pieces.title: Calculating an orbit into history: Katherine Johnson
pieces.short: Katherine Johnson
pieces.hook: When machines began to take over calculation, she showed that “a judgment you can check” is worth more than “the halo of a new technology”: first get clear on whether the equations are…
pieces.takeaway: When machines began to take over calculation, she showed that “a judgment you can check” is worth more than “the halo of a new technology”: first get clear on whether the equations are right, and only then decide whether to trust the machine.

parts: Katherine Johnson was born on August 26, 1918, in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia. A feel for numbers let her skip ahead the whole way: at 13 she was already at the high school attached to West Virginia State College, at 18 she entered the college, and in 1937 she graduated with highest honors, majoring in mathematics and French.

In 1939 the state university’s graduate school quietly began to integrate. She was one of the first three Black students admitted, but after the first semester she left to start a family, and taught school first.

What really changed her course was the summer of 1953: she entered the West Area Computing unit at the Langley laboratory of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA, later NASA), and became a “human computer.” After the Soviet Union launched Sputnik in 1957, the United States sped up its entry into the space race. Johnson did mathematical work on early notes on space technology, and she analyzed the trajectory for Alan Shepard’s Freedom 7 in 1961.

The scene more people know came in 1962. Before John Glenn flew Friendship 7 in orbit, he did not trust the early electronic computer, and he told the engineers to “get that girl” to check the equations in the program again on a hand-cranked calculator. She checked them, and only then was Glenn easy about the launch. What she herself valued more was the later calculation that helped the Apollo lunar module and the command and service module rendezvous and dock in lunar orbit. She also took part in work related to the space shuttle and Landsat, authored or coauthored 26 research reports, and retired in 1986.
In 2015 Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom. On February 24, 2020, she died at the age of 101.

blocks.title: Years mentioned in the text
items: Katherine Johnson was born on August 26, 1918, in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia.

A feel for numbers let her skip ahead the whole way: at 13 she was already at the high school attached to West Virginia State College, at 18 she entered the college, and in 1937 she graduated with highest honors, majoring in mathematics and French.

In 1939 the state university’s graduate school quietly began to integrate. She was one of the first three Black students admitted, but after the first semester she left to start a family, and taught school first.

What really changed her course was the summer of 1953: she entered the West Area Computing unit at the Langley laboratory of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA, later NASA), and became a “human computer.”

After the Soviet Union launched Sputnik in 1957, the United States sped up its entry into the space race. Johnson did mathematical work on early notes on space technology, and she analyzed the trajectory for Alan Shepard’s Freedom 7 in 1961.

The scene more people know came in 1962. Before John Glenn flew Friendship 7 in orbit, he did not trust the early electronic computer, and he told the engineers to “get that girl” to check the equations in the program again on a hand-cranked calculator. She checked them, and only then was Glenn easy about the launch.

critical.label: A critical look
items: The film Hidden Figures is what made the wider public remember her, but the telling readily turns “one person got the arithmetic right” into “one person saved the space program.” Real spaceflight is an ensemble of organization, engineering, and politics. She was a long-undervalued part of that, not the only hinge. On the other side, treating her only as “a symbol of breaking through racial and gender ceilings” narrows her too: she was first an exceptionally strong applied mathematician, and the trust came from calculations that could be checked, not from a slogan. There is a limit in the public record as well. It says little about how much say she had in project decisions, and the honors cluster in recognition conferred late in life.

pieces.title: How a needle and thread sewed a global garment industry: the sewing machine
pieces.short: The sewing machine
pieces.hook: Before the sewing machine, ready-to-wear clothes were almost all slow handwork.

parts: Before the sewing machine, ready-to-wear clothes were almost all slow handwork. In 1846 Elias Howe received a patent for a practical lockstitch sewing machine, turning “how needle and thread lock” from a craft into a mechanical action that could be copied. What really pushed the machine into homes and factories was Isaac Singer’s improvements around 1851 and, more decisive still, mass production, installment plans, and marketing. A technology can work, and people still have to be able to afford it, get it repaired, and be willing to drop an old habit.

The patent wars soon became a bottleneck for the whole trade. Around 1856 the principal patent holders formed a patent pool of the kind called the Sewing Machine Combination, and cross-licensing bought a stretch of peace and of expanding output.

This is a classic early case of a “patent pool.” Innovation is protected, and a few players can also block the door. The industry then split along two lines. Home machines moved toward electric power, a zigzag stitch, electronics, and computerized embroidery. Industrial machines were built into garment-factory lines and, together with cutting, pressing, and logistics, broke “a single garment” into a global sequence of steps.

The fast fashion in today’s stores still depends, at the core, on high-speed industrial sewing and on manufacturing clusters in East Asia and elsewhere. The home machine has become, more often, a tool for a hobby, for mending, and for small makers.

critical.label: A critical look
items: The sewing machine is often written up as “the household marvel that liberated women,” but on the factory side it also turned sewing into intense piecework. Those who gain are the brands and retail capital. Those under pressure are often the stitchers on the line. Another angle: the patent alliance both sped the spread and put off more open competition. “Cooperating on a standard” and “an oligopoly splitting the take” are sometimes the same coin.

Where things stand now: the industry is not breaking out on some brand-new principle of sewing. It is making small adjustments among automation, embroidery software, flexible small runs, and more sustainable cloth. The real bottleneck is usually the supply chain and labor standards, not a few stitches faster on the needle plate.

pieces.title: Oil is up by nearly 70%. How has Delta Air Lines still held a profit?
pieces.short: Oil is up by nearly 70%. How has Delta Air Lines…
pieces.hook: On October 9, Delta Air Lines (NYSE: DAL) released its earnings for the third quarter of 2026.

parts: On October 9, Delta Air Lines (NYSE: DAL) released its earnings for the third quarter of 2026. On a GAAP basis, operating revenue was 201.86 × 100 million U.S. dollars, up 21% from 166.73 × 100 million in the same period last year; operating profit was 14.54 × 100 million U.S. dollars, down 14% year over year; net profit was 7.56 × 100 million U.S. dollars, against 14.17 × 100 million a year earlier.

Adjusted earnings per share were 1.72 U.S. dollars, flat with last year. Fuel was the largest variable: the average price this quarter was 3.80 U.S. dollars a gallon, up 68% year over year, and the fuel bill rose 69%, to 43.51 × 100 million U.S. dollars.

The company expects fourth-quarter revenue to grow about 20%, and full-year pretax profit of about 45 × 100 million U.S. dollars, the equivalent of having absorbed a fuel-cost increase of about 60 × 100 million U.S. dollars. Full-year 2026 earnings-per-share guidance is 5.10 to 5.60 U.S. dollars, and the plan for the year is to repay more than 20 × 100 million U.S. dollars of debt.
(Sources: the press release on Delta’s own site, PR Newswire, and the 10-Q quarterly report.)

Fuel is up by nearly 70%, and profit has only been squeezed thinner. It has not collapsed. Delta CEO Ed Bastian calls this “structural resilience” built up over many years. In the past, airlines readily lost money whenever the oil price spiked. This time shows that the way a top carrier makes money has changed. They no longer rely only on selling seats. They also rely on premium cabins, a membership system, and hedging tools such as a refinery of their own.

GAAP revenue and adjusted revenue differ by about 26 × 100 million U.S. dollars, mostly from the company’s own refinery selling fuel outside. That slice is itself designed as a hedge on the price of oil.

Who gains, and who is under pressure: the gainers are travelers willing to pay more for the experience, and a large airline like Delta that has pricing power. Shareholders are under pressure. Net profit was nearly cut in half, partly because of investment losses. Price-sensitive travelers are under pressure too. Fourth-quarter revenue is expected to grow about 20%, and a large share of that comes from fares.
Smaller and midsize airlines, and the low-cost carriers, have no refinery and fewer premium customers, so a high oil price hurts them more.

Delta looks more and more like a “travel membership platform.” The airplane is the carrier. The real moat is the set of interfaces made of membership, co-branded credit cards, and a premium clientele. The higher the oil price, the more this structural gap will pull the industry apart.

critical.label: A critical note
items: Optimists will say that matching last year’s adjusted profit under an oil price rarely seen before shows that the model can really take the strain.
Pessimists will say the “adjusted” basis strips out both investment losses and refinery income, and that on the GAAP figures net profit is in fact down by nearly half.
From the traveler’s side, part of the so-called “strong demand” is people passively accepting higher prices.

Where the evidence is thin: fourth-quarter guidance rests on a forward oil price of about 4.25 U.S. dollars a gallon. If a shift in the Middle East makes the oil price swing, that premise no longer holds. The earnings report itself also cannot prove how long a “preference for spending on the experience” will last.

A lesson: when you read an earnings report, set the “adjusted” books and the GAAP books side by side. What is often most valuable in a company is not the hardware of the core business, but the layers of interface that a customer cannot leave.

pieces.title: Sanctioning the court itself: the United States steps up pressure on the International Criminal Court
pieces.short: The United States steps up pressure on the International Criminal Court
pieces.hook: According to the BBC, Al Jazeera, and others on October 9, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced further measures against the Int…

parts: According to the BBC, Al Jazeera, and others on October 9, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced tougher sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC). They no longer target only the roughly 17 judges and officials already sanctioned. They place the court as an entity itself under restriction, bar U.S. entities from transacting with it (banking, software, and other services are affected), and freeze related property interests it holds in the United States. Rubio said the aim was to “defend the sovereignty of the United States,” and he put it this way: “either the ICC stops the threats, or we end the ICC.”

The ICC replied that this was an attack on the rule of law and the international legal order, and said it would not be intimidated. UN Secretary-General António Guterres called it a heavy blow to international criminal justice. Britain, Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, and others expressed regret and restated their support for the court. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions.

The same day, the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to the South African jurist and former ICC judge Navi Pillay. The Nobel Committee stressed that international judicial bodies are under political attack. The U.S. side said some of the measures come with a grace period of about six months, so that states parties can negotiate a way to “resolve the concerns of the United States.” The Dutch foreign minister has already warned that the sanctions will hit hard at the operation of the court in The Hague.

Experts note that, in an extreme case, if the court cannot sustain fair trials, the cases of people awaiting trial (including Duterte and others) could be left in difficulty, even though the U.S. side has carved out partial exemptions for detention facilities and the like.

The United States, China, Russia, India, Israel, and others were never parties to the Rome Statute. The U.S. side has long resented the ICC investigation involving U.S. personnel in Afghanistan (since closed) and the arrest warrants for Israeli officials. Those who support the sanctions stress sovereignty and “politicized justice.” Those who oppose them stress remedy for victims, and the risk that “the powerful go unconstrained.”

critical.label: Narrative frames to watch
items: Reducing a complex dispute over jurisdiction to a war of labels over a “real court” and a “fake court.”
Letting a campaign, or the mood of allies, cover over the effect on victims in concrete cases (the Philippines, Sudan, and the Central African Republic, among others).
Automatically reading the Nobel Prize and the sanctions landing on the same day as a plot. A coincidence of timing is not a cause already proved.

A neutral reminder: this is an escalating institutional conflict between international justice that claims universal jurisdiction and great-power claims of exemption. It is not one media play. What to watch next: whether states parties in Europe and Africa will, in substance, “give a transfusion,” routing around the services of U.S. firms; whether any state follows by withdrawing; and whether the sanctions really bring particular trials to a halt.

pieces.title: A glass pyramid in the courtyard of the Louvre: I. M. Pei
pieces.short: I. M. Pei
pieces.hook: A good work is not only drawn. It also has to be negotiated through budget, power, and public opinion. I. M. Pei’s most underrated talent may…
pieces.takeaway: A good work is not only drawn. It also has to be negotiated through budget, power, and public opinion. I. M. Pei’s most underrated talent may be persuasion.

parts: I. M. Pei was born on April 26, 1917, in Guangzhou, with family roots in Suzhou. When he was one, the whole family moved to Hong Kong, and around the age of ten they went on to Shanghai. As a boy he often went back to Suzhou for the summer. The family’s Lion Grove Garden later seemed to him his earliest lesson in architecture: the human hand working with nature is the essence of creation.

In 1935 he went to the United States to study. In 1940 he received a bachelor’s degree in architecture from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and in 1946 a master’s from the Harvard Graduate School of Design. One of his teachers was Walter Gropius, a founder of the Bauhaus.

paras.lead: The first real turning point is one few people mention
parts: In 1948 he did not join a traditional architecture office. He went to the real-estate developer Webb & Knapp as head of the architecture division, and worked on urban projects in Chicago, Philadelphia, Washington, and other cities. That stretch taught him how to deal with developers, government, and a budget.
In 1955 he set up on his own. The firm was later renamed I. M. Pei & Partners.

The East Building of the National Gallery of Art in Washington (completed in 1978), the Kennedy Library in Boston (completed in 1979), the Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong, and the Suzhou Museum, which he went back to his home place to design late in life. The best known is still the Louvre. In 1981 French President François Mitterrand launched the renovation of the Louvre, and later chose Pei himself.

In the Cour Napoléon he placed a glass pyramid about 22 meters high as the new main entrance, with a whole underground extension beneath it. Around the opening of the pyramid in 1989, opinion in Paris was in an uproar. Many people felt that an object from another world had been set at the door of a classical palace.

Today it is one of the landmarks of Paris. In 1983 he received the Pritzker Architecture Prize, and with the prize money he set up a scholarship to fund Chinese students going to the United States to study architecture. On May 16, 2019, he died in New York at the age of 102.

items: I. M. Pei was born on April 26, 1917, in Guangzhou, with family roots in Suzhou.

In 1935 he went to the United States to study. In 1940 he received a bachelor’s degree in architecture from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and in 1946 a master’s from the Harvard Graduate School of Design. One of his teachers was Walter Gropius, a founder of the Bauhaus.

The first real turning point is one few people mention: in 1948 he did not join a traditional architecture office. He went to the real-estate developer Webb & Knapp as head of the architecture division, and worked on urban projects in Chicago, Philadelphia, Washington, and other cities.
In 1955 he set up on his own. The firm was later renamed I. M. Pei & Partners.

He has many signature buildings: the East Building of the National Gallery of Art in Washington (completed in 1978), the Kennedy Library in Boston (completed in 1979), the Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong, and the Suzhou Museum, which he went back to his home place to design late in life.
In 1981 French President François Mitterrand launched the renovation of the Louvre, and later chose Pei himself.

critical.label: Limits and disputes
items: The John Hancock Tower in Boston, designed by his firm (the lead designer was the partner Henry Cobb), shed pane after pane of its glass curtain wall during construction in 1973. It became a well-known accident in the profession, and the firm’s reputation was set back for a time. The urban-renewal projects he did for developers early in his career are disputed today as well: large-scale tearing down of the old to build the new, with the cost often falling on the communities that already lived there.

critical.label: A critical note
items: The Louvre pyramid is often told as a story of “a genius who overruled the crowd and was proved right in the end.” Seen another way, it got built in large part because a president decided it in person, power running from the top down, and not only because the design itself won the public over. “Everyone came to love it later” does not prove that the opposition at the time was wrong. Quite a few designs that were opposed really did fail. People simply do not remember them. “A fusion of East and West” is also the label the outside world most likes to put on him, while he himself more often stressed modernism, light, and geometry. The label may not have been what he intended.

pieces.title: A small industry in the hand, morning and night: the toothbrush
pieces.short: The toothbrush
pieces.hook: The bristle toothbrush first appeared in China.

parts: The bristle toothbrush first appeared in China. In Europe, for a long time, people rubbed their teeth with a cloth dipped in salt or coal ash. The modern Western toothbrush industry is usually dated from the Englishman William Addis.

He had been in the trade of stationery and rags. In 1780 he began making toothbrushes in Whitechapel, London, with handles of bone and bristles of animal hair. A widely told story says that, caught up in a riot and locked in Newgate Prison, he saw a broom and in a flash invented the toothbrush. Museums also say this is mostly legend.

The company he founded passed through seven generations, and later sold toothbrushes under the Wisdom brand. Material at the National Archives of the United Kingdom holds that its early success had to do with people eating more and more sugar in the 18th century, with more tooth decay, and with the middle class beginning to take hygiene seriously.

The first key juncture was the material. Before that, bristles were mainly hog bristle, most of it imported from Siberia, Poland, and China. On February 24, 1938, DuPont began mass production of the Dr. West's Miracle Tuft toothbrush, the first toothbrush with nylon bristles.
Nylon dries quickly, does not readily harbor bacteria, and lends itself to large-scale production. From then on the toothbrush truly became a cheap consumer good.

The second juncture was habit. During the Second World War the U.S. military issued toothbrushes to soldiers and required them to brush. Many accounts hold that Americans brushing every day, as a general practice, came after discharged soldiers carried the habit home.

The third juncture was going electric. In 1954 the Swiss physician Philippe-Guy Woog developed the Broxodent electric toothbrush. At first it was for people wearing braces, or whose hands were not nimble. Only later did it enter the mass market in the United States.

The manual toothbrush is a mature, thin-margin mass business, competing mainly on channel and brand. The electric toothbrush is moving in the direction of “consumer electronics,” and the selling points have become sonic vibration, pressure sensing, and an app. The bulk of the profit is often not in the handle but in the head that has to be replaced on a schedule, much like the razor model of selling the handle and earning on the blades.

blocks.title: Years mentioned in the text
items: He had been in the trade of stationery and rags. In 1780 he began making toothbrushes in Whitechapel, London, with handles of bone and bristles of animal hair.
On February 24, 1938, DuPont began mass production of the Dr. West's Miracle Tuft toothbrush, the first toothbrush with nylon bristles.

critical.label: A critical note
items: Marketing often implies that a higher price means cleaner teeth. How well someone brushes depends in large part on method and on how long they brush, and studies do not fully agree on how much better an electric toothbrush actually is. That should not be overstated. The environment is another angle: a plastic toothbrush is almost impossible to recycle. Alternatives such as a bamboo handle are on the rise, but the bristles are still mostly nylon. It is also worth seeing that the toothbrush spread not only because of the invention itself, but because armies, schools, and advertising shaped the habit over a long time. Behind an ordinary small object is really a history of promoting a whole set of ideas about hygiene.

pieces.title: Overseas overtakes Greater China for the first time: Uniqlo’s FY2026 report card
pieces.short: Uniqlo’s FY2026 re…
pieces.hook: Fast Retailing on October 8, 2026, released results for the period ended 202…

parts: Fast Retailing on October 8, 2026, released FY2026 results for the year ended August 31, 2026: consolidated revenue of 3.9633 trillion yen (+16.6%), operating profit of 7184 × 100 million yen (+30.4%), net profit attributable to owners of the parent of 5425 × 100 million yen (+25.3%), a record for the fifth year running. Overseas UNIQLO was the main engine: revenue of 2.4111 trillion yen (+26.2%), operating profit of 4398 × 100 million yen (+44.1%).

Revenue in North America grew about 35%, to 3649 × 100 million yen. Revenue in Europe grew about 39%, to 5126 × 100 million yen, and operating profit grew 69% to 917 × 100 million yen. Operating profit in Greater China grew 25% to 1120 × 100 million yen. The company stressed that combined sales in North America and Europe exceeded Greater China for the first time, and also exceeded the region made up of South Korea plus Southeast Asia, India, and Australia.

UNIQLO in Japan remained steady: revenue of 1.0848 trillion yen (+5.7%), with same-store sales up 5.1%. The proposed year-end dividend is 530 yen, and 850 yen for the full year (350 yen more than the year before).
Guidance for FY2027 is cautiously optimistic: revenue of 4.45 trillion yen (+12%), net profit of 5600 × 100 million yen (growth of only 3.2%); stores worldwide rising to about 3545 (+35).

The facts are bright. Inference should come half a beat slower. One reading: LifeWear’s “basic pieces, plus technical fabrics, plus a price that can be held” has found a larger pool of new demand in Europe and North America, and the regional center of gravity is moving west. The other side will note that the yen’s exchange rate, one-off factors, and the mix of stores and e-commerce all enlarge the year-on-year figures, and that profit in Europe is growing far faster than revenue, which may not extend in a straight line.

The sharper question: is overseas “overtaking Greater China” for the first time a structural victory, or a relative story told after growth in Greater China slowed? Net profit in the guidance rises only about 3%, which also sounds as if management itself does not treat a “record year” as a promise of acceleration without a limit.

critical.label: Worth thinking about
items: Is Uniqlo selling clothes, or a “standardized experience” that can be copied? If it is the latter, the test of the next stage is not only the number of stores opened. It is how, in Europe and North America where costs are higher, to hold gross margin and trust in the brand.

pieces.title: A diesel deal and “time for a new president”: two scripts for the same weekend
pieces.short: Two scripts for the same weekend
pieces.hook: On October 9 (Friday), Trump announced an agreement with Moscow to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports. The U.S.…

parts: On October 9 (Friday), Trump announced an agreement with Moscow to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports. The U.S. understanding is that the suspension runs until April 7, 2026. Russia would at once release about 30 × 10,000 tons of diesel to the United States and the global market, release about another 50 × 10,000 tons in November, with about a further 100 × 10,000 tons, and, depending on the state of the refineries, talk about at most about another 300 × 10,000 tons. Zelensky condemned this as a “gift” to Putin, the equivalent of funding the war. Kaja Kallas, the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, said “this is not the time to ease pressure on Russia,” and Europe intended to advance on Monday one of the largest sanctions packages since the war began.

On October 10 (Saturday), outside the White House, Trump said Zelensky was “making trouble for the world,” that he should stop striking Russian refineries, and that it was “time to change to a leader who can make a deal.” A Russian envoy publicly praised the cooperation.

After the conflict of the United States and Israel with Iran, the Strait of Hormuz is in substance blocked, and diesel is tight around the world. According to the American Automobile Association (AAA), the average U.S. diesel price is about 6.28 U.S. dollars a gallon. Ukraine is under continuing martial law and holds no ordinary general election. British Prime Minister Burnham spoke with Zelensky to voice support, and they took up matters such as an energy ceasefire.

critical.label: Several angles
items: The White House is putting “bring the oil price down, and protect the midterms” above the story of the alliance.
Kyiv treats strikes on Russian refineries as a matching counterblow against Russia’s war machine.
Brussels worries that a gap in the sanctions will become a pipe feeding Russia’s finances.
On the market side, some note that the first batch of tonnage is not large next to daily U.S. consumption, so the real effect on prices at the pump is in doubt.

critical.label: Narrative frames to watch
items: Reducing a complex transaction to the labels “for Ukraine” or “abandoning Ukraine.”
Speaking of “time to change the leader” as if a legal basis or a popular mandate were already in hand, while elections in Ukraine during the war are themselves constrained.
Treating tonnage not yet delivered, and with unclear conditions, as the same thing as “the oil price will fall at once.”

A neutral reading: this is a collision, in the same week, of three forces twisted together—an energy shortage, the election clock, and the logic of the war. The agreement is written about diesel. The argument is over who has the right to define “pressure” and “a deal.”

pieces.title: Turning a problem into a machine: Alan Turing
pieces.short: Alan Turing
pieces.hook: What is truly formidable is often not a better memory for the answer, but the nerve to turn a vague problem into a machine that can be tested.
pieces.takeaway: What is truly formidable is often not a better memory for the answer, but the nerve to turn a vague problem into a machine that can be tested.

parts: Alan Turing was born in London on June 23, 1912. He graduated with first-class honours in mathematics from King’s College, Cambridge, and in 1936, in the paper on “computable numbers,” he proposed an abstract machine: rewrite the instructions, and the same device can carry out different tasks.

Later generations call it a Turing machine, and it is one of the starting points of modern computing theory. In 1938 he received his doctorate at Princeton, and from that same year he worked part time for the British Government Code and Cypher School on the German Enigma cipher machine.

When the war broke out in September 1939, he joined Bletchley Park full time and later headed Hut 8, devoted to the German navy’s ciphers. Building on the earlier work of Polish cryptographers, he and Gordon Welchman, among others, pushed forward the design and improvement of the electromechanical deciphering machine known as the “bombe” (Bombe).

From 1940 the Allies could read a large volume of German military messages more systematically, and Atlantic convoys and the war at sea gained an intelligence advantage because of it. In 1945 he received the OBE for his wartime service. After the war he took part in designing the ACE computer, worked in the computing laboratory at Manchester, and in 1950 set out the line of thought for judging machine intelligence that was later called the “Turing test.”

The limits and the tragedy are equally stark. In 1952, for homosexual conduct that was illegal at the time, he was convicted of “gross indecency” and accepted probationary treatment of the kind called “chemical castration.” His security clearance was withdrawn, and he could never again work for the government’s communications department. On June 7, 1954, he died. The inquest concluded it was suicide by cyanide poisoning. He was only 41.

In 2013 the Queen granted him a posthumous pardon. In 2017, provisions of the Policing and Crime Act commonly called the “Turing law” extended a mass pardon to other outdated convictions of the same kind.

In 1938 he received his doctorate at Princeton, and from that same year he worked part time for the British Government Code and Cypher School on the German Enigma cipher machine.

In 1945 he received the OBE for his wartime service.

items: The official story often says that “he alone shortened the war by two years.” The claim is inflated, and hard to check. Codebreaking was a work of team engineering. The Polish pioneers, Welchman, the operators, and the commanders were just as essential. Turning Turing into a god as “the father of the computer” also tends to wipe out what his contemporaries contributed. The other side will ask whether the later pardon was a repair of justice, or the state wrapping a belated decency in a hero story. On the evidence, both his wartime contribution and the institutional harm done to him stand up. The line that “one person rewrote history” is the weakest.

pieces.title: Chocolate melting beside the radar: how the microwave oven entered the kitchen
pieces.short: How the microwave oven entered the kitchen
pieces.hook: The story of the microwave oven begins with a part from a radar set.

parts: The story of the microwave oven begins with a part from a radar set. In the Second World War the magnetron was the heart of Allied radar. Percy Spencer, an engineer at Raytheon, improved the mass production of the magnetron.

The story goes that one day the chocolate in his pocket melted beside a running magnetron. He later checked the effect with popcorn and an egg, and found that microwaves can heat food quickly. In 1945 Raytheon applied for a patent related to microwave cooking (granted in 1950, US 2,495,429).

Around 1947 the commercial Radarange appeared: nearly two meters tall, about 340 kilograms, cooled by water, priced at around five thousand U.S. dollars, and suited only to institutional kitchens such as those of a barracks or a hospital.

Real entry into the home had to wait until the size and the cost came down. In 1965 Raytheon acquired Amana, and in 1967 it brought out a countertop home Radarange, listed at about 495 U.S. dollars. For a middle-class household it was still not cheap, but at last it could go into an ordinary kitchen.

Around 1970 the United States was selling about 40,000 a year. Around 1975 the volume jumped to the order of about a million. By the 1980s, as safety standards were filled out, two-income households multiplied, and the demand to “save time” grew, the microwave became common. Makers in Japan and elsewhere then made the magnetron smaller and cheaper, and the center of global capacity gradually shifted east.

Today it is almost infrastructure in the kitchen: reheating leftovers, defrosting, making instant food, at very high efficiency. In browning, in the aroma of searing, and in texture, it still falls short of a traditional oven and an open flame. So what it has taken over is “time,” not the whole of “cooking.”

The hardware is already highly commoditized. Competition is concentrated on power, sensors, combined steam or light-wave functions, smart connectivity, and the recipes sold alongside. Growth comes more from penetration in emerging markets and from stacking functions on than from a burst of people “buying one for the first time.”

blocks.title: Years mentioned in the text
items: In 1945 Raytheon applied for a patent related to microwave cooking (granted in 1950, US 2,495,429).

Around 1947 the commercial Radarange appeared: nearly two meters tall, about 340 kilograms, cooled by water, priced at around five thousand U.S. dollars, and suited only to institutional kitchens such as those of a barracks or a hospital.

In 1965 Raytheon acquired Amana, and in 1967 it brought out a countertop home Radarange, listed at about 495 U.S. dollars. For a middle-class household it was still not cheap, but at last it could go into an ordinary kitchen.

Around 1970 the United States was selling about 40,000 a year. Around 1975 the volume jumped to the order of about a million. By the 1980s, as safety standards were filled out, two-income households multiplied, and the demand to “save time” grew, the microwave became common.

critical.label: A critical reflection
items: “An accident with chocolate led to the invention” is a good story, but the historical record also warns that legend is mixed in. The sounder account is that surplus capacity in wartime radar, plus the pressure to switch production in peacetime, led Raytheon to bet on a kitchen use of its own accord. Critics say the microwave has encouraged overprocessed food and a thinning of nutrition. Supporters stress that it lowered the threshold of cooking for people living alone and for busy households. On the evidence, the curve of the microwave’s spread lines up fairly clearly with the rise of the two-income society. “It ruined cookery” looks more like a cultural verdict, and is hard to treat as iron proof of a cause.

pieces.title: After 3 × 100 million paying users, what is Spotify still selling?
pieces.short: After 3 × 100 million paying users, Spo…
pieces.hook: According to second-quarter results Spotify published on August 4, 2026: paying subscribers (P…

parts: According to second-quarter results Spotify published on August 4, 2026: paying subscribers (Premium) reached 3 × 100 million, up about 9% from a year earlier; monthly active users were about 7.77 × 100 million, up about 12% from a year earlier; revenue was about 47.8 × 100 million euros, up about 14% from a year earlier (about 15% at constant exchange rates); gross margin rose to about 33.4%, up about 1.9 percentage points from a year earlier; operating profit was about 6.55 × 100 million euros. The company said this was a scale of paying users that audio streaming had never reached.

It is no longer only “a cheaper digital record shop.” It is slicing the day into scenes that can earn money, such as the commute, a workout, study, dinner, and sleep, and it is putting more weight on podcasts, audiobooks, conversational discovery, personalized podcasts, and a running mode. Even as paying users expand, free users who listen with ads still number nearly 5 × 100 million. Both engines are still turning.
3 × 100 million paying users mean a barrier of scale: licenses to the catalog, recommendation data, and a place in the mind form one flywheel.

Who gains, and who is under pressure: the gainers are the platform, and the leading forces in the creator ecosystem. Those under pressure are often musicians in the middle band (the dispute over how revenue is split has never stopped), and the traditional model that still makes its money on the release window of an album.

In a platform’s later stage, what it sells is not only a catalog of content, but the interface that “helps you decide what to hear in the next second.” The stickier the interface, the more smoothly a price rise and cross-selling can go.

critical.label: A critical reflection
items: The company’s story stresses healthy compound growth and “keeping you company all day.” The other side, especially independent musicians and some regulatory discussions, will say that the larger the scale, the more unequal the bargaining, and that a recommendation algorithm may also steepen the tilt toward the top. The subscription and profit figures are facts that can be checked. The evidence that it is “better for creators as a whole” is divided: it depends on whether you look at the head or the long tail, and at music or at podcasts. Equating growth in users directly with a flourishing of culture is a narrow frame.

pieces.title: A state of emergency, or a “soft coup”: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in Pakistan is taken over
pieces.short: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in Pakistan is…
pieces.hook: According to Reuters and others on October 12, Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari, on the advice of Prime Minister Shehb…

parts: According to Reuters and others on October 12, Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari, on the advice of the cabinet of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, on Sunday declared a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the northwestern province bordering Afghanistan, and suspended that province’s government. The federation said the governor would take charge. The law minister said the term would at first be about six months, and could be extended if needed. The interior ministry said the army would be deployed to the province.
The province is governed by Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), and it is the main province where PTI in practice formed a government after the general election of 2024.

The reason the federation gave is that the province failed to contain attacks by Islamist armed groups effectively. PTI spokesman Zulfikar Bukhari called it “a coup dressed up as a state of emergency,” aimed at breaking up a move, prepared about a week earlier, in which supporters would march on Islamabad to demand Imran Khan’s release. A large number of activists, and three of Khan’s sisters, had already been detained.

Maulana Fazlur Rehman, leader of a party of religious scholars, also criticized the emergency as “an ambush against democracy.” Islamabad has been heavily secured, with roads blocked by shipping containers, to keep protesters from approaching parliament.

Imran Khan is still in prison, and he denies the charges against him. His supporters accuse the military of manipulating the election; the military denies it. The federal government and the military accuse public security under PTI of having run out of control, and they imply that PTI sympathizes with the Taliban regime in Kabul and with forces linked to it inside Pakistan. PTI and the Afghan side both deny that.
The constitution allows the center, in an emergency, to take over provincial powers, so “whether the form is legal” and “whether the motive is political” will be argued at the same time.

In the short term, the risk of protest and clashes rises. Over the medium term, the question is whether Islamabad can use a “counterterrorism” story to weaken PTI’s last base of administration. Outwardly, it tugs at the security story of the border between Afghanistan and Pakistan.

critical.label: Narrative frames to watch
items: One frame writes it as “the center had no choice but to put a frontier out of control back in order.” Another writes it as “removing an opposition party’s province in the name of security.” Both sides may select the attack statistics and the arrest numbers that suit them.

A neutral reading checks the pieces apart first: whether attacks really are rising, whether the emergency procedure is constitutional, and whether the suppression of protest has gone too far. Only then judge the motive, rather than picking a camp and then hunting for evidence.

It is also unwise to treat a “state of emergency” as automatically the same thing as “a military coup has already taken place.” In form, this is still a civilian president announcing it on the advice of the cabinet. The risk that the space for democracy is being compressed is just as real.

pieces.title: A five-year voyage, exchanged for a book that rewrote the history of life: Charles Darwin
pieces.short: Charles Darwin
pieces.hook: Sitting on a big idea for twenty years is not delay. It is gathering, first, every piece of evidence an opponent could use to knock you down.
pieces.takeaway: Sitting on a big idea for twenty years is not delay. It is gathering, first, every piece of evidence an opponent could use to knock you down.

parts: On February 12, 1809, Darwin was born in Shrewsbury, England. The family was well off. His father was a physician, his grandfather Erasmus Darwin was a naturalist, and his other grandfather was Josiah Wedgwood, founder of the Wedgwood pottery.

As a young man he was hardly a “good student.” He studied medicine in Edinburgh and gave it up partway, unable to bear surgery without anesthetic. He transferred to Cambridge to prepare for the clergy, but what he cared about most was catching beetles.

The turning point was a letter of recommendation. The Cambridge botanist Henslow recommended him to sail on HMS Beagle as a naturalist. The voyage ran from the end of 1831 to October 1836, nearly five years in all.
Fossils in South America, and the finches and tortoises that differed slightly from island to island in the Galápagos (1835), led him to doubt the premise that “species do not change.”

After he returned, in 1838 he read Malthus’s An Essay on the Principle of Population, and the core idea of “natural selection” roughly took shape. He did not rush to publish. He spent another twenty years gathering evidence, eight of them on barnacles alone. In 1858 Wallace, far off in the Malay Archipelago, sent a paper whose line of thought was almost the same.

Through an arrangement by Lyell and Hooker, the two papers were read together at the Linnean Society in July of that year. On November 24, 1859, On the Origin of Species was published, and in 1871 The Descent of Man followed. In private life he and his cousin Emma Wedgwood had ten children. The early death of their daughter Annie, at 10, hit him very hard.
He was troubled for years by chronic illness. He died in 1882 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.

critical.label: Limits and disputes
items: He did not know how heredity worked (Mendel’s results went unnoticed at the time), so he could not answer the objection that “favorable variations would be diluted away by blending.” Some passages in The Descent of Man on race and sex carry an obvious bias of the Victorian age. The phrase “survival of the fittest” actually comes from Spencer, and Darwin adopted it only from the fifth edition on. Later, “social Darwinism” and eugenics borrowed his name. Galton, who proposed eugenics, was also his cousin.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Does the story of the “lone genius” hold? Wallace thought of natural selection independently, at almost the same time. Darwin’s advantage lay in the stock of evidence and in social position, and the history of science often gathers the credit onto a single name.

When a theory is misused, can the account be charged to him? Some say natural selection describes “what happens in nature,” not “how society ought to be,” and that the responsibility for misuse lies with others. Others point out that parts of his own writing already carry a sense of rank, so he cannot be cleared entirely.

On the evidence, the trunk of evolutionary theory has been confirmed again and again by genetics and molecular biology, while the details keep being revised, for example neutral evolution and horizontal gene transfer among bacteria. “Darwin was right about everything” and “evolutionary theory has been overturned” are both simplifications.

pieces.title: A “pencil” with not one gram of lead in it: more than four hundred years of a small wooden rod
pieces.short: More than four hundred years of a small wooden rod
pieces.hook: A pencil has never contained lead.

parts: A pencil has never contained lead. Around 1564, an extremely pure deposit of graphite in lumps was found at Borrowdale, in England’s Lake District. People at the time thought it was a kind of lead and called it plumbago (Latin for “lead ore”). The English word lead, and the German word Bleistift, both carry that mistake forward.

The graphite was pure enough to be sawn straight into sticks, but it was soft and brittle. At first it was wrapped in string, and later it was pushed into a hollowed wooden slip. The wooden pencil dates from that. It could also line the molds for cannonballs, so the British Crown tightly controlled the output, and a smuggling underground even grew up locally.

The first key juncture was a substitute for the raw material. During the wars between Britain and France, France could not buy British graphite. In 1795 Conté invented a method of mixing graphite powder with clay and firing it into a core. Hardtmuth in Austria worked out a similar process independently at nearly the same time. The company he founded in 1790 became Koh-i-Noor.
Change the proportion of graphite and clay, and you control how soft or hard the core is. Today’s HB and 2B both come from that. This step freed the pencil from dependence on a single mine.

The second juncture was branding and industrialization. Kaspar Faber, a carpenter in Nuremberg, began making pencils in 1761. After his great-grandson Lothar took over in 1839 and improved the process, the company name was printed on the barrel from 1847, and in 1856 he bought a high-quality graphite mine in Siberia. Nuremberg thus became the pencil center of Europe.

In 1858 the American Lipman received a patent for “a pencil with an eraser on the end.” In 1875 the U.S. Supreme Court held the patent invalid, on the rough ground that sticking two known things together is not an invention. At the Paris Exposition of 1889, Koh-i-Noor brought out a high-grade pencil with a yellow barrel. The impression that “yellow means a good pencil” formed then, and later even ordinary pencils were painted yellow to match.

The Chinese line begins with the National Goods Movement. Wu Gengmei learned to make pencils in Japan. In October 1935 he completed, in Shanghai, China’s first pencil factory able to make its own leads, slats, and barrels. In 1937 it was renamed the China Standard National Goods Pencil Factory, and the barrel was printed with “Chinese people use Chinese pencils.”
The Zhonghua 101 drawing pencil, introduced in 1954, gradually pushed imported drawing pencils out of the Chinese market.

Mature, thin in profit, and highly scaled. China is the world’s largest producer and exporter of pencils. According to the China Writing Instrument Association (as compiled by Zhiyan Consulting), national pencil output in 2021 was about 245 × 100 million pencils, of which colored pencils were about 54%, surpassing black-core pencils for the first time. Qingyuan, a single county in Zhejiang, produced about 70 × 100 million pencils in 2020.
The pencil is shifting from a “writing tool” toward a “tool for drawing, for education, and for making by hand.”

items: Will “the pencil be eliminated by the screen”? Black-core pencils are indeed shrinking, but colored pencils are growing. The claim itself is not wrong. It simply mixes the market for “writing” with the market for “drawing.”

In 1958 the economist Leonard Read wrote a famous essay, “I, Pencil,” saying that no one person in the world knows how to make a pencil from scratch, and that the market coordinates a worldwide division of labor. The other side notes that the hand of the state is just as plain in the history of the pencil: the British Crown controlled the mine, wartime France was pushed into a substitute process, and China got its start from the National Goods Movement.

A caution on the figures: the output numbers above come from an industry association, relayed through a consulting firm. The latest reach only to 2021. They are fine for a trend. Do not treat them as a precise value for right now.

pieces.title: 1.9 trillion U.S. dollars flow through in a year: what Stripe really sells is “the interface”
pieces.short: What Stripe really sells is “…
pieces.hook: Stripe is the online payments company the Irish brothers Patrick and John Collison founded in 2010.

parts: Stripe is the online payments company the Irish brothers Patrick and John Collison founded in 2010. In the annual letter published on February 24, 2026, it disclosed these figures (reported by the company itself): in 2025, businesses on the platform processed 1.9 trillion U.S. dollars in total payments, up 34% from a year earlier, equal to about 1.6% of global GDP.

More than 500 × 10,000 businesses use Stripe directly or through a platform, covering 90% of the Dow Jones constituents and 80% of the Nasdaq-100. Of companies newly registered in Delaware, about a quarter are registered through its Atlas service.
The “revenue suite” beyond payments—billing, invoicing, tax, and the like—is on track for annualized revenue of 10 × 100 million U.S. dollars this year.
The same day it announced a tender offer for employees’ shares, at a valuation of 1590 × 100 million U.S. dollars.

What Stripe first sold was not “cheaper collection,” but “collection that is easier to plug in.” A developer could take payments with a few lines of code, which was close to a miracle in the bank-acquiring systems of the time. Its moat is the interface. Once a company has hung billing, tax, and risk control on its application programming interface (API), the cost of moving away is high.

The new moves in the annual letter run along the same line: together with OpenAI, it is setting an “Agentic Commerce Protocol” (ACP), so that AI assistants and merchants have a shared technical language.
It introduced a “shared payment token,” so an AI agent can start a payment without exposing the user’s card number.
It introduced stablecoin micropayments aimed at API calls and at usage of MCP (the Model Context Protocol).
The metaphor of a “unified track gauge,” touched on earlier, fits right here. Whoever defines the interface stands on the road that other people’s business has to travel.

Who gains, and who is under pressure: the gainers are small teams and AI companies that want to “face the world the moment they go live.” The annual letter says that 57% of the businesses that newly joined Stripe in 2025 were outside the United States, and that this new cohort is growing about 50% faster than the cohort of the year before.

Those under pressure (this is an inference) are the traditional acquirers that live on relationships and offline process, and rivals such as Adyen and PayPal that are also competing for the position of a “one-stop financial interface.”

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Volume is not revenue. The 1.9 trillion is money that flowed across the platform. How much Stripe itself keeps (the fee rate), and what its net profit is, have not been made public. The annual letter only says it is “solidly profitable.” Comparing payment volume with GDP also mixes transaction value with value added. It sounds staggering, and its economic meaning is limited.

How far the data can be trusted: Stripe is not listed, and these figures have not been publicly audited. 1590 × 100 million U.S. dollars is the price at which employees’ shares changed hands. It is not a price set in the open market.

Cycle risk: the surge in 2025 owed a great deal to the AI boom. The Collison brothers themselves ask in the letter whether this is an anomaly or the start of a new normal. Stablecoins and agentic commerce are both still in a trial stage. Regulation and how widely they spread are both uncertain.

A lesson for you: when you size up a “platform” company, ask first how much code and how many processes a customer would have to change in order to leave it. The longer the answer, the deeper the moat.

pieces.title: Three weeks from the vote, federal agents searched Omar’s home
pieces.short: Three weeks from the vote, federal agents searched…
pieces.hook: The gist of the reporting (drawn from NPR, the Associated Press, PBS, The Hill, FOX 9, and others): On October…

parts: The gist of the reporting (drawn from NPR, the Associated Press, PBS, The Hill, FOX 9, and others): in the early morning of Monday, October 12, agents of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the investigative arm under U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement) searched the Washington home of Ilhan Omar, a Democratic member of the House from Minnesota. The Justice Department confirmed only that this was a search “authorized by a court,” part of an “ongoing federal investigation,” and gave no details.

According to what anonymous officials familiar with the matter told NPR, this is an investigation that has run for several years and includes complaints from whistleblowers, involving allegations of immigration fraud. Other people familiar with it said that part of it concerns immigration papers filled out in her childhood by her late father. Vice President Vance had earlier accused her in public of immigration fraud. Omar denied it.

Omar replied that this was “weaponizing federal law enforcement against a political opponent,” and that “I will not be silenced.” House Democratic leader Jeffries and others called it “deeply disturbing.” Republican Representative Emmer said, “No one is above the law, and accountability is coming.” Representative Mace said that if the fraud is true, her citizenship should be stripped and she should be deported.
The midterm elections are on November 3, and Omar is seeking another term.

The Justice Department has long had a practice: within about 60 days before an election, avoid investigative steps against a candidate that would become public. This is only an internal practice, not a law. Eliason, a professor at George Washington University and a former federal anti-corruption prosecutor, holds that this search broke with past practice, but that the practice itself has no mechanism of enforcement.
The side that supports the search stresses that “a judge issued a warrant.” A search warrant means a judge found probable cause. That carries real weight in procedure.

The side that opposes it stresses “the timing.” The same practice has, in different years, been used by each party to accuse the other. The most famous case is 11 days before the 2016 election, when FBI Director Comey announced that the investigation into Hillary’s emails was being reopened. The Hill also noted that the current attorney general, Blanche, when he was Trump’s private lawyer, had argued that any Justice Department move before an election amounted to interfering in the election.
The district Omar represents has a clear Democratic advantage. In the short run this is more likely to stir a backlash mobilization among her supporters than to change the result in that district.

Nationally, it will be fitted into two campaign stories: one of “a weaponized justice system,” and one of “the rule of law with no exceptions.” CNN reported in the same period that Republicans are scrambling to limit the damage in several districts that had been safe.
As for “stripping citizenship,” that would require a separate court proceeding, the bar is high, and things are still far from that step.

critical.label: Narrative frames to watch
items: The wording is the position. “A raid” (raid) and “a search under the law” (search) describe the same event.

The key information all comes from anonymous sources, and the specific content of the allegations has not been made public. “She must have done something wrong” and “this is pure political persecution” both lack evidence at this stage.
Facts worth following: whether charges are formally brought, whether the affidavit behind the warrant is unsealed, and whether the Justice Department explains why it chose this moment.

pieces.title: The man who turned explosives into a medal: Alfred Nobel
pieces.short: Alfred Nobel
pieces.hook: You may not get to decide how an invention is used. You do get to decide what is done with the wealth it brings. One choice late in life…
pieces.takeaway: You may not get to decide how an invention is used. You do get to decide what is done with the wealth it brings. One choice late in life can redefine what a whole life meant.

parts: The Nobel Prizes are being announced one after another this month (the physics prize on October 6, the peace prize on October 9), which is a good moment to talk about the person behind the name.

On October 21, 1833, Nobel was born in Stockholm. His father, Immanuel, was an inventor and engineer whose fortunes rose and fell. After the business failed he went to Saint Petersburg, in Russia, to build naval mines and machinery, and later brought the whole family over. Alfred hardly attended a regular school. He learned chemistry from private tutors, spoke several languages well, and as a youth traveled in Europe and the United States.

The main line of his life was “taming nitroglycerin.” The liquid is enormously powerful, and extremely unstable. In September 1864 the family factory in Stockholm exploded, and his brother Emil and others were killed.

He did not stop. He grew more intent on making it safe. In 1867 he absorbed nitroglycerin into diatomaceous earth and applied for a patent on dynamite. After that came the blasting cap, blasting gelatin (1875), and smokeless powder (1887). Explosives sharply raised the efficiency of driving tunnels, railways, and mines.
He built factories in more than twenty countries, held about 355 patents in his lifetime, and with his brothers invested in the oil fields of Baku.

paras.lead: The other side is just as real
parts: Explosives also went into the arsenal. In 1894 he bought the Swedish arms firm Bofors. He never married, lived alone for long stretches, and was constantly on the move. He was called “the richest vagabond in Europe.”

On November 27, 1895, he signed his will in Paris, placing the great bulk of the estate (about 3100 × 10,000 Swedish kronor) in a fund, to be awarded each year to the person who had “conferred the greatest benefit on humankind” in five fields: physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature, and peace. On December 10, 1896, he died in Sanremo, Italy.

After the will was made public, relatives opposed it, and Swedish opinion also accused him of being “unpatriotic” (the peace prize was to be awarded by a committee chosen by the Norwegian parliament). The executor, Ragnar Sohlman, spent several years in lawsuits and in taking stock of the assets. The first prizes were not given until 1901.

On December 10, 1896, he died in Sanremo, Italy.

critical.label: More than one side
items: The most popular account is that in 1888 his brother Ludwig died, a French newspaper mistakenly thought the dead man was Alfred, and it ran an obituary, “The merchant of death is dead.” The shock, the story goes, is what led him to make the will. The original paper that carried that obituary has been hard to confirm to this day. It looks more like a legend retold again and again. Do not treat it as settled.

His view of peace was also in tension. He is said to have told the peace campaigner Bertha von Suttner that a weapon frightful enough might make war impossible to start. This idea of “buying peace with deterrence” still has people who accept it and people who reject it.

The Nobel Prize itself is often criticized too. The science prizes have long leaned toward men in Europe and America, and the peace prize is thick with politics. The aim in founding it and the reality of how it runs can be judged apart.

pieces.title: The business of a single blade: one hundred and twenty years of the razor
pieces.short: One hundred and twenty years of the razor
pieces.hook: For several thousand years, shaving was a craft: from flint and bronze knives to the steel folding straight razor of 18th-century Sheffield, in England…

parts: For several thousand years, shaving was a craft: from flint and bronze knives to the steel folding straight razor of 18th-century Sheffield, in England. A straight razor is sharp, but it has to be honed every day, and a slip of the hand draws blood, so many men would rather go to the barber.

The turn came from a salesman. While King C. Gillette was selling bottle caps, he worked out the idea of “use it and throw it away,” and together with William Nickerson, an engineer trained at MIT, he solved the process of stamping thin steel in bulk, hardening it, and putting an edge on it. The Gillette company was founded in 1901, and in 1904 it received a patent for the safety razor: a T-shaped frame clamping a thin double-edged blade, to be replaced once it dulled.
During the First World War the U.S. military bought Gillette razors and blades in quantity and issued them to soldiers. A generation of young men came home already used to shaving themselves.

The next few decades were a race of technology and of channels. In 1931 Jacob Schick brought out a commercial electric razor and opened the side branch of the “dry shave.” In the early 1960s, coated stainless blades from Wilkinson in Britain for a time took a large slice of the market away from Gillette.

In 1975 Bic brought out a disposable plastic razor and drove the price extremely low. Gillette’s answer was to add blades, layer by layer: two (the Trac II of 1971), three (the Mach3 of 1998), five (the Fusion of 2006). Each generation came with its own cartridge, and patents were used to build the wall.
In 2005 Procter & Gamble bought Gillette for about 570 × 100 million U.S. dollars, and the industry entered a pattern of “giants plus premium multi-blade razors.”

In the 2010s, subscription commerce tore an opening. Dollar Shave Club got its start in 2012 with a video that went viral, mailing blades to the door once a month. In 2016 Unilever bought it for about 10 × 100 million U.S. dollars, and brands such as Harry's took the same road.
In 2019 Procter & Gamble took an impairment of about 80 × 100 million U.S. dollars against the Gillette business.

A mature market is fighting over the stock of customers it already has. Growth in men’s shaving in the developed countries is limited. The new volume comes from women’s hair removal, personal-care kits, and emerging markets. The weight of competition has also shifted from “how many blades” to brand, channel, and the subscription relationship.

In 1975 Bic brought out a disposable plastic razor and drove the price extremely low.

Gillette’s answer was to add blades, layer by layer: two (the Trac II of 1971), three (the Mach3 of 1998), five (the Fusion of 2006). Each generation came with its own cartridge, and patents were used to build the wall.
In 2005 Procter & Gamble bought Gillette for about 570 × 100 million U.S. dollars, and the industry entered a pattern of “giants plus premium multi-blade razors.”

critical.label: More than one side
items: “Give the razor away, and make the money on the blades” is often taken as the secret of how Gillette got started. The legal scholar Randal Picker looked at the record: during the life of the patent (1904–1921), a Gillette razor set sold for 5 U.S. dollars, about a third of a week’s wages for an ordinary industrial worker. It was not cheap at all. Only when the patent expired in November 1921 did the company bring out an old model at 1 U.S. dollar, while a new model at 5 U.S. dollars held the high end. So locking customers in with a low price looks more like a response after the patent expired than like the way the firm got started.

The stretch in which military purchasing trained a habit in users is often told as Gillette’s marketing genius. It can also be seen as a windfall that wartime state purchasing happened to confer, and that is hard to copy.

Of that impairment at Procter & Gamble, how much came from the fashion for growing beards, and how much from a price war with direct-to-consumer brands and from exchange rates, is weighted differently in different accounts. Be careful about assigning it to a single cause.

pieces.title: 962 × 100 million U.S. dollars in one quarter: what is hardest to replace at Nvidia is the habit of 600 × 10,000 developers
pieces.short: What is hardest to replace at Nvidia is 6…
pieces.hook: On August 26, Nvidia reported results for the second quarter of fiscal 2027 (ended in 2026, in July …

parts: On August 26, Nvidia reported results for the second quarter of fiscal 2027 (ended July 26, 2026). Revenue was 962 × 100 million U.S. dollars, up 106% from a year earlier. Data-center revenue was 890 × 100 million U.S. dollars, up 117% from a year earlier, more than nine-tenths of total revenue. Gross margin was 75.0%.

The company expects third-quarter revenue of 1080 × 100 million U.S. dollars (plus or minus 2%), and that figure includes no revenue at all from data-center computing products for China. Last quarter, shipments of Hopper chips to China were less than 1% of data-center revenue.

On the surface it sells GPUs. What really makes it hard for a customer to leave is CUDA. Nvidia released CUDA in November 2006, and in 2007 it opened the developer kit, so a programmer could drive a GPU for general computing in a style close to the C language.

Twenty years on, the company said at the GTC conference in March of this year that CUDA developers had passed 600 × 10,000. Jensen Huang said there were already about 1000 CUDA-X acceleration libraries, and that CUDA-compatible GPUs installed worldwide are counted in the hundreds of millions. New algorithms often appear first as CUDA code, and the tutorials, the answers, and the ready-made code are here too.
The more people use it, the less reason the next person has to switch. That is the network effect of a developer ecosystem.

Who gains, and who is under pressure: the gainers are Nvidia and suppliers such as TSMC, and the cloud firms and AI companies that get computing power first. Under pressure are the customers who have to buy cards at a high price, and rivals such as AMD. Even when the hardware specifications are close, the customer still has to count the cost of moving the code over.

Revenue is highly concentrated too. Of this quarter’s 890 × 100 million U.S. dollars in data-center revenue, hyperscale cloud firms contributed about 487 × 100 million, and those large customers are also designing their own chips.
The figures above come from Nvidia’s earnings report and from official statements. “CUDA is the moat” is a widespread judgment in the industry, but it is an inference.

critical.label: More than one side
items: The other side’s view: frameworks such as PyTorch, plus tools that “write once and compile to many chips,” such as OpenAI’s Triton and TileLang, open-sourced by a team at Peking University, are hiding CUDA underneath. Huawei Ascend and others are also building software stacks of their own. The moat may be slowly growing shallower.

Another view: the ability of AI to write low-level code may also make CUDA code cheaper and more plentiful, and so reinforce the ecosystem. People argue both directions. The evidence for either is not yet sufficient.

Where the evidence is thin: “600 × 10,000 developers” is a registration count the company reports itself. It is not the same as active users. Part of the extremely high growth also comes from pricing power when supply cannot meet demand. Once demand cools, concentration among customers will magnify the swing.

A lesson: when you look at a platform company, do not look only at the product. Also ask what it costs a user to leave. The cost of switching often explains long-run profit better than the performance of the product does.

pieces.title: Riyadh’s airport shut down: why the war in Yemen has burned into the Saudi heartland
pieces.short: Why the war in Yemen has burned into the Saudi heartland
pieces.hook: The gist (from Xinhua, the BBC, Al Jazeera, the Guardian, and the Associated Press, October 11–13…

parts: The gist (from reporting by Xinhua, the BBC, Al Jazeera, the Guardian, and the Associated Press from October 11 to 13): on Saturday, October 10, a Houthi missile hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. The Saudi civil aviation authority reported 12 dead and 309 injured. The death toll in BBC and Guardian reports was 13.
On the 11th the airport was struck again, and a man of Pakistani nationality was killed.

On the 12th, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted ballistic missiles fired at Riyadh and at Khamis Mushait. The Houthis said they had hit their targets, and warned that every Saudi airport except Mecca and Medina was “not safe.” Riyadh’s airport stayed closed, and Etihad Airways, Gulf Air, Qatar Airways, and others suspended flights in succession.

The Houthi side said Saudi Arabia had carried out 119 airstrikes on Yemen within 24 hours, and on the 13th it called Saudi Aramco’s oil facilities a “legitimate target.” The Saudi energy minister vowed a “serious response.” Trump said the United States might join the strikes. Iran said it was willing to mediate.

The civil war in Yemen began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa. In 2015 a coalition led by Saudi Arabia intervened. After a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022, large-scale fighting was largely frozen for four years. This July the Houthis announced a “maritime embargo” on Saudi Arabia, citing a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in the areas they control, and an airstrike on Sanaa airport (the Yemeni government said it had carried out that strike itself, in order to stop an Iranian plane from landing).

In September the Houthis took key ground and nearly controlled the Bab el-Mandeb. On October 4, government forces launched a “Yemen Dawn” counteroffensive, with targets that included the port of Mocha. The strike on the airport was an escalation at that point. The larger background is the war of the United States and Israel against Iran that broke out at the end of February this year, and the continuing blow to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia classifies the strike as an attack on civilian facilities and vows a forceful response. The Houthis call it a counterblow against “Saudi aggression” and the blockade, aimed at Saudi Arabia’s “most precious assets.” The Yemeni government is using the moment to push the recovery of lost ground.
Iran calls for dialogue and, at the same time, is closely tied to the Houthis. The United States wavers between supporting an ally and avoiding being drawn in.

In the short run, the risk premium on Gulf aviation hubs and energy facilities rises. If Saudi Aramco’s facilities really are hit, and that is stacked on a blocked Hormuz, oil prices and shipping will come under pressure again. Over the medium term, Saudi Arabia has in recent years put great effort into tourism and into conferences and exhibitions. “The airport is not safe,” by itself, is an economic blow.

Ratney, a former U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia, described an attack on a civilian airport as a “paradigm shift.” If the United States steps in, the conflict could spill out of Yemen’s civil war into a larger regional war.

critical.label: Narrative frames to watch
items: Explaining everything in one phrase, “an Iranian proxy war.” The Houthis are closely tied to Iran, but they have demands of their own at home and a logic of territory. Treating them simply as a proxy leaves out the politics inside Yemen.

Looking only at one side’s casualties. The dead and wounded at the Saudi airport have an official report, while figures such as “119 airstrikes” mostly come from the Houthis’ own media. Neither side’s account is easy to verify independently. Even among mainstream outlets the death toll differs, 12 against 13.
The technical topic of “why the missile was not intercepted” slides easily into a discussion of arms sales, and covers over a more basic question: why the ceasefire mechanism collapsed.

Something to think about: if you were a Saudi decision-maker, what would each of these three roads cost—striking back harder, asking the United States to step in, or returning to the negotiating table?

2026-10-15.fallbackLine: A lamp, a cup of tea, and a page of a book make a fine evening.

pieces.title: The mechanic who treated failure as tuition: Soichiro Honda
pieces.short: Soichiro Honda
pieces.hook: Failure itself is not the frightening part. What is frightening is failing and then not going back to study. After Honda botched his first batch of piston rings, he went back and learned metallurgy.
pieces.takeaway: Failure itself is not the frightening part. What is frightening is failing and then not going back to study. After Honda botched his first batch of piston rings, he went back and learned metallurgy.

parts: In 1906, Soichiro Honda was born in a small village in Shizuoka Prefecture (now part of Hamamatsu). His father was a blacksmith who also repaired bicycles. He was an ordinary student, but machines fascinated him. In 1922, at 15, he went to Tokyo to apprentice at an auto repair shop called Art Shokai, and in 1928 he returned to Hamamatsu and opened a branch.

In 1936 he founded Tokai Seiki to make piston rings, and the first batch failed the quality checks. He did not try to force it through. He went and sat in on metallurgy classes, filled in the materials science, and only then became a supplier to Toyota and other plants. After the war he sold that business. In 1946 he opened the Honda Technical Research Institute, mounted used small engines on bicycles, and sold them to people who could not afford a car.

Honda Motor Co. was founded in 1948. The next year he met Takeo Fujisawa: Honda handled the engineering, and Fujisawa handled the money and the sales. The pair later became one of the most famous partnerships in Japanese business history.

A few of the turning points went like this. In 1958 the company launched the Super Cub, a small motorcycle that was easy to ride, durable, and cheap. Cumulative production later passed 100 million. It entered the Isle of Man TT for the first time in 1959, and in 1961 it took the championship, knocking a large hole in the idea that Japanese goods were cheap but crude.

In the 1960s the Japanese government meant to limit new firms entering the auto industry. Honda moved first, launching light trucks and sports cars and forcing its way into the business. The CVCC engine of 1972 met the strict U.S. emissions standards of the time without a catalytic converter, and opened the American market for Honda.
In 1973 he and Fujisawa retired together. He did not hand the company to his son. He died in 1991 at the age of 84.
