critical.label: Another way to look at it
items: The "genius founder" story hides what the team contributed. Without Fujisawa watching the cash flow and the dealer network, many of Honda's experiments might never have lasted.

He had a stubborn side too. In the 1960s he insisted on air-cooled engines, while younger engineers argued for water cooling. The dispute went on for a long time, and in the end he gave way. Many people see this as the start of a Honda culture in which you can challenge the boss on technical grounds. It also shows that a founder's instincts are not always right.

He had a fierce temper and was hard on employees, in ways today's workplace standards might not accept. Biographies often write that style up as "a genuine character." It is worth a question mark as you read.

pieces.title: From miners' workwear to wardrobes worldwide: a hundred and fifty years of a pair of jeans
pieces.short: A hundred and fifty years of a pair of jeans
pieces.hook: Jeans did not start as fashion. They started because work pants kept tearing.

parts: Jeans did not start as fashion. They started because work pants kept tearing. In the early 1870s, Jacob Davis, a tailor in Reno, Nevada, found that copper rivets at the pocket corners kept the pants of people doing heavy work from ripping. He could not pay the patent fee himself, so he wrote to Levi Strauss, a fabric wholesaler in San Francisco, and proposed they apply together.
On May 20, 1873, U.S. Patent No. 139,121 was granted. That day is often taken as the birthday of jeans.

paras.lead: What followed falls roughly into several stages
parts: The workwear years (the 1870s through the 1920s): the rivet patent lapsed around 1890, and competitors poured in. Levi's gave this pant the lot number 501. From 1915, Levi's began buying denim from Cone in North Carolina, and that relationship lasted a century.

The symbol years (the 1930s through the 1970s): Westerns tied jeans to the cowboy. In the 1950s, Marlon Brando and James Dean wore them as the uniform of rebellious youth, and some schools even banned students from wearing jeans.
By the 1960s and 70s, they had also become a badge of the counterculture.
Designer labels sold a pair of work pants at luxury prices.

Production moved from the United States to Mexico and Asia. Xintang, in Guangdong, was for a time called the jeans capital. In the early 2000s Levi's closed its last U.S.-owned factories, and Cone's century-old White Oak mill stopped production in 2017.

paras.lead: Which stage it is in now
parts: Mature, but squeezed. Yoga pants and athleisure have taken over some everyday occasions, and the fashion swings back and forth between skinny and wide-leg. On the other side, environmental pressure keeps growing. In 2015 Levi's ran a calculation: one pair of 501s uses about 3,781 liters of water over its whole life, from growing the cotton through the customer's washing.
Secondhand and vintage denim, meanwhile, have become a new point of growth.

critical.label: Another way to look at it
items: "Levi invented jeans" is not accurate. The core improvement came from Davis, and sturdy twill work cloth was already around. When a brand tells the story, it naturally pulls the credit toward itself.
"Denim comes from Nîmes in France, and jeans from Genoa" is a widely told etymology, but scholars dispute the details. Take it as a story, not as settled fact.

A number like 3,781 liters depends heavily on where you draw the line. Cotton irrigation is most of it, and how the customer washes the jeans is counted in as well. Using it to compare brands directly is easy to get wrong.
The "symbol of rebellion" was half grown by the culture itself, and half pushed by movies and advertising.

pieces.title: The more it sells, the higher the price? Switch 2's platform accounts in year two
pieces.short: The more it sells, the higher the price? Switc…
pieces.hook: What happened (from Nintendo's earnings): In the fiscal year ending March 2026, Switch…

parts: In the fiscal year ending March 2026, Switch 2 sold 19.86 million units. That figure is shipments to retailers, not the number consumers actually bought. It beat the company's original forecast of 15 million units, and it also beat the 19 million figure to which the forecast had been raised midyear. Over the same period, Switch 2 software sold 48.71 million copies.

In the current fiscal year, though, Nintendo cut its hardware forecast to 16.5 million units (-16.9%) and raised its software forecast to 60 million copies (+23.2%). Full-year revenue is forecast at 2.05 trillion yen (-11.4%). Operating profit is forecast at 370 billion yen, a slight rise of 2.7%.

It also raised the price. The Japanese Switch 2 went from 49,980 yen to 59,980 yen, and the United States, Canada, and Europe raised prices from September 1 as well. President Shuntaro Furukawa gave the reason as more expensive memory and other parts, and shifts in exchange rates. The earnings report also counts tariffs among the costs.

From April through June 2026, Switch 2 shipments were 3.82 million units, 34.4% below the launch quarter. The launch quarter's base was high to begin with, and in August the company left its full-year forecast unchanged.

A game console is a classic platform business. The hardware is only the ticket. The real money is in the software sold afterward, copy by copy. Fewer consoles and more software in the second year is the normal pace as a platform matures.
Switch 2 can play games from the older Switch, which lowers the hurdle for players switching consoles. That is an important reason first-year sales beat expectations, and the company says so itself.

Who gains, and who is under pressure: first-party blockbusters and third parties willing to follow gain, because the installed base is already there. Consumers are under pressure, because a console usually gets cheaper the more it sells, and this time the price rose in year two. Retailers' hardware volume will feel it too.

Revenue down while operating profit is flat to slightly up is most likely explained by software taking a larger share, since software margins are far higher than hardware margins. One source of the rise in memory prices is AI servers competing for memory capacity. So the Nvidia chain you read about yesterday lands on ordinary people today as a higher price for a game console.

critical.label: Another way to look at it
items: Shipments are not the same as real demand. How much stock is sitting in the channel has to be read from later retail figures.
Nintendo's full-year forecasts have historically leaned conservative (this is an inference). The 16.5 million may in the end be a low opening number.
Others argue that raising the price in year two spends down users' goodwill, and over the long run may slow the growth of the installed base, which would hurt software revenue in turn.

pieces.title: Voting even when you know you will lose: where Sweden's government formation is stuck
pieces.short: Where Sweden's government formation is stuck
pieces.hook: Key points (Euronews, Al Jazeera, and Swedish local media): in the September 13 election, the Social…

parts: Key points (Euronews, Al Jazeera, and Swedish local media): in the September 13 election, the four-party camp led by the Social Democrats (the Social Democrats, the Left Party, the Green Party, and the Centre Party) won 176 seats, and the four parties on incumbent prime minister Kristersson's side (the Moderate Party, the Sweden Democrats, the Christian Democrats, and the Liberals) won 173. But Social Democratic leader Andersson failed twice to form a government. The Centre Party refused to join a government that had Left Party ministers, and the Left Party insisted it would not let a government through unless it was in the cabinet.

Speaker Norlén still put "a single-party Social Democratic government led by Andersson" to a parliamentary vote on the 15th. Andersson herself said, "I will lose." The Left Party and the Green Party said they would vote no, and the Liberals would oppose it too.
How does the counting work?

Sweden uses negative parliamentarism. A candidate for prime minister does not need support from more than half the house. The candidate gets through as long as the votes against are fewer than 175, an absolute majority. An abstention counts as letting the candidate through. So the real question is not who has more seats. It is who can get enough people to choose not to oppose.

That also explains why a "victory" of 176 to 173 is not the same thing as being able to form a government. A bloc is only shorthand used by the media. The split between the Centre Party and the Left Party, on economic policy and on whom to work with, may be wider than the split between either of them and some parties across the aisle.

The Left Party and the Green Party want this no vote to prove that without them, no one can form a government. The Left Party had earlier voted to keep Norlén, who comes from the Moderates, on as Speaker, which sent a complicated signal.
The Centre Party has held back from saying where it stands, keeping its chips as the party that can tip the balance.
If Andersson loses, the Speaker is expected to turn to Kristersson. But he, too, needs at least one party from the other side to abstain if he is to get through.
The constitution says that once four nominees for prime minister put forward by the Speaker have been rejected, there must be an early election.
Why vote when you know you will lose?

This picks up the "straw vote" you were interested in earlier. A vote that is bound to fail moves each party's position out of closed-door bargaining and onto the public record, and it makes "holding the line" costly. Andersson's own account is that a vote can put pressure on the parties and loosen the deadlock.

The government formation of 2018 dragged on for more than four months. Along the way a candidate for prime minister was rejected, and in the end a prime minister got through only because a large number of members abstained.

critical.label: Narrative frames to watch for
items: The claim that "the left clearly won, yet was blocked from governing" ignores that the system looks at who can keep a majority from opposing, not at which bloc has more seats.
The claim that "the left is fighting itself and cannot be trusted" is too quick as well. Several rounds of voting are normal in Sweden. They are not a collapse.
"The Sweden Democrats decide everything" is also worth doubting. Their influence is large, but this time the jam is inside the other bloc.
Tonight's vote is the first touchstone for these stories.

2026-10-16.fallbackLine: A bamboo staff and straw sandals, and I go lighter than on a horse. Who's afraid? A straw cloak through mist and rain, and I take life as it comes.

pieces.title: A watch for an ocean: John Harrison
pieces.short: John Harrison
pieces.hook: If the direction is wrong, more effort only adds parts to a giant clock. Harrison's turn came when he dared to make the thing small.
pieces.takeaway: If the direction is wrong, more effort only adds parts to a giant clock. Harrison's turn came when he dared to make the thing small.

parts: In 1707, several British warships misjudged their position near the Isles of Scilly, ran aground, and more than a thousand sailors died. Seven years later, in 1714, the British Parliament passed the Longitude Act, offering a prize of up to 20,000 pounds to anyone who could measure longitude accurately on the open ocean.

Latitude can be fixed from the sun and the North Star. Longitude is hard because you have to know what time it is, at that moment, back at the home port. Four minutes off is one degree off. The leading scientists of the day bet on astronomy. They thought a clock on a pitching, damp ship, swinging from hot to cold, could never keep accurate time.

John Harrison (1693–1776) was, of all things, a clockmaker who was almost entirely self-taught. Born in Yorkshire, he learned carpentry from his father. The longcase clocks of his early years used wooden gears in quantity, and he chose a hardwood that lubricated itself so he could skip the oil. In 1730 he took his design to London. The astronomer Halley introduced him to the noted watchmaker Graham, and Graham lent him the money to go on.

Over the next few decades he built three large sea clocks in succession, H1, H2, and H3. H3 alone took more than ten years. The real breakthrough came from making it small. He found that a precise large pocket watch actually ran steadier than a bulky clock, and so came H4.

At the end of 1761 his son William took H4 aboard the Deptford, bound for Jamaica. Over an 81-day voyage it was off by only about 5 seconds, far inside the standard set by the Act. But the Board of Longitude did not award the prize outright. It demanded a repeat trial (another run, to Barbados, in 1764), required him to disclose the principles, and insisted that other people be able to build one from them.

A new act in 1765 gave him only half the prize. Harrison believed the rules had been changed on the spot, and he kept arguing into old age. In 1772 King George III tested his H5 in person. In 1773 Parliament granted another 8,750 pounds. He died three years later.
What Captain Cook carried on his second voyage was K1, copied from H4, and he thought highly of it. The idea of "carrying accurate time on board" runs on to satellite positioning today.

critical.label: A critical look
items: The other side of the hero story. The bestseller Longitude (1995) casts Maskelyne, the Astronomer Royal, as the villain. But many historians of science argue that the Board's demands were not unreasonable. Success on one voyage is not the same as being able to build the thing in quantity, and a watch that only its inventor can make will not save a whole navy.

The astronomy route was not a joke either. The lunar-distance method that Maskelyne advanced, used with the Nautical Almanac published from the 1767 edition onward, was for a long time cheaper and more widely available. Sea clocks did not really become standard gear for ocean voyages until the 19th century. The two paths look more like parallel lines than a win and a loss.
Where the evidence is thin. Many of the details about his being "held down" come from statements by Harrison himself and his family. As you read, remember that this is one side's account.

pieces.title: A hundred and fifty years of one paper box: how the corrugated box moved modern commerce
pieces.short: How the corrugated box moved modern commerce
pieces.hook: Corrugated paper had nothing to do with packaging at the start.

parts: Corrugated paper had nothing to do with packaging at the start. An 1856 British patent used a collar-pleating iron to press flutes into paper, as padding in the sweatband of a man's hat. In 1871 the American Albert Jones was the first to patent it as a packaging material, for wrapping glass bottles and lampshades so they would not shatter.

In 1874 Oliver Long pasted a facing sheet onto the fluted paper so it would not get pulled flat. That was the seed of single-face and double-face corrugated board. Afterward Thompson, Norris, and the printer Robert Gair joined forces and used patents to monopolize bottle-wrapping paper, until the patents expired in the 1890s.

In 1894 Thompson & Norris made the first double-face corrugated boxes, for light-parcel express in New York. Wells Fargo tried them and then recommended them to other customers. In 1895 the first machine that could flute the paper and paste both faces at once appeared. It could manage only 10 feet a minute, but it is the ancestor of today's corrugator.

The real fight was institutional. At the time the railroads assumed freight would travel in wooden crates. Around 1903 a cereal plant obtained an "exception permit" to ship in paper boxes. In 1905 nine firms that had been competing with one another joined forces, set a common standard for materials, and went to lobby the railroads.

In 1906 the railroads gave way, but the freight rate for paper boxes was 10 percent higher. Railroad companies in the West, which held large timberlands and sawmills, went so far as to charge a premium of up to 400 percent. In 1914 the U.S. Interstate Commerce Commission issued the Pridham decision, finding no difference for transport between wooden crates and paper boxes and forbidding different charges. People in the trade call that day "Independence Day for the box industry."
In 1919 the rules of the various railroads were consolidated into Rule 41, which grades board by bursting strength. That standard is still in use.

paras.lead: The material kept being upgraded after that
parts: From the 1920s, stronger kraft board gradually replaced jute board. In 1930 mills began making the fluted medium from recycled old boxes. The Second World War then forced the development of waterproof board. By the 1970s, nearly every product in the United States left the factory in a corrugated box.

Today e-commerce carries the box all the way to the doorstep. The industry has entered a mature phase and keeps consolidating: in July 2024 Smurfit Kappa merged with WestRock, and in January 2025 International Paper completed its acquisition of DS Smith.

critical.label: A critical look
items: It was not technology alone that won. The paper box prevailed through standards, a regulatory ruling, and industry alliances, and the wooden crate did not lose only because it was worse. Those alliances had a dark side too. The government brought antitrust suits in 1939 and again in 1967. The 1976 class-action settlement set a record at US$550 million. In the 1990s people were again accused of colluding to close plants and push paper prices up. The researcher Twede even says we "had almost no chance to explore alternatives."

Whether "a cardboard box equals green" depends on what you compare it with. That it can be recycled is true. But over-packaging, how much virgin fiber is in the mix, and the bulk of hauling empty boxes all change the conclusion.

The record leans one way. Much of the early history comes from the recollections of people inside the industry. One of the authors was a secretary at the Gair company, so the view is bound to favor the trade itself.

pieces.title: Demand is outrunning capacity: TSMC's third-quarter accounts, and the risks off the books
pieces.short: TSMC's third-quarter accounts, and the risks off the…
pieces.hook: What happened (the facts, from the company's October 15 announcement): third-quarter revenue of 1.4942…

parts: What happened (the facts, from the company's October 15 announcement): third-quarter revenue was NT$1.4942 trillion (about US$46.72 billion), up 50.9 percent from a year earlier (up 41.2 percent in dollar terms) and up 17.6 percent from the previous quarter. Net income was NT$763.06 billion, up 68.7 percent from a year earlier, a record for net income for the sixth quarter in a row. Both revenue and net income came in above analysts' expectations.

Gross margin was 66.4 percent, operating margin 58.7 percent, and net margin 51.1 percent. By process, 3 nanometer accounted for 33 percent of wafer revenue, 5 nanometer for 28 percent, 7 nanometer for 10 percent, and 2 nanometer for 8 percent. Processes at 7 nanometer and more advanced together accounted for 79 percent.

By application, high-performance computing accounted for 68 percent and phones for 21 percent. Automotive chips grew 23 percent from the previous quarter, the fastest growth. Free cash flow was NT$476.56 billion, against only NT$139.38 billion a year earlier.

Fourth-quarter guidance is US$52.3 billion to US$54.3 billion. The midpoint would be about 14 percent above the previous quarter and about 58 percent above a year earlier. Full-year revenue in dollars is expected to grow about 44 percent. The company also said capital spending from 2026 through 2028 will be clearly higher than in the previous three years. The second Arizona fab is already built and equipment is going in, with volume production expected in the third quarter of 2027.

A foundry is, at bottom, an "interface business." Chip companies only design. TSMC supplies the process and the design rules. The more customers design chips to its rules, the more it costs them to switch fabs. Whoever wins in AI chips, most of those chips still have to get in line for its production.

paras.lead: Who gains, and who is under pressure
parts: AI-chip customers who secure capacity gain. Rivals still chasing the leading processes are under pressure, and customers are in a weak spot when they bargain. Worth noticing: gross margin fell 1.3 percentage points from the previous quarter's 67.7 percent. The announcement does not break out the cause. A common guess outside the company is that 2 nanometer is just starting its ramp and that overseas fabs cost more. That part is only an inference.

critical.label: A critical look
items: The case for the bulls. Analysts say that after TSMC checked whether customers have the money, and the supporting parts, to actually deploy these chips, it still believes demand is far above capacity. That suggests it is not expanding blindly.

The case for the bears. Semiconductor history keeps repeating a cycle of shortage, expansion, and glut. If spending on AI capital slows, today's high capital spending turns into a heavy depreciation charge. The fact that the company itself went to check whether customers can deploy the chips also shows that management is guarding against double orders.

Concentration risk. High-performance computing is 68 percent, so both customers and applications are highly concentrated. Capacity is also concentrated in Taiwan, and the geopolitical risk cannot be routed around. Building fabs overseas will keep pulling the profit margin down.
Where fact stops and inference starts. The figures above come from the company announcement and from CNBC. Why the gross margin fell, and when the cycle turns, are inferences.

A lesson: the most profitable place is not necessarily selling the hottest thing. It is becoming the step that everyone else has to follow your specification to get through. But once the customers are all crowded into the same basket, the risk lands entirely on you.

pieces.title: A man the United States lists as a terrorist has become Iraq's deputy prime minister
pieces.short: A man the United States lists as a terrorist has…
pieces.hook: On Thursday evening Iraq's parliament met, with 261 members present. Speaker Haibat al-Halb…

parts: On Thursday evening Iraq's parliament met, with 261 members present and Speaker Haibat al-Halbousi presiding. The session filled 11 cabinet posts that had been empty in Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's government, including Defense Minister Nayef al-Shammari, Interior Minister Yasir al-Maliki, and ministers for planning, culture, and higher education, among others. It also appointed three deputy prime ministers: Muhsin al-Mandalawi, Laith al-Khazali, and Mohammed Tamim al-Jubouri.

The vote on a minister of migration and displacement was put off because the parties could not agree. These posts had been empty since the government took office in May. Al-Zaidi said the deputy prime ministers draw no salary and get no dedicated budget or staff. Their work is mainly out in the field.

The controversy gathers on Laith al-Khazali alone. He is a senior figure in the pro-Iran armed group the League of the Righteous (Asaib Ahl al-Haq), and the brother of the group's leader, Qais al-Khazali.

In 2007 an attack in Karbala killed five U.S. soldiers, and U.S. forces arrested him for it. He was released in 2009. In 2019 the U.S. Treasury sanctioned him. In 2020 the United States designated the group a foreign terrorist organization, and both brothers were listed as Specially Designated Global Terrorists.
The U.S. side has had no official response for now. Republican representative Joe Wilson called him, on X, "a designated terrorist and an Iranian puppet."

Since the United States and Israel went to war with Iran on February 28, Iraq, caught in the middle, has had a harder time of it. Before the war Iraq exported about 3.5 million barrels of oil a day through the Strait of Hormuz, supporting 90 percent of government revenue. Cash is now tight, and al-Zaidi has already let the dinar fall nearly 15 percent against the dollar.

By his account, when the government took over, public debt was more than 208 trillion dinars (about US$139 billion), and wages plus necessary spending run about 10 trillion dinars a month. Al-Zaidi took office with Trump's support, and he is also keeping up relations with Iran. He has promised to complete the withdrawal of U.S. forces and to disarm non-state armed groups.
The League of the Righteous is one of the few armed groups that have said they are willing to hand over their weapons.
Why the arrangement looks like this.

Iraq has long formed governments by bargaining cabinet posts out among the parties, and political forces with armed backgrounds are themselves in parliament. Bringing them into government can be read as "absorb them first, then disarm them," or as "putting a legal coat on the militias." People argue for both readings, and the evidence on hand is not enough to say which is closer to reality.
What the effects might be.

Dealing with a deputy prime minister under U.S. sanctions puts U.S. agencies, banks, and companies in a hard spot on compliance. For a long time Iraq's oil revenue has moved in and out through an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, so Washington's reaction bears directly on the dollars Baghdad has in hand.
That layer of effect is still at the stage of inference. It depends on whether the United States speaks, and on how it speaks.

critical.label: Narrative frames to watch for
items: On one side, "an Iranian puppet enters the cabinet." On the other, "the state is absorbing the militias and moving toward normal politics." Both tellings pick the facts that suit them. "A terrorist becomes deputy prime minister" is an eye-catching headline, but the post is unpaid and has no staff, and how much real power it carries is not clear yet.

Where the evidence is thin. Whether the League of the Righteous will actually disarm, how much authority a deputy prime minister really has, and whether the United States will add further sanctions: none of that has reliable information yet. Better not to rush to a conclusion. Over the next few weeks, the public statements from Washington and Tehran will be more useful.

pieces.title: So surgery would no longer be a bet with your life: Joseph Lister (1827–1912)
pieces.short: Joseph Lister (1827–…
pieces.hook: Take a new finding from another field and put it to work on your own problem, and accept it calmly when a better method replaces yours.
pieces.takeaway: Take a new finding from another field and put it to work on your own problem, and accept it calmly when a better method replaces yours.

parts: In 1827 Lister was born into a Quaker family in Essex, England. His father's trade was wine, but in his spare time he improved the lenses of the achromatic microscope, so Lister grew up used to looking through one. That habit later proved very useful.

He studied medicine at University College London, graduated in 1852, then went to Edinburgh to work under the noted surgeon James Syme, and married Syme's daughter Agnes. In 1860 he became professor of surgery at the University of Glasgow.

paras.lead: The most awkward fact about surgery in those years was this
parts: Anesthesia already let operations run longer and on a larger scale, but many patients survived the surgery only to die of wound infection. Suppuration, gangrene, and septicemia were ordinary sights on the wards. The prevailing account blamed "miasma," that is, bad air.

The turn came in 1865. Lister read Pasteur's work on fermentation and microbes, and guessed that pus in a wound might also be the work of tiny living things. He settled on carbolic acid (phenol), which some cities were already using to treat sewage and cut the smell.

On August 12, 1865, James Greenlees, a boy of 11, had an open fracture of the lower leg. By the experience of the time, a wound like that was likely to mean amputation, or even death. Lister dressed it with bandages soaked in carbolic acid. The wound did not suppurate, and the boy kept his leg.

In 1867 he published a series of articles in The Lancet setting out "the antiseptic principle." By statistics he released in 1870, the death rate for amputations fell from about 45 percent to about 15 percent.

After that he returned first to Edinburgh, and in 1877 went on to King's College London, promoting the method wherever he went. He was later made a baron, one of the first doctors to enter the British House of Lords for medical achievement. He died in 1912. Incidentally, Listerine mouthwash was named after him by someone else in 1879. He did not invent it.

blocks.title: Years mentioned in the text
items: In 1827 Lister was born into a Quaker family in Essex, England.
He studied medicine at University College London, graduated in 1852, then went to Edinburgh to work under the noted surgeon James Syme, and married Syme's daughter Agnes.
In 1860 he became professor of surgery at the University of Glasgow.
The turn came in 1865.
On August 12, 1865, James Greenlees, a boy of 11, had an open fracture of the lower leg. By the experience of the time, a wound like that was likely to mean amputation, or even death.
In 1867 he published a series of articles in The Lancet setting out "the antiseptic principle."

critical.label: Another way to look at it
items: Who gets the credit? As early as 1847, Semmelweis in Vienna had doctors wash their hands in a chloride-of-lime solution and sharply cut the death rate among women in childbirth, only to be rejected by his colleagues. What was distinctive about Lister was that he joined the theory that germs cause disease to a concrete procedure, and kept promoting it. So "one man started it" is too simple.

Is the evidence hard enough? People questioned his mortality figures at the time: the sample was small, there was no control group, and hospital hygiene was improving at the same time. The British medical world argued over those statistics for more than twenty years. It is a reminder that a correct conclusion does not mean the original evidence was airtight.

The method itself was also surpassed. Carbolic acid irritates the skin, and the carbolic spray he promoted was miserable for doctors and nurses. He himself gave up the spray around 1890. Surgery later turned to asepsis: steam sterilization, gowns, and gloves. The idea shifted from "kill the germs in the wound" to "don't let the germs in."

pieces.title: A hundred and fifty years of a light bulb: from Edison to the LED
pieces.short: From Edison to the LED
pieces.hook: The start was the arc lamp of the early 19th century, glaring and hungry for current, fit only for streets and lighthouses.

parts: The start was the arc lamp of the early 19th century, glaring and hungry for current, fit only for streets and lighthouses. The real problem was getting a thin filament to keep glowing inside a glass bulb without burning through. In February 1879 the Englishman Swan demonstrated a carbon-filament lamp in Newcastle. On October 22 of the same year, Edison's team used a filament of carbonized cotton thread and kept a lamp lit for 13.5 hours. On January 27, 1880, they received U.S. Patent No. 223,898.

What Edison was really good at was not "inventing the light bulb." It was making a high-resistance filament, then pairing it with a power station, the lines, and the meter, so the whole thing was one system. In 1882 the Pearl Street Station in New York began supplying power. In Britain, the patent dispute between the two men ended in 1883 when they joined to form the Ediswan company.

The second stage was a contest of materials. In the early 20th century tungsten filament replaced carbon. General Electric (GE) made tungsten that could be drawn into wire, and later filled the bulb with inert gas. The lamps were brighter and lasted longer.

The third stage is a discreditable episode. In December 1924, Osram, Philips, firms in the GE group, and others formed the Phoebus cartel in Geneva. They fixed the life of a household bulb at 1,000 hours, and fined any maker that went over.
According to IEEE Spectrum, the average life of the reference bulbs fell from 1,800 hours in 1926 to 1,205 hours in 1933–34. The cartel did not break up until the Second World War began.

The fourth stage was a contest of efficiency. First came fluorescent lamps and compact fluorescent lamps. Then, in the 1990s, Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano, and Shuji Nakamura made an efficient blue LED, and white LED lighting became possible. The three received the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Policy pushed too. From 2009 the European Union phased out incandescent bulbs. From August 1, 2023, the United States has enforced a standard of at least 45 lumens per watt, while an ordinary incandescent manages only about 15 lumens per watt. Figures from the International Energy Agency (IEA) show LEDs rising from 1.1 percent of global lighting sales in 2010 to about 50.5 percent in 2022.

What stage is it in now? The bulb is turning from "a consumable you replace every so often" into "an electronic product that can last many years." Industry profit is shifting from selling bulbs to smart lighting, fixtures, and whole engineering packages.
The old giants have been pulling back from lighting too. Philips Lighting listed on its own and then renamed itself Signify, and GE sold its lighting business to Savant.

items: In February 1879 the Englishman Swan demonstrated a carbon-filament lamp in Newcastle. On October 22 of the same year, Edison's team used a filament of carbonized cotton thread and kept a lamp lit for 13.5 hours. On January 27, 1880, they received U.S. Patent No. 223,898.
In 1882 the Pearl Street Station in New York began supplying power.
In Britain, the patent dispute between the two men ended in 1883 when they joined to form the Ediswan company.
In December 1924, Osram, Philips, firms in the GE group, and others formed the Phoebus cartel in Geneva. They fixed the life of a household bulb at 1,000 hours, and fined any maker that went over.
According to IEEE Spectrum, the average life of the reference bulbs fell from 1,800 hours in 1926 to 1,205 hours in 1933–34.

First came fluorescent lamps and compact fluorescent lamps. Then, in the 1990s, Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano, and Shuji Nakamura made an efficient blue LED, and white LED lighting became possible. The three received the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.

critical.label: Another way to look at it
items: Is planned obsolescence all a conspiracy? An incandescent bulb really does involve a physical tradeoff. The hotter the filament, the brighter and more efficient it is, but the shorter it lives, so 1,000 hours may itself have been a reasonable compromise. The problem is that the cartel set that number by fines, rather than letting market competition choose it.
A more efficient lamp does not mean the total electricity used for lighting falls.
The BBC has reported on the "rebound effect": when light gets cheap, people install more lamps and leave them on longer, and total energy use for lighting does not fall as far as expected.

Banning the sale of incandescent bulbs is disputed too. Supporters care about efficiency and cutting emissions. Opponents care about consumer choice and the quality of the light's color. Both sides are talking about things that really exist.

pieces.title: The customer pays first, and the coffee comes later: the accounts behind Starbucks stored-value cards
pieces.short: The accounts behind Starbucks stored-value cards
pieces.hook: Start with the facts.

parts: Start with the facts. Starbucks's annual report for fiscal 2025 (through 2025-09-28) shows a deferred-revenue balance of US$1.75 billion tied to stored-value cards and to the Stars of the membership program. About US$1.6 billion of that will be redeemed within a year.

Over the year, new cards, reloads, and Stars that customers earned added about US$15.25 billion to deferred revenue, and about US$15.20 billion was recognized as it was redeemed. Separately, balances expected never to be spent are called "breakage" in accounting. Company-operated stores recognized about US$200 million of it, and licensed stores about US$22 million.
Over the same period the company's total revenue was about US$37.2 billion. Active U.S. members over 90 days numbered 34.2 million, up only 1 percent from a year earlier.

Why is it worth looking at? The mechanism is, at bottom, "take the money first, deliver later," and it brings four things at once. Cash arrives early, a short-term fund on which no interest is paid. Money sitting on the card makes a customer more likely to come back, which is a lock-in effect. The app, the membership, and the payment are tied together, so the company knows who bought what, and when. Small balances that get forgotten eventually become nearly pure profit. In some places they have to be turned over under unclaimed-property rules.

Now the inference (what follows is inference, not something the company disclosed). A balance of US$1.75 billion is about 4.7 percent of annual revenue. A rough calculation at a 4 percent annual return puts the "interest value" at about US$70 million a year, a small sum beside US$37.2 billion of revenue.
So the popular line that "Starbucks is really a bank" overstates it. What makes the stored-value card valuable is locking in customers and accumulating data, not collecting interest.

Who gains, and who is under pressure? Starbucks gets the cash and the data. Customers get convenience and rewards, but the balance earns no interest, and if they forget to use it, it simply sits there.
For a competitor to copy the play, the precondition is a user base that is already large enough.

critical.label: Another way to look at it
items: A flywheel can top out too. Active members grew only 1 percent, which suggests that the "stored value plus points" play is nearing its ceiling in the United States.

Discounts can "train" customers the wrong way. Push a membership system too hard, and price-sensitive customers may come only when there is a deal, which over time presses down the average ticket and the brand's premium. That is a common worry in the trade. Whether Starbucks has already reached that point takes finer data to judge.

Don't turn one measure into a fetish. A high level of cash taken in advance shows that customers are willing to trust the company early. But the store experience, the product, and the price are the source of that trust. If the main business goes wrong, the stored-value balance will not hold the situation up.

A takeaway for you: when you read a company's accounts, look at "cash collected in advance, deferred revenue." It reflects how much customers trust the company. The same applies to you. Loading money onto a prepaid card is an interest-free loan to the merchant. Before you load it, ask whether you will really use it up.

pieces.title: The first woman prime minister takes office. Has Morocco's map of power changed?
pieces.short: The first woman prime minister takes office, and Morocco's…
pieces.hook: On Friday, October 16, King Mohammed VI of Morocco formally appointed a new government. Prime Minister Fatima-…

parts: On Friday, October 16, King Mohammed VI of Morocco formally appointed a new government, and Prime Minister Fatima-Zahra Mansouri became the first woman to head a government in Morocco's history. Her center-right Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) took 97 of 395 seats in the election of September 23, and with the right-wing Independence Party (65 seats) and two smaller parties of the left formed a coalition of 210 seats. The majority line is 198.

Of the 31 ministers in the previous cabinet, 13 stayed on, including Foreign Minister Bourita and Interior Minister Laftit. Lekjaa, president of the football federation, was promoted to economy minister. The new cabinet, prime minister included, has 7 women, the same as the last one. Turnout in this election was about 38 percent, the lowest in nearly twenty years.

Morocco's 2011 constitution requires the king to appoint the prime minister from the largest party in parliament. But major matters such as foreign affairs, security, and religion are still led by the palace, and "sovereign ministries" such as foreign affairs and the interior have long been held by people close to the court. This list of holdovers shows exactly that.

Reports from Reuters, Radio France Internationale, and others note that PAM and the previous ruling party, the National Rally of Independents (RNI), are close in outlook, and that the founding figures of both have ties to the palace. This time the RNI fell from 102 seats to 66. The Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) recovered from 13 seats to 54.

Looking further back, from late September 2025 Morocco saw the youth-led "Gen Z 212" protests. The demands included poor health care and education, corruption, and too much money spent building stadiums for the 2030 World Cup. According to the Associated Press and Human Rights Watch, 3 protesters died and hundreds were arrested.
Separate local reports say that in this election people aged 18–24 were only about 4 percent of registered voters.
The new government's side: it stresses the first woman prime minister and an orderly handover, and promises an "ambitious program of government" in answer to livelihood demands.
According to Agence France-Presse, party leader Benkirane welcomed his party's recovery in seats, and at the same time ruled out joining a government led by PAM.
Many people used not voting to express disappointment, judging that a vote would change nothing. Human-rights groups, for their part, criticized how the authorities handled last year's protests.

The new government has three hard problems in hand: jobs and prices, the balance between World Cup investment and social spending, and how to draw young people back into politics. The governing coalition is only 12 seats above the majority line, so holding it together will be a real test.

critical.label: Narrative frames to watch for
items: "First woman prime minister = the structure of power has changed." The symbolism is real, but a prime minister's actual power is limited, and the number of women in the cabinet is the same as last time.
"Low turnout = a crisis of the regime." It may only be a long-running political chill. Turnout in 2007 was even lower than this.
The either-or of "the World Cup versus hospitals" simplifies a complicated fiscal problem into a single opposition.
"The election result was entirely arranged by the palace" ignores a fact: voters did use their ballots to punish the previous ruling party hard.

[A short note on institutional design] "The largest party in parliament supplies the prime minister," plus "sovereign ministries are led by the palace." The effect of that combination is that an election can change who governs, but does not easily change the country's broad direction. You have been interested in how institutions are designed. This is a very typical case.

pieces.title: Bread from the air, and poison gas onto the battlefield: Fritz Haber
pieces.short: Fritz Haber
pieces.hook: The same skill can save lives or take them. What really sets the direction is not the ability, but whom you are willing to hand it…
pieces.takeaway: The same skill can save lives or take them. What really sets the direction is not the ability, but whom you are willing to hand it to.
pieces.imageAlt: Fritz Haber
pieces.imageCredit: Nobel Foundation · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On December 9, 1868, Haber was born in Breslau, Prussia (today Wrocław, Poland), into a family of Jewish merchants. His mother died soon after he was born. As a young man he studied chemistry. In the German academic world of the time, thick with antisemitism, he was baptized into Christianity, determined to prove himself "the most German of Germans."

At the end of the 19th century, European farming depended on natural nitrogen fertilizers such as Chilean nitrate and guano. In 1898 the British chemist Crookes warned in public that if nitrogen fertilizer could not keep up, there would sooner or later not be enough wheat to eat. Nearly four-fifths of the air is nitrogen, but it is so stable that plants cannot use it.

In 1909, in his laboratory at Karlsruhe, Haber used high pressure and a catalyst to synthesize ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen. Carl Bosch of BASF scaled that laboratory result up into an industrial process, and in 1913 the Oppau plant started production. The Haber–Bosch process has been the foundation of the fertilizer industry ever since.
A 2008 paper in Nature Geoscience estimated that in that year about 48 percent of the world's population was fed by the extra harvest that synthetic nitrogen fertilizer made possible.

The same man had another side. After the First World War broke out, Haber threw himself into poison-gas research. On April 22, 1915, the German army released chlorine at Ypres in Belgium, and he went to the front himself to direct it.

A few days later, in early May, his wife Clara Immerwahr, the first woman to earn a doctorate in chemistry at the University of Breslau, killed herself with his service pistol. The 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded in 1919, went to his work on synthesizing ammonia, and drew plenty of criticism at the time.

After the war he tried to extract gold from seawater to help Germany pay reparations, and failed. When the Nazis took power in 1933, he was a veteran of the First World War and could have been exempted, but he refused an order to dismiss his Jewish colleagues, resigned as director of his institute, and left Germany. On January 29, 1934, he died of heart failure in Basel, Switzerland.
The bitter part is that Zyklon B, later used by the Nazis in the gas chambers, had its roots in early cyanide-insecticide research at his institute. Some of his relatives also died in the camps.

items: about 48%
Share of the 2008 world population fed by the extra yield from synthetic nitrogen fertilizer (a paper's estimate)
Born in Breslau on December 9
Ammonia synthesized in the laboratory
The Oppau plant starts production
Chlorine at Ypres; his wife dies by suicide in early May
Nobel Prize in Chemistry (awarded in 1919)
Refuses to dismiss Jewish colleagues and leaves Germany
Dies in Basel on January 29

blocks.title: The choice in 1933
blocks.text: After the Nazis took power, he was a veteran of the First World War and could have been exempted, but he refused an order to dismiss his Jewish colleagues, resigned as director of his institute, and left Germany.

critical.label: From several angles
items: The credit for "feeding half the world" should not all sit on his head alone. Bosch's work of scaling the process up mattered just as much, and Bosch himself won a Nobel Prize in 1931. The figure of 48 percent is a model's estimate of the extra yield. It does not mean that every person was kept alive by Haber directly.

People defending him say that in that era scientists in many countries were researching weapons for their own armies. Critics say he pushed gas warfare actively and eagerly, and was not merely obeying. On that point the record is quite clear.

Clara's suicide is often told as "a death in protest against the gas," but she left very little direct evidence, and her motive is still disputed. Stories like this are moving, and precisely because they are moving, they need care not to be simplified.

Synthesizing ammonia now consumes a sizable share of fossil energy. A figure often cited is 1 to 2 percent of global energy use. The eutrophication of water from nitrogen fertilizer running off is part of the legacy he left as well.

pieces.title: Giving a day's strength back: more than a hundred years of the washing machine
pieces.short: More than a hundred years of the washing machine
pieces.hook: More than a hundred years ago, "laundry day" was real physical labor: hauling water, heating it, the washboard, wringing, and hanging clothes out. A household often…
pieces.imageAlt: Advertisement for the Thor electric washer, "Wash Without Work"
pieces.imageCredit: Seattle Electric Supply Co. · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: More than a hundred years ago, "laundry day" was real physical labor: hauling water, heating it, the washboard, wringing, and hanging clothes out. A household often used up a whole day, and the people doing the work were almost all women.
Stage one, the hand-crank era (the 19th century).
Europe and America produced all sorts of hand-cranked drums and agitator tubs. They saved some of the scrubbing, but the power was still a person.
Stage two, electricity (around 1908).

The Hurley Machine Company of Chicago brought out the Thor electric washer, designed by Alva Fisher. Mass sales began in 1908, and it received a patent in 1910. It used a perforated drum that reversed direction, so the clothes would not tangle into a lump, but it was a long way from "automatic." Filling, changing the water, and wringing with rollers all had to be done by hand. Early motors were often left exposed, with a risk of shock.
Stage three, fully automatic (1937).

Bendix brought out the first fully automatic home washer, putting wash, rinse, and spin into one program. The first machine shipped on September 27, 1937. Early models shook hard in the spin cycle and had to be bolted to the floor.
After the Second World War, washing machines spread through American homes on a large scale.
Stage four, into East Asian homes.

In Japan in the 1950s, the black-and-white television, the washing machine, and the refrigerator were together called the "three sacred treasures," a symbol of the new middle-class life. After that, twin-tub machines and pulsator machines became popular across Asia, while Europe preferred front-loading drum machines. Water quality, the size of homes, and laundry habits in different places shaped different product lines.
Stage five, now: a mature replacement market.

China is already the largest producer. According to the National Bureau of Statistics, national output of household washing machines in 2025 was 125.168 million units, up 4.8 percent year on year. Competition has shifted from "whether you have one" to saving water and electricity, combined washer-dryers, heat-pump drying, and smart programs. Microplastic fibers shed from clothing have also begun to enter the regulatory discussion.

blocks.title: A whole day of "laundry day"
blocks.text: Hauling water, heating it, the washboard, wringing, and hanging clothes out. A household often used up a whole day, and the people doing the work were almost all women.

Hand-cranked drums and agitator tubs
The Thor electric washer goes into mass sales
Bendix fully automatic home washer; ships on September 27
One of Japan's "three sacred treasures"

critical.label: From several angles
items: The optimistic side: in his 2010 TED talk "The Magic Washing Machine," the statistician Hans Rosling treated it as a key invention for freeing women's time. The economist Ha-Joon Chang goes further in 23 Things They Don't Tell You About Capitalism, saying the washing machine changed society more than the internet did. Economics papers (Greenwood and others, 2005, "Engines of Liberation") have tried to show that household appliances pushed women's employment.

The skeptical side: in More Work for Mother (1983), the historian Ruth Schwartz Cowan pointed out that once the machine spread, the standard of "clean" rose with it. Clothes were changed more often and washed more, housework time did not fall as much as people imagine, and most of it still fell on women.

On the evidence, the causal claim that "the washing machine sent women out of the home" is hard to prove. The same period also saw schooling spread, service industries expand, and ideas change. It is hard to enter the credit on one machine alone.

pieces.title: After commissions went to zero, how Charles Schwab makes its money
pieces.short: After commissions went to zero, what does Charles Schwab…
pieces.hook: What happened (the facts): one of the largest retail brokerages in the United States, Charles Schwab…
pieces.imageAlt: A Charles Schwab branch on Nassau Street, New York
pieces.imageCredit: Djkeddie · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 15, 2026, Charles Schwab, one of the largest retail brokerages in the United States, released its third-quarter results. Net revenue was US$7.171 billion, up 17 percent year on year. Net income was US$2.906 billion, up 23 percent. Earnings per share were US$1.62, up 29 percent. The pretax margin was 52.7 percent. Total client assets were US$13.33 trillion, up 15 percent year on year. Core net new assets for the quarter were US$190.4 billion, up 38 percent. About 1.24 million new brokerage accounts were opened.

paras.lead: Why it is worth a look
parts: In October 2019 Schwab led the way in cutting online commissions on U.S. stocks to zero, and the rest of the trade followed. "If there is no fee, where does the money come from?" The answer is in the revenue mix of this report. Net interest income was US$3.476 billion, nearly half of total revenue, and the net interest margin was 3.04 percent.

Idle cash in client accounts is "swept" into the Schwab system. At month-end that cash was about US$492.8 billion. Take bank deposits as an example. The average balance this quarter was about US$244.3 billion, interest expense was only US$139 million, and the annualized cost works out to about 0.23 percent.
In the same quarter, the yield on margin loans to clients was 5.70 percent.
Asset-management and administration fees were US$1.913 billion, up 14 percent, from funds, advice, and custody.

Trading revenue was US$1.158 billion, up 16 percent. But the average trade earned only US$1.69, against US$2.11 a year earlier. The gain came from a surge in volume: about 10.69 million trades a day, up 44 percent.

paras.lead: Who gains, and who is under pressure
parts: Retail clients got zero commissions. Independent registered investment advisers (RIAs) use Schwab as a back-office platform. Advisory business this quarter brought in about US$120.1 billion of net new assets, the bulk of it. That is a platform-and-interface business. Under pressure are the small brokerages with no balance sheet of their own. They have a hard time subsidizing zero commissions out of an interest spread.

Clients who leave a lot of cash in a low-interest sweep account are quietly paying too. In recent years more than one U.S. brokerage has faced lawsuits or regulatory inquiries over sweep rates that were too low.

US$2.906 billion

items: Net interest income

critical.label: What to watch for
items: Dependence on interest rates. Net interest income is very sensitive to rates, and the spread can narrow in a cutting cycle. During the Silicon Valley Bank turmoil of 2023, Schwab's stock fell hard because clients moved cash into higher-yielding products while the firm held a large book of bonds with unrealized losses, and it was forced to borrow heavily. Federal Home Loan Bank borrowings were largely paid off this quarter, so that particular pass is over, but the model's sensitivity is still there.

Leverage on the high side. Margin-loan balances were US$187.9 billion, up 14 percent in the quarter (US$60.7 billion of that tied to long-short strategies). In a strong market that is revenue. In a sharp drop it can become forced liquidation and risk.
This quarter is a report card from a strong market. It cannot be extended in a straight line.

A takeaway for you: "free" usually means the charge has moved somewhere else. The next time you use any zero-commission, zero-fee product, ask first: the idle money I leave there, what rate does it earn?

pieces.title: Five days of street clashes in a row: why Albanian students want Rama out
pieces.short: Why Albanian students want Ra…
pieces.hook: Key points (drawn from the BBC, the Associated Press, Al Jazeera, the Albanian Telegraphic Agency, and local police statements): The…
pieces.imageAlt: Street protest in Tirana, 2026
pieces.imageCredit: Vyolltsa · CC0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Key points (drawn from the BBC, the Associated Press, Al Jazeera, the Albanian Telegraphic Agency, and local police statements): by October 17, anti-government protests in the capital, Tirana, had turned into clashes for the fifth day running. The main body was high-school and university students, and the focus had moved from the Education Ministry building to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama.

Protesters threw stones, Molotov cocktails, and fireworks. Police used tear gas and water cannons, and on the 17th used rubber bullets for the first time. Police chief Hita called it "limited use." He said that over the five days 167 people were arrested and 132 police officers injured, and that another 7 officers were suspended on suspicion of exceeding their authority.
The clashes have spread to the port city of Durrës.

The students' demands include high tuition, poor teaching conditions, and scarce jobs. In the courtyard of the Education Ministry they burned a suitcase, to say they did not want to be pushed into leaving the country. The wider background is the "Flamingo" movement, which began this June in opposition to a luxury tourism development on the southern coast, a project tied to the investment firm founded by Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law.
The movement later widened into an anti-corruption protest demanding that Rama step down.

At the same time, the special prosecution office that Albania set up in 2019 under European and American pressure recently arrested Flora Hyseni, head of the national intelligence service, accusing her of helping Ergis Agasi, a businessman and a friend of Rama's, evade justice. Agasi denies corruption. Rama admits knowing him, but denies knowing of any illegal dealings.

Rama has been in power for 13 years and is now in a fourth term. He refuses to resign, blames the violence on the opposition Democratic Party and on unnamed "foreign forces," and restates the goal of joining the European Union in 2030. The governing Socialist Party holds 83 of 140 seats in parliament. The next general election is not until 2029.

Background: Albanian politics has long been dominated in turn by two men, Rama on the left and former prime minister Berisha on the right. Young people shouting against "the whole corrupt political class" are saying they do not believe a change of party in office would solve the problem. A steady outflow of people makes the failures of education and jobs especially sharp. The burned suitcase is the symbol.

The government holds a solid parliamentary majority and is under no procedural duty to call an early election. It stresses order and the gains on the path into the EU. Protesters think the channels inside the system have already failed. "We protested peacefully for 135 days," a 19-year-old student told the BBC.

Some journalists have proposed a neutral caretaker government for a year, and then an election. The EU is in an awkward spot. Rama has long been its "star pupil of reform," and the special prosecution office pursuing Hyseni is precisely an anti-corruption result that the EU pushed to create.

In the short run the ruling party is unlikely to dissolve parliament under street pressure. Two variables matter: whether the special prosecution office's investigation keeps climbing, and whether cracks appear inside the ruling party. If the violence escalates, the government may take the chance to stress "keeping order," and public sympathy for the protest may shrink.
For the EU, how to judge a government that is both advancing accession talks and deep in corruption allegations will be a test of how credible its enlargement policy is.

items: Arrested over five days
Police injured
Officers suspended on suspicion of exceeding their authority

blocks.title: What the ruling party can count on

critical.label: Narrative frames to watch for
items: "Stirred up by foreign forces." The government has produced no evidence, and has not named anyone. The line is often used to dodge demands at home, but that does not let you conclude there is no external factor at all.

The romance of a "youth revolution." Protesters themselves admit that some people in the crowd used the disorder to smash shops and banks. Whether the violence is justified, and whether the demands are, have to be judged apart.
Treating "the Kushner project" as the whole cause. It was one of the sparks. Tuition, jobs, corruption, and the fatigue of long rule are the deeper soil.
How the numbers are counted. The arrest and injury figures come mainly from police statements. An independent count of injuries on the protesters' side is still missing.

pieces.title: A bookbinding apprentice lit the century of electricity: Michael Faraday
pieces.short: Michael Faraday
pieces.hook: Do the notes in front of you carefully, and bind them into a volume. Sometimes that volume is the calling card that opens the next door.
pieces.takeaway: Do the notes in front of you carefully, and bind them into a volume. Sometimes that volume is the calling card that opens the next door.
pieces.imageAlt: Portrait of Faraday by Thomas Phillips
pieces.imageCredit: Thomas Phillips · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: In 1791 Faraday was born in Newington Butts, south of London. His father was a blacksmith and belonged to a very small sect, the Sandemanians. The family was poor. He had only a few years of basic schooling, and at 14 he went to the bookseller Riebau as a bookbinding apprentice (1805–1812).
Binding books let him read through the volumes that passed through his hands, and that is how he taught himself chemistry and electricity.
The turn came in 1812. Someone gave him tickets to hear Humphry Davy lecture at the Royal Institution. He wrote the notes up, bound them, and sent them to Davy, asking for a job.
In March 1813 he entered the Royal Institution as a laboratory assistant, and then traveled Europe with Davy for a year and a half, part assistant and part servant.

Over the next few decades, in the Institution's basement laboratory, he all but rewrote electromagnetism. In 1821 he produced "electromagnetic rotation," the seed of the electric motor. In 1825 he isolated benzene.

In 1831 he discovered electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field can produce an electric current, and every generator today works on that principle. He also set down the laws of electrolysis, and coined the words "electrode," "cathode," and "ion." In 1845 he discovered the magneto-optical effect and diamagnetism.
More important still, he proposed a picture of "lines of force" and of the "field." To the orthodoxy of action at a distance, that was close to heresy.

He was also a born explainer. In the mid-1820s he founded the Friday Evening Discourses and the Christmas Lectures, which still run. The Chemical History of a Candle is still in print. Twice he declined the presidency of the Royal Society. In his later years he lived in a house at Hampton Court that Queen Victoria had given him, and he died there on August 25, 1867.

blocks.title: A bound set of notes
blocks.text: He wrote up the notes from Davy's lectures, bound them, and sent them to Davy, asking for a job. In March 1813 he entered the Royal Institution as a laboratory assistant.

items: Born in Newington Butts, London
Bookbinding apprentice
Enters the Royal Institution
Electromagnetic rotation, the seed of a motor
Isolates benzene
Discovers electromagnetic induction
The magneto-optical effect and diamagnetism
Dies on August 25

critical.label: Another angle
items: Tell the "poor boy makes good" story too often, and it is easy to miss what the institution did. Without a platform like the Royal Institution, and without Davy's introduction, the talent might well have stayed buried in the bindery.

His relationship with Davy was not only a fond tale of master and pupil. After he published on electromagnetic rotation in 1821, some people accused him of borrowing Wollaston's idea, and the quarrel put a distance between him and Davy.

"He refused a knighthood" is widely repeated, but the Royal Institution, drawing on the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, points out that he did say in public, more than once, that he would not accept a title, yet no evidence has been found that a title was ever actually offered. In a famous anecdote, separate what the person said from what the record shows.
His mathematics was weak. The idea of the "field" did not really become a theory until Maxwell wrote it as equations in 1865. Intuition and mathematics: leave either one out and it does not work.

pieces.title: Bringing winter into the kitchen: two hundred years of the refrigerator
pieces.short: Two hundred years of the refrigerator
pieces.hook: Before the refrigerator, "cold" was something gathered from nature.
pieces.imageAlt: A GE Monitor Top refrigerator
pieces.imageCredit: Mr.Shoval · CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Before the refrigerator, "cold" was something gathered from nature. In 1806 Frederic Tudor, a Boston merchant, shipped natural ice from New England to the Caribbean, and later made a global business of ice. Cutting ice off the lakes in winter, storing it in icehouses insulated with sawdust, and selling it to iceboxes in the city: that was the earliest cold chain.

The technical turning point was "making cold by machine." In 1834 Jacob Perkins received a British patent for vapor-compression refrigeration: a liquid absorbs heat as it evaporates, gives the heat off again when it is compressed, and the cycle repeats. The refrigerator in a home today still uses that principle.
In the second half of the 19th century, ammonia refrigeration moved into breweries, meatpacking plants, and refrigerated ships, and the cold chain grew out from the industrial end.

Getting into the home had to wait for electricity. In 1913 Fred Wolf of Chicago brought out the DOMELRE, an electric refrigerating machine fitted onto an old-style icebox. In 1927 General Electric's Monitor Top refrigerator put the compressor on top of the cabinet, and the price and the reliability both came within reach of an ordinary household.

But the early refrigerants (ammonia, sulfur dioxide, methyl chloride) were poisonous, and a leak could kill. In 1928 Thomas Midgley's team synthesized Freon (a chlorofluorocarbon) for Frigidaire. "Safe and nontoxic" let the refrigerator spread fast.

The irony is that this "safety" later became a global problem. In 1974 Rowland and Molina showed that chlorofluorocarbons damage the ozone layer. That led to the Montreal Protocol of 1987, and then to the Kigali Amendment of 2016, which began cutting hydrofluorocarbons, whose greenhouse effect is very strong.
Many household refrigerators now use hydrocarbon refrigerants such as isobutane.

The Chinese line started late and ran fast. In 1956 Beijing trial-produced a refrigerator under the Snowflake brand, often called the first one made in China. In 1985 Zhang Ruimin, at the Qingdao Refrigerator General Factory (the predecessor of Haier), publicly smashed 76 refrigerators that had failed inspection. It became a symbol of Chinese manufacturing's "awakening to quality."

In 2016 Haier acquired General Electric's appliance business. According to the National Bureau of Statistics, China's output of household refrigerators in 2025 was 109.244 million units, up 1.6 percent year on year, and China is the world's largest producer.

paras.lead: What stage it is in now
parts: Growth in new demand has topped out, and the business runs on replacement and upgrading. The contest is no longer "can it get cold." It is zoned freshness, efficiency, smart features, and selling abroad.

items: Tudor ships natural ice to the Caribbean
Perkins's patent for vapor-compression refrigeration
The DOMELRE electric refrigerating machine
The GE Monitor Top refrigerator
Freon is synthesized
Chlorofluorocarbons are shown to damage the ozone layer
The Montreal Protocol
The Kigali Amendment

blocks.title: 76 refrigerators smashed
blocks.text: In 1985 Zhang Ruimin, at the Qingdao Refrigerator General Factory (the predecessor of Haier), publicly smashed 76 refrigerators that had failed inspection. It became a symbol of Chinese manufacturing's "awakening to quality."

critical.label: Another angle
items: The refrigerator is often described as a hero that "freed the household and improved nutrition," but it also brought a large environmental mistake. From "nontoxic" to "damaging the ozone layer" is a reminder that technology has to be judged on a scale of decades.

The cold chain lets people buy a week's food at once. It is also credited with encouraging big supermarkets and suburbanization, and it brought a new kind of waste: food that expires in the refrigerator gets thrown out all the same.

Some research links the decline in stomach cancer to the spread of refrigeration (less preserved food), but findings of that kind are mostly correlations. They should not be stated as "the refrigerator lowered cancer."

pieces.title: 120 million people are playing. Who is making the money: the accounts of Roblox's creator platform
pieces.short: The accounts of Roblox's creator platform
pieces.hook: Roblox itself barely makes games.
pieces.imageAlt: The Roblox building in San Mateo
pieces.imageCredit: 4300streetcar · CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Roblox itself barely makes games. It supplies the engine, the servers, the payments, and the traffic. The games are made by users and by studios. Players spend real money on a virtual currency, Robux, and spend it inside games. Robux that creators earn can be turned into dollars through the Developer Exchange (DevEx).
This is a typical "platform plus interface" model, the same kind of thing as Lego and Stripe, which interest you.

The latest complete report is the second quarter of 2026, released on July 30. The main figures: daily active users were 123 million, up 10 percent year on year, and hours of use were 29 billion, up 5 percent. Daily actives in Japan and India grew more than 60 percent. The United States and Canada grew only 6 percent.

GAAP revenue was US$1.469 billion, up 36 percent. But bookings, which better reflect sales in the period, were US$1.557 billion, up only 8 percent, at the bottom of the guidance range. The gap is so wide because most revenue is recognized over the average life of a paying user (27 months), so the revenue includes a good deal of money from the hit-game period of 2025.

DevEx paid to creators was US$363 million, about 23 percent of bookings, up 15 percent. Spending on infrastructure and safety was US$236 million, up 54 percent. The quarter's net loss was US$185 million, and free cash flow was US$294 million.
Bookings down 14 percent to 18 percent year on year.

The company's explanation is that the recommendation algorithm was changed to favor games with "high retention" rather than games that "pull in the most money," and that the hit games of 2025 were fading, so revenue per hour from younger users in the U.S. and Canada fell sharply. In other words, the platform deliberately gave up short-term revenue in exchange for a healthier ecosystem.

paras.lead: Who gains, and who is under pressure
parts: Long-tail creators gain. The share of hours taken by the top 10 games has fallen from about 30 percent three years ago to about 20 percent, and hours in games outside the top 10 grew 25 percent. Adult users are a focus too. The company says U.S. users 18 and older monetize more than 50 percent higher than minors.

Under pressure are studios that depend on a hit, and shareholders' short-term patience. Another large pressure is child safety. In 2026 Roblox has settled with Nevada (US$10 million) and with Alabama and West Virginia (US$23 million combined), among other states, and is rolling out age checks worldwide (by the end of the second quarter, 57 percent of global daily actives had completed one). Legal-settlement costs booked in the first half were US$91 million.
The facts: users are rising, and revenue per user is falling. Safety costs are rising. The share paid out to creators is rising.

Roblox is moving from "a game company that lives on hits" toward "a platform that taxes like an app store." The platform's moat depends on whether it can reassure parents and let creators make money at the same time. The two sometimes pull against each other. Age checks, for example, reduce chat and social play, and in the second quarter the company itself admitted that communication on the platform was below the level before the checks.

items: 123 million
Daily actives, +10%
29 billion hours
Hours of use, +5%
US$1.469 billion
GAAP revenue, +36%
US$1.557 billion
bookings, +8%

blocks.title: Second quarter: where the money went
The bill for child safety
blocks.text: In 2026 Roblox has settled with Nevada (US$10 million) and with Alabama and West Virginia (US$23 million combined), among other states, and is rolling out age checks worldwide. By the end of the second quarter, 57 percent of global daily actives had completed one.

critical.label: Another angle
items: The bulls think that once the market of younger users is saturated, adult users, 2D games, and one-click AI game making (Build) can open new room.

The bears think the platform still takes a share far above what creators receive, that the company has lost money under GAAP year after year, and that stock-based pay is high. The story of "a loss, but positive cash flow" has to be held up by growth that keeps going.

The "123 million daily actives" are counted by account, not by person, and the company admits in its filings that accounts used to inflate the numbers exist. When you look at a platform's figures, look at the definition first.

A takeaway for you: to judge a platform, don't look only at scale. Look at whom it shares the money with, and whether it is willing to sacrifice the short term for the long term. The next third-quarter report will be the first exam paper for this claim.

pieces.title: Students in the street, a city hall on fire: what this French protest is arguing over
pieces.short: What this French protest is arguing over
pieces.hook: Key points (from the Associated Press, The Guardian, NPR, and other reports): on Saturday, October 17, in many parts of France…
pieces.imageAlt: Limoges city hall
pieces.imageCredit: Aratar · CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Key points (from the Associated Press, The Guardian, NPR, and other reports): on Saturday, October 17, protests broke out across France. The Interior Ministry estimated about 550,000 people took part. The CGT union said about 800,000.

The protest began, after the new school year opened in September, in schools in poor districts of the northern suburbs of Paris: teachers absent, buildings run down. It later widened into a national movement against the cost of living, fuel prices, and cuts to public services. On social media, some people called for a restart of the Yellow Vests of 2018.

Most of the marches were peaceful, but groups on the fringe set fires, looted, and attacked police cars and public buildings. On Saturday night Prime Minister Lecornu said 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers injured. On Sunday Interior Minister Nunez updated the arrests to about 1,800, close to the Yellow Vests' single-day record of nearly 2,000 in December 2018.

In Limoges a 143-year-old city hall was mostly burned, and the roof collapsed. Marseille's city hall was stormed for a time. In Paris one person died of a heart attack, and prosecutors are investigating.

On October 18 Macron gave a televised address. He spoke of "anger" and "shame," said that "looters will pay for the damage, and those who try to overturn the Republic will be held to account," and blamed the violence on "rioters inside radical far-left groups, and on numerous criminals." He authorized prefects to ban gatherings when necessary. The government said it would not declare a state of emergency for now.

Macron has entered the last stretch of his term. Parliament is fragmented, and the campaign atmosphere for the 2027 presidential election is already up. During the student protests of the previous weeks, the police oversight body has been investigating at least twenty-some allegations of police violence. After a 15-year-old student lost a hand, the Interior Ministry suspended the use of a kind of stun grenade against students, but allowed it again during Saturday's protest.
A survey of 2,000 people in October found that about 45 percent of the French worry that the cost of living will rise.

The government: it stresses that "the right to protest is a fundamental right, and systematic violence is not," and puts the weight on going after looters and on the organizing role of the "far left."
Mélenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed: he supports the students, but says looting "goes against our methods."
She condemns the rioters and accuses Mélenchon's party of "making violence legitimate."
It sets the demands on higher wages, higher pensions, lower prices, and protecting public services.

In the short run, the security question will crowd out the question of demands. The government is more likely to add weight to keeping order than to produce a plan for education and livelihoods right away. Over the medium term, both the far left and the far right are using this movement to lay track for 2027: one side competing for angry young people, the other for voters who want order.
That could hollow out the center further.

items: about 1,800
Arrested (interior minister's update on Sunday)
Police injured (Saturday night)
143 years
Age of the Limoges city hall that burned

critical.label: Narrative frames to watch for
items: The "riot" frame and the "popular grievance" frame each take half the facts. Peaceful marches of 550,000 to 800,000 people, and a few thousand setting fires and looting, are two things that happened on the same day. Telling only one of them is incomplete.
"Orchestrated by the far left" is for now mainly an official characterization. How many organizers there were, and how they organized, has to wait on the judicial investigation that follows.
The numbers don't share one definition. Official and union counts of participants differ by 250,000, and the arrest total also moved within a day. When you cite them, name the source and the time.

Set beside yesterday's student protests in Albania: students are often the spark, but whether that becomes a movement of the whole public depends on whether a broader economic discontent sits behind it. That is what the two countries share. Their political systems and their demands differ a great deal, though, and a simple analogy is a bad idea.
