pieces.title: A book that let spring be heard again: Rachel Carson
pieces.short: Rachel Carson
pieces.hook: Solid evidence, plus writing an ordinary person can read, is what turns a specialist question into a public one.
pieces.takeaway: Solid evidence, plus writing an ordinary person can read, is what turns a specialist question into a public one.
pieces.imageAlt: Rachel Carson
pieces.imageCredit: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On May 27, 1907, Rachel Carson was born in the small town of Springdale, Pennsylvania. She wanted to be a writer from childhood, studied English at college, and later, drawn by a biology course, changed her field. In 1932 she earned a master's degree in zoology from Johns Hopkins University. But in the Depression the family was short of money, and after her father died in 1935 the burden of supporting them fell on her.

The turn was a "scientific job that involved writing." In 1935 she wrote radio scripts for the U.S. Bureau of Fisheries, and in 1936 she became a junior aquatic biologist, one of the few women in a professional post. By day she wrote official papers. At night she wrote the sea. Under the Sea-Wind, in 1941, came out just as Pearl Harbor happened, and sales were dismal.

The Sea Around Us, in 1951, was a sudden success. It won the National Book Award and stayed on the New York Times bestseller list for 86 weeks. Once she was financially independent, she resigned and wrote full time.

What really changed history was 1962. Silent Spring was serialized first in The New Yorker, and the book came out on September 27. She took the evidence that DDT and other pesticides concentrate up the food chain and harm birds and other living things, and wrote it as a story an ordinary person could read.

The chemical industry hit back hard. Some companies threatened to sue, and some people attacked her as "hysterical" and not professional enough. In May 1963 the science advisory committee to President Kennedy issued a report that largely supported her concerns. On June 4 she testified in the Senate. She already had cancer, and she did not make the illness public.
On April 14, 1964, she died, at only 56. After that the United States established the Environmental Protection Agency in 1970, and in 1972 banned most agricultural uses of DDT.

blocks.title: The freedom The Sea Around Us bought
blocks.text: The Sea Around Us, in 1951, won the National Book Award and stayed on the New York Times bestseller list for 86 weeks. Once she was financially independent, she resigned and wrote full time.

items: Born in Springdale
Earns a master's in zoology
Becomes a junior aquatic biologist
The Sea Around Us wins the National Book Award
Silent Spring is published on September 27
Testifies in the Senate on June 4
Dies on April 14
The United States bans most agricultural uses of DDT

critical.label: Several ways of seeing her
items: The charge most often made against her is that "banning DDT killed people in malarial regions." But Carson did not argue for banning every pesticide. She warned against overuse, and against mosquitoes developing resistance. The Stockholm Convention of 2001 also kept an exemption for DDT in malaria control.

Not every judgment of hers has been confirmed by later research. The evidence that DDT causes cancer in humans is still not a closed case. In 2015 the International Agency for Research on Cancer listed it as "probably carcinogenic" (Group 2A), not "carcinogenic." The harm to birds and to ecosystems rests on much firmer evidence.
"One book set off the environmental movement" simplifies the history too. Scientists, birdwatching groups, and local lawsuits were already building the pressure.

pieces.title: Flip the switch and wait for the rice: seventy years of the rice cooker
pieces.short: Seventy years of the rice cooker
pieces.hook: The idea of cooking rice with electricity came early.
pieces.imageAlt: A rice-cooker advertisement from 1956
pieces.imageCredit: Uploader's scan · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: The idea of cooking rice with electricity came early. By the end of Japan's Taisho era there was already an "electric pot" with a heating element sealed into the base. It only swapped fire for electricity. Someone still had to stand by, so the rice would not scorch or turn to porridge.

The real breakthrough was "automatic." In 1950 Toshiba put a rice cooker on its list of new products. Rivals had failed again and again, and inside the company people hesitated, so the development was handed to a partner factory, Koshinsha. In 1953 its president, Yoshitada Minami, ran experiments with his whole family, and broke the cook's feel for the heat down into a principle: hold the rice at about 98°C for about 20 minutes, and it cooks through.

How could the pot know, by itself, that the rice was "done"? His method was to put a cup of water in the outer pot, enough to evaporate in about 20 minutes. Once the water was gone and the temperature rose past 100°C, a bimetal strip bent in the heat and cut the power. Later, to cope with faster heat loss in winter, he changed the double pot into a three-layer "indirect heating" structure.

On December 10, 1955, the first 700 Toshiba ER-4 cookers went on sale. Appliance shops would not take them at first, so Toshiba went through the electric-power companies. Shogo Yamada, who ran the marketing, went into the countryside himself to demonstrate them, and after that sales took off, peaking at 200,000 units a month.

In 1956 Matsushita brought out a "direct heating" model. In 1959 it entered Hong Kong and was adapted to local taste. A timer switch appeared in 1961. In 1970 Zojirushi brought out an electronic rice warmer, and in 1972 cooking and keeping warm were combined in one machine.

In the late 1980s, IH (induction heating, so the inner pot itself produces the heat) arrived, with fiercer heat and finer control. After the 1990s, China's low-priced capacity rose and Japanese brands turned upmarket. Around 2015, Chinese tourists buying up rice cookers in Japan became news for a time.

paras.lead: Which stage it is in now
parts: China is already a replacement market. Online monitoring figures cited by the trade press put 2025 online retail sales of rice cookers at about 5.7 billion yuan, up about 4 percent year on year; unit sales at about 19.65 million, down nearly 9 percent; and the average price at about 290 yuan, up about 14 percent.
Fewer units, at a higher price, and the share of IH models is still rising. The industry has moved from "getting one into every home" to "trading up."

blocks.title: A cup of water as a timer
blocks.text: Put a cup of water in the outer pot, enough to evaporate in about 20 minutes. Once the water is gone and the temperature rises past 100°C, a bimetal strip bends in the heat and cuts the power.

critical.label: A critical look
items: Toshiba's materials say that about four years after the ER-4 went on sale it had reached half of Japanese households. The same materials also show that in 1960 the share of Japanese households owning a rice cooker had only just passed 25 percent, and that in 1969 it was 55.2 percent. When a company's story and the statistics do not match, go with the statistics.
How much "better" a high-end model tastes is largely a subjective matter of the mouth. Whether the gap between a few thousand yuan and a few hundred is worth it depends on the person.
"Freeing the housewife" is real, but, just as the piece on washing machines said, the time saved is often eaten up by a higher standard of housework.

pieces.title: Once China cools, can LVMH's combination punch still hold?
pieces.short: Once China cools, can LVMH's combi…
pieces.hook: What happened (the facts): on October 12, LVMH, the world's largest luxury group, reported third-…
pieces.imageAlt: The Louis Vuitton store at Hudson Yards, New York
pieces.imageCredit: Kidfly182 · CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 12, LVMH, the world's largest luxury group, reported third-quarter revenue of about €18.5 billion. Organic growth, which strips out exchange rates and acquisitions, was only 1 percent. Fashion and leather goods, nearly half of revenue (Louis Vuitton, Dior, and others), brought in €8.245 billion, an organic decline of 5 percent, much worse than the 1.8 percent decline analysts had expected.

By region, Asia excluding Japan fell 5 percent, the United States grew 5 percent, Japan grew 6 percent, and Europe grew 4 percent. Revenue for the first nine months was €57.1 billion, down 2 percent on a reported basis and up 2 percent on an organic basis. According to CNBC, LVMH's share price is down about 40 percent for the year.

LVMH's model is not a single brand. It is a combination running across wine, fashion, perfume, watches and jewelry, and selective retailing (Sephora and others). The effect of that combination was plain this quarter. Fashion and leather goods fell, while watches and jewelry (organic +6 percent), selective retailing (+8 percent), and wines and spirits (+6 percent) rose, and pulled the whole back to growth.
That is the "hedge" value of a multi-brand group.
Who gains, and who is under pressure: under pressure is the core leather-goods line that depends most on Chinese consumers and that raised prices again and again over the past few years.
Relative gainers are the U.S. and Japanese markets, and jewelry, which has a higher unit price and looks more like a "store of value."
The group is also pulling in the edges of the business. On September 1 it sold Marc Jacobs to WHP Global.

The trouble in leather goods may not be only "the Chinese economy cooling." It may also be that prices were pushed too hard over the past few years, and that middle-class "entry" customers walked away. The official report mentions only a slowing of Chinese demand. It does not admit this.

The combination can cushion a blow, but it cannot replace the core engine. If leather goods fall for several quarters in a row, Sephora and jewelry will have a hard time holding profits up for long, because leather goods usually carry the highest margin. That point has to wait on the full-year profit figures.

The case against is that luxury has always been a cyclical business, and one quarter of data is not enough to declare that "brand power is slipping." The design reset at Louis Vuitton and Dior is still early, and may need longer to show.

When you look at a diversified company, don't look only at the total. Split it open and see which division is carrying the load and which is dragging. Behind "overall growth of 1 percent" there may be a main engine stalling.

pieces.title: A U.S.–China–Russia summit? Trump says he will talk only about nuclear weapons
pieces.short: A U.S.–China–Russia summit? Trump says only…
pieces.hook: On October 19, Trump told reporters at the White House that he was willing to meet Putin and Xi Jinping in a three-way meeting, and that it would…
pieces.imageAlt: The north front of the White House
pieces.imageCredit: Nishkid64 · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 19, Trump told reporters at the White House that he was willing to hold a three-way meeting with Putin and Xi Jinping, and that it would be "on the basis of denuclearization." He said: "I would go, but not really for Ukraine, because honestly Russia is doing all right on the Ukraine question. They haven't moved much.

" Pressed further, he also said he would do his best to end the war. Earlier, The Wall Street Journal reported that Putin, on a phone call with Trump this month, proposed a three-way meeting to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. Kremlin spokesman Peskov said the three leaders might all attend the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 18–19, that the topic had indeed come up, but that there was "no substantive proposal or agreement."

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said the ministry had no information on the matter. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Sybiha objected outright, saying a meeting of the United States, China, and Russia "would only encourage Putin to go on with this war."

The last nuclear-arms-control treaty between the United States and Russia, the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), expired on February 5, 2026. For the first time in more than half a century, the two countries have no binding ceiling on strategic nuclear weapons. The U.S. side says the old treaty is out of date, and wants to negotiate a new agreement that would bring China in as well.

By estimates from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, China's warheads rose from about 600 at the start of 2025 to about 620 at the start of 2026. The U.S. Department of Defense expects the number to pass 1,000 before 2030. Even so, the U.S. and Russian arsenals are each still far larger than China's.
The United States: it wants to pull the subject from Ukraine over to nuclear arms control, and to get China to the table.
It would rather use a three-way frame to talk about Ukraine. According to The Wall Street Journal, that means ceasefire terms favorable to Moscow.

Its long-standing public position is that its nuclear forces are far smaller than those of the United States and Russia, and that it should not join three-way nuclear-disarmament talks. This time officials said only that they had no information.
It worries about being "arranged" by the great powers in its own absence.

Whether a meeting will happen, and what it would discuss, are both still unset. Even if it is held, nuclear-arms talks are usually measured in years, and a result is hard to get in one sitting. The more practical effect is inside the United States. With the midterms near, Trump's earlier waiver of sanctions on Russia, meant to push diesel prices down, has already stirred worry among Republican lawmakers that support for Ukraine is wobbling.

critical.label: Narrative frames to watch for
items: The great-power story that "the Big Three can sit down and solve the world's problems" easily overlooks the standing of Ukraine, of Europe, and of the other states that have nuclear weapons.
The reverse, calling any dialogue "selling out an ally," is too simple as well. Communication among great powers about nuclear risk has value in itself.
The evidence is still thin. So far there are only statements and anonymous reports, no agenda and no date. It should not be over-read as "the summit is set."

pieces.title: Exiled three times, he still turned ordinary days into poetry: Su Shi
pieces.short: Su Shi
pieces.hook: You cannot choose your circumstances, but arriving somewhere new and still taking the work, the meals, and the writing seriously is a skill in itself.
pieces.takeaway: You cannot choose your circumstances, but arriving somewhere new and still taking the work, the meals, and the writing seriously is a skill in itself.
pieces.imageAlt: Portrait of Su Shi by Zhao Mengfu
pieces.imageCredit: Zhao Mengfu · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Su Shi was born in 1037 in Meishan, Meizhou (today Meishan, Sichuan). His father Su Xun and his younger brother Su Zhe would both later be named among the Eight Masters of Tang and Song prose. In 1057, Su Shi, just past twenty, and his brother passed the jinshi examination on the same list. That year’s chief examiner, Ouyang Xiu, read his essays and said he ought to “step aside and let this man stand a head taller.” From then on, Su Shi’s name filled the capital.

Most of the turns in his official career were tied to Wang Anshi’s reforms. Su Shi did not oppose reform itself, but he thought the New Policies were being pushed through too fast and too uniformly. He submitted memorial after memorial in criticism, then asked to be posted out of the capital, serving in turn as a local official in Hangzhou, Mizhou, Xuzhou, and Huzhou. In 1079, censors lifted lines from his poems and prose and charged him with mocking court policy. That was the Crow Terrace Poetry Case.
He spent more than a hundred days in prison and for a time believed he would die. In the end he was demoted to deputy militia commissioner of Huangzhou.

Huangzhou was the low point of his life and the high point of his writing. He cleared a slope of land east of the city and farmed it, taking the name Lay Buddhist of the Eastern Slope. “Nian Nu Jiao: Recalling Antiquity at Red Cliff” and both the former and the latter “Red Cliff Rhapsodies” were written in these years. Later the conservative faction returned to power and he was recalled to court, but he opposed Sima Guang’s wholesale repeal of the hired-service law. He pleased neither side, and was sent out to a provincial post again.

During his term in Hangzhou he dredged West Lake and built a long causeway from the silt he dug out. That is today’s Su Causeway. In his later years the political tide turned again. He was first demoted to Huizhou, then to Danzhou on Hainan, at the time nearly the most distant place of exile. He was pardoned and started north in 1100, and died the following year in Changzhou.

What he left behind was not only poems, essays, and calligraphy, but a way of living in earnest even in adversity: working out what to eat in Huangzhou, and opening a school in Danzhou. For later generations, Dongpo became a byword for an open, unburdened spirit.

blocks.title: The Crow Terrace Poetry Case
blocks.text: Censors lifted lines from his poems and prose and charged him with mocking court policy. He spent more than a hundred days in prison and for a time believed he would die. In the end he was demoted to deputy militia commissioner of Huangzhou.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Su Shi’s easy spirit is often romanticized. In his letters from Huangzhou he also wrote of fear, poverty, and loneliness. The “unburdened” image is, in part, one that later readers assembled by choosing what to read.

Some take his refusal to side with either the new faction or the old as a matter of principle. Others fault his politics for leaning on moral argument and literary style, with plans for governing that were not systematic enough.

The Crow Terrace Poetry Case is often told as a pure miscarriage of justice over words, but his poems did contain lines satirizing the New Policies. The question is whether speech should be a crime, not whether he said it.
Anecdotes such as Dongpo pork mostly come from later embellishment, and the historical evidence is uneven. Best heard as stories.

pieces.title: From a horse-drawn vacuum to robots underfoot: 120 years of the vacuum cleaner
pieces.short: 120 years of the vacuum cleaner
pieces.hook: In 1901, British engineer Hubert Cecil Booth watched a demonstration in London of a “dust-blowing” machine: it blew the dust…
pieces.imageAlt: Booth’s horse-drawn vacuum cleaner in 1901
pieces.imageCredit: Author unknown · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: In 1901, British engineer Hubert Cecil Booth watched a demonstration in London of a “dust-blowing” machine: it blew the dust into the air and then counted on the dust settling into a bag. Booth thought the direction was backward. The dust should be sucked in, then stopped by a filter cloth.

On August 30 of the same year he received a British patent, and then founded the British Vacuum Cleaner Company. The earliest machines were mounted on horse-drawn carriages and parked outside well-off homes, with a long hose run in through a window. Hiring someone to come and vacuum once then cost about as much as a junior maid’s wages for a year.
Its most famous job sent 15 machines over four weeks to suck 26 tonnes of dust off the steel beams of London’s Crystal Palace.

What actually brought the vacuum into ordinary homes was American. In 1908, James Spangler, a janitor with asthma, applied for a patent on a light electric upright vacuum. William Hoover had been in the harness and leather-goods business. Seeing the automobile rise and looking for a new trade, he bought the patent and launched the Model 0 at $60, still a luxury at the time.

Hoover put real effort into advertising, so much so that in Britain “hoover” later became the verb for vacuuming itself. By the 1920s the industry had settled into two main designs, the upright and the canister, and for decades after that the changes were small ones in power, attachments, and looks.

The next big change came from James Dyson. He disliked the way suction fell as soon as the dust bag clogged. He spent more than ten years and built about five thousand prototypes before working out a cyclonic separation design. In 1982 he pitched the technology to Hotpoint and was turned down flat. In 1993 he finally launched his own bagless vacuum, the DC01.
Bagless, cyclonic, and cordless became the new axes of competition.

The stop after that was robots. iRobot launched the Roomba in 2002 and created the category of home robot vacuums, but the lead eventually passed to Chinese companies. According to IDC, in the first three quarters of 2025 the top five shippers of smart robot vacuums worldwide were all Chinese brands: Roborock at 21.7%, Ecovacs at 14.1%, Dreame at 12.4%, Xiaomi at 10%, and Narwal at 7.5%.

By the third quarter iRobot’s share had fallen to 7.9%, dropping it out of the top five. In December 2025 it filed for bankruptcy reorganization and was acquired by its contract manufacturer, Picea, under Shenzhen Shanchuan. In 2025, global shipments of cleaning robots were 32.72 million units, up 20.1% year over year. Of those, robot vacuums accounted for 24.12 million. The fastest growth was in mowing robots and window-cleaning robots.
So the industry is now shifting from a “vacuuming tool” into a “home robot platform.” The contest is over navigation algorithms, base stations, the speed of the supply chain, and price tiers.

items: Do vacuums really save housework? Some research argues that as home appliances spread, standards of cleanliness rose with them, and time spent on housework did not fall in proportion.

iRobot’s failure is often told as “Chinese manufacturing beat American innovation,” but IDC also pointed to problems of its own: a long refusal to use lidar for navigation, an insistence on high prices, and on top of that the collapse of the Amazon acquisition and the shock of tariffs.
Robot vacuums map your home and carry cameras. In 2022 it came out that indoor photos taken by Roomba test units had leaked. The privacy cost is worth weighing.

pieces.title: Selling the engine is only the start: GE Aerospace’s third-quarter aftermarket accounts
pieces.short: GE Aerospace’s third-quarter aftermarket accounts
pieces.hook: On October 20, 2026, GE Aerospace reported third-quarter results: total orders of $19 billion…
pieces.imageAlt: A LEAP-1B engine on a Boeing 737 MAX
pieces.imageCredit: Captain Galaxy · CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 20, 2026, GE Aerospace reported third-quarter results: total orders of $19 billion, up 49% year over year; adjusted revenue of $13.3 billion, up 18%; and adjusted earnings per share of $2.25, up 36%. The company raised its full-year guidance for the third time, projecting adjusted earnings per share of $8.00 to $8.10.

paras.lead: Why it is worth a look
parts: The most interesting thing in this report is not how large the numbers are, but where the money comes from. The commercial engines and services segment posted revenue of $10.3 billion this quarter, up 21%. Within that, services revenue rose 17% and spare-parts revenue rose more than 20%, and the segment’s operating margin was 27.9%.
The company said the commercial-services backlog has passed $170 billion. It has roughly 50,000 civil engines and 30,000 military engines in service worldwide.

This is the aircraft-engine industry’s typical “installed base plus aftermarket” model. New engines sold to aircraft makers and airlines often carry very thin margins, and early in a new model’s life they may even lose money (a common claim in the industry; GE did not disclose it separately in the earnings report).

The real money is in the overhauls, replacement parts, and long-term service agreements over the twenty or thirty years that follow. This quarter offered an example: Turkish Airlines ordered more than 300 LEAP-1B engines and, at the same time, signed a long-term service agreement covering its fleet of more than 600 LEAP-1B engines. Sell once, and service for decades.
(The LEAP is built by CFM, a joint venture owned in equal halves by GE and France’s Safran.)

Who benefits, and who is under pressure: the ones who benefit are GE and its shareholders. Deliveries of new aircraft worldwide have stayed troubled, so older planes have to keep flying a few more years, which in turn brings more demand for maintenance.

The ones under pressure are the airlines. Queues for overhaul and rising parts prices push their costs up directly. The supply chain is stretched tight as well. GE has just announced it will acquire the castings maker CPP to expand capacity, a sign that the bottleneck is real.

GE’s moat is less a matter of a technical lead than of the barrier created by its installed base and by airworthiness certification. As long as an engine hangs under the wing, the maintenance business is hard to take away. The risk is that if aircraft deliveries recover sharply, the thin margins on new engines will pull the overall margin down. Discontent among regulators and airlines over an aftermarket monopoly could also heat up.

blocks.title: Sell once, service for decades
blocks.text: Turkish Airlines ordered more than 300 LEAP-1B engines and, at the same time, signed a long-term service agreement covering its fleet of more than 600 LEAP-1B engines.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Part of the strong growth in services revenue comes from engines entering the shop early. Durability problems with the LEAP in hot, sandy regions have drawn complaints from some airlines, so “more maintenance” is not entirely good news.

On a GAAP (U.S. generally accepted accounting principles) basis, the margin this quarter actually fell from 20.7% to 19.9%, and free cash flow was down 14% year over year. Looking only at the adjusted figures gives too rosy a picture.
A takeaway for you: when you look at a business, do not only ask what it sells. Also ask, after the sale, how many years the customer will keep paying.

pieces.title: Streets lit by the price at the pump: unrest in France and Europe’s cost-of-living protests
pieces.short: Unrest in France and Europe’s cost-of-living protests
pieces.hook: On October 17, about 550,000 people took to the streets across France to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, and schools…
pieces.imageAlt: A march in Paris on October 17, 2026
pieces.imageCredit: FreCha · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 17, about 550,000 people took to the streets across France to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, and the deterioration of public services such as schools. The marches were largely peaceful, but smashing, looting, and arson broke out in Paris, Marseille, Lille, and elsewhere. A 19th-century city hall in Limoges was set on fire.

According to the French Interior Ministry, about 2,400 people were arrested. On the 18th, Macron gave a national address, speaking of “legitimate demands” and “those who smash and loot” as separate things. Prime Minister Lecornu pointed the blame at the “far left,” announced a curfew in parts of Paris, and set a meeting with the unions for October 21.

Le Pen and Bardella of the far-right National Rally boycotted the meeting of party leaders called by the government, while the General Confederation of Labour (CGT) accused the government of running a “strategy of chaos.” The same weekend, cost-of-living or housing protests also appeared in Milan, Lisbon, and parts of Spain.

This round of protests began with students in the northern suburbs of Paris complaining about poor school buildings, then quickly spread into a nationwide cost-of-living protest. The economic figures supplied the “fuel” for the mood: in September, French consumer prices rose 3.1% year over year, with energy up 21.3%; the unemployment rate in the second quarter was 8.3%, and youth unemployment was 21.6%.

The European Commission estimates that the U.S.–Iran conflict that broke out in February this year has already cost Europe about 100 billion euros. Natural gas prices are up about 140%, and diesel prices have doubled.
The government: it puts order first, blames the violence on far-left groups, and at the same time grants that livelihood demands are legitimate.
They argue that the government is using the violence to shift the focus and avoid livelihood issues.
They boycott the government on one side and demand tougher policing on the other. Some far-right parties in Europe also favor resuming imports of Russian energy.
Their view is cooler. Capital Economics argues there was no single trigger. The rise in energy prices this time is actually smaller than in 2022, when similar violence did not appear.

In the short run, the government may roll out fuel or livelihood subsidies, but France’s public finances are already tight, so subsidies and deficit control pull in opposite directions. Over the medium term, France, Italy, and Poland all have elections next year, and the cost of living is likely to keep lifting support for the far right. There is an echo abroad as well: Trump has already cited the French unrest at rallies for the U.S. midterm elections.

People in the streets on October 17

rows: September consumer prices, year over year

critical.label: Narrative frames to watch
items: “All far-left thugs” and “all angry citizens” are both simplifications. The several hundred thousand people who marched in peace and the few who smashed things should be looked at separately.
Blaming everything on the U.S.–Iran conflict pushing up energy prices leaves out longer-running structural problems: schools, housing, and youth unemployment.
Claims such as “Europe is collapsing” are often taken up by politicians abroad to serve their own campaigns. When you quote them, look at what the speaker is trying to prove.

Different sources give different figures for the size of the protests and the number of arrests. When you use the official numbers as a baseline, remember that they come from one of the parties involved.

pieces.title: The girl who picked fossils under the cliffs, and helped the world grasp extinction: Mary Anning
pieces.short: Mary Anning
pieces.hook: Someone who stays at the site itself long enough will, in the end, have the firsthand evidence speak for her.
pieces.takeaway: Someone who stays at the site itself long enough will, in the end, have the firsthand evidence speak for her.
pieces.imageAlt: Portrait of Mary Anning
pieces.imageCredit: Signed Mr. Grey · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On May 21, 1799, Mary Anning was born in Lyme Regis, a seaside town in Dorset, England. Her father, Richard, was a carpenter, and he also dug fossils from the cliffs along the shore to sell to visitors and help with the household expenses. The Annings did not belong to the Church of England. At the time they were both poor and pushed aside.

On August 19, 1800, at 15 months old, she was in a neighbor’s arms watching a horse display when lightning struck beneath the tree. The neighbor holding her and two other women were killed on the spot. She survived. The story is still told in the town.

In 1810 her father died and left debts behind. In 1811 her brother Joseph dug out a skull about 1.2 meters long. A few months later Mary, around 12, found the rest of the skeleton nearby. It measured about 5.2 meters in all. The local paper presented it as a “crocodile.” Later it was exhibited in London and caused a sensation. It was the first ichthyosaur fossil to draw the attention of London’s scientific community.

From then on she made her living by digging up fossils and selling them. Winter storms and landslides would expose new ones, and they had to be rescued before the waves carried them off. The work was dangerous, and it depended on luck.

On December 10, 1823, she found the first complete plesiosaur skeleton. The neck had 35 vertebrae. Cuvier, the leading French authority on anatomy, at one point suspected it was a fake pieced together, and accepted it only after the matter was discussed. In 1826 she saved enough to buy a house with a glass shop window and opened Anning’s Fossil Shop. In December 1828 she found the first pterosaur fossil in Britain.
She taught herself anatomy and read the papers, and she helped scholars establish that what were then called “bezoar stones” were in fact fossilized feces.

But as a woman and a member of the working class, she could not join the Geological Society of London (the society did not admit women until 1904), and scholars often left her name off the papers they published. In 1835 she lost about £300 in savings. Old friends, Buckland among them, went to work on her behalf and secured her a government annuity of £25 a year.
On March 9, 1847, she died of breast cancer, only 47. De la Beche, president of the Geological Society, read a eulogy for her. It was the first time the society eulogized a woman.

Her ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs, and pterosaurs became key evidence for the ideas that species can go extinct and that the Earth once had an age of reptiles. Before Darwin, they changed how people understood the history of life. In 2010 the Royal Society named her one of the ten British women who most influenced the history of science. On May 21, 2022, her statue was unveiled in Lyme Regis. The fundraising was started by a local girl who began the effort at 11.

blocks.title: The society’s closed door, and its eulogy
blocks.text: She could not join the Geological Society of London (the society did not admit women until 1904), and scholars often left her name off the papers they published. But after she died, the president, De la Beche, read a eulogy for her. It was the first time the society eulogized a woman.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The phrase “a buried genius” needs a discount. In her lifetime she was already well known in geological circles in Britain and Europe. Scholars came to her door to consult her, and in 1844 the King of Saxony visited the shop in person and bought an ichthyosaur skeleton. What she mainly lacked was her name on the work, and a place in the institutions, not total obscurity.

She lived by selling fossils, and the specimens went into private collections in many places. Some argue that commercial collecting loses the record of where a find came from and hurts research. Others answer that without this market, nobody would take the risk under cliffs that collapse in winter.

Where the evidence is thin: she left very little writing of her own. The only thing published in her lifetime was an excerpt from a letter in 1839, and many of the “things she said” come from other people’s retelling. A widespread claim is that the tongue twister “She sells seashells” is about her, but researchers at the American Folklife Center point out that there is no reliable evidence for it.

pieces.title: Drop in a coin, and the machine hands you something: two thousand years of the vending machine
pieces.short: Two thousand years of the vending machine
pieces.hook: The earliest “vending machine” appeared in Roman Egypt around the 1st century CE.
pieces.imageAlt: A vending machine on a roadside in Japan
pieces.imageCredit: Marie-Sophie Mejan · CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: The earliest “vending machine” appeared in Roman Egypt around the 1st century CE. Hero of Alexandria described a device: a coin dropped in landed on the pan of a lever, pressed a valve open, and let out a little holy water or wine. The pan then tipped, the coin slid off, and the valve closed again.
Take the money and hand over the goods, with no person in between. That core idea has not changed in two thousand years.

The modern vending machine was born in London in the 1880s. In 1883 Percival Everitt invented a coin-operated machine that sold postcards. It soon filled railway stations and post offices, selling envelopes, postcards, and notepaper. In 1887 Britain got its first company devoted to installing and maintaining vending machines.

By 1893 the German chocolate maker Stollwerck was selling chocolate in 15,000 machines. In 1888 the Thomas Adams chewing-gum company in the United States put vending machines on the train platforms of New York.

The second pattern was the automat. In 1895 Berlin opened the world’s first, Quisisana. On June 12, 1902, Horn & Hardart opened the first American one in Philadelphia, and New York at one point had 40. But fast-food restaurants could take cards and were more flexible, and inflation made a handful of coins buy less and less. The last automat in New York closed in 1991.

The main character of the third stage is Japan. As early as 1888 someone in Japan applied for a patent on an “automatic goods-vending machine.” Juice machines became popular in the 1950s–60s, and by 2000 there were about 5.6 million machines nationwide. A dense population, low crime, and heavy rail traffic made the machine on the corner both safe and a real business.

Today this “kingdom of vending machines” is shrinking. Figures from the Japan Vending System Manufacturers Association (JVMA) show that at the end of 2025, vending machines and automatic service machines together numbered 3.8817 million, down 0.7% from a year earlier. Of those, the machines that actually sell goods numbered 2.5852 million, beverage machines 2.1788 million, and cigarette machines only 57,100, down 13.4% in a year.

The SOMPO Institute points out that the total is more than 20% lower than ten years ago. The reasons are that convenience stores and drugstores keep opening, and rising prices push people toward cheaper channels. Sapporo Holdings has left the vending-machine business, and DyDo and Ito En have also booked impairment charges tied to vending machines.

paras.lead: The United States took another path
parts: Industry estimates cited by Wikipedia put the United States in 2023 at about 3 million vending machines and a market of about $18.2 billion, with average monthly revenue of about $525 per machine, and a shift toward “smart retail kiosks” that take cards, connect to a network, and carry a touchscreen. Overall, the industry is moving from competing on how many machines it has to competing on how much each machine earns. There are fewer machines, but each one has to be smarter and better at selling.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: A falling machine count does not mean demand has vanished. What gets removed is mostly the locations that do poor business, and the machines that remain may sell more per unit. JVMA’s tables of machine counts do not show sales revenue. Looking only at the count makes it easy to misjudge how healthy the industry is.

Japan’s experience is hard to copy. Low crime, high density, and the habit of using coins are the preconditions. Where QR-code payment and delivery services are well developed, “buy anytime, anywhere” already has a cheaper substitute.

The energy dispute: machines that cool or heat around the clock use electricity. Makers have been pushing energy-saving models in recent years, but the parties do not count the savings on the same basis, and the figures should be treated with care.

Where the evidence is thin: the U.S. figures of $18.2 billion and 3 million machines are industry estimates, and different organizations define them very differently. Japan’s 5.6 million machines in 2000 and the 2025 JVMA figures may not have been counted on exactly the same basis either.

pieces.title: Ads keep fetching higher prices, but the cash is not enough to spend: Meta’s third-quarter AI ledger
pieces.short: Meta’s third-quarter AI …
pieces.hook: On October 21, U.S. time, Meta reported its third-quarter results.
pieces.imageAlt: Meta’s headquarters in Menlo Park
pieces.imageCredit: LPS.1 · CC0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 21, U.S. time, Meta reported its third-quarter results. Revenue was $64.60 billion, up 26% year over year. Of that, advertising revenue was $63.06 billion, also up 26%. Broken out, ad impressions rose 10%, and the average price of each ad rose 14%.

The apps in its family had 3.64 billion daily active people on average in September, only 3% more than last year. In other words, it is already hard to add more users. The money comes mainly from “the same people seeing more ads, and more expensive ones.” Meta credits AI recommendations and ad delivery with raising engagement and the efficiency of monetization.

paras.lead: The other side of the income statement is stark
parts: Costs and expenses were $51.61 billion, up 68% year over year. Inside that is a one-time charge of $9.89 billion, from a settlement reached in August with 52 state attorneys general over lawsuits about teen mental health (a total of up to about $18.59 billion).
Excluding that charge, operating profit was $22.88 billion, still above the $20.54 billion of the same quarter last year, and earnings per share were $7.40.

What really deserves watching is the cash. Capital expenditure this quarter, including principal on finance leases, was $34.91 billion, more than operating cash flow of $32.79 billion. Free cash flow was a negative $2.12 billion, against a positive $10.63 billion in the same quarter last year.

Over the first nine months the company issued about $24.9 billion in new long-term debt, and it bought back no stock this quarter. It narrowed its 2026 capital-expenditure guidance to $135–145 billion, and said that 2027 will still bring “aggressive investment.”
Reality Labs, which makes VR and AR, lost $4.13 billion this quarter, and the full-year loss is expected to be $18–19 billion. Fourth-quarter revenue guidance is $73–76 billion.

The same day, the board announced a new listed but non-voting Class C share, planned to take effect on January 19, 2027: one Class C share for each Class A or Class B share held. The Class A price is expected to adjust as it would in a two-for-one split. The company said outright that the new shares can be used for financing, employee compensation, and acquisitions, while it “continues the founder-led model.”

Meta is using the profits of its core advertising business to fund AI infrastructure, and the Class C share offers a tool for issuing stock and raising money without diluting Zuckerberg’s voting power. The beneficiaries are chips, data centers, and the electricity supply chain. The pressure falls on shareholders who care about dividends and buybacks, and about corporate governance.

Legal risk is building as well. According to Axios and Business Recorder, in a New Mexico case about misleading privacy practices, Meta was ordered to pay about $25 billion. The takeaway for you: when you look at a company, do not only look at how fast revenue is growing. Also look at whether the cash is coming in faster than it is going out.

blocks.title: Class C shares with no vote
blocks.text: For each Class A or Class B share held, one Class C share is issued, planned to take effect on January 19, 2027. The new shares have no voting rights. The company says they can be used for financing, employee compensation, and acquisitions, while it “continues the founder-led model.”

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The optimistic view: a 14% rise in the price of an ad shows that AI is already turning into money in a concrete way, and the heavy spending is building a moat. Meta still has $82.45 billion in cash and marketable securities, and can carry it.

The cautious view: free cash flow has turned negative, the company has started borrowing, and buybacks are paused, which shows that the pace of investment has already outrun the pace of making money. The company itself admits that the new AI spending has “a longer payback period than the core business.”

The governance view: shares with no vote let the founder make long-term bets freely, and they also mean outside shareholders have a harder time correcting course. The company cites “a share price up more than 1,700% since listing” as proof that founder control works, but past results do not stand for the future.

Where the evidence is thin: the earnings report does not break out a specific figure for how much “incremental ad revenue” AI has brought. Outsiders can only infer it indirectly from the price per ad and the number of impressions.

pieces.title: Five months, four nominations: Romania finally has a new government, resting on a promise not to bring it down
pieces.short: Romania finally has a new government, resting…
pieces.hook: On October 20, a joint session of Romania’s Senate and Chamber of Deputies voted by secret ballot, 280 in favor and 58 against…
pieces.event: October 20, 2026 (confidence vote in the Romanian parliament)
pieces.imageAlt: The Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest
pieces.imageCredit: William John Gauthier · CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 20, a joint session of Romania’s Senate and Chamber of Deputies voted by secret ballot, 280 in favor and 58 against, to pass a motion of confidence in Prime Minister Luca Niculescu and his cabinet (464 members of parliament in all; the legal threshold was 233). The new cabinet is made up of people from the Social Democratic Party (PSD) and technocrats: 16 ministers plus 2 delegates of ministerial rank. The National Liberal Party (PNL) and the Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Romania (UDMR) voted in support, but they are not in the cabinet.
The cabinet then went to the presidential palace and was sworn in before President Nicușor Dan. Niculescu said he would hold the first cabinet meeting that evening.

On May 5 this year, the government of the center-right prime minister, Bolojan, fell on a motion of no confidence brought by the PSD and the right-wing nationalist party AUR. Behind it was the conflict set off by austerity measures meant to bring the fiscal deficit down. After that, President Dan nominated three people in a row, and none of them managed to form a government. The cabinet of the third nominee, Mureșan, was rejected by parliament.

On October 5 he nominated Niculescu, 55: a journalist by background, ambassador to France from 2016 to 2022, and after that a state secretary at the foreign ministry, responsible for Romania’s path into the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), and a member of no party.

The PSD took most of the ministerial posts. Party chair Grindeanu himself stayed outside the cabinet. In parliament he said, “Cutting the deficit is absolutely necessary, but it cannot be done by making Romanians poorer.” The PNL offers support from the opposition, in exchange for the new government’s promise that the 2027 budget will meet the European Union’s deficit target. The PNL in turn promised not to seek to bring the government down before March 2027, but some of its local organizations publicly oppose this government.

USR and AUR said they would not vote in favor. Members of the SOS Romania party held up signs in the chamber reading “early general election.” Niculescu said Romania faces not only a budget crisis but “a crisis of its model of development”: for every 10 lei the state takes in, nearly 1 leu goes to pay interest.
He promised that from 2027 pensions will be raised by indexation, but within the path of deficit reduction.

In the short run, four things are most urgent: amending this year’s budget without widening the deficit, passing next year’s budget, securing energy for the winter, and finishing the European Union’s Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP) on schedule so the money is not lost. Over the medium term, this is a “minority government plus outside support” arrangement, a little like the “confidence and supply” agreements common in parliamentary countries. The PNL is not in the cabinet, but it promises not to bring the government down for a period, which gives the government about five months of safety.
It lowers the risk of falling again right away, but every budget and every reform has to be negotiated over again.

critical.label: Narrative frames to watch
items: First, “technocrat equals neutral expertise”: the prime minister belongs to no party, but most of the cabinet is PSD people. Second, “the crisis is over”: much of the support inside the 280 votes is conditional, and the PNL’s promise runs only until March next year. Third, the either-or of “austerity or livelihoods”: it hides the middle options, tax collection, the efficiency of spending, and attracting investment, which is exactly the direction the new government itself stresses.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The supporters’ view: ending half a year of a government treading water, protecting European Union funds, and steadying what the markets expect costs less than dragging things out further, or than an early election.

The critics’ view: SOS Romania held up signs demanding an early general election, and USR and AUR also refused to vote in favor. In their view the choice should be handed back to the voters. Some local organizations of the PNL likewise withhold their support from this government in public.

From the design of the system: “outside support in exchange for a promise not to bring the government down” can buy time, but it has no legal force. It can lapse when the term ends, or when a dispute over the budget appears. How stable the government is depends on the next round of bargaining.

Where the evidence is thin: the new government has not yet published a specific numerical path for cutting the deficit, and it has not given the size of the pension increase either. It is too early to judge success or failure.

pieces.title: He painted that wave at seventy, and at the end still thought it was not good enough: Katsushika Hokusai
pieces.short: Katsushika Hokusai
pieces.hook: Treat “not good enough yet” as a reason to keep practicing, not a reason to stop: the wave at seventy was accumulated over more than sixty years of daily brush…
pieces.takeaway: Treat “not good enough yet” as a reason to keep practicing, not a reason to stop: the wave at seventy was accumulated over more than sixty years of daily brushwork.
pieces.imageAlt: Katsushika Hokusai, “The Great Wave off Kanagawa”
pieces.imageCredit: Katsushika Hokusai · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Katsushika Hokusai was born around October 31, 1760, in the Katsushika district of Edo. By about six he loved drawing the things in front of him. At twelve he did odd jobs in a bookshop, at fourteen he learned to carve woodblocks, and at eighteen he entered the studio of Katsukawa Shunshō, a master of ukiyo-e.

In 1779 he published his first prints under the name Shunrō. After Shunshō died in 1793, he was expelled from the Katsukawa school by the senior pupil Katsukawa Shunkō. The reason may have had to do with his studying, on the side, the rival Kanō school. He later said that what really pushed his style forward was precisely the humiliation he suffered under Shunkō.

He used at least 30 art names in his life. From about 1800 he called himself Katsushika Hokusai, and over time he took on about 50 pupils. The “Hokusai Manga,” published from 1814, drew people, birds and beasts, and the movements of ordinary life. By 1820, twelve volumes were out.

paras.lead: A peak inside the low point
parts: In 1826 he fell into financial trouble. In 1827 he seems to have had a stroke, and the next year his wife died. Just after that, around the age of seventy, he brought out “Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji.” Among them, “The Great Wave off Kanagawa” used Prussian blue, which was imported in quantity only from 1829, and it was a great success as soon as it appeared.

These pictures were goods printed in bulk. The first printing of “The Great Wave” was about 1,000 sheets, and across the run an estimated 8,000 were printed. How much of the work in the studio was done by his daughter Ōi and the others is hard to sort out sheet by sheet. In 1839 the studio burned. Younger artists such as Hiroshige took the spotlight. At 83, invited by Takai Kōzan, he traveled far to Obuse in Shinshū to paint.

He died on May 10, 1849, at the age of 88, and on his deathbed he still said, “Give me five more years, and I can become a real painter.” His wave influenced Monet and van Gogh. Debussy specifically asked that it be used on the cover of the score of his symphonic sketches “La Mer.” From 2024 it has been printed on the back of Japan’s new 1,000-yen note.

blocks.title: What the “old man mad about painting” said of himself
blocks.text: In his later years he signed himself “Gakyō Rōjin Manji.” In the afterword to “One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji” he wrote that nothing he painted before seventy was worth mentioning; that only at seventy-three did he begin, a little, to understand the structure of birds, beasts, insects, and fish, and the way grasses and trees grow; and that by one hundred and ten, every dot and every stroke would have a life of its own.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Art historians and authentication researchers | View: Hokusai’s late studio was a collaborative workshop, and a signature reading “Hokusai” does not mean every stroke came from his own hand. ; Interest: getting the attribution straight, and keeping the credibility of scholarship and of authentication. ; Worry: the story of the “lonely genius” hides the labor of his daughter Ōi and of about 50 pupils. ; Basis: Ōi long served as a production assistant in her father’s studio, and a number of works signed by her also survive, divided among the Tokyo National Museum, the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, and elsewhere (the Wikipedia entry “Katsushika Ōi”).

Publishers, and the block carvers and printers | View: “The Great Wave” was first of all a successfully planned product, made by dividing the work among many people. ; Interest: sales and reprinting. The better the series sold, the more extra impressions were printed. ; Worry: if all the credit is entered under the painter’s name alone, the contributions of planning, carving the blocks, and printing get passed over. ; Basis: the publisher Nishimuraya Yohachi advertised the new “Prussian blue” heavily at the start of 1831. The series sold well, and 10 more designs were printed beyond the thirty-six. The total printing of “The Great Wave” is estimated at about 8,000.

Western collectors and museums | View: Hokusai is a key figure who entered the history of world art by way of Japonisme. ; Interest: the collection, and market value. As of 2022, 113 first-edition impressions were known to survive, 35 of them in American museums. In 2023 one sold for a record $2.8 million. ; Worry: how early or late the impression is, its condition, and whether it is genuine all bear directly on the valuation. ; Basis: the collections and comments of Bracquemond, Monet, van Gogh, Degas, and others; the cover of the score of Debussy’s “La Mer.”

Japan’s state and cultural institutions | View: Hokusai is a representative symbol of Japanese culture. ; Interest: the national image, and cultural tourism. ; Worry: the meaning of Hokusai has long been defined by a story of Western “discovery.” ; Basis: from 2024, the back of the 1,000-yen note in circulation carries “The Great Wave.” Obuse, where he painted in his later years, has a Hokusai museum.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: When researchers ask to “take the signature apart,” they run into the interests of the collecting world. If a work is reassigned from Hokusai to Ōi or to a pupil, the gallery label, the catalogue, and the valuation all have to change with it. The two sides also cannot do without each other. Research depends on what the museums hold, and the credibility of those holdings depends on research to stand behind it.

The publisher’s view and the “genius” view are arguing over how to divide the credit. The first stresses the pigment, the advertising, and the decision to print more. The second stresses the painter’s composition and eye. The two accounts use the same body of sources.

Western institutions and Japanese institutions each have an account of “who made Hokusai into Hokusai,” but both benefit from the same fame, so the conflict mostly stays at the level of the story, and joint exhibitions are still common. The 2017 Hokusai exhibition in Melbourne showed two impressions of “The Great Wave” at once, one from its own collection and one from the Japan Ukiyo-e Museum.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Which works Ōi actually took part in has no written record sheet by sheet, so the argument over attribution is hard to settle.

“The West discovered Hokusai” and “Hokusai was already selling briskly in Japan” each have evidence. “Thirty-six Views” was a great success in Japan as soon as it came out, and its reputation in the world really is tied to the fever for collecting it in Europe.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The deathbed words come from later accounts. A common version is “Give me ten more years… even five,” and the wording is not consistent.
As for why he was expelled from the school, the account we have only says it “may” have had to do with his going to study the Kanō school.
The number of surviving first-edition impressions changes as new ones are found. 113 is the count from 2022.

pieces.title: From the operating table into a phone: one hundred and eighty years of a roll of tape
pieces.short: One hundred and eighty years of a roll of tape
pieces.hook: In 1845, the American surgeon Horace Day made a pressure-sensitive adhesive: no water, no heat, and a light press was enough to make it stick…
pieces.imageAlt: A roll of Scotch duct tape
pieces.imageCredit: Evan-Amos · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

paras.lead: The start was on the operating table
parts: In 1845, the American surgeon Horace Day made a pressure-sensitive adhesive: no water, no heat, and a light press was enough to make it stick. In the early twentieth century, commercial tapes made with this kind of adhesive came onto the market one after another. The first large users were hospitals.

In the 1920s, two-tone car paint was the fashion in the United States. Spray painters masked the work with paper and strong glue, and when they pulled it off they often tore away paint that had just been sprayed. Richard Drew, an engineer at 3M, spent two years and in 1925 made a paper tape with a mild tack. The first version had adhesive only along the edges, and it fell off the car. A painter told him to go back and tell those “Scotch bosses” — Scotch meaning stingy — to put more adhesive on it. That is how the Scotch brand got its name.

paras.lead: Clear tape and the Great Depression
parts: In 1930 Drew made the world’s first roll of clear cellophane tape. In 1932 his colleague John Borden invented the snail-shaped tape dispenser. In the Great Depression people used it to mend books, curtains, and clothes. “Fix it and use it again” made the little roll sell even better.

paras.lead: Gray cloth tape in the war
parts: In 1943 Vesta Stoudt, a woman working in a munitions plant, wrote to President Roosevelt and suggested sealing ammunition boxes with cloth tape. The Revolite division of Johnson & Johnson used the idea to make an olive-drab cloth tape that was waterproof and could be torn by hand. After the war it was wrapped around the ducts of heaters and air conditioners, and the name “duct tape” caught on in the 1950s.

paras.lead: Every country has its own word for it
parts: In Britain, clear tape is called Sellotape. It was born in London in the 1930s, and it could be registered as a trademark only by changing the C in Cellophane to an S. In 1980 it entered the Oxford English Dictionary. In Germany it is called tesa. In 1906 a clerk, Elsa Tesmer, built the name from letters in her surname and her given name, and in 2001 tesa was split off from Beiersdorf as its own subsidiary.

Tape left the stationery shop long ago. tesa has about 7,000 products. Its customers include Apple, Samsung, and car plants, and many of the batteries, screens, and parts inside a phone are held in place by adhesive. In the first half of 2026, tesa’s sales were 839 million euros, an organic decline of 0.9%, with the second quarter recovering to +2.5%. The parent company warned that the supply of chips may fall short, and that the electronics business will be dragged down in the second half.

paras.lead: The other side of the giant
parts: On October 20, 3M reported its third quarter: adjusted sales of about $6.6 billion, adjusted organic growth of 3.3%, and organic growth of only 0.2% on a GAAP basis. The difference between the two comes from excluding PFAS products, commonly called “forever chemicals,” that it is taking out of production. The highlights in the press release are already optical interconnects for data centers and display materials. Tape is only one piece of its vast portfolio of materials.

blocks.title: Peeling tape can produce X-rays
blocks.text: In 1953, Soviet scientists found that peeling a roll of Scotch tape in a vacuum produces X-rays from the light of friction. In 2008, American scientists ran an experiment and confirmed that the rays were strong enough to leave an X-ray image of a finger on photographic paper.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The tape and materials giants (3M, tesa) | View: tape is a high-technology material. It can stand in for screws, and help a product get lighter and thinner. ; Interest: long-term orders from large customers in electronics and cars, and a higher value added on the product. ; Worry: swings in demand from electronics, and shortages of chips. 3M also has to absorb the cost of leaving PFAS, and the lawsuits. ; Basis: Beiersdorf’s note on tesa’s electronics business in its half-year report for 2026; the special charges for PFAS and litigation in 3M’s third-quarter press release.

Phone and car makers | View: adhesive bonding makes a product thinner and lighter, and makes the seal and the waterproofing better. ; Interest: cost, yield, and freedom in the design of the product. ; Worry: if the delivery or the quality of upstream materials goes wrong, it can pull the whole production line with it (an inference; public sources show no specific statement from the manufacturers). ; Basis: tesa supplies bonding materials to Apple, Samsung, and the auto industry (the Wikipedia entry “Tesa SE”).

Right-to-repair advocates and European Union regulators | View: batteries and other parts are glued down so firmly that users can hardly replace them themselves. ; Interest: longer product lives, and less electronic waste. ; Worry: a design that is “glued shut” makes repair harder and more expensive. ; Basis: the European Union’s Battery Regulation (EU 2023/1542) requires that, from February 2027, batteries in portable devices should in principle be removable and replaceable by the user, with a number of exemptions.

Archivists and conservators | View: tape is a hidden problem left behind when paper is mended. ; Interest: keeping documents and works of art for the long term. ; Worry: the adhesive yellows, seeps into the paper, hardens, and can even dissolve the ink. ; Basis: the Wikipedia entry “Pressure-sensitive tape”: from the late 1920s, archives used tape to mend paper, and it later became a problem for conservation.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Materials giants and device makers trade “it sticks fast” for thinness and waterproofing. The repair side, and European Union rules, demand “it comes apart.” The two sides meet in adhesives that can be stretched, peeled, and released, such as the pull-tab adhesive under a phone battery.
The rules leave exemptions for cases such as waterproofing, so “what counts as easy to take apart” has become a place where device makers and regulators pull back and forth.
Ordinary users want “stick it on and it is done.” Conservators want something reversible, which can be removed without damage. Their judgments of the same roll of tape are exactly opposed.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Bond strength and the ability to take something apart pull against each other physically. It is hard for both to be pushed to the limit at once.
The cycle of the electronics industry, and the supply of chips, are not decided by the tape plant. In its half-year report, tesa can only list them as a risk.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: 3M does not publish tape sales on their own, and tesa’s figures also include other adhesive products, such as glue sticks. There is no public figure, on one common basis, for the size of the “tape industry” as a whole.
The origin of the name Scotch is a story passed around inside the company, and it is hard to check independently.
There are different accounts of whether the name duct tape or the name duck tape came first. The Oxford English Dictionary records a use of duck tape earlier than duct tape.

pieces.title: This quarter, volume is pulling the cart: Nestlé’s third-quarter “volume” and “price”
pieces.short: Nestlé’s third-quarter “volume” and “price”
pieces.hook: When you look at growth at a consumer company, first split “volume” from “price”: growth held up by raising prices is more fragile, and growth that comes from selling more…
pieces.takeaway: When you look at growth at a consumer company, first split “volume” from “price”: growth held up by raising prices is more fragile, and growth that comes from selling more is more solid, while one quarter of good numbers still has to be watched to see whether it can keep coming.
pieces.event: October 22, 2026 (Nestlé releases results for the first nine months)
pieces.imageAlt: Nestlé’s headquarters in Vevey
pieces.imageCredit: Robert Cutts · CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 22, Nestlé reported results for the first nine months. Organic growth in the third quarter was 4.0%. Of that, real internal growth (RIG, which mainly reflects volume and product mix) was 2.8%, and price increases contributed 1.1%. The market had expected organic growth of 3.4%, of which volume was only 1.5%.

paras.lead: The facts: where the growth came from
parts: In the third quarter, organic growth was 6.8% in emerging markets and 2.2% in developed markets. India grew about 20%, and Greater China 4.2%. By category, pet food was 5.3%, snacks and food 5.0%, coffee 3.4%, and nutrition only 0.3%. A recall of infant formula dragged the group’s growth by about 0.2 percentage points.

paras.lead: The facts: the exchange rate ate the growth
parts: Sales for the first nine months were 65.865 billion Swiss francs, almost the same as 65.869 billion a year earlier. Organic growth of 3.7% was exactly offset by a currency effect of 3.7%. E-commerce was the bright spot. It grew 15.3% in the third quarter, and it already accounts for 21.6% of this year’s sales.

Navratil, who became CEO in September 2025, is shrinking the ice cream, bottled water, and vitamin businesses. This time the company announced the sale of its mainstream vitamin business to Yellow Wood Partners for $1 billion. It includes Nature's Bounty and six other brands, seven in all, with sales of $1.2 billion in 2025. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027.

In September, Russia placed Nestlé’s Russian business under “temporary external management” by presidential decree. Nestlé says it is still the owner in law, but it has lost operating control, and from the end of September it no longer consolidates the business. This business is about 2% of group sales, and 3%–4% of operating profit and free cash flow. Nestlé wrote off about 1.6 billion Swiss francs of net assets, and recognized a further non-cash foreign-exchange loss of about 1.4 billion Swiss francs.

This is the first time since 2024 that volume’s contribution to growth has exceeded price. Growth that comes from selling more is less easily broken off by consumers voting with their feet than growth that comes from raising prices, so the market reads it as a sign of recovery.

paras.lead: The inference: who benefits, and who is squeezed
parts: What benefits are the fast-growing emerging markets and categories such as pet food and snacks. Resources will tilt further toward them. What gets squeezed are the slow-growing businesses being sold or shrunk. For retailers and consumers, the pressure of higher prices has not gone away. CFO Manz said prices would be raised on the condition of “not harming medium-term consumer penetration,” and that in 2027 “we are very likely to see more price increases.”

The share price rose about 1.5% that day, a three-month high, and the gain for the year to date is more than 7%. Vontobel said the recovery “has become more credible, but consistency is the real test.” Ackerman, an analyst at Barclays, said that for 2027 “pricing is still the key debate.”
The full-year targets are unchanged: organic growth of 3%–4%, and free cash flow of more than 9 billion Swiss francs.

blocks.title: The accounts of the Russian business
blocks.text: From September it is under the temporary management of LEV Management in Moscow, and from the end of September Nestlé no longer consolidates it. The business is about 2% of group sales and 3%–4% of operating profit and free cash flow. About 1.6 billion Swiss francs of net assets were written off, and a further non-cash foreign-exchange loss of about 1.4 billion Swiss francs was recognized. Net debt at year-end is therefore worse by about 900 million Swiss francs.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Nestlé’s management | View: growth is starting to be driven by volume, and a recovery is on the way. ; Interest: delivering the full-year growth target of 3%–4%, and steadying investor confidence. ; Worry: raising prices too far would hurt consumer penetration and drive away the volume that has just come back. ; Basis: CEO Navratil: “I am pleased… but I am not satisfied.” CFO Manz’s remarks on price increases in 2027.

Investors and analysts | View: one good quarter of figures is not yet a trend. ; Interest: the share price and the valuation, already up more than 7% this year. ; Worry: whether the growth can last, and how much room is left to raise prices in 2027. ; Basis: Vontobel: “The recovery has become more credible, but consistency is the real test.” Barclays’ Ackerman: “Pricing is still the key debate.”

Retailers and consumers | View: price is where buyer and seller bargain. ; Interest: holding the price on the shelf, and the spending in the basket. ; Worry: a new round of price increases next year. ; Basis: the CFO’s remark that 2027 will “very likely” bring more price increases; price increases this quarter contributed only 1.1%, below the 1.9% the market expected. This side has made no direct public statement, so the basis is weaker.

The Russian government | View: by presidential decree, it places foreign-owned firms under “temporary external management.” ; Interest: keeping the business running locally, and keeping operating control inside the country. ; Worry: the public record does not show a specific demand from it. ; Basis: the presidential decree in September handed Nestlé’s Russian business to LEV Management in Moscow (the Wikipedia entry “Nestlé”); Nestlé’s press release says it is still the legal owner.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Management and investors: investors want “consistency.” Management points to the businesses being sold, e-commerce growth of 15.3%, and the unchanged full-year targets, to show this is not a one-off piece of luck.
Management, and retailers and consumers: raising prices can repair profit, but it can also drive volume away. The CFO’s phrase “without harming penetration” draws a line between the two.

Nestlé and Russia: Nestlé has lost control but kept legal ownership, and net debt at year-end is therefore worse by about 900 million Swiss francs. What the two sides can still exchange depends on how this asset is dealt with afterward.

Yellow Wood, the buyer of the vitamin business, takes a portfolio of brands with annual sales of $1.2 billion for $1 billion. What Nestlé gets in exchange is a more focused business, and less management attention spent on it.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The choice between volume and price: profit calls for higher prices, volume calls for restraint, and there is no answer yet for how to balance them in 2027.
There is no timetable for who will finally own the Russian assets. On its books, Nestlé has already moved them out.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: RIG includes changes in the product mix. It is not exactly the number of units sold.
“Market expectations” are a consensus figure compiled across institutions, and different sources may not count them the same way.
There is little direct public data on how retailers and consumers responded.

pieces.title: Parliament has passed it; the president’s gate has not: two votes on reforming Poland’s abortion law
pieces.short: Two votes on reforming Poland’s abortion law
pieces.hook: On October 20, the Polish Sejm passed two bills easing the limits on abortion.
pieces.event: October 20–22, 2026 (the Sejm vote on the 20th, nationwide protests on the 22nd)
pieces.imageAlt: The All-Poland Women’s Strike protest in Warsaw, 2020
pieces.imageCredit: RoodyAlien · CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 20, the Polish Sejm passed two bills easing the limits on abortion. The first passed by 217 in favor, 213 against, and 3 abstentions. It removes criminal liability for “assisting an abortion” (at present punishable by up to 3 years) and also protects doctors. The second passed 233 to 203. It restores the right to end a pregnancy lawfully in cases of “severe fetal anomaly,” sets a time limit for hospitals to act, and requires a refusal to be explained in writing.

On October 22, 2020, the Constitutional Tribunal ruled that the “fetal anomaly” clause was unconstitutional. The ruling took effect in January 2021, and Poland became the strictest country in Europe after Malta. The protests that year were the largest since the end of communism. In 2019, before the ruling, 1,074 of the country’s 1,110 legal abortions were for fetal anomaly.

The first bill was put forward by the Civic Coalition (KO) and the Left. The second was put forward by the more conservative Poland 2050 and the Polish People’s Party (PSL). KO, the Left, and Razem all voted in favor, and Poland 2050 almost all voted in favor. Fourteen members of the PSL voted against the first bill, including the party leader and deputy prime minister, Kosiniak-Kamysz.
Twenty-seven members were absent in all, 10 of them from Law and Justice (PiS), including the party leader, Kaczyński. In July 2024 a similar decriminalization bill had failed, 215 to 218.

The Senate can amend a bill, but it cannot reject one. The key is President Nawrocki. He can sign, veto, or send the bills to the Constitutional Tribunal. Overriding a veto takes a three-fifths majority, and the governing coalition does not have that many votes.

The Constitutional Tribunal is itself in dispute. The government does not recognize some of its rulings, and the president and the chief justice refuse to seat 5 new judges chosen by parliament. If the bills are sent for review, they will get tangled up in this fight over legitimacy.

Bogucki, head of the presidential office, said the president “supports protecting life from conception to natural death,” and charged that Tusk wants to cover his own incompetence by raising “ideological issues” again. Kotula, the government’s plenipotentiary for equality and a Left member of parliament, said “the state trusts women.” The abortion-rights group Legalna Aborcja said that for women who need an abortion now, this “changes nothing.” The Abortion Dream Team called it “a symbolic gesture.”

October 22 was the sixth anniversary of the ruling. Twenty-six cities in Poland, and London, held protests to “show the abortion ban a red card.” Polls show that a majority of Poles support easing the law. The next parliamentary election is at the end of 2027.

First is the binary of “protecting life” against “women’s rights.” Inside that frame, the specific content of the bills is easy to pass over. Polish law already does not punish the woman who has the abortion. This decriminalization is aimed at the people who assist and at doctors, and it does not open abortion on demand. Second, “an ideological distraction” and “a symbolic gesture” are both in circulation. They come from the president’s camp and from abortion-rights groups, and they point in opposite directions.
Third is “a majority of public opinion.” Support for easing the law is a majority, but how far that easing should go, and the wording and the figures of the various polls, do not line up.
