blocks.title: Three cards in the president’s hand
blocks.text: Sign, and the bills take effect. Veto, and they go back to the Sejm, where a three-fifths majority is needed to override. Send them to the Constitutional Tribunal, and the result of the review is pulled into the dispute over that court’s own legitimacy.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The Tusk government, with KO and the Left | View: restoring some of the rules from before 2020, and decriminalizing, is how campaign promises get kept. ; Interest: holding supporters, and building a record for the election at the end of 2027. ; Worry: a presidential veto leaves the reform on paper. ; Basis: the vote counts on the two bills; Kotula, the plenipotentiary for equality, saying “the state trusts women”; Education Minister Nowacka saying she would vote in favor of “every change, however small.”

The Polish People’s Party (PSL), a partner in the coalition | View: many in the party oppose decriminalization, and fewer oppose restoring the fetal-anomaly clause. ; Interest: keeping its more conservative rural voters. ; Worry: being seen inside the coalition as a drag, or losing ground with its own voters (an inference, drawn from how the votes fell). ; Basis: 14 votes against the first bill, including party leader Kosiniak-Kamysz; 5 votes against the second.

President Nawrocki and PiS | View: “protect life from conception to natural death,” and a claim that the government is using ideological issues to change the subject. ; Interest: consolidating conservative voters. ; Worry: standing opposite a majority that the polls say supports easing the law (an inference). ; Basis: Bogucki’s remarks; 10 members of PiS were absent from the vote.

Abortion-rights groups (Legalna Aborcja, the Abortion Dream Team) | View: the two bills are “a symbolic gesture,” and for people who need an abortion now they “change nothing.” ; Interest: actually opening early abortion. ; Worry: politicians trading a small change for a reputation of having “already done something.” ; Basis: public statements from both groups; the protests on October 22 in 26 cities plus London.

The Constitutional Tribunal | View: if the president sends the bills for review, it may become the final decider. ; Interest: keeping its own authority. ; Worry: the public record shows no statement from it on these two bills. ; Basis: the government does not recognize some of its rulings; the president and the chief justice refuse to seat 5 new judges.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The government pushes the bills. The president holds the veto. Overriding a veto takes a three-fifths majority, which the coalition does not have. If the bills are sent for review instead, they fall into the dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal’s legitimacy. Each side has a way to block the others, and no side can finish the matter alone.

The PSL is the swing vote inside the coalition. The first bill passed by a margin of only 4 votes, with 14 from the PSL against it. The second bill the same day had fewer opponents in the PSL, and the margin widened to 30 votes.
Abortion-rights groups ask the government for “more,” but the government is held back by the PSL and can put forward, for now, only a version the coalition itself can pass.

The president’s camp calls the bills “a distraction.” Abortion-rights groups say they are “too little.” The two criticisms point in opposite directions, and both of them weaken the claim that “the reform succeeded.”

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The veto, plus the three-fifths threshold: before the election at the end of 2027, the current spread of seats is unlikely to change that arithmetic.
There is no shared view of the Constitutional Tribunal’s legitimacy, so the judicial path is blocked as well.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The president has not yet said formally whether he will sign. The position in the reporting comes from remarks by the head of his office.
“A majority supports easing the law” is a poll conclusion passed along by the reporting. The specific share varies widely with how the question is asked.
The number of clandestine abortions, and of abortions abroad, is only an estimate. The estimates reported by the BBC run from 10,000 to 150,000 cases a year, a very wide gap.

2026-10-24.fallbackLine: The bright moon shines through the pines, and a clear spring runs over the stones.
2026-10-24.fallbackBy: Wang Wei, “Autumn Dusk at a Mountain Dwelling”

pieces.title: The brothers who repaired bicycles figured out “control” first: the Wright brothers
pieces.short: The Wright brothers
pieces.hook: Find the hardest problem first, then test it again and again by the cheapest means you have: the brothers had no more money than anyone else, but they were earlier than anyone else…
pieces.takeaway: Find the hardest problem first, then test it again and again by the cheapest means you have: the brothers had no more money than anyone else, but they were earlier than anyone else in treating “control” as the core.
pieces.imageAlt: The Wright brothers’ first flight, 1903
pieces.imageCredit: John T. Daniels · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: The older brother, Wilbur, was born in Indiana in 1867. The younger, Orville, was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1871. In 1878 their father, a minister, brought home a toy helicopter. The brothers later said that was where their fascination with flight began.

In 1889 they opened a print shop and put out a weekly paper. In December 1892 they opened a bicycle shop, and from 1896 they sold bicycles under their own brand. The income from the shop later became the entire fund for building the airplane.

When the German gliding pioneer Lilienthal was killed in a crash in 1896, the brothers decided that the hardest part was “control”: once you were in the air, how to stay balanced, and how to turn. In the shop, Wilbur idly twisted a long cardboard box for inner tubes, and thought of twisting the two ends of a wing in opposite directions, to control the bank.

In 1901 they found that earlier figures for lift were inaccurate, so they built a wind tunnel and measured again themselves. At 10:35 on the morning of December 17, 1903, Orville flew the Flyer for 12 seconds, about 37 meters.
The last flight of the day was Wilbur’s: 59 seconds, about 260 meters. The engine was built in six weeks by Charlie Taylor, a mechanic at the bicycle shop.

For several years after that, the outside world did not believe them. French newspapers called them “bluffers.” On August 8, 1908, Wilbur gave a public demonstration at a racecourse near Le Mans, and the doubts fell away. In September of the same year, during a demonstration for the Army at Fort Myer, a crash killed Lieutenant Selfridge, who was in the airplane with him. He became the first person to die in an airplane accident.

Their control system received a U.S. patent in 1906. After that they spent years in court with Curtiss and other rivals, and won at the first trial in February 1913. In the First World War the United States could not field a satisfactory airplane of its own. The government pushed for a manufacturers’ aircraft association, with licensing pooled in one place.

Another quarrel was with the Smithsonian Institution. For a long time the Institution gave “the first machine capable of carrying a person in flight” to its former secretary, Langley. In anger, Orville lent the Flyer to the Science Museum in London.

In 1942 the Smithsonian corrected the record in public. The Flyer returned to Washington for display in 1948, the year Orville died. Wilbur had died of typhoid back in 1912, only 45. They put control of pitch, yaw, and roll together, and that idea is still the foundation of the fixed-wing airplane.

blocks.title: The first air-cargo job
blocks.text: On November 7, 1910, an airplane of the Wright Company carried two bolts of silk from Dayton to Columbus, 105 kilometers away. The customer was a department store, and the freight charge was $5,000. The silk was later cut into small pieces and sold as souvenirs.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The Wright brothers and the Wright Company | View: they were the first to solve controlled, powered flight, and what the patent protects is exactly that core. ; Interest: license fees and the company’s business. In 1909 the brothers sold the patent to the Wright Company for $100,000. ; Worry: being copied, and having the credit shared away. ; Basis: the U.S. patent granted in 1906; in February 1913 a judge ruled that ailerons also fell within the patent.

Curtiss and other competitors | View: controlling bank with ailerons is not the same thing as warping the wing, and should not be bound by the Wright patent. ; Interest: building airplanes of their own, and selling them. ; Worry: license fees and lawsuits holding new makers down. ; Basis: in 1908 Curtiss took part, inside the association chaired by Bell, in reinventing the wingtip aileron; the Wright brothers promptly warned him that he was infringing.

The Smithsonian Institution | View: the “Aerodrome” of its former secretary, Langley, was in principle the first machine capable of carrying a person in flight. ; Interest: protecting the reputation of the former secretary and of the Institution. ; Worry: having the historical account rewritten. ; Basis: the Institution relied on a brief 1914 test flight of the “Aerodrome” by Curtiss’s team, and did not disclose that extensive modifications had been made before that flight. Only in 1942 did it publish the list of modifications and correct the record.

European aviation circles | View: until they saw it with their own eyes, they stayed doubtful of what the brothers claimed. ; Interest: the honor of their own country’s aviation, and the standing to speak of it. ; Worry: giving “first” to a rival who would not fly in public. ; Basis: a 1906 editorial in the Paris edition of the New York Herald: “The Wright brothers either flew, or they did not.” Some people also hold that Santos-Dumont and others made the real first flight.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The patent was the Wright brothers’ bargaining chip. Competitors wore it down by changing the design and by lawsuits that ran for years. The First World War needed airplanes in quantity, the government stepped in to push cross-licensing, and every side gave some ground.

Between Orville and the Smithsonian, the chip on the table was the Flyer itself. The Institution wanted its version of the history. Orville sent the airplane to London. In the end the Institution corrected its account, and only then did the airplane come home.

To protect the patent, the brothers were unwilling to demonstrate in public, and the outside world doubted them all the more. The deeper the doubt, the greater the shock when they did fly in public in 1908.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: What standard “the first flight” should meet: whether it must take off on its own, be controlled, be sustained, and have witnesses in public. Different standards point to different people.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: On the day in 1903 there were only five witnesses and one photograph. The detailed record comes mainly from the brothers themselves.
How much the patent war actually slowed American aviation is hard to separate from other factors, such as money and what the military asked for.

pieces.title: From a can opener to one pull of the hand: ninety years of the easy-open can
pieces.short: Ninety years of the easy-open can
pieces.hook: In 1935, Richmond, Virginia, began selling canned beer. It was the first canned beer to be sold commercially.
pieces.imageAlt: A detachable pull-tab and a stay-on tab
pieces.imageCredit: Mitsuzuka · CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

paras.lead: The start: a can of beer
parts: In 1935, Richmond, Virginia, began selling canned beer. It was the first canned beer to be sold commercially. The same year, the Felinfoel Brewery in Wales became the first brewery outside the United States to sell canned beer. The cans then were tin-plated steel, and before you drank you had to punch a hole in the top with a tool commonly called a “church key.”

paras.lead: A change of material: from steel to aluminum
parts: In 1959 the Coors company brought out a recyclable aluminum can of 7 ounces. In 1964, R.C. Cola and Diet-Rite, from the Royal Crown Cola company, became the first soft drinks put into all-aluminum cans. Today about 75% of beverage cans worldwide are aluminum and 25% are steel, and the inner wall is coated with a layer of epoxy or polymer so the drink never touches the metal.

paras.lead: The revolution in the opening: the pull-tab
parts: In 1959, Ermal Fraze of Dayton, Ohio, thought of a way to open a can with no opener. The story goes that at a picnic he forgot the opener and had to pry the beer open on a car’s bumper. He received the patent in 1963 and licensed it to Alcoa and to the Pittsburgh Brewing Company. The latter’s Iron City beer was the first to use it.

paras.lead: A new trouble: tabs all over the ground
parts: Early pull-tabs tore off in one piece, were dropped on the ground, and cut hands and feet. In 1976 the Journal of the American Medical Association also recorded children swallowing tabs that had fallen into the can. Some people switched to a “push-button” opening, but a pressing finger met a sharp cut edge, and it never caught on.

paras.lead: The form that stuck: the tab that does not come off
parts: In 1975 the “stay-on tab,” designed by Daniel Cudzik, an engineer at Reynolds Metals, was first used on Falls City beer. The tab presses the opening in and then stays on the top of the can. That is the form most common today. The size most common in China is 330 milliliters.

ever more are made, and recycling is stuck] Around the world, about 370 billion beverage cans are produced each year, and the leading makers are still growing: Ball Corporation’s global shipments of aluminum packaging rose 4.3% year over year in the second quarter of 2026. But the U.S. recycling rate is slipping. In 2023 it was only 43%, below the average of about 52% since the figures began in 1990. That year more than 46 billion were recycled, and more than 61 billion were thrown away.

blocks.title: How much difference a deposit can make
blocks.text: On 2021 figures, the Container Recycling Institute estimates that in the United States the recycling rate for aluminum cans is about 74% where there is a deposit, and only about 26% where there is not. The industry association has set itself a target of a nationwide recycling rate of 70% by 2030.

items: Aluminum cans
Glass bottles
PET plastic bottles

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Can makers (Ball, Crown, and others) | View: aluminum can be melted down again and again, and the aluminum can is the most sustainable drinks package. ; Interest: growing shipments, and passing the cost of the aluminum price on to customers. ; Worry: a falling recycling rate weakens the environmental selling point, and the supply of recycled material gets tight. ; Basis: an industry report puts the closed-loop recycling rate for aluminum cans at 96.7%. Ball’s North American sales grew in the second quarter, mainly from passing on a higher aluminum price (Ball’s quarterly report).

Beverage brands | View: packaging has to be cheap, easy to ship, and easy to drink from. ; Interest: costs kept in hand, and a good look on the shelf. ; Worry: a rising aluminum price, and new charges for deposits and for producer responsibility. ; Basis: Ball’s quarterly report: the change in North American price and mix came mainly from the aluminum price, and was passed on to customers under contract.

The recycling trade and sorting centers | View: the aluminum can is the most valuable thing in the recycling bin, yet large numbers are lost during sorting. ; Interest: revenue from recycling. ; Worry: aging sorting equipment, and mis-sorting. ; Basis: about $1,338 a tonne for aluminum cans, about $215 for plastic bottles, and a negative $23 for glass. From 25%–33% of aluminum cans are mis-sorted at sorting centers (a report by the Container Recycling Institute).

Environmental groups and supporters of deposit systems | View: to actually pull the recycling rate up, a deposit system is the most direct way. ; Interest: less litter, and less mining of primary aluminum. ; Worry: the industry’s target stays on paper. ; Basis: about 74% with a deposit, about 26% without (a 2021 estimate). Nationwide in 2023 it was only 43%.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Can makers need a high recycling rate to hold up the environmental selling point and the supply of recycled material, but the cost of deposits and of producer responsibility lands in the end on beverage brands and consumers. How the brands feel about it decides how fast a new rule moves.
The recycling trade wants more aluminum cans in the system, but upgrading the sorting equipment needs someone to pay, and local budgets and companies push the bill onto each other.
Supporters of deposit systems and the can-making industry share the aim of “raising the recycling rate,” and they differ on “who pays, and who runs it.”

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Most American states have no deposit system. Recycling depends mainly on people choosing to drop cans off, and on curbside collection. From 2014–2023 the national recycling rate fell from 56.7% to 43%.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Recycling rates are not counted on one basis. The industry association’s figure for 2021 is 41.6%. After the Container Recycling Institute adjusted the basis, it was 37.2%.
“370 billion” is a global estimate. Markets such as China lack public recycling statistics on the same basis.

pieces.title: Broadband is losing people, and Peacock is making money: the give and take of Comcast’s third quarter
pieces.short: Comcast’s third quarter, the give…
pieces.hook: When you look at a company whose old business is shrinking and whose new business is growing, do not look only at total revenue: first strip out disposals and one-off events, then read the…
pieces.takeaway: When you look at a company whose old business is shrinking and whose new business is growing, do not look only at total revenue: first strip out disposals and one-off events, then read the trend one piece at a time.
pieces.imageAlt: Comcast Center in Philadelphia
pieces.imageCredit: ajay_suresh · CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 22, Comcast, the American cable-television and media group, reported third-quarter results: revenue of $29.3 billion, down 6.1% year over year; adjusted earnings per share of $1.07, down 4.0%. Both were a little better than analysts had expected, and the share price closed up about 3% that day.

The fall in revenue came mainly because, on January 2, it spun off the cable-channel company Versant, and at the end of May it sold the Sky business in Germany. With those two taken out, revenue and adjusted EBITDA were flat with last year.

Peacock] The streaming service Peacock had revenue of $1.8 billion (against $1.4 billion last year). Adjusted EBITDA was a profit of $261 million, against a loss of $217 million in the same quarter last year. This is its second profitable quarter in a row. Paid subscribers were 48 million, 17% more than last year. The price increase in August and the World Cup broadcasts both played a part.

paras.lead: The piece that hurts most: broadband
parts: Domestic broadband households had a net loss of 144,000, and cable-television subscribers fell by 274,000. The company is using the mobile business to hold on to customers: wireless lines gained a net 368,000, for a total of 10.6 million. Nearly 45% of broadband customers are on a plan of a gigabit or faster.

paras.lead: Parks and films: one cold, one hot
parts: Theme-park revenue was about $2.6 billion, down 4.4%, and adjusted EBITDA fell 17.1%, because ticket revenue was down and promotions were up. On the film side, “The Odyssey” became the highest-grossing film in the history of Universal Pictures, with a worldwide total this year of nearly $1.8 billion. Studio EBITDA grew 18.6%, to $402 million.

paras.lead: Which parts are fact, and which are inference
parts: The figures above come from the company’s earnings report and from CNBC. “Whether Peacock can keep making money” and “when the loss of broadband customers will stop” are inferences in the market: a tournament on the scale of the World Cup does not come every quarter. Next, the company plans to split NBCUniversal and Sky off as an independent company, expected to be finished by the middle of 2027. It still needs approval, and financing.

blocks.title: The World Cup’s quarter
blocks.text: The World Cup brought the media business $224 million in added revenue. With that taken out, media revenue still grew 8.3%. Domestic advertising revenue, once it was taken out, was roughly flat: growth at Peacock offset the decline at the traditional television networks.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Comcast’s management | View: the short-term results reflect a deliberate investment in broadband and mobile, and customer satisfaction is improving. A split would make the two companies more flexible. ; Interest: steadying shareholders, and completing the split smoothly. ; Worry: broadband keeps being lost, and the parks recover slowly. ; Basis: what management says in the press release; the split is “still on plan.”

Investors and analysts | View: what matters is the quality of the profit, not only whether the numbers beat expectations. ; Interest: the share price, and the return to shareholders. ; Worry: revenue brought by the World Cup will not last, and the slide in broadband drags on the valuation. ; Basis: revenue and earnings per share were slightly ahead of expectations, and the share price closed up about 3% (CNBC). With the World Cup’s $224 million taken out, media revenue grew 8.3%.

Broadband and mobile customers | View: they want both speed and price, and they have more and more choices. ; Interest: a lower price, and a faster connection. ; Worry: plans grow more complicated, and once they are bundled it is hard to compare prices. ; Basis: the earnings report: domestic broadband revenue fell because the average charge was lower and there were fewer customers. The company stepped up promotions, and the conversion of free mobile lines into paid ones.

Park visitors and competitors | View: the same holiday budget gets compared across several parks. ; Interest: a good time, at a fair price. ; Worry: a new park whose experience is uneven, and expensive tickets. ; Basis: the earnings report: park ticket revenue was down, and promotions were up. CNBC reported that the company mentioned technical problems at Epic Universe and competitors’ marketing pushes, and that it expects growth to return in the second half of 2027.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Management uses cheap, even free, mobile lines to hold on to broadband customers, which presses profit down in the short run. Investors have to supply patience somewhere between “keeping the customer” and “the profit.”
Peacock reached a profit by raising prices and by a major tournament. Raise the price again, and it meets what subscribers will bear. The two sides test each other on price.
A split lets investors value the cable business and the entertainment business separately. The cost is that the cable business loses the pull of the entertainment.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The loss of broadband customers has not stopped. Peacock had the World Cup behind it this quarter. Next quarter it will not.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Peacock’s profit includes revenue tied to the World Cup. How much it would have earned on its own with that taken out, the company has not published.
How much of the parks’ decline comes from competition, and how much from problems at the new park itself, is not broken out.
What the businesses would be worth after the split is only what the market expects.

pieces.title: The Lords have nodded, and the government has not: the “three locks” on the Chagos Islands
pieces.short: The “three locks” on the Chagos Islands
pieces.hook: On October 23, the House of Lords gave a second reading to the British Sovereignty Protection (Cha…
pieces.event: October 23, 2026 (second reading in the British House of Lords)
pieces.imageAlt: An aerial view of Diego Garcia
pieces.imageCredit: U.S. Navy · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 23, the House of Lords gave a second reading to the British Sovereignty Protection (Chagos Islands) Bill, introduced by Lord Weir of the Democratic Unionist Party, and it was not put to a division. The bill sets “three locks” on handing over sovereignty: specific legislation by Parliament, the agreement of a representative government of the Chagossians, and approval in a referendum of the Chagossians.
It would also allow Chagossians to go and work on Diego Garcia.

Very unlikely. Private members’ bills in the House of Lords rarely become law. Next comes committee stage, and without the government’s support it is hard to get far. In the debate the government was clear that it opposes a referendum. Baroness Winterton, for the Foreign Office, said the treaty is a matter of national security, and that “doing nothing is not an option.”

paras.lead: Background: one archipelago and one base
parts: The Chagos Islands came under Britain in 1814. In November 1965, before Mauritius became independent, Britain detached the islands for £3 million. Between 1967 and 1973, about 1,500 to 1,750 islanders were removed, to make way for the American and British military base on Diego Garcia.

The treaty signed in May 2025 gives sovereignty to Mauritius, Diego Garcia included. Britain would go on using the base for 99 years. The government’s figure for the average cost is about £101 million a year, a net present value of £3.4 billion. The bill to put it into effect lapsed when the parliamentary session ended on April 29. The treaty has still not come into force.

In January this year Trump called it “an act of great stupidity,” and later asked Britain to reconsider this “bad deal.” The Burnham government has agreed to a review. On October 2, the prime minister of Mauritius, Ramgoolam, told Powell, the British national security adviser, in London that sovereignty is “not negotiable,” and that if the matter drags on they will go to law.

Opponents often say “giving the territory away, and paying on top of it.” Supporters often say “if we do not sign, we will lose the base in an international court.” Both simplify. The money depends on the method of counting: a net present value of £3.4 billion, and a cash total of about £34.7 billion. The International Court of Justice’s opinion in 2019 is advisory. It is not binding. But the General Assembly supported it by a wide margin.

blocks.title: The “three locks” in the bill
blocks.note: This is a bill introduced by an individual member of the House of Lords, not a government bill.
rows: Ceding or leasing sovereignty requires specific legislation by Parliament
It must be approved by a representative government of the Chagossians, or of the British Indian Ocean Territory
It must be approved by a referendum of the Chagossians. Citizens of the territory aged 18 and over may vote

items: The islands are detached from Mauritius
The islanders are removed
Mauritius becomes independent
Chagossians receive British citizenship
Advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice; the General Assembly passes a resolution, 116 votes to 6
Britain and Mauritius sign the treaty on May 22
The implementing bill lapses in April; second reading in the House of Lords on October 23

blocks.title: How the Chagossians themselves see it
blocks.text: The Chagossians do not agree among themselves. Chagossian refugee groups in Mauritius support the treaty. Some Chagossians in Britain want to decide the future of the islands themselves. In February 2026, four Chagossians landed without permission on Coin Island in the Peros Banhos atoll, hoping to settle there. By 2025 the Chagossian community in Crawley, West Sussex, numbered about 3,500.

blocks.title: Three ways of counting the cost of the treaty
items: Government: net present value
Government Actuary’s Department: cash total
TaxPayers’ Alliance estimate

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The British Labour government | View: the treaty is the surest way to keep the base on Diego Garcia, and “doing nothing is not an option.” ; Interest: the long-term legal security of the base, and relations with the United States and with Mauritius. ; Worry: legal uncertainty, and American opposition. ; Basis: Winterton’s speech in the House of Lords; the defence secretary, Streeting, has said that Britain will not, “at this stage,” pay the sums agreed.

The Conservatives, the Democratic Unionist Party, and other opponents | View: the opinion of the International Court of Justice is not binding. Sovereignty should not be handed over, and still less should money be paid. ; Interest: sovereignty, and the public finances. ; Worry: the cost has been understated, and the security of the base is affected. ; Basis: Lord Weir’s bill; in the debate, members cited the TaxPayers’ Alliance estimate of about £47 billion.

The government of Mauritius | View: sovereignty is “not negotiable.” ; Interest: a complete territory, and the income from rent. ; Worry: Britain delaying ratification indefinitely. ; Basis: what Ramgoolam said after meeting Powell on October 2: if it cannot be settled soon, going to law will be unavoidable (the Mauricien).

The United States | View: it takes a negative view of this agreement. ; Interest: the use of the base on Diego Garcia. ; Worry: the public remarks focus on the agreement itself, and the specific concerns are not set out in an official document. ; Basis: on January 20 Trump called it “an act of great stupidity,” and later called it “a bad deal.”

The Chagossians | View: opinion is divided. Some want to decide the islands’ future themselves. Some support the arrangements for return that the treaty would bring. ; Interest: the right to go home, status, and compensation. ; Worry: being bypassed in the talks between Britain and Mauritius. ; Basis: in December 2025 the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination called for ratification of the treaty to be paused; in February 2026 four people landed on an island; on the day of the second reading, Chagossians celebrated in Westminster Hall.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The British government needs the United States and Mauritius to agree at the same time. If the United States opposes it, the treaty cannot be pushed through. If it is not pushed through, Mauritius threatens to go to court.

The opposition uses the “three locks” to make the Chagossians’ consent a precondition. That gives the Chagossians a bargaining chip. But the Chagossians do not agree among themselves, and the result of a referendum is hard to predict.

Mauritius holds the opinion of the International Court of Justice and the General Assembly resolution. Britain holds actual control of the base, and the power to ratify the treaty. Neither side has a means of forcing the other to give way.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The implementing bill has already lapsed. The government is reviewing the matter. The American position has not changed. And a private member’s bill will have a hard time going far.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The cost figures depend on assumptions about discounting and inflation. The several methods differ by more than tenfold.
There is no reliable count of what share of Chagossians are for the treaty and what share are against it.
The content of the government’s review, and its timetable, have not been published.

pieces.title: Counting peas in the monastery garden: Mendel
pieces.short: Mendel
pieces.hook: When a question will not come clear, turn it into something you can count: Mendel had no better microscope. What he had was the patience to count…
pieces.takeaway: When a question will not come clear, turn it into something you can count: Mendel had no better microscope. What he had was the patience to count tens of thousands of pea plants, and then to tell the story in ratios.

parts: Gregor Mendel was born on July 20, 1822, to a farming family in Silesia, in the Austrian Empire (now part of the Czech Republic). The family could not afford the school fees. His sister Theresia put up her dowry so he could finish the philosophy course at Olomouc.

paras.lead: A monk, so that he could study
parts: In 1843 he entered the Augustinian Abbey of St. Thomas in Brno. He later said he did it to escape “the perpetual anxiety over making a living.” He failed the teaching qualification twice, in 1850 and 1856. In between he was sent to the University of Vienna for two years. One of his physics teachers was Doppler, who proposed the Doppler effect.

From 1856 to 1863, in the abbey’s experimental garden of about 2 hectares, he grew about 28,000 plants, most of them peas, and watched seven traits: the shape and color of the seed, the height of the plant, and others. He found that when a pure-breeding yellow pea was crossed with a green one, the first generation was all yellow. In the second generation the green came back, in a ratio of about 1 to 3.
For seed color, the second generation had 6,022 yellow seeds and 2,001 green ones.

In February and March 1865 he gave two talks to the Natural Science Society of Brno. About 40 people were there. The paper was published in 1866, and almost no one paid it any mind. He corresponded with Nägeli, the leading botanist of the time, and Nägeli did not see the weight of it either.
He turned to experiments with hawkweed. The results were not like the peas. Only later was it understood that hawkweed mostly sets seed without being fertilized. That left him puzzled too.

In 1868 he was elected abbot. Busy with administration, and with a dispute with the government over the abbey’s taxes, he largely stopped the research. He was also a founder of the Austrian Meteorological Society, and he kept bees. On January 6, 1884, he died of chronic nephritis. The composer Janáček played the organ at the funeral. The abbot who succeeded him later burned his papers.

blocks.title: “My time will come”
blocks.text: He is said to have told a friend this. In 1900, de Vries, Correns, and Tschermak each rediscovered his work on their own. In Britain, Bateson spread his theory and coined the word “genetics.” The genes corresponding to the seven pea traits were not all identified until 2025.

items: Yellow
Green

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Mendel himself | View: traits are decided by “factors” in pairs, which separate in fixed ratios and can be described with mathematics. ; Interest: finishing the experiments, and getting the scholarly world to accept them. ; Worry: the hawkweed results did not match the peas, and he himself had doubts. ; Basis: the 1866 paper “Experiments on Plant Hybridization”; he is said to have told a friend, “My time will come.”

The scholars of his own time (the Brno audience, Nägeli) | View: they took the paper as a report on hybridization, and did not see a general law. ; Interest: the lines of research that were mainstream then, and the theories already in place. ; Worry: a conclusion drawn by a monk from one plant might not generalize. ; Basis: about 40 people heard the talks and did not respond; in the correspondence, Nägeli did not accept the discovery.

The rediscoverers of 1900 | View: their own experiments produced the same laws, and Mendel had written them down long before. ; Interest: priority in the discovery, and scholarly reputation. ; Worry: how the credit for who was first would be divided. ; Basis: de Vries, Correns, and Tschermak each published in 1900; Bateson then spread the work and named it “genetics.”

Fisher and the skeptics | View: the data sit too close to the theoretical value of 3 : 1, “too good to be true.” ; Interest: rigor in statistical evidence. ; Worry: the experimental record was “tidied,” on purpose or not. ; Basis: Fisher’s reanalysis in 1936; Edwards’s comparison: if a gambler wins every day, you have reason to suspect.

Defenders such as Hartl and Fairbanks | View: Fisher misread the design of the experiments, and the charge of fraud lacks strong evidence. ; Interest: recovering what Mendel actually did. ; Worry: judging a 19th-century record by today’s standards. ; Basis: their analysis holds that the fraud charge “can be laid to rest”; in 2008 the two, with other scholars, coauthored “Ending the Mendel–Fisher Controversy.”

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The skeptics’ chip is statistical probability. The defenders’ chip is a reconstruction of the experimental detail. The original records were burned, so neither side has the decisive firsthand material.
The rediscoverers needed Mendel’s paper to establish that the laws were general, and in doing so they gave the priority to a monk who was already dead.
After Mendel became abbot, the tax dispute with the government took the time he would have used to keep answering the scholarly world.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The original experimental notes no longer exist. “Why the data are so tidy” can only be approached by conjecture and by analyzing them again.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “My time will come” is a retelling. There is no record in Mendel’s own hand.
His motive for entering the monastery rests mainly on what he said himself, and an outsider can hardly check it.

pieces.title: From a glass plate to an instant print: nearly two hundred years of a roll of film
pieces.short: Nearly two hundred years of a roll of film
pieces.hook: In 1839 the daguerreotype process was published, and photography entered the public view.

parts: In 1839 the daguerreotype process was published, and photography entered the public view. But the early light-sensitive materials were metal plates, and later glass plates, heavy and easy to break. Taking one photograph was like running a chemistry experiment.

The American George Eastman made paper-based roll film in 1885, and in 1889 switched to a transparent base of cellulose nitrate. Nitrate stock catches fire. In 1908 Kodak brought out a safer acetate base. The 35-millimeter nitrate film used in cinemas was not discontinued until 1951.

The first Kodak camera, in 1888, sold for $25, and it left the factory already loaded with film for 100 pictures. When the roll was finished you mailed the whole camera back to Rochester, paid $10, and received the prints, the negatives, and a new roll of film. The line “You press the button, we do the rest” was soon known in every household.

In 1935 Kodak brought out Kodachrome color film for motion pictures, and in 1936 a version for 35-millimeter still cameras. The same year, Agfa in Germany brought out Agfacolor Neu, a color film with the color couplers inside the emulsion. By the 1970s, color film had taken over the mass market.

Kodak’s annual revenue reached a peak of about $16 billion in 1996. In 1997 it entered a price war with Fuji, and its share of the U.S. market fell in one year from 80.1% to 74.7%. In 1975, Kodak engineer Sasson built the first prototype of a handheld digital camera, using a sensor of 10,000 pixels.
From 2001, film sales began to slide. Kodachrome was discontinued in 2009. On January 19, 2012, Kodak filed for bankruptcy protection, and it emerged in September 2013 after a reorganization.

paras.lead: Now: instant film is hotter than roll film
parts: Fuji launched the Instax Mini instant camera in 1998. By April 2025 it had sold a cumulative 100 million cameras and printers. From April to June 2026, revenue in Fuji’s imaging division grew 16.2%, mainly on Instax. Traditional film is warming again too: in 2022 Kodak hired more than 300 people for the film lines and switched them to running around the clock.

blocks.text: As early as 2006, Fuji said film was only 3% of the company’s sales. From 2022, some of Fuji’s color negative film was made under contract by its old rival, Kodak.

blocks.title: Kodak’s share of the U.S. film market

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Kodak (Eastman Kodak) | View: there is a real revival in demand for film, and it is worth investing again. ; Interest: revenue from the film business, and a revival of the brand. ; Worry: limited capacity, and rising costs such as the price of silver. ; Basis: in 2022 it hired more than 300 people and ran production 24 hours a day; from September 2025 it distributes consumer film itself in the United States and Canada.

Fujifilm | View: the engine of growth is Instax, not traditional film. ; Interest: continued sales of instant cameras and instant paper. ; Worry: demand changes quickly, and capacity cannot keep up. ; Basis: imaging-division revenue grew 16.2% from April to June 2026; from 2022 to 2025 it expanded Instax paper capacity three times, about 50% in all (compiled by Fstoppers).

Film enthusiasts and processing labs | View: film has a feel and a process that digital cannot replace. ; Interest: a price they can bear, and convenient processing. ; Worry: higher prices, stock running out, and fewer and fewer labs. ; Basis: a 2025 survey by FilmFocus in Japan: 71% of respondents use Kodak film, 68% use Fuji; quite a few have turned to cheaper film, or to processing it themselves.

Suppliers of processing chemicals | View: the whole chain is more fragile than it looks. ; Interest: steady orders. ; Worry: the scale is too small, and the return on investment is low. ; Basis: according to RedShark News, only two companies can produce processing chemicals at scale: Fuji in Belgium, and Photo Systems in Michigan, in the United States.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Kodak and Fuji are rivals and, at the same time, upstream and downstream of each other. Fuji has some of its color negative made by Kodak, so Kodak’s capacity also decides the supply of Fuji film.
What enthusiasts want pushes the makers to expand production, but higher prices push the amount of shooting back down. Makers and users test each other on price.
Film and processing chemicals have to exist together. If a supplier drops out of either link, the whole chain is affected.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Demand is coming back, but an investment in a production line can take years to pay for itself, and the makers do not agree on “how long the revival can last.”

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: There is no single public count of annual film sales worldwide. The scale of the revival comes mostly from what the makers say, and from small surveys.
“Kodak missed digital” is a common line, but Kodak in fact put money into digital research very early. There is more than one account of why it declined.

pieces.title: More tests, but a lower price each: the third-quarter “volume” and “price” at Quest, the blood-test company
pieces.short: Quest, the blood-test company, third quarter…
pieces.hook: When you look at a company’s growth, split “volume” from “price”: a falling price per unit is not necessarily bad news. First ask who pulled down…
pieces.takeaway: When you look at a company’s growth, split “volume” from “price”: a falling price per unit is not necessarily bad news. First ask who pulled down the average.

parts: On October 22, Quest Diagnostics, one of the largest independent testing companies in the United States, reported third-quarter results: revenue of $3.097 billion, up 10.0% year over year; adjusted earnings per share of $3.00, up 15.4%. The company also raised its full-year guidance for revenue and for earnings per share.

The number of test requisitions grew 14.5%, but revenue per requisition fell 4.2%. The company explained that this was mainly two new large customers: the Michigan health system Corewell Health, and the dialysis company Fresenius Medical Care. Requisitions of this kind have a lower average value.

paras.lead: And if those two are taken out?
parts: The two contributed about 9.5 percentage points of the growth in requisitions. With them taken out, requisitions grew about 5%, and revenue per requisition actually grew 1.7%, because each requisition carried more tests. The reimbursement price of a single test was roughly flat.

Adjusted operating profit was $517 million, and the margin rose from 16.3% to 16.7%. CEO Jim Davis attributed the growth to an aging population, to demand for prevention and for managing health, and to efficiency from automation and AI.
Full-year revenue guidance was raised to $12.065 billion to $12.105 billion, and adjusted earnings per share to $11.25 to $11.35.

paras.lead: Which parts are fact, and which are inference
parts: The figures and events above come from the company’s press release and from an 8-K filing. “Whether the large customers at a low price can slowly become profitable” and “whether the data incident will bring lawsuits and regulatory costs” are inferences. The company has not yet given figures on either.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Quest’s management | View: aging and demand for prevention bring long-term growth, and automation and AI are raising efficiency. ; Interest: meeting the full-year guidance, and absorbing the new customers. ; Worry: the new customers pull down the average price, and the data incident hurts trust. ; Basis: what the CEO says in the press release; full-year revenue guidance was raised to $12.065 billion to $12.105 billion.

Investors and analysts | View: what they care about is the quality of the growth: was the volume bought, or did it grow on its own? ; Interest: profit, and the valuation. ; Worry: the price per unit keeps sliding, and the margin comes under pressure. ; Basis: with the two large customers taken out, requisitions grew about 5% and revenue per requisition was +1.7% (the press release).

Health-system customers (Corewell, Fresenius Medical Care, and others) | View: sending testing out to a specialist company can cut cost and raise efficiency. ; Interest: a lower cost of testing, and reports that come back faster. ; Worry: once the work is sent out, control over the quality of service weakens. ; Basis: the press release: the two customers brought about 9.5 percentage points of the growth in requisitions.

Patients and regulators | View: testing data are sensitive, and security has to come first. ; Interest: the protection of privacy, and accurate reports. ; Worry: what follows once data have been accessed. ; Basis: the 8-K: on October 21 the Quanum system was found to have been accessed without authorization, some patient records were affected, and law enforcement was notified.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Health systems send their testing out to Quest, and what they get is high volume at a low price. Quest gives up price per unit in exchange for scale, and uses automation to hold the margin.

Investors are willing to pay for growth, on the condition that the underlying growth is still there once the large customers are taken out. That is why management published the figures with them excluded.
The data-security incident has raised the attention of patients and regulators, and it may offset some of the trust that scale had brought.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The long-run contribution to profit of the large customers at a low price is still unclear, and the reach of the data incident has not been published either.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The company has not published the margin of each of the two large customers.
The 8-K does not say how many patients were affected.

pieces.title: Both sides are a few seats short: the last polls before Israel’s election
pieces.short: The last polls before Israel’s election
pieces.hook: Israel will hold a parliamentary election on Tuesday, October 27.
pieces.event: October 23–24, 2026 (the last polls and the rally before the vote; polling day is October 27)

parts: Israel will hold a parliamentary election on Tuesday, October 27. Friday, October 23, was the last day the law allows polls to be published. Polls from three television stations all showed that Yashar, the party led by the former chief of staff Eisenkot, is in line to be the largest party, with Netanyahu’s Likud second. But neither of the two blocs reaches the 61 seats needed to form a government.

The parliament has 120 seats, allotted by nationwide proportional representation. A party must clear a threshold of 3.25% of the vote to enter. This parliament is the first since 1988 to serve out its term. From Saturday, publishing polls is forbidden, until 10 p.m. on Tuesday, when voting ends and the exit polls are released.

Both sides are a few seats short. The key is the Arab parties, and the small parties near the threshold. Abbas, the leader of Ra'am, has said he is willing to join a coalition government of the anti-Netanyahu camp, but several parties in that camp have said clearly that they will not work with it.

On October 24, thousands rallied in Tel Aviv to demand a state commission of inquiry into the security failures of the attack on October 7, 2023. Opposition leaders including Eisenkot were there. On October 22, President Herzog, at the Rabin memorial, called for restraint and said “words can kill.” The same day, the High Court ruled that polling-station staff may not send voter data to the parties on election day.

“Eisenkot is ahead” refers to the seats of a single party. It does not mean he can form a government. The margin of error in the polls runs from 2.3% to 4.4%, and a gap of a few seats sits inside that margin. What actually decides the result is the bargaining after the vote.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Netanyahu and the governing coalition | View: stay in office, and stop the opposition from forming a government. ; Interest: keeping power, and keeping the existing coalition. ; Worry: the polls do not give them enough seats, and small right-wing parties may waste votes by missing the threshold. ; Basis: in all three polls the governing coalition has 50 seats. He has pressed some small right-wing parties to withdraw. The People’s State party and the Haredi Public party say they will stay in the race (the Times of Israel).

Eisenkot and the anti-Netanyahu camp | View: Israel needs a different government, and an inquiry into the security failures of October 7. ; Interest: winning the right to form the government. ; Worry: even as the largest party, they cannot assemble 61 seats. ; Basis: Eisenkot attended the Tel Aviv rally on October 24 (the Associated Press, the Times of Israel). He criticized Netanyahu for “taking apart the Israeli economy.”

The Arab parties (Ra'am, the Joint List) | View: the votes of Arab citizens ought to enter the government’s decisions. ; Interest: seats, and influence. ; Worry: being left out of a coalition government. ; Basis: the polls put them at 14–16 seats together. Abbas is willing to join an opposition government, but several of those parties refuse to work with him. The Central Elections Committee cancelled the two parties’ right to run in September; the Supreme Court overturned that on October 2.

Small parties near the threshold | View: stay in the race, and represent their own voters. ; Interest: clearing the 3.25% threshold and entering parliament. ; Worry: not enough votes, which would instead cost their own bloc those votes. ; Basis: in all three polls, the parties of Winter and of Leitner are below the threshold. Hendel’s reservists’ party gets 4 seats only in the Kan poll, and has not said which side it supports.

The courts, the president, and other parts of the system | View: the election has to be finished fairly and safely. ; Interest: keeping the election in order. ; Worry: political violence, and misuse of voter data. ; Basis: the High Court’s ruling of October 22; Herzog’s speech at the Rabin memorial.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Either bloc can reach 61 seats only by breaking a campaign promise: sitting down with a party it had refused to work with, or drawing in a small party whose position is not yet fixed.
A small party that stays in the race can keep its own voters, but it may leave its bloc’s votes stranded. That is exactly why there is pressure to withdraw.
The Arab parties’ seats are enough to change the result, but the opposition does not agree inside itself on whether to work with them. That split gives the governing coalition time.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: In none of the three polls can either side count on 61 seats. The bargaining after the vote, and a possible second election, are both unsettled.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The polls’ margin of error is 2.3%–4.4%, and with small parties near the threshold, the final seats may shift noticeably.
Whether the sides will change their promises of “no cooperation” after the vote is, for now, only a statement. There is no agreement.

pieces.title: Eleven years, six voyages, and he still went after he lost his sight: Jianzhen
pieces.short: Jianzhen
pieces.hook: If a thing is worth doing, do not wait until the conditions are complete before you set out: Jianzhen failed five times and lost his sight, and on the sixth he still boarded the ship.
pieces.takeaway: If a thing is worth doing, do not wait until the conditions are complete before you set out: Jianzhen failed five times and lost his sight, and on the sixth he still boarded the ship.
pieces.imageAlt: The golden hall of Tōshōdai-ji in Nara
pieces.imageCredit: 663highland · CC BY 2.5, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Jianzhen was born in Yangzhou in 688, of the lay surname Chunyu. Around fourteen he became a monk at Dayun Temple. Around twenty he went to Chang'an to study, returned to Yangzhou a few years later, and in time became abbot of Daming Temple.

paras.lead: More than a preacher of sutras
parts: He knew medicine, and at Daming Temple he set up a “Hall of the Compassionate Field” to take in the sick. According to the records, more than forty thousand people received the precepts from him, and his name was great along the Yangtze and the Huai.

In 742 the Japanese monks Yōei and Fushō came to Yangzhou, asking someone to go to Japan and transmit the precepts. None of the monks at Daming Temple answered. Jianzhen, already past fifty, said: “This is for the sake of the Dharma. Why should I begrudge my body and my life?”

On the voyage of 748, a north wind blew the ship on the East China Sea for more than ten days, and it drifted to what is now Sanya, on Hainan. He made his way back to Yangzhou overland, preaching as he went. On the road Yōei died of illness, and his leading disciple Xiangyan died as well.

By the time he returned to Yangzhou he was blind in both eyes. The traditional account is that he caught an infection on the journey and was then mistreated by a poor doctor. Fukushima Giichi, a Japanese historian of ophthalmology, has suggested it may have been cataracts of old age.

In 753 a Japanese embassy to the Tang asked him again to go east. Emperor Xuanzong would not let him put to sea, so he secretly boarded the embassy’s ship. On December 20 he landed in the Kagoshima area of Kyushu, and in the spring of the next year he reached Nara.

He set up an ordination platform at Tōdai-ji and conferred the precepts on about 500 people, among them the retired emperor Shōmu, the empress dowager Kōmyō, and the empress Kōken. At the time quite a few people became monks to escape taxes and labor service. Receiving the precepts under the proper rule was a way of putting a threshold on entering the clergy.

In 758 the empress Kōken, who had supported him, lost power, and he was removed from the office of chief administrator of monks. In 759, on land that had been granted to him, he built Tōshōdai-ji. He died there in 763. In 1980 his dry-lacquer statue went back to Yangzhou on a “visit home.”

blocks.title: Six voyages east
blocks.note: According to the Chinese Wikipedia entry “Jianzhen,” based mainly on The Eastward Journey of the Great Tang Monk.

blocks.title: A debate
blocks.text: Japan already had a tradition of “ordination by one’s own vow,” and Kenkei of Kōfuku-ji and others strongly opposed the new rule. Jianzhen debated them in public. He granted that ordination by one’s own vow could continue, but a formal ordination required “three masters and seven witnesses.” According to the record, the opponents accepted this in the end.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Jianzhen himself | View: transmitting the precepts was a great matter of spreading the Dharma, worth risking his life. ; Interest: giving Japan a system of ordination that accorded with the rules. ; Worry: the road was dangerous, and disciples died one after another. ; Basis: “This is for the sake of the Dharma. Why should I begrudge my body and my life?” as relayed in The Eastward Journey of the Great Tang Monk.

The Japanese court (the retired emperor Shōmu, the empress Kōken) | View: they needed an authoritative master of the rules to put the community of monks in order. ; Interest: using proper ordination to hold down the number of people entering the clergy, and to reduce escape from taxes and labor service. ; Worry: the local community of monks would not submit, and court struggles would drag him in. ; Basis: Kōken ordered that “from now on, the transmission of the precepts is entrusted entirely to the master”; after the political shift of 758, Jianzhen was removed from office.

The local party of “ordination by one’s own vow” (Kenkei and others) | View: ordination by one’s own vow had a tradition of its own, and there was no need to follow a rule from outside in every particular. ; Interest: the standing and the practice they already had. ; Worry: the right to speak being taken by an eminent monk from abroad. ; Basis: the record of the public debate at Kōfuku-ji.

The Tang authorities, and the disciples who stayed behind | View: they did not want an eminent monk to risk the sea, and they did not want him to leave. ; Interest: local reputation, the bond of master and disciple, and control of who put to sea. ; Worry: an eminent monk dying at sea; leaving the country without permission. ; Basis: on the fourth attempt the disciple Lingyou asked the authorities to bring him back; on the sixth, Xuanzong would not allow him to sail.

Later scholars | View: Jianzhen is a key figure in cultural exchange between China and Japan, and the details should be read with care. ; Interest: recovering what actually happened. ; Worry: the main source comes from the side of his disciples, and may have been embellished. ; Basis: the cause of his blindness has an infection account and a cataract account (Fukushima Giichi); the years of the six voyages differ slightly from one text to another.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The Japanese court used Jianzhen’s hand to bring the community of monks under control. Opposition from local monks then forced him, in the debate, to give ground, and ordination by one’s own vow was kept.
The Tang authorities and his disciples blocked him again and again. The aim was to protect him. In practice it stretched the voyage east over eleven years.
Jianzhen’s standing rose and fell with the political fate of his patrons. When Kōken lost power, he was removed from office. When Kōken returned, his disciples were promoted to important posts again.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The people who invited him needed him to set rules. The people who would be ruled by them did not want the constraint. The contradiction was eased, for a time, only by debate and by concession.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Sayings such as “why begrudge this life” come mostly from retellings in the Eastward Journey, and they are hard to set beside a record from a third party.
The exact cause of the blindness, and when it happened, are still not settled.

pieces.title: From a spinning disk to a set as thin as a picture frame: one hundred years of a television
pieces.short: One hundred years of a television
pieces.hook: On January 26, 1926, the Scotsman Baird demonstrated, in London, to about 40…
pieces.imageAlt: A black-and-white television of the 1950s
pieces.imageCredit: John Atherton · CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

paras.lead: A face on a spinning disk
parts: On January 26, 1926, the Scotsman Baird demonstrated, in London, to about 40 scientists of the Royal Institution, sending a living face onto another screen with a spinning disk full of holes, a Nipkow disk. This is often taken as the world’s first public demonstration of television.

In December of the same year, Takayanagi Kenjirō in Japan displayed a 40-line image with a cathode-ray tube, a CRT. The picture from the disk was small and blurred, and the fully electronic path soon won.

In 1934 Telefunken in Germany built the first batch of commercial electronic televisions. On November 2, 1936, the BBC began regular high-definition broadcasts from Alexandra Palace in London. In February 1937 Baird’s mechanical system was formally dropped.

On January 1, 1954, the United States made the first nationwide color broadcast, of the Rose Parade. RCA’s CT-100 color set then needed 36 electron tubes. The price was high, and color programs were few. Color sets did not sell in volume until the middle of the 1960s.

paras.lead: From a thick box to a thin screen
parts: In 1997 Philips brought out a 42-inch plasma television using a Fujitsu panel. Liquid crystal then caught up. In 2007, worldwide sales of LCD televisions passed CRT televisions for the first time. OLED needs no backlight, and its black is purer. In 2014 curved OLED televisions appeared.

According to Omdia, global television shipments in the fourth quarter of 2025 were 61.50 million units, flat with a year earlier. In China, after the subsidies ended and people had already replaced their sets early, shipments fell hard, by 25.3%. Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Middle East and Africa, grew 12.5% and 9.4%.

TCL and Hisense, under pressure at home, still grew their combined shipments by 2.2%, and their share of shipments in North America rose from 28.6% to 30.7%. Citing Omdia, Samsung said that in 2025, with a share of 29.1%, it ranked first in the world for the twentieth year in a row.

Television is a mature industry. The total barely grows anymore. The contest has shifted to large sizes and to high-end picture quality, which is to say the contest between Mini LED and OLED, and to the expansion of Chinese brands overseas.

It is called China’s first domestically made television.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Chinese brands (TCL, Hisense) | View: demand at home has fallen back, and growth has to come from overseas and from large screens. ; Interest: the scale of shipments, and share overseas. ; Worry: compliance costs in the United States are rising, parts such as memory are getting more expensive, and margins are thinning. ; Basis: Omdia, 2026-03-03: the two companies’ combined shipments were +2.2%, and their North American share rose from 28.6% to 30.7%.

Samsung | View: hold first place in the world, and hold the high end. ; Interest: share in the high price bands, and the premium on the brand. ; Worry: Chinese brands catching up in the middle and the high end. ; Basis: Samsung, citing Omdia: a 2025 share of 29.1%; 52.2% of the band above $1,500, and 54.3% of the band above $2,500.

The OLED camp | View: the picture quality of a self-lit screen is the direction of high-end television. ; Interest: people willing to spend. ; Worry: as more RGB Mini LED televisions enter the market, that high-end clientele gets divided away. ; Basis: Omdia: OLED shipments in the fourth quarter were +8.6%, and Western Europe was +11.5%.

The Mini LED camp | View: make the flagship with Mini LED plus quantum dots, and the value is better. ; Interest: taking the high-end market out of OLED’s hands. ; Worry: whether the high-end margin can hold. ; Basis: Omdia notes that at CES 2026 TCL made Mini LED plus enhanced quantum dots its flagship.

Chinese consumers, and the subsidy policy | View: during the subsidy, people replaced their televisions early. ; Interest: a new set for less money. ; Worry: once the subsidy ends, demand falls off a cliff. ; Basis: Omdia: after the subsidies ended, China’s shipments in the fourth quarter were -25.3%.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Once the Chinese market turned cold, Chinese brands sent the goods toward the United States and other markets overseas, and ran straight into Samsung’s advantage at the high end and into stricter American compliance.
OLED and Mini LED are competing for the same people willing to spend money. Growth on one side often has to be taken from the other side’s customers.
The subsidy pulled demand forward, and what it left the brands is a gap the following year.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: In an industry whose total is not growing, share moves from one side to the other, and profit is squeezed from both ends by rising parts prices and by compliance costs.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Each company’s “first” is counted differently, by units shipped or by sales value, and figures from different organizations cannot be compared directly.
Full-year figures for 2026 are not out yet. Whether the growth overseas can last still has to be watched.

pieces.title: The annual fee is rising twice as fast as spending: American Express’s third-quarter “membership fee” accounts
pieces.short: American Express’s third-quarter “membership fee” accounts
pieces.hook: When you look at the business of a “membership card,” do not look only at how much in fees was collected. Also look at how much was spent on the benefits given out in return for those fees.
pieces.takeaway: When you look at the business of a “membership card,” do not look only at how much in fees was collected. Also look at how much was spent on the benefits given out in return for those fees.
pieces.imageAlt: The entrance to an American Express Centurion lounge
pieces.imageCredit: ajay_suresh · CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 23, American Express reported third-quarter results: revenue after interest expense of $20.06 billion, up 9%. Card members’ spending was $454 billion, up 8%. Annual-fee revenue was $2.969 billion, up 16%, twice the pace of spending.

paras.lead: Where the annual fee comes from
parts: The number of cards American Express itself issues grew by less than 2%, but the average annual fee per card rose 14%. What lines up in time is the redesign of the Platinum Card. In September 2025 the annual fee on the U.S. Platinum Card rose to $895. Existing members pay the new price starting with the first renewal after January 2, 2026.

paras.lead: The benefits got more expensive too
parts: The price rise came with a new batch of statement credits. The result was that the cost of “card member services” rose 36%, an extra $529 million, more than the extra $418 million collected in annual fees. American Express said in the report that the growth of this spending will slow next quarter, because the same quarter last year already included the effect of the redesign.

On the earnings call, management said that a year after the Platinum redesign, the spending retention on this group of cards was still 99%. Millennials and Generation Z are the largest and fastest-growing group in the U.S. consumer business. Travel and entertainment spending grew 10%, and airline tickets within that grew 13%.

The write-off rate on U.S. consumer cards fell from 1.8% to 1.6%. Separately, on October 8 American Express disclosed a consent order with the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. A bank under it paid a $350 million fine, over financial-crime compliance.

paras.lead: Who benefits, and who is under pressure
parts: Heavy users who actually use the benefits may get credits worth more than the annual fee. People who barely use them are, in effect, paying more. For American Express, whether the books can balance depends on when the growth in the cost of the benefits comes down.

The growth in the annual fee, and the growth in cost, are figures from the earnings report. “The growth in the annual fee comes mainly from the Platinum Card” is an inference from the timing. American Express did not disclose Platinum Card figures on their own.

blocks.title: The key figures
blocks.note: Figures are from the schedules to American Express’s third-quarter report, as compiled by StockTitan.

blocks.title: Why earnings per share rose 31%
blocks.text: Reported earnings per share were $5.42, up 31%, but that includes a $982 million gain on the sale of a stake in GBTG, a business-travel company, and $336 million in restructuring charges. Take those two out, and adjusted earnings per share were $4.68, up 13%.

blocks.title: American Express’s third quarter, growth from a year earlier
items: Card member services cost
Annual-fee revenue
Average annual fee per card
Card member spending

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: American Express management | View: the premium-membership model is working. Members are willing to pay a higher annual fee, and both spending and retention are steady. ; Interest: annual fees, merchant discount fees, and interest, three streams of revenue rising together. ; Worry: the cost of the benefits is rising too fast. ; Basis: CEO Squeri, in the press release, pointed to strength in spending, new customers, and retention. On the call, the spending retention on the Platinum Card was put at 99%.

Heavy users | View: the credits and the lounges after the price rise are worth the fare. ; Interest: concrete benefits in travel, dining, and the like. ; Worry: the terms of the benefits being tightened later. ; Basis: card member services cost was +36%, which shows the benefits were heavily used.

Light users | View: an annual fee of $895 does not pay for itself. ; Interest: spending less. ; Worry: paying for benefits they will not use. ; Basis: American Express has not disclosed how many people renewed at the new price. It has given only the spending-retention rate.

Investors and analysts | View: the results beat expectations, but once one-time items are taken out the growth is less bright. ; Interest: whether the profit can last. ; Worry: the cost of benefits outrunning the annual fee, and profit being diluted. ; Basis: adjusted earnings per share of $4.68, above the $4.47 consensus compiled by Zacks. StockTitan calculates that pretax profit, after one-time items, rose only about 1.6%.

Regulators | View: the bank’s financial-crime compliance has to be put right. ; Interest: the safety of the financial system. ; Worry: gaps in compliance. ; Basis: the October 8 consent order of the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and a $350 million fine.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: American Express trades more expensive benefits for a higher annual fee. Heavy users get more. Light users are subsidizing the system.
Management stresses retention and spending. Analysts care more about the pace of profit once one-time gains are taken out. The two accounts use the same earnings report.
The regulatory fine does not change the full-year guidance, but putting compliance right will take management’s attention.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Whether the rise in the annual fee can keep covering the cost of the benefits will be clear only after the effect of the redesign has entered the base of the same quarter a year earlier.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: American Express has not broken out the annual fee and the cost of the Platinum Card on their own. “The Platinum Card drove the growth in the annual fee” is an inference.
“Spending retention of 99%” is management’s figure. It has not been checked from outside.

pieces.title: After fourteen years in power, a concession: Serbia’s “student list” won the election
pieces.short: Serbia’s “student list” has won…
pieces.hook: About an hour and a half after voting ended in Serbia’s parliamentary election on October 25, Vučić conceded defeat.
pieces.event: October 25, 2026 (polling day in the parliamentary election; official results not yet published)
pieces.imageAlt: The building of the National Assembly of Serbia
pieces.imageCredit: kallerna · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: The Associated Press reported that about an hour and a half after voting ended in Serbia’s parliamentary election on October 25, Vučić conceded defeat. He said that, on the basis of a sample, the “student list” would take 135 to 140 seats, his Serbian Progressive Party about 105, in a parliament of 250 seats.

According to the Guardian, citing the television station N1, the projection by Ipsos and CeSID is 52% and 138 seats for the student list, and 39.3% and 104 seats for Vučić’s list. A majority takes 126 seats. The official election commission has not yet published the result.

On November 1, 2024, not long after the Novi Sad railway station had been renovated, the canopy collapsed and 16 people were killed. Students blamed corruption in the renovation, and the protests have gone on for nearly two years.

The students themselves are not on the candidate list. The candidates are little-known experts, athletes, farmers, and artists. The list is headed by Ilija Srdanović, a professor at the medical faculty of the University of Novi Sad, and he may become the new prime minister.

He conceded that “the student list won,” and at the same time blamed the defeat on independent media, on interference by European countries he did not name, and on “the American deep state.” His supporters value his pragmatism and the growth of the economy.

The prime minister of Hungary, Magyar, and the prime minister and the president of Montenegro quickly posted their congratulations. The head of the European Union’s delegation to Serbia, on polling day, expressed deep concern about violence at polling stations. As of that night, there was no formal response to be seen from the European Commission or from Moscow.

The new government has to be formed, and a presidential election also has to be held before the end of the year. The political-risk firm Teneo thinks a student-led government would push anti-corruption work and a reshaping of public institutions and state companies, but that it may meet strong resistance from the bureaucracy.

One telling is “foreign forces overthrew the government.” Another is “democracy was bound to win.” Both easily cover over the concrete questions: how corruption will be answered for, whether the new government can function, and whether the foreign-policy line will change.

Prime Minister Vučević announces his resignation
The Belgrade protest, estimated at more than 325,000 people
Parliament is dissolved; an early election
Vučić resigns as president, and heads the campaign for prime minister
The vote; Vučić concedes that night

blocks.title: The other side of polling day
blocks.text: Independent observers reported dozens of irregularities, such as photographing ballots, which suggests someone was applying pressure, and attempts to buy votes. Turnout is expected at about 70%, a level not seen since 2000.

blocks.title: Seats projected by Ipsos and CeSID
items: Student list
Vučić’s list

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The student list | View: this is a rejection of corruption and of “rule by one person,” and a call to rebuild democracy and the economy. ; Interest: anti-corruption, a free press, and accountability for the dead. ; Worry: a lack of experience in government, and a bureaucracy that will not cooperate. ; Basis: the campaign program as reported by the Associated Press and Euronews; a mother of one of the dead said, “I hope every one of them is held to account.”

Vučić and the Serbian Progressive Party | View: the defeat came from independent media and from foreign interference. ; Interest: keeping the political base, and contesting the presidential election at the end of the year. ; Worry: the problems of the long years in power being settled up. ; Basis: Vučić’s speech on election night; he said the vote was about 1.72 million to 2.2 million.

The European Union | View: Serbia is a candidate for membership, and the election has to be fair. ; Interest: stability in the western Balkans, and Serbia moving closer to the European Union. ; Worry: violence and irregularities in the election, and a foreign-policy line of the new government that is not yet clear. ; Basis: the statement on polling day by the head of the European Union’s delegation to Serbia; the Daily Telegraph said that no one is clear on the student list’s foreign-policy line.

Russia | View: Vučić is one of its few friendly leaders in Europe. ; Interest: influence in the Balkans. ; Worry: Serbia turning toward the West. ; Basis: the Associated Press: Putin had endorsed Vučić; as of that night there was no response from Moscow.

The neighbors (Hungary, Montenegro) | View: this is the will of the citizens, and they look forward to a new chapter in relations between the countries. ; Interest: better bilateral relations. ; Worry: tensions getting worse. ; Basis: Magyar’s congratulations on X; the statements of Montenegro’s prime minister, Spajić, and its president, Milatović.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Vučić’s talk of “foreign interference” and the European Union’s concern for a fair election point at the same election, and they give opposite readings of it.
The student list won voters with the image of “not a party.” To form a government and govern, it still has to deal with parties and with the bureaucracy.
Russia and the European Union are both waiting to see the new government’s choice in foreign policy, while the student list’s campaign talked almost only about domestic issues.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The result still has to wait for the official announcement, and the presidential election at the end of the year may shift the balance of power again.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The seat figures so far come from projections and from Vučić himself. They are not the official result.
How serious the irregularities reported by observers were, and whether they affected the result, has not yet been fully assessed.
