pieces.title: She learned needle and thread in an orphanage, and got women out of the corset: Coco Chanel
pieces.short: Coco Chanel
pieces.hook: A material other people thought unfit to be seen becomes something new in the right place: jersey had been used only for men’s underwear, and in her hands it became…
pieces.takeaway: A material other people thought unfit to be seen becomes something new in the right place: jersey had been used only for men’s underwear, and in her hands it became women’s everyday dress.
pieces.imageAlt: Chanel in 1931
pieces.imageCredit: Los Angeles Times · CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Gabrielle Chanel was born on August 19, 1883, in the charity hospital of a poorhouse in Saumur, France. Her mother was a laundress. Her father was a peddler who went from street to street.
The year she was 11, her mother died, and her father sent his three daughters to the orphanage run by the convent at Aubazine. Life was hard and the rules were strict. There she learned to sew.

After she left the orphanage at 18, she worked as a seamstress by day and sang in a café in Moulins at night. “Coco,” it is said, came from a song she often sang. She herself preferred to say her father had given her the name.

In 1910 she received a milliner’s license and opened a hat shop at 21 rue Cambon in Paris. In 1913, with money from her lover Capel, she opened a shop in the seaside town of Deauville, selling clothes suited to leisure and to sport.

paras.lead: A perfume, and a contract on paper
parts: In 1921 she brought out the perfume “No. 5.” In 1924 she and the Wertheimer brothers set up a perfume company together. They put up all the capital and took 70% of the profit. The man who made the introduction, Bader, took 20%. She took only 10%, and for decades afterward she tried to get the control back.

When the Second World War broke out in 1939, she closed the fashion house, and about 4,000 women workers lost their jobs. During the occupation she lived at the Ritz and was involved with the German diplomat Dincklage. In 1941 she also tried, by way of “Aryan” status, to take for herself the perfume company of the Wertheimer family, who were Jewish.

As early as May 1940 the Wertheimers had transferred the company to the French businessman Amiot, and her application came to nothing. The biographer Vaughan, drawing on declassified files, said she had been a German intelligence agent, number F-7124. Some scholars think the evidence is not enough.

After the war she lived in Switzerland for nearly ten years. In 1954, past 70, she reopened the fashion house. The money came from Pierre Wertheimer, the old rival of those years. The French press was cool. The American and British press called it a breakthrough.

The tweed suit introduced in 1923, and the 2.55 chain bag revised in February 1955, are both still in use. On January 10, 1971, she died at the Ritz, at 87. In Time magazine’s “100 most influential people of the 20th century,” she was the only fashion designer.

blocks.title: Underwear cloth, made into outerwear
blocks.text: The knit she used, jersey, was then used mainly for men’s underwear. It was cheap, soft, and elastic. Made into a loose dress, it meant a woman no longer had to cinch her waist, and could walk and ride a bicycle at ease.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Chanel herself | View: a woman’s clothes should be comfortable and allow movement. She should not have to suffer in order to look good. ; Interest: her own brand, her name, and the income from perfume. ; Worry: partners taking the profit, and being called to account after the war. ; Basis: she called the cinched waists, padded busts, and stiff jackets of male designers “illogical,” as Wikipedia records it in the account of her 1954 return.

The Wertheimer family | View: the perfume business had to be made large with capital and with channels of sale. ; Interest: the profit on No. 5, and control of the company. ; Worry: during the occupation, the company being seized as Jewish property. ; Basis: in May 1940 the company was transferred to Amiot; in 1947 the contract was renegotiated, giving her 2% of worldwide sales of No. 5 and paying her living expenses for life.

The women workers of the fashion house | View: wages and hours should be improved. ; Interest: a livelihood, and the conditions of the work. ; Worry: the boss taking revenge when she had the chance. ; Basis: the general strike in France in 1936; after the house closed in 1939, about 4,000 people were out of work. The biographer Vaughan thinks this was connected to the strike.

The French press after the war, and the British and American press | View: the French press had reservations about her wartime record; the fashion press in Britain and America cared more about the design. ; Interest: the taste and the position of their own readers. ; Worry: whitewashing a collaborator, or missing an important designer. ; Basis: when she returned in 1954 the French coverage was cool, and Ballard, an editor at American Vogue, stood firmly behind her.

Biographers and scholars | View: her identity as an intelligence agent has to be read from the files. ; Interest: recovering what happened. ; Worry: the evidence being read for more than it holds. ; Basis: Vaughan cites, in the French police files, “code name Westminster, number F 7124.” Others think the files are not enough to prove she was a formal agent.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: She wanted the perfume company back from the Wertheimers, and in wartime she moved under the anti-Jewish laws. The money for her return after the war came from the same Wertheimer.
In her designs she freed women’s bodies. As an employer she stood opposite the women workers who asked for higher pay.
Enthusiasm in the British and American markets let her rise again. The reservations in France itself about her wartime record never went away.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: To talk about Chanel today, the contribution of the design and the conduct in wartime are hard to judge apart. The brand’s story and historical research are often telling two versions.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The childhood she told was in many places invented. The early details often rest only on what biographers have been able to establish.
Scholars do not read the files on her relation to German intelligence the same way.

pieces.title: The instrument that can play soft and can play loud: more than three hundred years of the piano
pieces.short: More than three hundred years of the piano
pieces.hook: Cristofori, an instrument maker in Florence, Italy, worked for the Medici family.
pieces.imageAlt: Cristofori’s piano of 1720
pieces.imageCredit: Shriram Rajagopalan · CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

paras.lead: A new instrument in the Medici court
parts: Cristofori, an instrument maker in Florence, Italy, worked for the Medici family. An inventory of the family’s property in 1700 already lists a piano he had built. The three that survive were all built in the 1720s.

paras.lead: The name was the selling point
parts: He called it “a cypress keyboard instrument that can play soft and can play loud.” It was later shortened to pianoforte, and then to piano. The harpsichord before it plucked the string, and the volume barely changed. The piano strikes the string with a small hammer, and the weight of the finger becomes the size of the sound.

Around 1777, Broadwood in London and others put the piano into the long case of a harpsichord. That is the origin of the grand piano. In 1821 Érard in Paris invented the double-escapement action. The key can be struck again before it has fully risen, and fast repeated notes became possible.

The strings were pulled tighter and tighter, and wood could not bear it. In 1825 Babcock of Boston patented a one-piece cast-iron frame for the square piano. In 1843 the Chickering company put a full iron frame on the grand piano. Today the strings of a grand piano can pull, all together, with more than 20 tonnes of tension.

In 1853 the German piano maker Steinweg founded Steinway in New York. In 1859 his son applied for a U.S. patent on cross-stringing for the grand piano. In 1900 Yamaha in Japan built the country’s first piano.

paras.lead: The stretch of the story in China
parts: The predecessor of Pearl River Piano, the Guangzhou piano factory, was founded in 1956. It later became one of the largest piano factories in the world by output, with a yearly capacity of more than 100,000 instruments. Essex, the entry-level brand under Steinway, has also been made at Pearl River’s Guangzhou factory since 2005.

Pearl River Piano’s annual report for 2025: revenue of 570 million yuan, down 15.88%; a net loss attributable to shareholders of 374 million yuan. Piano sales were 23,174 units, 38.6% fewer than the 37,743 of 2024. Digital pianos sold 22,026 units, a smaller decline, of 16.9%.

The acoustic piano in China has entered a deep adjustment. A new piano has to compete for buyers with a large number of used pianos on offer, and with cheaper digital pianos. Pearl River said in its annual report that it would turn from “the world’s largest piano manufacturer” toward music and cultural services, and open new businesses such as stage lighting and cultural tourism.

blocks.title: After the bonus-point policy left the stage
blocks.text: According to Jiemian News, citing the China Musical Instrument Association’s industry white paper for 2024, domestic piano sales fell from 356,000 units in 2018 to 128,000 in 2023, a drop of 64%, and in 2024 they were expected to fall below 100,000. The report puts the causes on the cancellation in 2018 of bonus points for artistic talent, on the “double reduction” policy, and on factors such as household income.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Piano makers (Pearl River Piano and others) | View: demand for the main business keeps shrinking, and new growth has to be found in smart products and in cultural services. ; Interest: the use of capacity, and profit. ; Worry: shrinking capacity pushes up the cost per unit, and assets keep being written down. ; Basis: Pearl River’s report of the board for 2025: revenue of 570 million yuan, a loss of 374 million yuan, and a plan to expand into stage lighting, cultural tourism, and other businesses.

Families with a child learning the piano | View: the return from piano study, in the form of school admission, has got smaller, and the spending has to be more careful. ; Interest: the child’s interest, and the household’s outlay. ; Worry: a piano bought for tens of thousands of yuan sitting idle in the end. ; Basis: Jiemian News: after the 2018 cancellation of bonus points for artistic talent, and the “double reduction” policy, demand cooled markedly.

Sellers of used pianos, and the platforms | View: an idle piano needs a way out, and it has to be sold even at a low price. ; Interest: recovering part of the cost, and earning the spread. ; Worry: too many listings, and no sale. ; Basis: Jiemian News: listings on used-goods platforms have surged, and the asking price is often less than a tenth of the original.

The digital-piano camp | View: cheaper, smaller, and practice with headphones, better suited to a city household. ; Interest: taking entry-level users. ; Worry: overall demand sliding together. ; Basis: Pearl River’s digital-piano sales in 2025 were -16.9%, a smaller decline than the -38.6% for acoustic pianos.

The China Musical Instrument Association | View: the adjustment is an inevitable stage in the cycle of the piano industry. ; Interest: stability for the industry, and a transition. ; Worry: firms that cannot last through the adjustment. ; Basis: remarks by the chairman, Wang Shicheng, as reported by Jiemian News.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The more used pianos there are, the harder a new piano is to sell. When makers shrink capacity, the cost per unit is pushed up again.
Digital pianos take entry-level users away. But they depend, like the acoustic piano, on the number of people learning. When overall demand falls, both sides are hit.
Makers are turning to new businesses such as cultural tourism and lighting. Whether that can fill the gap in the main business has no answer yet.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The root of demand is the number of people learning the piano, and that number is shaped by school-admission policy and by household income. Neither is something a piano factory can control.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The national sales figures come from the industry association’s monitoring. Complete national figures for 2024 and 2025 have not, so far, been found in a public source.
“Less than a tenth of the original price” for a used piano is an observation in the press. There is no systematic count.

pieces.title: Revenue more than doubled, and the cash still flowed out: Bloom Energy’s third-quarter “deliver first, collect later”
pieces.short: Bloom Energy …
pieces.hook: When you look at a fast-growing company, look past the income statement to the cash-flow statement: a sale is not the same thing as money received.
pieces.takeaway: When you look at a fast-growing company, look past the income statement to the cash-flow statement: a sale is not the same thing as money received.
pieces.imageAlt: A Bloom Energy server at eBay headquarters
pieces.imageCredit: Bloom Energy · CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 22, the American fuel-cell company Bloom Energy reported third-quarter results: revenue of $1.236 billion, up 138.1% from $519 million a year earlier; net profit of $250 million, against a loss of $23.1 million a year earlier.

Its “energy server” is a solid-oxide fuel cell. At about 800°C it generates electricity from natural gas, biogas, or hydrogen, and it is installed on the customer’s own site. The company was founded in 2001. The founder, Sridhar, had been studying oxygen-making technology for Mars at NASA. It went public only in 2018.

More and more of the buyers are data centers that need electricity. In November 2024 the power company AEP signed an agreement for up to 1 gigawatt. In April 2026 Oracle announced a collaboration of 2.8 gigawatts. The CEO said in the press release that electricity is shifting from centralized power plants to distributed generation on site.

There was a profit, but operating cash flow was an outflow of $27.1 million. The quarter before, it had still been an inflow of about $226 million. The gap sits mainly in “contract assets” and in inventory. The first of those is money for goods already delivered and revenue already recognized, but not yet at the point where an invoice can be sent.

Capital expenditure this quarter was $153 million, mostly equipment, and the expansion of capacity at the Fremont and Newark plants. Operating cash flow plus capital expenditure leaves free cash flow as an outflow of $181 million. The first three quarters of this year together are still a positive $42 million. Cash at the end of the quarter was $2.5 billion.

The finance chief said revenue is recognized when the customer obtains control, while invoicing follows the milestones in the contract and may fall in the next quarter. These gaps will be smoothed out as invoices are sent and cash comes in. The CEO said capacity would be added a little at a time, following demand, and not in one large outlay.

In its risk factors the company listed a slowing of demand for AI, air-emission permits, and financing, among other things. Critics also note that it burns mainly natural gas, and that the effect on emissions depends on which grid it is compared with.

Revenue, profit, cash flow, and capital expenditure are figures the company published. “Contract assets will turn into cash on schedule” is what management says. It can be checked only by looking at collections over the quarters that follow.

blocks.title: The key figures
blocks.note: Figures are from Bloom Energy’s third-quarter press release and from the earnings call.

blocks.title: The results beat expectations, and the share price still fell
blocks.text: Adjusted earnings per share were $0.94, above the market’s expectation of about $0.69. Full-year revenue guidance was raised to $4.4–4.6 billion, the third raise this year. But on Friday, October 23, the share price fell about 11%. JPMorgan, Roth, and BTIG all cut their price targets.

blocks.title: Bloom’s third quarter ($100 million)
items: Revenue
Net profit
Capital expenditure
Free cash flow (outflow)

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Bloom’s management | View: demand is strong, and the swing in cash flow is only the gap in time between delivery and invoicing. It will smooth out. ; Interest: keeping the high growth, and the pace of adding capacity. ; Worry: the market taking a short-term outflow of cash for a trend. ; Basis: the earnings call: contract assets and receivables turn into cash after the invoicing milestones; free cash flow for the first three quarters was +$42 million.

Investors and analysts | View: the growth is not the problem, but they want to see profit turn into cash. ; Interest: the valuation, and the share price. ; Worry: the high growth is being held up by tying up working capital and by continuing capital expenditure. ; Basis: on October 23 the share price fell about 11%. JPMorgan’s target went from $314 to $292, Roth’s from $260 to $230, and BTIG’s from $295 to $250 (TipRanks).

Data-center customers (Oracle and others) | View: connecting to the grid is too slow, and generation on site can put electricity to use faster. ; Interest: powering AI machine rooms as soon as possible. ; Worry: delivery of the equipment, and the running of it, not keeping up. ; Basis: in April 2026 Oracle announced a collaboration of 2.8 gigawatts; the CEO said electricity is shifting to generation on site.

Power companies (AEP and others) | View: fuel cells can be a supplement for supplying large customers. ; Interest: keeping large customers, and supplying them faster. ; Worry: the economics of a long-term contract. ; Basis: in November 2024 AEP signed an agreement for up to 1 gigawatt.

Critics on the environmental side | View: a fuel cell that burns natural gas is not the same thing as zero emissions. ; Interest: a real effect on cutting emissions. ; Worry: expanding fossil-fuel electricity under the name of “clean energy.” ; Basis: figures for Delaware in 2014, cited by Wikipedia: about 823 pounds of carbon dioxide per megawatt-hour, against about 1,000 pounds for the local grid.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Customers want electricity in a hurry, so Bloom has to stock the goods first and deliver first. The money comes back only at the invoicing milestone. The faster the growth, the more money is tied up.
Management says the added capacity follows demand. Investors are already marking the price down for the cash flowing out.
Data centers buy it in order to get electricity quickly. Environmental criticism is aimed at the emissions of generating with natural gas. The two sides are not looking at the same account.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Whether contract assets turn into cash on schedule depends on collections over the next several quarters. This one quarter cannot say.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “The gap in time will smooth out” is what management says. The company has not disclosed the collection milestones customer by customer.
The emissions figures are fairly old, and comparisons with different grids are counted in very different ways.

pieces.title: Behind in the first round, ahead in the second: Lula elected for a fourth time, and his opponent will not concede
pieces.short: Lula elected for a fourth time, and his opponent will not concede
pieces.hook: In the second round of Brazil’s presidential election on October 25, Lula, at 80, with 51.79% (about 64.26…
pieces.event: October 25, 2026 (the second round of Brazil’s presidential election); reactions on October 26
pieces.imageAlt: The Brazilian runoff debate
pieces.imageCredit: Lula Oficial · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: The Associated Press reported: in the second round of Brazil’s presidential election on October 25, Lula, at 80, with 51.79% (about 64.26 million votes) to 48.21% (about 59.83 million votes), defeated Flávio, 45, a senator and the son of former president Bolsonaro. The margin was about 4.4 million votes. He will begin a fourth term on January 5, 2027.

In the first round, on October 4, Flávio had about 47% and Lula about 45%. According to the reporting, this is the first time since Brazil restored democracy that the second-place finisher in the first round has overturned the result in the runoff.

The Associated Press said Lula picked up about 10.4 million more votes between the two rounds, and turnout rose as well. In the key state of Minas Gerais he was 6 points behind in the first round, and 1 point ahead in the second.

On the afternoon of polling day, Supreme Court justice Zanin extended voting from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. Both camps had asked for more time. According to a count by g1, only about 35,500 votes were cast after 5 p.m.

Flávio refused to accept the result and asked that the election be declared void, on the ground of the extension. The president of the electoral court, Nunes Marques, who was appointed by Bolsonaro, said the extension did not affect the result. On October 26, Justice Moraes ordered Flávio to hand over his passport.

Latin America has turned markedly to the right in recent years. Argentina in 2023, Chile in 2025, and Colombia in 2026 all elected leaders of the right. Brazil this time went against that current, but the margin was only 3.6 percentage points, and the country is still split in two.

One telling is “the extension stole the election.” Another is “democracy won a great victory.” The first does not fit the gap between 35,500 votes and 4.4 million votes. The second easily overlooks this: nearly half the voters chose the other side, and the new government still has to deal with the division at home and with relations with the United States.

blocks.title: A remark from Trump
blocks.text: On October 26, Trump said this election “looks like another rigged election,” and at the same time said he had “not taken a side,” that he “likes Lula,” and that “Brazil is not under my charge.” He offered no evidence. Vice President Alckmin called the claim “completely wrong.” The former foreign minister, Amorim, said Trump was “poorly informed.”

First round: Flávio about 47%, Lula about 45%
The runoff debate on TV Globo
The runoff; voting extended by two hours; Lula wins with 51.79%
Flávio asks that the election be declared void; Trump says it “looks rigged”
The new term begins

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Lula’s camp | View: voters used the ballot to refuse the Bolsonaro family, and the extension had nothing to do with the result. ; Interest: a fourth term starting smoothly, and steady relations with the United States. ; Worry: an opponent who will not concede, and a politics that stays divided. ; Basis: the Associated Press: about 10.4 million more votes. Alckmin called Trump’s claim “completely wrong,” and said he hoped to negotiate with the United States.

Flávio Bolsonaro’s camp | View: extending the last two hours damaged the fairness of the election. ; Interest: keeping the family’s political base, and seeking to overturn the result. ; Worry: the legal pressure being increased further. ; Basis: the demand that the election be declared void; on October 26 Moraes ordered him to hand over his passport.

The electoral court and the Supreme Court | View: the procedure was lawful. Both sides had asked for the extension, and it does not affect the result. ; Interest: public confidence in the result of the election. ; Worry: being accused by one side of favoritism. ; Basis: the president of the electoral court, Nunes Marques (appointed by Bolsonaro), said the extension did not affect the result; g1: about 35,500 votes after 5 p.m.

Trump and the United States government | View: the election “looks rigged,” but he “did not take a side.” ; Interest: influence in Latin America, and relations with allies on the right. ; Worry: Brazil moving further away from the United States. ; Basis: Trump’s remarks of October 26 (reported by USA Today). He provided no evidence.

Swing voters (as in the state of Minas Gerais) | View: between the two rounds they changed their choice, or decided to go and vote. ; Interest: matters close to them, such as the economy and corruption scandals. ; Worry: the opposition of the two camps growing deeper. ; Basis: the Associated Press: in Minas Gerais, Lula was 6 points behind in the first round and 1 point ahead in the second.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Flávio charged that the extension was fraud. But his own side had also asked for the extension, and the court president who came out to say it had no effect is a man Bolsonaro appointed.
Trump questioned the election and also said he “likes Lula.” The Brazilian government rebutted him and, at the same time, said it wanted to negotiate with the United States.
Lula won the presidency. What he faces is an electorate split almost in half.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The legal room for overturning the result is small. But the posture of not conceding will carry into the new term, and it will affect the mood at home and the talks with the United States.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Claims such as “the first time a second-place finisher overturned the result” come from the way the press counts it.
The specific grounds of the passport order are not yet complete in the public reporting.

pieces.title: A swan-neck flask, and lab notes locked away for decades: Louis Pasteur
pieces.short: Louis Pasteur
pieces.hook: Let the result speak for itself: in the argument over whether life can simply appear on its own, the swan-neck flask rested on a flask of broth that did not spoil, and…
pieces.takeaway: Let the result speak for itself: in the argument over whether life can simply appear on its own, the swan-neck flask rested on a flask of broth that did not spoil, not on a loud voice.
pieces.imageAlt: Portrait of Pasteur
pieces.imageCredit: Paul Nadar · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On December 27, 1822, Pasteur was born in Dole, in the Jura of France. His father was a poor tanner. As a boy his schoolwork was ordinary, and he preferred drawing and fishing.
In 1841 he sat the entrance exam for the École Normale Supérieure in Paris for the first time, and failed. He sat it again in 1843, placed well up the list, and got in.

paras.lead: Left and right in a crystal
parts: In 1848, working with crystals of tartaric acid, he found that one and the same molecule can take two forms that mirror each other, a “left hand” and a “right hand.” It was the first proof that molecules have “chirality.”

In 1854 he went to Lille as dean of the faculty of science, and left the line that became famous: “Chance favors only the prepared mind.” In 1856 a beet-alcohol maker came to him for help. From then on he studied fermentation, and published the results in 1857–58.

paras.lead: A flask of broth that did not spoil
parts: Many people at the time believed in “spontaneous generation”: that rotting matter would grow life of itself. He bent the neck of a flask into a swan’s neck. Air could enter, but dust lodged in the bend, and broth that had been boiled never spoiled. In 1862 he received the Alhumbert Prize for it.
In 1865 he took out a patent for treating the “sickness” of wine: heat the wine, and kill the microbes that were causing the trouble. That became what is now called “pasteurization.”

paras.lead: A public trial on a farm
parts: On May 5, 1881, at the farm of Pouilly-le-Fort, he ran a public trial of an anthrax vaccine on sheep, goats, and cattle. On June 2, more than 200 spectators saw that the vaccinated animals had survived.

On July 6, 1885, Joseph Meister, a boy of 9 who had been bitten by a mad dog, was brought in. Pasteur was not a practicing physician. The physician Grancher did the work, giving 13 injections over 11 days, and the child lived.

In 1886 he treated 350 people, and only 1 developed the disease. On November 14, 1888, the Pasteur Institute opened. As early as 1878 he had told his family not to publish the laboratory notes. The notes were given to the Bibliothèque nationale de France in 1964, and opened only after 1971.

In 1995 the historian Geison published The Private Science of Louis Pasteur, setting out the discrepancies above. The Nobel laureate Perutz and others wrote in his defense. Pasteur died on September 28, 1895. Of his five children, three died young, two of them of typhoid.

blocks.title: Saving the silkworms also took a wrong turn
blocks.text: From 1865 to 1870 he studied silkworm disease at Alès, in the south of France. At first he denied that pébrine was caused by a parasite, and only later changed his mind. In 1868 he had a stroke, and the left side of his body was paralyzed.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Pasteur himself | View: microbes cause fermentation and disease, and that can be shown by experiment and prevented by vaccine. ; Interest: scientific reputation, research funds, and the institute that came later. ; Worry: rivals getting there first, or taking the credit. ; Basis: the swan-neck flask experiment won a prize in 1862; in 1881 he chose a public trial; in 1878 he told his family not to publish the notes.

Peers and rivals (Koch, Toussaint, Béchamp) | View: each person’s methods and discoveries ought to be recognized. ; Interest: priority of discovery, and academic standing. ; Worry: the credit being taken entirely by Pasteur’s side. ; Basis: from 1881 to 1883 he debated Koch of Germany in public; the notes show the anthrax vaccine method was close to that of the veterinarian Toussaint; the chemist Béchamp disputed priority with him for years.

Assistants and physicians (Roux, Chamberland, Grancher) | View: treatment should meet medical standards, and the assistants’ contribution should be seen. ; Interest: professional duty, and credit in publication. ; Worry: rushing to use it on a person when the animal trials were not enough. ; Basis: Meister was inoculated by the physician Grancher; Roux refused to take part in this treatment; the anthrax vaccine used Chamberland’s method.

Patients and the public | View: saving a life is what matters. ; Interest: a chance of treatment. ; Worry: the risk of the treatment itself. ; Basis: in 1886, 350 people were treated and 1 developed the disease; the institute was then built.

Historians of science | View: the picture of Pasteur should rest on the original notes. ; Interest: recovering what happened, and explaining how science works. ; Worry: judging the practice of that time by today’s ethics, or, the other way, covering for him. ; Basis: the notes were opened after 1971; in 1995 Geison’s book raised the doubts, and Perutz and others answered them.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Pasteur needed public trials to win the public and the funding, and he did not want the notes published. The gap between those two practices became the source of the later dispute.
He was not a physician. The rabies treatment could not go ahead without a doctor’s hands. Whether a doctor took part decided whether this risk could be taken.
The priority disputes with Koch and Béchamp made both sides more eager to publish first.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: By the standard of the time, this risk saved a child. By the rules of a clinical trial today, the number of animal trials and the procedure for consent would both be questioned. The two standards are hard to set side by side.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Whether Meister would have developed the disease if he had not been treated cannot be known for certain.
Reading the notes depends on a few scholars, and the disagreement between Geison and his critics is still there.

pieces.title: It struck at a touch, and it once killed: two hundred years of the match
pieces.short: Two hundred years of the match
pieces.hook: Behind a product that is “cheap and handy,” someone may be paying the price: white-phosphorus matches would strike anywhere, and the price fell on the workers’ jaws…
pieces.takeaway: Behind a product that is “cheap and handy,” someone may be paying the price: white-phosphorus matches would strike anywhere, and the price fell on the workers’ jawbones, until reporting, a strike, and a ban put it on the table.
pieces.imageAlt: Matchboxes at the Jönköping Match Museum
pieces.imageCredit: Clemensfranz · CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

paras.lead: The “light-bringer” of more than a thousand years ago
parts: Around the year 950, Tao Gu recorded in Qingyi lu a kind of small pine stick dipped in sulfur, called a “light-bringer.” It caught only if it touched an existing flame. By the Southern Song, people were already selling them on the streets of Hangzhou.
On April 7, 1827, the English pharmacist John Walker sold the first box of friction matches, but he did not take out a patent. Others copied them quickly, and gave them the name “Lucifer.”

Around 1830, the Frenchman Sauria put white phosphorus into the match head. A strike anywhere would light it, and it was cheap. But white phosphorus is poisonous. In 1845 a physician reported “phossy jaw” for the first time: the workers’ jawbones died, and in severe cases it killed them.

In 1844 Pasch proposed putting the red phosphorus on the striking surface at the side of the box, so the match head itself contained no phosphorus. The Lundström brothers of Jönköping, in Sweden, took out the patent in 1855, and by 1858 were turning out about 12 million boxes a year.

paras.lead: Women workers take to the street
parts: On June 23, 1888, Annie Besant wrote in the weekly The Link, exposing the conditions of the match women at Bryant & May in London. In July the women struck, and later formed a union.

paras.lead: The ban came step by step
parts: In September 1906 several European countries signed a convention at Bern banning white phosphorus. Britain legislated in 1908. The United States switched to a heavy tax in 1913. China did not ban it until 1925.

The Swede Kreuger formed Swedish Match in 1917, lending money to governments in exchange for match monopolies. By 1930 he had lent about $387 million, and controlled about 60% of world output. After his death in 1932 the empire broke up, and by 1938 the share was down to two tenths.

According to a 2025 report in The New Indian Express, the Sivakasi area of Tamil Nadu in India has about 300 factories, supporting about 300,000 people directly and indirectly, and more than 9 in 10 of the workers are women.

When raw materials rose in price, the makers did not raise the price. They cut the count: a box went from 50 sticks to 40, then 35, and now it is 25. Over ten years about 1,000 hand-packing workshops closed. A fully automatic plant, with 30 people, can do the work of a manual plant with 150.

paras.lead: Lighters, and a giant steps away
parts: According to DT Next, a lighter costing 5–10 rupees can stand in for about 20 boxes of matches, and local match sales have fallen by about 70%. In March 2026 Philip Morris sold the parent company of the Brazilian match brand Fiat Lux to local investors, saying it fitted the direction of its “smoke-free future.”

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Match manufacturers and capital | View: push the cost down with cheaper materials and with machines. ; Interest: profit, and market share. ; Worry: bans, higher prices, and substitutes. ; Basis: white-phosphorus matches spread because they were cheap; Kreuger traded loans for monopolies; Indian makers cut each box from 50 sticks to 25.

Workers (most of them women) | View: the work should be safe, and the wage should be enough to live on. ; Interest: health, and a livelihood. ; Worry: poisoning, or being replaced by machines. ; Basis: the London women struck in 1888; more than 9 in 10 of the workers in Tamil Nadu are women, and about 1,000 hand workshops closed over ten years.

Governments and international bodies | View: use the law to restrain a dangerous material, and also protect the local industry. ; Interest: public health, employment, and tax revenue. ; Worry: a ban leaving the home product at a price disadvantage. ; Basis: the Bern convention of 1906; the national bans were nearly twenty years apart; in 2025 the finance minister of Tamil Nadu said the state would try to ban the sale of lighters.

Substitutes, and the tobacco giants | View: a tool for making fire can be more convenient. ; Interest: the lighter market; Philip Morris turning toward smoke-free products. ; Worry: the match business dragging on the shift. ; Basis: according to DT Next, one lighter stands in for about 20 boxes of matches; in March 2026 Philip Morris sold its Brazilian match business.

Consumers | View: cheap and convenient is enough. ; Interest: price, and safety. ; Worry: matches growing fewer, and harder to buy. ; Basis: the count in a box shrank while the price stayed put; the fall in sales shows that quite a few people have switched to lighters.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: White phosphorus was cheap, so manufacturers had a reason to use it. Bans came country by country, and a country that banned first feared losing its market to one that banned later, which is why a multi-country arrangement such as the Bern convention was needed.
Indian manufacturers want the government to ban the sale of lighters, and they also use machines to cut the workforce. The workers’ livelihood is squeezed from both sides.
Kreuger traded loans for monopolies. Governments got the money, and competition was shut out.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Jobs in the match industry are concentrated in a few places. Banning the sale of lighters can protect the work, but it limits what consumers can choose. The two interests are hard to look after at once.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Figures such as the “about 70%” fall in Indian sales come from people in the trade, and there is no official count.
The price Philip Morris got for the Brazilian business has not been made public.

pieces.title: Cabins filled to 112%, and resorts going up on shore: Royal Caribbean’s third quarter
pieces.short: Royal Caribbean’s third quarter
pieces.hook: To read a company’s growth, first separate “selling more” from “selling dearer”: Royal Caribbean’s revenue rose 9% this quarter,…
pieces.takeaway: To read a company’s growth, first separate “selling more” from “selling dearer”: Royal Caribbean’s revenue rose 9% this quarter, while net revenue per berth rose only 0.9%.
pieces.event: October 27, 2026 (Royal Caribbean Group reports third-quarter results)
pieces.imageAlt: The cruise ship Icon of the Seas
pieces.imageCredit: Chakie2 · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 27, Royal Caribbean Group reported third-quarter results: revenue of $5.591 billion, up 9%; adjusted earnings per share of $6.57, above the analysts’ average estimate of $6.38. Revenue was about $10 million short of expectations, and the share price still rose about 7% before the open.

[Where the 112% comes from (the facts)] The cruise business counts a standard berth as two people to a cabin. Occupancy above 100% means that quite a few cabins took a third or a fourth guest. On the earnings call, management said the flagship Icon of the Seas reached occupancy of 133%.
Ticket revenue was $3.885 billion, up about 7% from a year earlier. Onboard spending and other revenue was $1.706 billion, up about 14%, about twice the pace of the tickets.

[Not much more earned per guest (the facts)] “Net yield,” the measure of net revenue per berth, rose only 0.9% (0.6% at constant currency). Over the same period capacity rose 8%, and the company carried about 2.68 million guests.
Fuel this quarter cost $347 million, against $297 million a year earlier. The company expects fuel for the full year of about $1.35 billion, and 58% of the fourth quarter’s fuel has been hedged.

paras.lead: The money comes in first, and the debt comes with it
parts: Deposits guests have paid ahead come to $6.034 billion. On the other side, long-term and short-term debt together come to about $22.36 billion, with $7.4 billion of liquidity on hand.

The company plans to buy half of the Caribbean all-inclusive resort brands Sandals and Beaches for about $3 billion, 18 resorts in all, and expects to close early in 2027. The chief executive, Liberty, said the company now captures only 20%–25% of what a guest spends on vacation in a year, and that adding the resorts could reach about half.

paras.lead: Inference: what the growth rests on
parts: On the figures above, the growth in revenue comes more from more ships, more people, and more spending on board. The rise in the ticket price itself is comparatively limited. That is an inference from the published figures. The company has not split them out this way.

On the earnings call, Liberty said guests are not comparing them with other cruise lines. They are comparing them with a vacation on land. Buying the resorts can be read as widening the competition from the sea to the shore.

In May 2026 the Mexican environment ministry withheld approval, citing the risk to mangroves, coral reefs, and an underground aquifer. The public consultation drew 14,411 comments. In October the Supreme Court of Mexico took up again a lawsuit over the change of land use there.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The company’s management | View: demand is strong, and growth can continue by “adding capacity in moderation, raising prices in moderation, and holding costs tight.” ; Interest: growing profit, the share price, and a larger share of the “vacation wallet.” ; Worry: fuel, exchange rates, and geopolitical events. ; Basis: bookings for 2027 sailings are up year over year by a figure “in the high teens of percentage points”; the full-year outlook was raised; on the call they said fuel and exchange rates are still a headwind.

Investors and analysts | View: profit above expectations, and a raised outlook, are good news. ; Interest: the share price, and the return. ; Worry: the pressure of fuel and of debt, and a valuation that looks high. ; Basis: the share price rose about 7% before the open; revenue was a little below the expected $5.61 billion; before the release, 24/7 Wall St. flagged the risk under the headline “the debt anchor.”

The Mexican environment ministry, and local opponents | View: the project would harm mangroves, coral reefs, and the aquifer. ; Interest: ecological protection, and the public interest. ; Worry: a protected area being developed, and the gains from tourism not reaching the place itself. ; Basis: approval was withheld in May 2026, listing several environmental effects for which no mitigation had been offered; 14,411 public comments.

The Stewart family, of Sandals | View: bring in capital and technology, and keep the brand independent. ; Interest: expanding the resorts, and the family brand. ; Worry: cruise traffic watering the brand down. ; Basis: they keep the other half of the equity; Liberty said the ships would not be brought to the door of a Sandals resort to ferry guests.

Guests | View: they are willing to pay more for a better experience. ; Interest: value for money, and the experience. ; Worry: more and more extras being added on board. ; Basis: onboard spending rose about 14%; management said half the guests are millennials or younger, and short itineraries are a larger share.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Management uses deposits paid ahead, and borrowed money, to build new ships and buy resorts. Investors like the profit, and they are also watching more than $22 billion of debt.
The company wants to expand in Mexico. The environment ministry and local residents hold the approvals and the public argument, and the lawsuit at the Supreme Court has added another variable.
The Sandals deal has to satisfy Royal Caribbean’s aim of “cross-selling” and the Stewart family’s demand that the brand stay independent, at the same time.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Ever larger ships, and ever more destinations, have no ready balance with protecting the Caribbean coast and with local resentment of too much tourism. In its risk factors the company itself lists “growing anti-tourism sentiment.”

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “Onboard spending was stronger than expected” comes from what management said, and an outsider cannot check it item by item.
The “several hundred million dollars” of benefit from working with Sandals is only management’s estimate, and the deal is not yet closed.

pieces.title: Acknowledging the “suffering,” but no apology and no reparations: the British king’s Caribbean tour and the argument over reparations
pieces.short: The British king’s Caribbean tour and reparations…
pieces.hook: On October 27, King Charles III of the United Kingdom arrived in the Bahamas and began a nine-day Caribbean tour. It is his…
pieces.event: October 27, 2026 (Charles III arrives in the Bahamas and begins the Caribbean tour); October 22–27, statements from the various sides
pieces.imageAlt: Charles III
pieces.imageCredit: The White House · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 27, King Charles III of the United Kingdom arrived in the Bahamas and began a nine-day Caribbean tour, his first visit to the region as monarch since his accession. According to the BBC, he is expected to say that acknowledging “the immense suffering of the past” is “the right thing to do.”

On the British government’s position, this trip will bring no formal apology, and it will not discuss reparations. The king is a constitutional monarch, and a statement of this kind has to stay in line with the government.

After the Bahamas he goes to Guyana, with the emphasis on the environment, and then to Antigua and Barbuda, for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting from November 1 to 4, and he will speak at the opening on November 3.

Hilary Beckles, chair of the CARICOM Reparations Commission, has called this meeting a “reparations summit,” and said there would be no deliberate attempt to embarrass the king. In July of this year, CARICOM adopted a revised “ten-point plan for reparations.”

The communiqué of the 2024 Samoa summit said: “The time has come for a meaningful, truthful, and mutually respectful conversation,” so as to build a shared future on a fair footing. The British prime minister at the time, Starmer, said the matter was “not about the money.” Charles said that no one can change the past.
The president of Guyana, Ali, hopes the talks will produce progress, and that the first step is an apology. The Commonwealth secretary-general, Botchwey, said an apology “would do no harm.”

According to The Guardian, the Labour member of Parliament Ribeiro-Addy said: “The king of the Netherlands apologized, and their world did not collapse.” The scholar Beckford has proposed a truth and reconciliation commission.

paras.lead: It is not on the agenda
parts: The Guardian says reparations are not on the summit’s formal agenda. O'Marde, a member of the Reparations Commission, said there are only some side events. The Rastafari leader McKinney is organizing a protest.

paras.lead: A form of words worth noticing
parts: The British side speaks of “acknowledging the suffering.” The Caribbean side wants an “apology” and “reparatory justice.” The official theme of the summit is “accelerating partnerships and investment, for a prosperous Commonwealth.” At one and the same meeting, the parties are pressing different points.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The British government | View: history can be acknowledged, but there will be no apology and no reparations, and the weight goes on cooperation turned toward the future. ; Interest: fiscal and legal risk, and the relationship with the Commonwealth. ; Worry: an apology being taken as an acceptance of legal liability, and drawing claims for reparations. ; Basis: the BBC reports that this trip is in line with the government’s position; in 2024 Starmer said it was “not about the money.”

Charles III and the royal household | View: as head of the Commonwealth, express an acknowledgment of history. ; Interest: the standing of the monarchy, and the cohesion of the Commonwealth. ; Worry: protests and a cold reception, or stepping past what the government has authorized. ; Basis: he is expected to say that acknowledging the suffering is “the right thing to do”; in 2021, in Barbados, he spoke of “the darkest days”; the 2022 Caribbean tour by the Prince and Princess of Wales drew criticism.

CARICOM and its Reparations Commission | View: Britain should apologize, and open a substantive dialogue on reparatory justice. ; Interest: development funds, debt, and historical acknowledgment. ; Worry: the subject being passed over once again with a courteous form of words. ; Basis: the revised ten-point plan was approved in July 2026; Beckles called it a “reparations summit,” and called on the king to support the dialogue as a “brother of the human family.”

The Commonwealth Secretariat | View: let the dialogue move, and at the same time hold the summit’s agenda of cooperation. ; Interest: the unity of the organization, and its presence. ; Worry: member countries splitting over this issue. ; Basis: Botchwey said an apology “would do no harm”; the official theme is partnership and investment, and reparations are not on the agenda.

Advocates in Britain and locally | View: the monarchy and the government should apologize, or set up a truth and reconciliation mechanism. ; Interest: historical justice, and the claims of communities. ; Worry: the king’s visit amounting to nothing but ceremony. ; Basis: Ribeiro-Addy cited the apology by the king of the Netherlands; Beckford proposed a truth and reconciliation commission; McKinney is organizing a protest.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: What the king may say is bound by the government’s position. The Caribbean side places its hopes on the king, while the British government holds the decision.
Caribbean countries need British investment and cooperation, and they also have to answer demands for reparations at home. The summit’s theme and the demand for reparations sit at the same table.
The Secretariat has to answer the member countries and also keep a single issue from filling the agenda, so reparations appear only in side events.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: There is one step between “acknowledging the suffering” and an “apology,” and another between an “apology” and “reparations.” The British side fears that the earlier step will be taken as the ground for the later one. The Caribbean side holds that without the earlier step there is no conversation to be had.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: What the king will say comes, for now, from press previews of the speech. The formal address on November 3 has not yet been given.
On the concrete form and the sum of any reparations, the public reporting contains no plan that the parties have agreed.

pieces.title: A machine that was never built, and the “first program” written for it: Ada Lovelace
pieces.short: Ada Lovelace
pieces.hook: See what a tool can do beyond the use in front of you: everyone was fixed on “doing arithmetic,” and she wrote down “handling symbols.”
pieces.takeaway: See what a tool can do beyond the use in front of you: everyone was fixed on “doing arithmetic,” and she wrote down “handling symbols.”
pieces.imageAlt: Daguerreotype of Ada Lovelace
pieces.imageCredit: Antoine Claudet · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On December 10, 1815, Ada was born in London. Her father was the poet Byron. About five weeks after the birth, her mother, Annabella, took her back to her own family’s house. Byron soon left Britain for good, and when he died in 1824 Ada was only 8.

paras.lead: Using mathematics to “keep” the imagination in hand
parts: Her mother feared the daughter would be “mad” as the father had been, and set her to mathematics early. Among her tutors were the science writer Somerville and the mathematician De Morgan.

paras.lead: At twelve she wanted to fly
parts: In February 1828, at 12, she set about designing wings, comparing paper, oiled silk, and feathers, studying the proportions of a bird’s body, and planning a book to be called Flyology. After measles in 1829 she was paralyzed and kept to her bed for nearly a year. Only in 1831 could she walk with a crutch.

On June 5, 1833, Ada, then 17, met the mathematician Charles Babbage at an evening party. A few weeks later she went to see the prototype of his “Difference Engine.” Babbage later called her, in a letter, “the Enchantress of Numbers.”

paras.lead: The translation was only a quarter
parts: In 1842 the Italian engineer Menabrea published, in French, a record of Babbage’s lectures on the “Analytical Engine.” Ada spent 9 months turning it into English, and added seven notes, A through G, about three times as long as the translation. It appeared in September 1843, signed “AAL.”

Note G sets out, step by step, how to use the Analytical Engine to compute the “Bernoulli numbers,” and it has often since been called “the first computer program to be published.” But the Analytical Engine was never built, and the program was never run.

She wrote that if the relations among pitches could be expressed in symbols, the machine “might compose elaborate and scientific pieces of music of any degree of complexity or extent.” Swade, a specialist on Babbage, says the shift from “computing numbers” to “handling symbols by a rule” is something she set down plainly in this paper.

The historian Bromley pointed out that Babbage had already written dozens of sample programs for the Analytical Engine in 1837–1840, that nearly all the programs in the notes were his, and that Ada found an error in one of them. In his autobiography Babbage also said the Bernoulli-number algorithm was his.

In the 1840s she took to betting on horses, and lost more than 3,000 pounds. In 1851 she tried again to stake a large sum on a mathematical model, and ended several thousand pounds in debt. On November 27, 1852, she died of cancer, at 36, and was buried beside her father, as she had asked.

In 1953 her notes were reprinted, and drew attention again. In 1980 a programming language of the U.S. Department of Defense was named “Ada,” and the military standard number MIL-STD-1815 was taken from the year of her birth. Since 2009, the second Tuesday of every October has been “Ada Lovelace Day.”

blocks.title: “Lady Lovelace’s objection”
blocks.text: She also wrote that the Analytical Engine “has no pretensions whatever to originate anything,” and can do only what we know how to order it to do. In 1950, in a paper on whether machines can think, Turing named this objection after her and answered it.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Ada herself | View: the Analytical Engine was not only a calculator. It could handle anything that can be expressed in symbols, but it would not “originate” anything on its own. ; Interest: publishing under her own name as author, and what she called “poetical science.” ; Worry: being taken for nothing more than an aristocratic young woman trading on her father’s fame. ; Basis: in 1843 the notes appeared signed AAL; when Babbage wanted to attach his own statement as an unsigned preface, she refused to withdraw the paper.

Babbage | View: the Analytical Engine was his invention, and he needed someone to explain it and to win support. ; Interest: funding and recognition for the Analytical Engine from the government and from scholars. ; Worry: the machine going ununderstood, and getting no money. ; Basis: he asked Ada to write the translation and the notes, and called her “the Enchantress of Numbers”; in his autobiography he said the Bernoulli-number algorithm was his.

Skeptical historians (Bromley, Collier) | View: the claim of “the first programmer” does not fit the record. ; Interest: recovering, from the original manuscripts and letters, who did what. ; Worry: a commemorative story taking the place of what happened. ; Basis: dozens of sample programs by Babbage in 1837–1840, earlier than the notes; her correspondence with Babbage.

Scholars who credit her (Swade, Wolfram) | View: her contribution was to see the generality of the machine, and to write the abstract principle clearly. ; Interest: explaining how the idea of “computation” took shape. ; Worry: judging only by “who wrote the first line of code,” and missing a contribution of thought. ; Basis: the passages in the notes on music and on symbols; Wolfram’s analysis of her manuscripts (Idea Makers).

Those who commemorate her later (the U.S. Department of Defense, the organizers of Ada Lovelace Day) | View: she is an emblematic figure in the history of computing, and for women in science and technology. ; Interest: finding a figure that new work, and women in technology, can identify with. ; Worry: being criticized for reducing a historical person to a symbol. ; Basis: the Ada language was named in 1980; since 2009 the aim of Ada Lovelace Day has been “to raise new role models for girls and women.”

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Babbage needed her writing and her name to publicize the machine. She needed Babbage’s machine in order to put her mathematics to work. The two of them clashed over the signature on the preface, and later made it up.
A commemoration needs a clear “first.” Skeptical historians insist on the manuscripts. The two sides define “contribution” differently.
In 1950 Turing answered her objection, so her name also appears in the discussion of “whether machines can think.”

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: There is no single standard for whether “writing a program” and “publishing a program, and explaining the principle” count as the same kind of contribution.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The Analytical Engine was never built, and the program in Note G was never run. Whether it is correct can only be worked out by later people.
Many of their discussions were face to face, and only part of the correspondence survives, so the detail of who did what is hard to recover in full.

pieces.title: From tree sap to synthetic rubber: a hundred and fifty years of a stick of chewing gum
pieces.short: A hundred and fifty years of a stick of chewing gum
pieces.hook: At Kierikki in Finland, a piece of birch-bark tar “chewing gum” about 5,000 years old has been dug up, and it still has tooth marks.
pieces.imageAlt: A 1928 Wrigley chewing-gum advertisement
pieces.imageCredit: Wrigley Company advertisement (scanned and uploaded by Don O’Brien) · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

paras.lead: Tooth marks from five thousand years ago
parts: At Kierikki in Finland, a piece of birch-bark tar “chewing gum” about 5,000 years old has been dug up, and it still has tooth marks. The ancient Greeks chewed mastic resin. The Maya and the Aztecs chewed the gum of the sapodilla tree, called chicle, from a Nahuatl word for “sticky stuff.”

In 1848 the American John Curtis began selling “State of Maine Pure Spruce Gum,” the first commercial chewing gum. Around 1850, gum made of paraffin overtook it. There was no sweetness then, and people chewed it while dipping it in powdered sugar.

paras.lead: The rubber that did not work out
parts: In the 1860s the former president of Mexico, Santa Anna, brought chicle to New York and handed it to the inventor Thomas Adams, hoping to make a substitute for rubber. It did not work. Adams cut it into strips, and in 1871 began selling “Adams’ New York Gum.”

paras.lead: The free gift sold better than the goods
parts: In 1891 William Wrigley Jr., aged 29, arrived in Chicago with $32 to sell soap, and later switched to baking powder, giving two packs of chewing gum with each can. The gum turned out more popular than the baking powder, so he changed trades altogether. In 1893 he brought out Juicy Fruit.

paras.lead: It went out into the world with the soldiers
parts: In the Second World War, chewing gum went into American military rations, and soldiers traded it with local people wherever they were. Wrigley gave the army its entire output of Spearmint, Doublemint, and Juicy Fruit.

paras.lead: The tree gave way to the chemical plant
parts: After Guatemala’s land reform in 1952, Wrigley stopped buying local chicle, and it had been the only buyer there. By the 1960s most American makers had switched to cheaper butadiene-based synthetic rubber. Today only a few small brands still use natural gum.

paras.lead: The first thing a scanner ever read
parts: On June 26, 1974, a supermarket in Ohio made the first barcode scan at a checkout in the United States. What it scanned was a 10-stick pack of Juicy Fruit.

After the Singapore metro opened in 1987, people stuck chewing gum on the door sensors. The doors would not close, and the people were hard to catch. From January 3, 1992, Singapore banned the import and sale of chewing gum. Chewing itself is not illegal. From 2004, pharmacists may sell gum for dental use and for giving up smoking.

In the early 2000s, chewing-gum sales in the United States fell. Some put it down to the phone: people look down at a screen while they wait in line, and the impulse to pick up a pack is weaker. During the pandemic, U.S. sales fell again, by about 30%.

paras.lead: Higher prices made up the difference
parts: In 2023, U.S. chewing-gum sales returned to the pre-pandemic level, mainly because the average price of a pack had risen $1.01 from 2018, to $2.71. Global volume was 10% below 2018.

In 2008 Mars bought Wrigley for about $23 billion. On October 2, 2023, Mondelez sold its chewing-gum business in North America and Europe, including Trident and Dentyne, to Perfetti Van Melle, the Italian-Dutch company that makes Mentos.

blocks.title: The pink was an accident
blocks.text: In 1928 Walter Diemer, an accountant at the Fleer company in Philadelphia, tried out a recipe that was not too sticky and could be stretched. That was bubble gum. The original mix was a dull gray. The only coloring he had to hand was red, and so bubble gum became pink.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The confectionery giants (Mars Wrigley, Perfetti Van Melle, Mondelez) | View: chewing gum is a mature category, to be held up by brand, pricing, and the channel. ; Interest: profit margin, and a place on the shelf. ; Worry: falling volume, and less impulse buying at the checkout. ; Basis: Mars bought Wrigley in 2008; in 2023 Mondelez sold its chewing-gum business in North America and Europe; from 2018 to 2023 the average U.S. price rose $1.01.

City managers (the government of Singapore, as an example) | View: gum residue brings cleaning costs and broken equipment. ; Interest: public facilities that work, and the cost of maintaining them. ; Worry: the ban being criticized as overreach. ; Basis: Lee Kuan Yew’s memoir says a ban on sales was proposed as early as 1983, and he thought it “too drastic” at the time; after metro doors were stuck in 1987, the ban took effect in 1992.

The producing regions, and the tappers | View: natural gum was once an important source of income. ; Interest: a steady buyer, and a price. ; Worry: when the only large buyer leaves, the livelihood goes with it. ; Basis: after Wrigley stopped buying Guatemalan chicle in 1952, the local government had to put out large-scale aid for the tappers.

Oral health, and medicine | View: sugar-free gum has some use, but it cannot take the place of brushing. ; Interest: oral hygiene, and therapeutic uses such as giving up smoking. ; Worry: sugared gum bringing a risk of cavities. ; Basis: from 2004 Singapore allowed pharmacists to sell dental gum and nicotine gum; xylitol and saliva research cited in the Chinese Wikipedia entry on chewing gum.

Consumers | View: people chew gum to freshen the breath, to pass the time, or to wake themselves up. ; Interest: price, flavor, and being able to buy it easily. ; Worry: rising prices, and a change in shopping habits. ; Basis: some attribute the fall in volume to phones reducing impulse buys at the checkout; during the pandemic people went out less and socialized less, and demand fell.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Makers hold up the sales figure by raising the price, and consumers answer by buying less. That is one reason falling volume and flat sales can sit side by side.
City managers put the cleaning cost down to chewing gum, and makers and consumers bear the cost of a ban or a fine.
Once makers switched to a synthetic base, the cost was lower and the supply steadier, while the regions that produced natural gum lost their main buyer.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Who pays to clean up the residue: the person who spat it out, the producer, or the taxpayer. Places do it differently.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “Phones reduced impulse buying” is one explanation, and there is no direct study of the cause.
Whether the lump of birch tar from 5,000 years ago was “chewed for the sake of chewing” can only be inferred from the tooth marks.

pieces.title: The guests came back, and the profit got thinner: Chipotle’s third-quarter “account of the new stores”
pieces.short: Chipotle’s third quarter…
pieces.hook: After the U.S. market closed on October 28, the burrito chain Chipotle reported third-quarter results:…
pieces.imageAlt: A Chipotle store
pieces.imageCredit: Phillip Pessar · CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: After the U.S. market closed on October 28, the burrito chain Chipotle reported third-quarter results: revenue of $3.29 billion, up 9.6%; same-store sales up 2.1%, above the analysts’ average estimate of 1.4% (Reuters, citing LSEG).

paras.lead: But it earned less per share
parts: Adjusted earnings per share were $0.27, 6.9% less than a year earlier, and also below the expected $0.29. Even so, the share price still rose about 4% after hours. Bloomberg had reported earlier that the stock is down 24% this year, near a three-year low.

paras.lead: The revenue rests mainly on new stores
parts: The company said the growth in revenue came mainly from newly opened stores, and that same-store growth was secondary. This quarter it opened 84 company-owned stores, 53 of them with a “Chipotlane,” a lane where a customer who ordered online drives up and collects the food.

paras.lead: The guests came back a little
parts: Of the 2.1% same-store growth, the average check contributed 1.3% and traffic contributed 0.8%. The chief executive, Boatwright, said this was the third quarter in a row of rising traffic. Digital orders were 38.8% of food and beverage revenue, against 36.7% a year earlier.

Restaurant-level margin fell from 24.5% to 23.3%, and operating margin from 15.9% to 13.7%. Food and packaging fell from 30.0% to 29.5% of revenue, on price increases and tariff relief. Labor rose from 25.2% to 25.7%, and general and administrative expenses from $147 million to $185 million (stock-based pay and bonuses).

Reuters reported that promotions, member marketing, and limited-time items such as “honey chicken” brought traffic, and that younger customers who prefer high-protein meals are also increasing. But consumers are tightening their spending, and an earlier multi-state outbreak of cyclosporiasis also weighed on confidence.

The week before the results, a TD Cowen analyst cut the rating from “buy” to “hold,” worried about a weak start to the fourth quarter and too much dependence on promotions. Bloomberg’s data show that, of the analysts covering the stock, 23 say buy, 12 say hold, and 1 says sell.

The company kept its outlook for low-single-digit same-store growth for the full year, and for 350–370 new stores this year. For 2027 it plans 340–360 new company-owned stores in the United States and Canada.

Opening new stores can hold revenue up, but what each store earns depends on same-store sales and on traffic. Pulling guests back with promotions, while holding the pricing of “premium ingredients,” is the balance Chipotle has to strike next.

blocks.text: On the figures in the release, net profit was down about 11%, while earnings per share were down only 6.9%. The difference comes from buybacks. Over the first nine months the company spent about $1.46 billion buying back stock. Diluted average shares this quarter were about 1.27 billion, against about 1.34 billion a year earlier.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The company’s management | View: the “growth formula” strategy is working, and traffic has risen for three quarters in a row. ; Interest: showing that the new strategy works, and supporting the plan to open stores. ; Worry: the consumer climate turning worse, and promotions losing their effect. ; Basis: Boatwright’s remarks in the earnings release; guidance for 350–370 new stores this year.

The more cautious analysts (TD Cowen) | View: a premium brand is leaning too hard on promotions, and the growth expected for 2027 is on the high side. ; Interest: judging future same-store growth accurately. ; Worry: a weak start to the fourth quarter, and unproven sources of growth such as new equipment and delivery. ; Basis: in late October the rating was cut to “hold,” and the fourth-quarter same-store growth estimate was cut from 4% to 1% (Bloomberg).

The more optimistic investors | View: same-store sales beat expectations and traffic is back, so a slip in profit is acceptable. ; Interest: the share price bouncing off a low. ; Worry: costs keeping on rising, and the margin not coming back. ; Basis: the share price rose about 4% after hours (Reuters); Bloomberg’s data show 23 buy ratings.

Store employees | View: wages and bonuses are rising, and the promotions also need more hands. ; Interest: pay, and the amount of work. ; Worry: being short of staff, or being replaced by equipment meant to raise efficiency. ; Basis: the release says the rise in labor cost comes from wage inflation, performance bonuses, extra staff for the promotions, and insurance; the company is rolling out “high-efficiency equipment.”

Customers | View: willing to pay for fresh ingredients, but more sensitive to price. ; Interest: price, portion, and food safety. ; Worry: a bowl getting more and more expensive, or another food-safety incident. ; Basis: Bloomberg said earlier customer unhappiness with the “high-priced bowl” had dragged sales down; Reuters mentioned that the cyclosporiasis outbreak weighed on confidence.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Management uses promotions to pull customers back. The more cautious analysts worry that this will weaken a premium brand’s power to set prices. Both sides are looking at the same traffic figures.
Price increases and tariff relief pushed down the share taken by ingredients, while wages and bonuses pushed up the share taken by labor. One cost gives way as the other rises.
Buybacks made earnings per share fall by less than net profit. Investors got some support, and the company has less cash on hand.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Whether the return of traffic is a short-term effect of promotions, or customers genuinely coming back, cannot be told from one quarter’s figures.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “Younger customers are increasing” comes from analysts’ views in the reporting. The company has not published the ages of its customers.
How the fourth quarter has opened is, for now, only analysts’ judgment and what was said on the call. The formal figures wait for the next report.

pieces.title: 53, 48, 19: after Israel’s election, no one can muster 61 seats
pieces.short: After Israel’s election, no one can muster …
pieces.hook: On October 27 Israel held a parliamentary election.
pieces.event: Voting on October 27, 2026; preliminary count released on October 28 (as of October 29, ballots were still uncounted)
pieces.imageAlt: The Israeli parliament building
pieces.imageCredit: Clema12 · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 27 Israel held a parliamentary election. As of about October 28, some 88.6% of the ballots had been counted: the governing bloc led by Netanyahu had 53 seats, the opposition bloc led by the former chief of staff Eisenkot had 48, and the Arab parties had 19.
Forming a government takes 61 of the 120 seats. No one has enough.

The “double-envelope” ballots cast by soldiers, diplomats posted abroad, prisoners, and others, about 430,000 to 480,000 of them, still have to be checked and counted separately. Each seat is worth about 40,000 votes, and that can change the seats of particular parties. But according to The Times of Israel, experts think the overall shape is unlikely to flip. The official result is not expected before November 4.
According to The Guardian, turnout this time was close to 78%, the highest since 1999. The Arab parties took 19 seats. The previous record was 15 seats in 2020.

paras.lead: The background: five elections in five years, and then this
parts: From 2019 to 2022, Israel held five elections in a row because it could not form a stable government. The parliament just ending was the first since 1988 to serve out four years.
On September 23 the Central Elections Committee cancelled the right of two Arab parties, Ra'am and the Joint List, to stand. On October 2 the Supreme Court overturned that decision.

paras.lead: The governing bloc: the election was “stolen”
parts: After the preliminary result, Netanyahu said the Arab parties had “stolen the election.” Likud said it had submitted “hundreds of testimonies” to the elections committee and to the security services, but it has not made the evidence public. Officials of the elections committee, according to reports, said there was no sign of violations on a large scale.

whether to work with the Arab parties] As the count came in, Eisenkot declared a “Zionist majority” the winner, and largely ruled out forming a government with the Arab parties. Golan, leader of the Democrats in his bloc, publicly called for talks with Ra'am and the Joint List. Jabareen, leader of the Joint List, said they “cannot be ignored under any circumstances.”

President Herzog said that, once the official result arrives next week, he will begin consulting the parties, and then name one person to form a government within about 6 weeks. If that fails, the chance passes to the rival. He called on the parties to come “with an open mind,” and to do everything possible to avoid another election. Until a new government is formed, the caretaker government led by Netanyahu stays in office.

According to Ynet, Netanyahu has already met the finance minister, Smotrich, and the national security minister, Ben-Gvir. The opposition is considering joining forces first to replace the speaker. The American president, Trump, said his public support before the vote “helped Netanyahu a great deal.”

paras.lead: A way of putting it that is worth watching
parts: The same set of figures can be told two ways. Count the Arab parties with the opposition, and it is 67 to 53. Count only the Jewish parties, and it is 53 to 48. The conclusion about “who won” changes with that. “The election was stolen” is, for now, only an accusation, with no evidence made public. The final seats also wait until the double-envelope ballots are counted.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Netanyahu’s bloc (Likud and its allies) | View: the right holds a majority among “the Zionist public,” and should form a “strong right-wing government.” ; Interest: staying in office, and winning defectors from the other bloc. ; Worry: the opposition joining hands with the Arab parties. ; Basis: Netanyahu said he does not see the election as a defeat; Likud said the election was “stolen” by the Arab parties and demanded an investigation (Wikipedia, The Guardian).

Eisenkot’s bloc (the opposition) | View: the election was a vote of no confidence in Netanyahu, and a “Zionist majority” should form the government. ; Interest: replacing the present government, while holding on to centrist and right-wing voters. ; Worry: working with the Arab parties would lose voters; not working with them leaves too few seats. ; Basis: Eisenkot declared a “Zionist majority” the winner; Golan publicly argued for talks with the Arab parties (The Guardian).

The Arab parties (Ra'am, the Joint List) | View: 19 seats means they cannot be left outside politics. ; Interest: the rights and the representation of Arab citizens. ; Worry: their votes being called “illegitimate,” or being treated as optional. ; Basis: Jabareen said they “cannot be ignored under any circumstances”; before the vote they were disqualified, and the Supreme Court later restored them (Wikipedia).

The president and the election bodies (Herzog, the Central Elections Committee) | View: avoid another election if possible, and finish the count and the consultations by the procedure. ; Interest: the credibility of the result, and a government that can function. ; Worry: a deadlock dragging on, or the count being challenged. ; Basis: Herzog called for an “open mind”; officials of the elections committee said there was no sign of violations on a large scale (INN, ABC, Wikipedia).

The United States (the Trump administration) | View: it supported Netanyahu in public, and thinks that helped him. ; Interest: not spelled out in the public remarks. ; Worry: not spelled out in the public remarks. ; Basis: Trump said his endorsement “helped him a great deal” (The Guardian).

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: To reach 61 seats, the opposition can hardly do without the Arab parties’ support. But once it cooperates, it confirms the governing bloc’s claim that it is “being steered by the Arab parties.”

Netanyahu goes on governing as caretaker. The longer the deadlock, the more time he has to win defectors, or to wait for another election. The Guardian noted that Israelis living abroad who came home to vote may not come back next time.
The president has to choose the person “most likely to form a government.” But both large blocs are well short, and his judgment will itself be read by every side.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Whether the Arab parties’ seats count toward the chance of forming a government decides “who won,” and the parties have no agreement on that.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: All the seat counts are preliminary. The double-envelope ballots have not been counted.

The charge that “the election was stolen” has, for now, no evidence made public. The elections committee says it has not seen violations on a large scale, and the conclusion of any inquiry has not been published.
