pieces.title: Alternating current won, and he moved into a hotel: Nikola Tesla
pieces.short: Nikola Tesla
pieces.hook: For a good idea to become something large, it cannot do without a partner willing to put up money for a long time, and able to bear the waiting. The invention alone will not carry it that…
pieces.takeaway: For a good idea to become something large, it cannot do without a partner willing to put up money for a long time, and able to bear the waiting. The invention alone will not carry it that far.
pieces.imageAlt: Portrait of Tesla, about 1890
pieces.imageCredit: Napoleon Sarony · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On July 10, 1856, Tesla was born in the village of Smiljan (now in Croatia). His father was an Orthodox priest. His mother had never been to school, but she could make household tools herself.

paras.lead: A promise that came out of an illness
parts: At 17 he caught cholera and was in bed for nine months. His father promised him: once he recovered, he would be sent to study engineering, not to become a priest.

In 1875 he entered the polytechnic in Graz, and later did not manage to graduate. He left at the end of 1878. After that he worked as an engineer at the telephone exchange in Budapest, and at Edison’s company in Europe, in Paris.

In June 1884 he arrived in New York and joined the Edison Machine Works. He resigned about half a year later. The widely told story that a “$50,000 bonus was a joke” comes from his own later recollection, and there is no other witness.

In 1886 the investors formed another company and left behind the one named for him. His patents, exchanged for shares, passed out of his control, and he got by on ditch-digging at $2 a day. The next year he and new partners founded the Tesla Electric Company.

In May 1888 he received a patent for an alternating-current induction motor, and demonstrated it at the American Institute of Electrical Engineers. In July, Westinghouse bought the license: $60,000, plus a royalty of $2.50 per horsepower, and hired him as a consultant at $2,000 a month.

paras.lead: He gave up the royalty himself
parts: In 1891 Westinghouse was short of money, and Tesla agreed to give up the royalty calculated by the horsepower. In 1897 Westinghouse paid him a lump sum of $216,000 to buy out the patents. The lighting at the Chicago world’s fair in 1893 was Westinghouse alternating current.

paras.lead: A tower that was never finished
parts: In 1901 the banker Morgan put up $150,000 in exchange for 51% of the interest in his wireless patents, and he began building the Wardenclyffe Tower on Long Island. In December of the same year, Marconi was the first to send the letter “S” from Britain to Newfoundland.

Wall Street’s money flowed toward Marconi, and in 1905 the project stopped. He mortgaged the property to the Waldorf hotel, against about $20,000 in room charges. For years after that he moved from hotel to hotel, often behind on the rent, and in 1923 the St. Regis put him out.

He went every day to feed the pigeons, and said he had spent more than $2,000 on one white pigeon. From 1934 he lived at the Hotel New Yorker. Westinghouse paid him a consultant’s fee of $125 a month, and paid his rent for him.

In 1937 he was injured by a taxi. On January 7, 1943, he died alone in his hotel room, at 86. The same year, the U.S. Supreme Court restored some of the radio patents that he and two other men had held before Marconi. In 1960 the unit of magnetic flux density was named the “tesla.”

blocks.title: The war of the currents
blocks.text: Over the same years, Edison’s company pushed direct current, and claimed that high-voltage alternating current was dangerous. The engineer Brown, with technical help from Edison’s company, electrocuted animals in public, and also helped bring it about that the first electric chair used a Westinghouse alternating-current generator.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Tesla himself | View: alternating current and wireless transmission of power could change the world, and the money in front of him mattered less. ; Interest: turning the idea into a real thing, and being recognized as the inventor. ; Worry: the funds running out, and the credit being taken by someone else. ; Basis: he gave up the Westinghouse royalty; he thought Marconi’s system copied his own; in later years he still wrote to Morgan and his son asking for support.

Westinghouse | View: alternating current was a better business than direct current, and the key patents had to be secured. ; Interest: winning the war of the currents, while controlling the cost of the patents. ; Worry: the royalty wrecking the cash flow, and being swallowed by a rival. ; Basis: the license contract of 1888; in 1891 it asked Tesla to give up the royalty; the $216,000 buyout of 1897; in his later years it paid $125 a month and paid the rent for him.

Edison’s company | View: direct current was safer, and the alternating-current system also infringed its patents. ; Interest: holding on to the direct-current network already laid out. ; Worry: alternating current taking the market by the advantage of sending power a long way. ; Basis: early in 1888 it said in public that high-voltage alternating current was dangerous; it gave Brown technical help with the animal experiments.

The backer, Morgan | View: an investment has to show a return, and wireless communication has to succeed before the rival. ; Interest: the patent interest, and a commercial return. ; Worry: the money going in, and the technology still falling behind Marconi. ; Basis: in 1901, $150,000 for 51% of the patent interest; after Marconi completed the first transatlantic transmission in December 1901, the funds did not continue.

Later commemorators, and historians | View: Tesla’s contribution was undervalued for a long time, and it is also often mythologized. ; Interest: recovering a true history of the technology, or shaping an inventor-hero. ; Worry: legend covering what happened. ; Basis: in 1943 the Supreme Court restored some of his patents; the unit was named in 1960; the “$50,000” story is only his own account.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Westinghouse needed Tesla’s patents to beat Edison, and it also needed him to give ground if it was to survive. Tesla gave up the royalty, and what he got in exchange was Westinghouse going on to spread alternating current.
Morgan’s money set the pace of the Wardenclyffe Tower. Marconi succeeded first, and the investors’ patience went with that.
Later commemoration has made his fame larger and larger. Historians remind us that many of the moving stories come from his own recollection.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Whether giving up the royalty counts as “yielding for the larger cause” or “missing a fortune” depends on how one estimates whether Westinghouse would have failed at the time, and the record does not settle it.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Many details of his quarrel with Edison come only from Tesla’s own telling.
Claims about “how much he could have made if he had not given up the royalty” are all calculations after the fact, with no reliable accounts behind them.

pieces.title: A machine for a year’s income: a hundred and fifty years of the typewriter
pieces.short: A hundred and fifty years of the typewriter
pieces.hook: By one estimate, the typewriter was invented independently 52 times.
pieces.imageAlt: An 1874 Sholes and Glidden typewriter
pieces.imageCredit: Dr. Bernd Gross · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: By one estimate, the typewriter was invented independently 52 times. As early as 1714 the Englishman Henry Mill took out a patent for a machine described in terms very like a typewriter.

paras.lead: The earliest were for the blind
parts: Early in the nineteenth century, the Italian Turri made a writing machine for a blind countess, so she could write her own letters. Quite a few early machines of this kind were designed for blind people.
A record from 1853 says that writing with a pen ran to at most about 30 words a minute, while a stenographer could take down 130. The speed of copying could not keep up with the speed of speech.

The “writing ball” invented by the Danish pastor Hansen went on commercial sale in 1870. It was the first typewriter sold commercially, and it stayed in use in Europe into the early twentieth century.

In 1868 the American newspaperman Sholes, Glidden, and others applied for a typewriter patent in Wisconsin. Later a partner sold his share. Sholes and the backer Densmore went to Remington, which made guns and sewing machines.

On March 1, 1873, Remington began production at Ilion, New York, of the “Sholes and Glidden Type-Writer.” It already used the QWERTY keyboard, but as you typed you could not see the characters just struck.

paras.lead: Why the keyboard is not in alphabetical order
parts: Sholes’s earliest prototype put the keys in alphabetical order. Over the next five years he adjusted it again and again, and Remington’s technicians changed it once more. The reasons given are many. The most widely told, “to keep the type bars from jamming,” may have been made up later.

paras.lead: The shift key, and the woman typist
parts: The Remington No. 2 of 1878 added a shift key, and QWERTY spread with it. Remington assumed from the start that the person typing would be a woman. During the two world wars, more and more women entered the workplace as typists.

On July 31, 1961, IBM brought out the Selectric electric typewriter, replacing the rows of type bars with an interchangeable spherical type head. It later took 75% of the U.S. market for commercial electric typewriters, and by 1986 more than 13 million had been sold.

Chinese has several thousand characters in common use, and there is no way to give each character its own key. In 1914 Zhou Houkun, who had studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, built a prototype that arranged the characters by radical and by stroke on a cylinder. In 1919 the Commercial Press improved it and put it into production.

From the 1980s, personal computers and word-processing software replaced the typewriter. In April 2011 the Godrej company in Mumbai closed its typewriter factory, reported as the last factory in the world making a standard manual typewriter.

blocks.title: One machine, one year’s income
blocks.text: By December 1874 only 400 had been sold. One cost about $125, about a year’s income per person in the United States at the time, and they often broke down. The writer Mark Twain was one of the earliest buyers, and called it “a curious little contraption.”

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Inventors and the early backers (Sholes, Densmore) | View: a machine could speed writing a great deal, and was worth improving steadily. ; Interest: the patents, and sales. ; Worry: not selling, not being repairable, and the money not holding out. ; Basis: Sholes adjusted the keyboard again and again over five years; in 1873 Densmore sold the production rights to Remington.

Manufacturers (Remington, IBM, and others) | View: the typewriter was office equipment that could be made at scale. ; Interest: market share, and the power to set the standard. ; Worry: a product that was expensive and often broke down; later, being replaced by electronic products. ; Basis: by the end of 1874 only 400 had been sold; the Selectric took 75% of U.S. commercial electric typewriters; in 1991 IBM spun off the typewriter business.

Typists (mostly women) | View: typing was a skill that could get a person into the workplace. ; Interest: a job, and an income. ; Worry: being confined to copying work. ; Basis: Remington assumed from the start that the typist would be a woman; during the world wars, women entered employment in large numbers as typists.

Users of Chinese, and the people who improved the machine (Zhou Houkun and others) | View: a Western typewriter does not suit Chinese characters, and another way has to be found. ; Interest: letting Chinese be written by machine as well. ; Worry: a machine too heavy and too slow, and some people arguing that Chinese characters should simply be abolished. ; Basis: Zhou Houkun’s prototype weighed about 18 kilograms; Qian Xuantong argued in New Youth for “abolishing Chinese characters.”

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Manufacturers held the market by the spread of QWERTY. Later arrivals might have other keyboard designs, but users had already learned the old one.
The typewriter brought women a chance of work, and it also fixed them for a long time in the place of “the copyist.”
The difficulty of the Chinese typewriter led some reformers to aim at the characters themselves, while others improved the machine.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Why QWERTY was arranged as it was has, to this day, no answer everyone accepts. The record can only rule some of the accounts out.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “Invented 52 times” is an estimate, and it depends on what counts as a “typewriter.”
The claim of “the last typewriter factory” was disputed as soon as it was published, and only later narrowed to “a standard manual typewriter.”

pieces.title: The company that sells home generators got a large order from Amazon: Generac’s third quarter
pieces.short: Generac’s third quarter
pieces.hook: Generac was founded in 1959 in Wisconsin, and began by making portable generators under contract for Sears.
pieces.imageAlt: A Generac commercial generator
pieces.imageCredit: Dwight Burdette · CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

paras.lead: What kind of company this is
parts: Generac was founded in 1959 in Wisconsin, and began by making portable generators under contract for Sears. It is best known for the standby generator mounted outside a house, which starts by itself in a power cut. It also makes commercial and industrial sets.

On October 28, Generac reported third-quarter results: revenue of $1.29 billion, up 16%, a quarterly record; net profit of $109 million, against $66 million a year earlier. Adjusted earnings per share were $2.54, above the analysts’ estimate of $2.43, while revenue was a little below the expected $1.32 billion.

paras.lead: Where the growth mainly came from
parts: External sales in the commercial and industrial segment rose 28%, to $552 million. The residential segment rose 9%, to $743 million. Gross margin rose from 38.3% to 39.9%. The company said part of the reason was a fall in tariff costs.
Shipments of energy-storage products, meanwhile, are shrinking.

The company announced a long-term supply agreement with Amazon, to provide standby generators for data centers. The first batch is to be delivered in 2027–2028, for $2.4 billion. Amazon also received warrants for up to about 1.7 million shares, which can be exercised in full only if cumulative purchases reach $8 billion within 7 years.

The data-center order backlog is about $4.5 billion, nearly three times what it was 90 days earlier. The company expects data-center revenue this year of close to $500 million, and in 2027 “well above $2 billion.” A new plant for high-power sets in Sussex, Wisconsin, went into production at the end of the third quarter.

According to market data, on the day of the announcement the share price first fell about 2% before the open, and then closed up about 3.9%, at $201.34. The company narrowed the expected range for the full-year adjusted margin before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization to 20.5%–21.0%.

paras.lead: Where the risk is written down
parts: In the risk factors of the announcement, the company wrote of “uncertainty about growth in the data-center market,” and of the cancellation terms in data-center contracts. That is to say, a backlog is not the same as revenue. Under certain conditions a customer can cancel.

A company that sold home generators on “anxiety about power cuts” has sold the same skill to AI data centers. The growth is faster, and it also depends more on the investment pace of a few large customers.

Amazon | View: data centers need a reliable standby power supply, and the supply has to be locked in. ; Interest: steady delivery, and a price. ; Worry: the supplier’s capacity not keeping up with the pace of building. ; Basis: the long-term supply agreement and the warrants: they can be exercised in full only with cumulative purchases of $8 billion over 7 years.

Investors and analysts | View: order growth beat expectations, and revenue was a little below expectations. ; Interest: whether the valuation already reflects the data-center growth. ; Worry: the backlog not turning into revenue on time. ; Basis: adjusted earnings per share of $2.54, above the expected $2.43; revenue of $1.29 billion, a little below the expected $1.32 billion; the share price fell and then rose on the day.

Household users, and the residential business | View: a power cut calls for a reliable home generator. ; Interest: the price of the product, and the service after the sale. ; Worry: once the company’s weight shifts to data centers, the residential business being neglected. ; Basis: the residential segment grew 9% this quarter, and its margin rose from 23.4% to 27.0%; shipments of energy-storage products fell.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Amazon trades warrants for a long-term purchasing commitment. Generac gets the orders, and also gives a large customer a share of future gains.
Data-center orders have lifted what investors expect. If customers slow their investment, the effect on the share price will be larger too.
The residential business has the higher margin for now, and the data-center business is growing faster. The two have to be balanced in capacity and in money.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: How much of the $4.5 billion backlog will in the end become revenue depends on the speed of data-center construction and on the cancellation terms. For now there is only the company’s own expectation.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The rise and fall of the share price comes from market websites, not from the company’s announcement.
“Well above $2 billion” is the company’s expectation for 2027, not a result that has already happened.

pieces.title: Two “Dan Sullivans” on the ballot: the same-name fight in Alaska’s Senate election
pieces.short: The same-name fight in Alaska’s Senate election
pieces.hook: Alaska’s Senate election is voted on November 3, and the ballot has two Dan Sullivans: one is the Republican incumbent…
pieces.event: A New York Times report on October 28, 2026; state and federal inquiries escalated on October 29; voting on November 3
pieces.imageAlt: The Alaska State Capitol
pieces.imageCredit: Kevin Lam · CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Alaska’s Senate election is voted on November 3, and the ballot has two Dan Sullivans: one is the Republican incumbent senator, and one is a retired teacher. On October 28 The New York Times reported that people from the campaign of the Democratic candidate, Peltola, had taken part in recruiting the namesake. On the 29th, inquiries by the governor and by the Department of Justice both escalated.

The incumbent senator, Dan S. Sullivan, was first elected in 2014 and is seeking a third term. His opponent, Peltola, is a former member of the U.S. House, and entered the race early in 2026. In the primary on August 18, Peltola took 49.5% and Sullivan 41.4%.

Dan J. Sullivan is a retired elementary-school teacher in Petersburg, born in 1957, who filed as a Republican three days before the deadline. He said he had been considering it for 12 years, and that he is a “pragmatic Republican centrist.” The elections division had taken him off the ballot on the ground of “an intent to confuse voters.” A state court overturned that, and the state supreme court upheld the reversal in July.

paras.lead: How the ballot tells them apart
parts: The elections division lists him as “Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.,” with no party. The incumbent is listed as “Sullivan, Dan S.” and marked “incumbent.” According to reports, this is the first time in at least ten years that the division has added such a label for an incumbent.

paras.lead: What The New York Times said
parts: The report, citing 12 people with knowledge or a part in it, and dozens of text messages, said that people from Peltola’s campaign and a senior adviser to the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee had taken part in a “ballot composition plan,” recruiting candidates who might split the Republican vote, including this namesake teacher.

Peltola’s team said they “have no relationship with either Sullivan campaign.” The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee also denied taking part, and said the Republican side had likewise backed candidates who split the vote. The teacher himself said running was his own decision.

On October 29 the Republican governor, Dunleavy, ordered the state Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the matter broke state law. “The evidence will decide what happens next.” The Department of Justice had already issued grand-jury subpoenas in August, and after the report it issued dozens of new subpoenas and notices to preserve documents.

Last week the Department of Justice sued, asking that if the incumbent loses by a narrow margin, certification of the result be held back, on the ground that voters might be confused by the namesake. State election officials, for their part, hold that the federal government “has no authority at all to step into a state election, let alone to step in on behalf of a particular candidate.”

Trump called for the people involved to be prosecuted. The incumbent senator, Sullivan, called it a “covert operation to deceive Alaskans.” On the other side, during the primary, outside groups also spent money to boost fringe candidates who might split the vote of Peltola or of Sullivan.

blocks.text: Richer, a former Arizona elections official and an NBC commentator, thinks that if there is no “inducement” such as money or a threat, and the candidate runs of his own accord, the recruiting itself may not be illegal. The New York Times report found no evidence of coercion.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The incumbent senator, Sullivan, and the Republicans | View: the namesake is a “fake candidate,” used to confuse voters. ; Interest: holding the seat, and a Senate majority. ; Worry: voters marking the wrong person, and a narrow defeat. ; Basis: Sullivan called it a “covert operation”; the governor ordered an inquiry; Comer, chair of the House Oversight Committee, asked the former campaign manager and others to testify.

Peltola’s team, and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee | View: they did not take part in the recruiting, and the Republicans also backed candidates who split the vote. ; Interest: winning a seat the Democrats have not won since 2008. ; Worry: the inquiry and the lawsuit dragging on the race before the vote. ; Basis: Peltola’s team stated they “have no relationship with either Sullivan campaign”; the committee pointed out that the Republican side has done similar things.

The namesake candidate, Dan J. Sullivan | View: he is a pragmatic centrist who chose to run. ; Interest: being taken seriously as a candidate. ; Worry: being treated as a piece in someone else’s hand. ; Basis: he said he had considered running for 12 years; the state supreme court confirmed his right to be on the ballot; the record shows he once gave Peltola a small donation.

The federal government (the Department of Justice, the White House) | View: voters may have been misled, and the federal government should step in to investigate. ; Interest: the “fairness” of the result, and a Senate majority. ; Worry: a result that is hard to change once certified. ; Basis: the lawsuit asks that certification may be held back; Trump said he ordered it; dozens of new subpoenas.

State election officials, and the courts | View: elections are the state’s business, and a candidate’s qualification has to be decided by law. ; Interest: the authority and the stability of the election procedure. ; Worry: federal intervention and the publicity making voters doubt the election. ; Basis: election officials said the federal government “has no authority to step in”; the state supreme court kept him on the ballot on the ground that a standard of “good-faith candidacy” had no basis in law.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The Republican side needs to prove “deliberate confusion.” The Democratic side stresses that the candidate ran of his own accord. The legal point is whether there was inducement.

The federal government presses with a lawsuit and an inquiry. State election officials and the courts hold the line that “elections are the state’s business.” The powers of the two levels of government are colliding.
Peltola’s team wants to pull attention back to policy before the vote. The more news there is of the inquiry, the harder that is to do.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Whether voters really marked the wrong person is hard to calculate on its own under ranked-choice voting, and that is exactly the core of the Department of Justice lawsuit.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Rios, a former campaign manager and one of the key sources for The New York Times report, later retracted everything he had said.
All the inquiries are still under way. No one has been charged, and no evidence has been made public of inducement by money or by threats.

pieces.title: Not the cheapest, but the best: the engineer Brunel
pieces.short: The engineer Brunel
pieces.hook: Dare to work to the highest standard, and also think early about whether others will follow. The broad gauge was faster, and in the end it still lost to the narrow gauge that everyone…
pieces.takeaway: Dare to work to the highest standard, and also think early about whether others will follow. The broad gauge was faster, and in the end it still lost to the narrow gauge that everyone was using.
pieces.imageAlt: Brunel standing before the launching chains of the Great Eastern, 1857
pieces.imageCredit: Robert Howlett · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On April 9, 1806, Brunel was born in Portsmouth, England. His father, Marc, was an engineer who had come as an exile from France. He studied in France, and was also apprenticed to Breguet, the famous watchmaker.

His father had the contract for the tunnel under the Thames, and in 1827 Brunel became the resident engineer. In January 1828 the tunnel flooded. 6 miners died, he was badly hurt, and he spent half a year recovering.

In 1829 Bristol invited designs for a suspension bridge over the Clifton gorge. The judge, the famous engineer Telford, thought his span too long. He lost the second round as well, then went in person to persuade the judges to reverse themselves. Work began in 1831.

paras.lead: Riots, and a lack of money
parts: The same year, riots broke out in Bristol, and the work stopped. The bridge was finished only in 1864, after his death, with money raised by his fellow engineers.

The Great Western Railway had meant to give the engineer’s post to the cheapest proposal. He wrote back: “The line I have surveyed will not be the cheapest, but it will be the best.” In March 1833, at 26, he was hired.
He chose a broad gauge of about 2.14 meters, nearly half again as wide as the usual 1.435 meters, for the sake of being faster and steadier.

paras.lead: A better technology lost to a standard
parts: In a speed trial in 1845, a broad-gauge locomotive averaged 53 miles an hour, and a narrow-gauge locomotive left the rails when it reached that speed. But the 1846 report of the Royal Commission still argued that the whole country should use the narrow gauge, because more of it had already been laid.
The Great Western Railway did not finish the conversion until 1892.

He also wanted a traveler to go by train from London to Bristol, and then change to a ship for America. In 1845 the Great Britain took 14 days and 21 hours from Liverpool to New York. It was the first iron-hulled, screw-driven ship to cross the Atlantic.

The Great Eastern was about 210 meters long, and could carry more than 4,000 people. A sideways launch failed in November 1857, and she did not enter the water until January of the next year. In September 1859 he had a stroke on board, and died on September 15, at 53.

blocks.title: A coin stuck in the windpipe
blocks.text: In April 1843, doing a trick for a child, he got half a sovereign stuck in his windpipe. Forceps, and a shaking machine of his own design, did no good. In the end, on his father’s idea, he was strapped to a board and turned upside down, and the coin fell out.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Brunel himself | View: good engineering should be done to the highest standard, and the broad gauge was faster and steadier. ; Interest: making work that led its time, and leaving a name. ; Worry: being told to save money, and to accommodate the old standard. ; Basis: when he applied, he wrote that it “will not be the cheapest, but it will be the best”; in the 1845 speed trial a broad-gauge locomotive averaged 53 miles an hour; after the report he still wrote a 50-page rebuttal.

The Great Western board, and the shareholders | View: the line should open as soon as possible, and the cost should be held down. ; Interest: getting the investment back early. ; Worry: the work running over budget, and the schedule slipping again and again. ; Basis: both completion dates, 1840 and 1841, were missed; the whole line cost about £5.887 million; when he was appointed, another engineer was also arranged to work alongside him.

Parliament, and the Royal Commission | View: the country’s railways had to be able to connect with one another. ; Interest: one standard, and less trouble changing trains. ; Worry: two gauges side by side, with goods and passengers having to change at the boundary. ; Basis: the 1846 report argued for a uniform narrow gauge, on the ground that the narrow-gauge mileage was already large, and the cost of widening it would be too great.

Critics (the science writer Lardner, and others) | View: his ideas were too risky, and some of them could not work at all. ; Interest: defending their own professional judgment, and their reputations. ; Worry: the safety of passengers, and investment wasted. ; Basis: Lardner once backed the claim that “a train would run away on the long gradient of Box Tunnel, and the passengers would be unable to breathe,” and also asserted that a steamship could not carry enough fuel to cross the Atlantic, the latter of which Brunel refuted by calculation; Brunel’s “atmospheric railway” was taken out of use less than a year after it opened.

Biographers, and later judges | View: he is a symbol of Britain’s industrial age, but the credit has also been enlarged. ; Interest: making clear which works really came from his hand. ; Worry: myth covering the facts. ; Basis: in the BBC poll of 2002 he placed second, behind only Churchill; biographers do not agree on how much of the Clifton Suspension Bridge is his original design.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The board needed his talent to make the railway famous, and it was also repeatedly trapped by the overruns he brought. He won the quality of the line, and he also acquired a reputation for “spending too much.”
Parliament cared whether the whole country could be connected. He cared how fast a single line could run. The two standards met head-on in the fight over the gauge.
The critics’ doubts were sometimes overturned by the facts (the long tunnel was built), and sometimes confirmed (the atmospheric railway failed). Each side had its wins and its losses.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Whether the broad gauge was “better” or “more expensive” depends on whether one looks at the speed of one line, or at the cost of connecting a national network. The two accounts are hard to set side by side.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: How much of the finished Clifton Suspension Bridge is his original design is something the biographers do not agree on.
The 1845 speed trial ran the two sides over different stretches, of different lengths (about 85 kilometers against 71), and is hard to treat as a strict comparison.

pieces.title: From “please connect me” to a pocket: a hundred and fifty years of the telephone
pieces.short: A hundred and fifty years of the telephone
pieces.hook: On March 7, 1876, Bell received the U.S. telephone patent, number 174,465.
pieces.imageAlt: A woman operator at a switchboard, about 1905
pieces.imageCredit: Webster & Stevens · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On March 7, 1876, Bell received the U.S. telephone patent, number 174,465. Three days later he spoke into the transmitter the famous line, “Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.”

paras.lead: Who invented it first is still disputed
parts: The same day, another inventor, Gray, filed a similar idea with the patent office. The Italian Meucci had experimented earlier still. In 2002 the U.S. House of Representatives passed a resolution recognizing his contribution, and the Canadian parliament then passed a motion to the contrary.

paras.lead: First there had to be a “switchboard”
parts: Two telephones can only talk to each other. To speak with many people, there has to be someone in the middle. On January 28, 1878, New Haven, Connecticut, opened the first commercial telephone exchange: 21 subscribers, at $1.50 a month.

The earliest operators were boys, quick-tempered, fond of pranks, and given to swearing. On September 1, 1878, Emma Nutt became the first woman operator, in Boston. Customers responded well, and the work soon became mostly women’s.

The American undertaker Strowger decided that an operator had switched a business call meant for him to someone else, so he invented an automatic exchange himself, and took out a patent in 1891. In 1892 La Porte, Indiana, opened the first automatic exchange, with about 75 subscribers.

In 1915 the United States completed its first long-distance call from coast to coast. In 1927 the transatlantic telephone opened. The Bell System later monopolized the American telephone business, and on January 1, 1984, under a consent decree, it was split into 7 regional companies.

In 1973, Motorola’s Cooper made a call on a New York street with a handheld telephone weighing about 2 kilograms. In 1983 the first commercial mobile phone, the DynaTAC 8000x, went on sale. In 1991 Finland opened GSM, and the mobile phone entered the digital age.

According to the 2025 statistical bulletin on the communications industry from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, China had 1.827 billion mobile-phone subscribers, 37.25 million more than the year before, and 160 million fixed-line subscribers, 6.337 million fewer in a year, only 11.4 sets per 100 people.

The same bulletin says that in 2025 the nation’s mobile-phone calls lasted 2.02 trillion minutes, 5.1% less than the year before, and voice revenue was only 7.2% of telecommunications revenue. The telephone is still there, but more and more of the “calls” happen inside network applications.

blocks.title: “No hello girl”
blocks.text: Early advertising called it “a telephone with no hello girl, no swearing, that does not break, and that you do not wait for.” In 1896 Strowger sold the patent for $1,800. In 1916 those patents changed hands for $2.5 million.

Many subscribers could call one another
A human operator was no longer needed

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Inventors and patent holders (Bell, Gray, Meucci) | View: the telephone was one’s own invention, and the credit and the patent should belong to oneself. ; Interest: patent rights, and a place in history. ; Worry: being beaten to it by someone else, or losing in court. ; Basis: Bell received the patent in 1876; Gray filed his idea the same day; in 2002 a resolution of the U.S. House recognized Meucci, and the Canadian parliament passed a motion to the contrary.

Telephone companies (the Bell System, and others) | View: a network run as one is the most reliable. ; Interest: scale, and control of the market. ; Worry: being broken up by antitrust, or being bypassed by a new technology. ; Basis: the Bell System monopolized the American telephone business for a long time; the Department of Justice sued in 1974, and in 1984 it was split into 7 regional companies.

Operators (mostly women) | View: operating was respectable work, and it called for patience. ; Interest: employment, and income. ; Worry: being replaced by the automatic exchange. ; Basis: Nutt started in 1878, at $10 a month and 54 hours a week; advertising for the automatic exchange said outright, “no hello girl.”

Users | View: a telephone should be convenient, cheap, and free of mistakes. ; Interest: the quality of the call, the price, and privacy. ; Worry: being delayed by a human operator, overheard, or priced by a monopoly. ; Basis: Strowger suspected an operator of diverting his business; the first New Haven subscribers paid $1.50 a month.

The new-technology companies (Motorola, and the mobile-phone makers) | View: a person should be able to make a call, rather than a place. ; Interest: opening a new market. ; Worry: the network and the spectrum being in the hands of the old telephone companies. ; Basis: Cooper’s street call in 1973; the DynaTAC went on sale in 1983; today China’s mobile subscribers are more than 11 times its fixed-line subscribers.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The telephone companies needed operators to hold the network up, and they were also the first to replace them with automatic exchanges. The labor cost saved was exchanged for a larger network.
The monopoly brought a unified network, and it also brought the antitrust lawsuit. After the breakup, new companies had a chance to enter.
Patent lawsuits among the inventors decided who could run the telephone business, while users cared more about price and convenience.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: “Who invented the telephone” depends on how one defines “telephone”: an experimental device that can carry sound, or a commercial product that can be used. The accounts are hard to bring into one for that reason.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The story that Strowger “had his business diverted by an operator” was later given a different explanation by the local Bell manager, who said the real reason lay elsewhere.
Meucci’s contribution rests mainly on a patent caveat of 1871 and on later testimony. The original device was not preserved.

pieces.title: Volume down by a tenth, profit doubled: Hershey’s third quarter, before Halloween
pieces.short: Hershey’s third quarter, before Halloween
pieces.hook: Hershey was founded in 1894 by Milton Hershey, with its headquarters in the town of Hershey, Pennsylvania. Its brands include Hershey, Ki…
pieces.imageAlt: Hershey’s Kisses on a shelf
pieces.imageCredit: Mike Mozart · CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

paras.lead: What kind of company this is
parts: Hershey was founded in 1894 by Milton Hershey, with its headquarters in the town of Hershey, Pennsylvania. Its brands include Hershey, Kisses, Reese’s, and other chocolate and candy brands, and in recent years it has also bought quite a few salty snacks.

On October 29, Hershey reported third-quarter results: revenue of $3.28 billion, up 3.0%; excluding acquisitions and exchange rates, growth was only 0.8%. Net profit was $581 million, against $276 million a year earlier. Adjusted earnings per share were $2.64, up 103%.

Almost all the growth in revenue came from higher prices: price contributed about 11 points, volume dragged about 10 points, and the acquired snack brand LesserEvil added another 2.1 points. The North American candy segment raised prices by about 13%, and volume was down about 11%.

The reasons the company listed were: the price increases, mark-to-market gains on cocoa-futures hedges, cost savings, a tariff refund of about $57 million, and a fall in the cost of cocoa. Of these, the tariff refund contributed about $0.22 a share.
Spending on advertising and consumer marketing rose 17.1%. Management said the fourth quarter would put still more in, to push a new cream-filled chocolate bar and Reese’s Oreo.

According to Reuters, the chief executive, Tanner, said on the earnings call that the number of people celebrating Halloween this year is expected to be flat with last year, but that “financial pressure may affect how much they buy at the end,” and that the last few days are “very critical.” In September, sales of candy, gum, and mints in U.S. convenience stores fell nearly 5%.

Analysts had expected $2.11 a share, and the result was more than 20% higher. But the share price fell about 2% at one point in the morning session, and was then roughly flat. Modi, an analyst at RBC, said that cutting the organic-growth target, and a more cautious tone on 2027, was “hardly inspiring.”

The doubling of profit came mainly from price and from cost, not from selling more chocolate. Cheaper cocoa will make the books look better, but whether customers can be pulled back depends on the volume ahead.

items: +11 points
Revenue from higher prices
−10 points
Revenue from volume
Gross margin (32.6% last year)

blocks.title: Third quarter: this year vs last year
blocks.note: Unit: dollars; source: Hershey’s third-quarter earnings release. Last year’s operating profit is inferred from this year’s $818 million and an increase of 88.1%.

blocks.title: Cocoa got cheaper (the company’s account)
blocks.text: The chief financial officer said the 2025/26 cocoa crop was especially good, that the world may have a record surplus of 500,000 to 600,000 tonnes, and that costs will keep falling next year. That is the company’s judgment. The cocoa price will also be affected by weather and by the producing regions.

blocks.title: Hershey’s third quarter: last year’s net profit vs this year’s ($100 million)

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Hershey’s management | View: profit and gross margin are recovering on schedule, and cocoa is moving back toward normal. ; Interest: holding the price, and pulling the margin back. ; Worry: consumers buying less candy under the pressure of fuel prices, inflation, and interest rates. ; Basis: the earnings release and the call: gross margin of 46.1%; a tariff refund of about $57 million; an expected record cocoa surplus of 500,000–600,000 tonnes.

Consumers | View: candy is getting more expensive, and people are buying more carefully. ; Interest: something that tastes good and is not too dear. ; Worry: prices keeping on rising. ; Basis: in September, sales of candy, gum, and mints in U.S. convenience stores fell nearly 5%; North American candy volume this quarter was down about 11%.

Retailers (supermarkets, convenience stores) | View: holiday candy is an important seasonal business. ; Interest: shelves that turn over quickly, and stock that does not pile up. ; Worry: customers finding it too dear and not buying, and a large stock left after the holiday. ; Basis: management said retailers’ inventories this year are healthier than last year’s; the advertising mentioned large packs and sizes at a lower price point.

Investors and analysts | View: profit far beat expectations, but the quality of the growth is ordinary. ; Interest: whether volume and profit can last over the next few years. ; Worry: profit being held up by one-off factors. ; Basis: $2.64 a share, above the expected $2.11; the share price fell about 2% in the morning and then was flat; RBC said the outlook was “hardly inspiring.”

Cocoa-producing regions, and the supply chain | View: high cocoa prices have pushed output up, and new producing regions. ; Interest: selling at a good price, and keeping on investing in planting. ; Worry: income falling once the price comes back down. ; Basis: the company’s call mentioned expanded planting in emerging regions, and improvements in fertilizer and in growing methods in West Africa.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Hershey bought its profit back by raising prices, and consumers answered by buying less. The company does not plan a general price cut, and is turning instead to promotions and to changing pack sizes to strike a balance.
Cheaper cocoa lowers Hershey’s costs, and it also means less income for farmers in the producing regions. The two sides’ interests in the price run exactly opposite.

Investors want the profit, and they also want to see volume come back. Management is putting more into advertising. That will press profit a little in the short run, in exchange for next year’s volume.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: How much of the fall in volume is from the price increases, and how much from a high base of new products last year and from different shipping dates, is something the company has given several reasons for, without splitting out the specific figures.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The “record surplus” of cocoa is the judgment of the company’s management, not a count by an independent body.
How Halloween finally sold will not have figures until the fourth-quarter report. For now there are only management’s expectations and industry surveys.

pieces.title: A letter to an Iranian hard-liner: can Vance hold off the next round of air strikes
pieces.short: Can Vance hold off the next round of air strikes
pieces.hook: According to The Wall Street Journal’s first report on October 28, U.S. Vice President Vance wrote to the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council…
pieces.event: The letter delivered on October 25, 2026; The Wall Street Journal’s first report on October 28; Iran’s reply and later reporting on October 29–30
pieces.imageAlt: The Strait of Hormuz, photographed by satellite
pieces.imageCredit: MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: According to The Wall Street Journal’s first report on October 28, U.S. Vice President Vance wrote a letter to Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, proposing to restart talks. The letter was passed on by Qatari mediators, and delivered on October 25, a Sunday.
On the 29th, the Iranian side said it had received the letter and had not yet replied.

The text of the letter has not been made public. According to The New York Times and The Guardian, Vance proposed direct talks, led by him, with the nuclear question on the table from the start. The place might be Qatar or Turkey, and the talks could begin as soon as next week.

Rezaei was once commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. David Ignatius, a columnist at The Washington Post, wrote on October 30 that the American side judges him to be “the key node” in Tehran, the only person who might gather a consensus inside Iran and bring an agreement about.

The Wall Street Journal said the letter was written on Trump’s instructions. Asked by reporters, Trump said “no,” and called it a matter of help Iran needed with medical supplies and the like. But he agreed that Vance should make contact with Iran.

According to an Iranian security official cited by the Fars News Agency, Iran received the letter, has not yet replied, and said that the media’s guesses about the contents are not accurate. The speaker of parliament, Ghalibaf, wrote on social media: “The carrot and the stick do not work on Iran.” There can be progress only if Iran’s seven conditions are accepted.

paras.lead: Where the two sides are stuck
parts: The American side wants Iran first to make a concrete commitment on the nuclear program, for example by shipping out the stock of highly enriched uranium. Iran fears that its own concessions will not be returned, while the American lifting of sanctions can be reversed, and has proposed diluting the stock to a level at which a nuclear weapon cannot be made. The Guardian said someone has proposed a third-party guarantee, and China is often mentioned.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Trump has already warned Gulf allies to prepare for a short, high-intensity military action after the U.S. midterm elections on November 3. Vaez of the International Crisis Group said the risk is “dangerously high.”

blocks.title: Background: a war that is not over
blocks.text: On February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel went to war with Iran, and the United States then blockaded shipping in the area of the Strait of Hormuz. In April and June of this year, Vance took part in two rounds of talks. The two sides signed a memorandum of understanding, which later lapsed amid fighting in the strait.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The U.S. White House (Trump, Vance) | View: the nuclear question has to be settled first, while the military option is kept. ; Interest: keeping Iran from having a nuclear weapon, and ending an unpopular war. ; Worry: the talks dragging on, and Iran picking up advantages in the meantime. ; Basis: Vance’s letter asks that the nuclear question be discussed “from the start”; Trump said the letter had to do with medical supplies; Gulf allies were warned to prepare militarily.

Iran’s leadership (Rezaei, Ghalibaf, Araghchi) | View: lift the blockade, the sanctions, and the frozen assets first, and only then talk about the nuclear question. ; Interest: an economic recovery and national sovereignty, and keeping the bargaining chips. ; Worry: giving way first, and then the American side going back on it, or striking again. ; Basis: Ghalibaf, “the carrot and the stick do not work”; Araghchi said Iran “continues to give diplomacy a chance”; the proposal put to the General Assembly in September.

Israel (Netanyahu) | View: only a change of regime in Iran can remove the threat for good. ; Interest: national security, and an advantage in the region. ; Worry: an agreement between the United States and Iran leaving Iran’s nuclear capability in place. ; Basis: Ignatius’s column of October 30 said Netanyahu argues for regime change.

Mediators such as Qatar, and the Gulf states | View: if the conflict starts again, the Gulf states are the first to be hit. ; Interest: keeping oil fields, desalination plants, and undersea cables from being hit in retaliation. ; Worry: the United States using force again, and Iran retaliating against Gulf facilities. ; Basis: Qatar passed the letter on; officials from Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Pakistan, and Turkey went to Tehran for talks in late October (Al Jazeera).

The U.S. Congress, and the voters | View: the war plan costs too much, and it needs congressional oversight. ; Interest: Americans’ safety, and the political gains and losses in an election. ; Worry: the war escalating, and without authorization from Congress. ; Basis: Senator Murphy called the war plan “insane”; a New York Times/Siena poll found 65% do not approve of the way Trump is handling the Iran war.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The American side uses “force is possible” to press the talks. Iran uses “seven conditions” to hold its chips. Each side wants the other to give way first.
Vance is seen in Iran as a relatively credible person to talk to, but Iran also doubts whether he can persuade Trump, and that limits the weight of this letter.
The Gulf states both rely on American security and fear Iranian retaliation most. So they cooperate with the United States, and they also mediate actively.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Whether a nuclear commitment comes first, or the lifting of sanctions comes first, is the largest disagreement. A third-party guarantee has been proposed, but who would guarantee it, and how, is not settled.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The text of the letter has not been made public. The contents all come from unnamed officials, and the Iranian side has also said the media’s guesses are not accurate.
Whether Trump instructed Vance to write the letter is something on which The Wall Street Journal’s report and Trump’s own account do not agree.
Whether force will be used after the midterms is, for now, only press reporting and the judgment of analysts.

pieces.title: A child taken captive, and seven voyages to the Western Ocean: Zheng He
pieces.short: Zheng He
pieces.hook: You cannot choose where you start. What you can choose is to take the task given to you and do it to the limit: a eunuch who began as a captive took the fleet several thousand…
pieces.takeaway: You cannot choose where you start. What you can choose is to take the task given to you and do it to the limit: a eunuch who began as a captive took the fleet several thousand kilometers away, to East Africa.
pieces.imageAlt: The Zheng He memorial statue in Malacca, Malaysia
pieces.imageCredit: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas · CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: In 1371 Zheng He was born in Kunyang, Yunnan (now Jinning, in Kunming). His family name was Ma, his childhood name Sanbao, and the household was Muslim. In 1381 the Ming army attacked Yunnan. His father died in the fighting. He, about ten, was taken captive, castrated, and sent to serve in the household of Zhu Di, the Prince of Yan.

In 1399 the Prince of Yan rose to seize the throne, and Zheng He distinguished himself at the battle of Zhengcunba, near Beiping. In 1402 Zhu Di took Nanjing and became the Yongle emperor. Early in 1404 the emperor granted him the surname “Zheng.”

paras.lead: More than two hundred ships put to sea
parts: On July 11, 1405, the first voyage set out. The records speak of 317 ships and about 28,000 people. From then until 1433 he made seven voyages to the Western Ocean, reaching Southeast Asia, India, the Arabian Peninsula, and East Africa.

The fleet carried silk and porcelain, and it also used force: it captured the pirate chief Chen Zuyi, fought a land battle in Ceylon, and brought the king back to China. From the fourth voyage on, envoys from more than thirty countries came to court with the ships.
The fourth voyage was the first to reach Malindi, in East Africa. In 1415 envoys from Malindi brought a giraffe, which the court took for the auspicious “qilin.”

paras.lead: How big the ships were is still argued
parts: A novel of 1597 writes that the treasure ships were 44 zhang long, about 127 meters, nearly twice HMS Victory (about 69 meters), the British flagship launched in 1765. Quite a few scholars think a wooden ship could not be built that large, and estimate 60 to 75 meters.
The dock at the Nanjing treasure-ship yard is long enough, but not wide enough for a ship that large.

In 1424 the Hongxi emperor called off the voyages. The Xuande emperor sent a last one in 1430. Zheng He most likely died on the return of that voyage, about 1433, and may have been buried at sea. The tomb in Nanjing is empty. Official histories after that rarely mention him, until in 1904 Liang Qichao wrote Biography of Zheng He, the Great Navigator of the Motherland, and he became famous again.

blocks.title: A clerk’s diary
blocks.text: Ma Huan, an interpreter who sailed with the fleet, was a Muslim and knew Arabic. He wrote the products and customs of the countries along the way into The Overall Survey of the Ocean’s Shores. It was finished in 1416, and it is an important source today for these voyages.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The Yongle court | View: the voyages could proclaim the state’s prestige, and bring the countries to court. ; Interest: securing a throne taken by force, and building a tributary order. ; Worry: resistance overseas, and pirates making trouble. ; Basis: six fleets were sent in succession in the Yongle years; from the fourth voyage on, envoys from more than thirty countries came to court; the Malindi “qilin” was taken as an auspicious sign.

The Ministry of Revenue, and the civil officials | View: the voyages cost too much, and went against the ancestral instructions. ; Interest: spending the money on the northern frontier and on the people’s livelihood. ; Worry: eunuchs using the voyages to expand their power. ; Basis: in 1424 the Hongxi emperor ordered the voyages stopped; the records say the voyages did “not accord” with the Ancestral Instructions of the Imperial Ming left by the founding emperor.

The countries and ports along the way | View: dealings with the Ming could mean trade, and recognition. ; Interest: trade, and diplomatic standing. ; Worry: the fleet using force, and interfering in internal affairs. ; Basis: the sultan of Malacca came to China in person, with his people; the king of Ceylon was taken captive and brought to China.

Modern historians | View: the picture of Zheng He has been prettified, or misread. ; Interest: separating what happened from the legend. ; Worry: judging history by a “missed chance.” ; Basis: scholars think the figure of 127 meters comes from a novel and is not to be trusted; some scholars stress the military color of the voyages; others say the voyages “reshaped Asia.”

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The emperor needed the voyages to keep up appearances. The civil officials had to guard the treasury and the ancestral instructions. Zheng He’s fleet was caught between the court and the ministers, and when the emperor changed, it stopped.
Small states along the way used Ming recognition to raise themselves, and they also had to bear the fleet’s force. Diplomacy and deterrence were in the same fleet.
People today want to use Zheng He to tell of “peaceful voyages,” and some use him to ask “why China did not turn to the sea.” The two tellings pull against each other.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The size of the treasure ships depends on how long one zhang of the Ming actually was. Standards differed from place to place, and the conversion can come out nearly twice as long.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Official histories say little about the voyages. Some of the archives were later lost, and the number of ships and of people rests largely on later compilation.
There is no definite record of how Zheng He died, of the year, or of where he was buried.

pieces.title: From a smoky tunnel to more than ten million trips a day: more than a hundred and sixty years of the metro
pieces.short: More than a hundred and sixty years of the metro
pieces.hook: On January 10, 1863, the Metropolitan Railway in London opened. It was the world’s first underground railway to carry passengers.
pieces.imageAlt: Baker Street Underground station, London, about 1863
pieces.imageCredit: Anonymous · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On January 10, 1863, the Metropolitan Railway in London opened. It was the world’s first underground railway to carry passengers. The carriages were made of wood, lit by gas, and pulled by steam locomotives.

paras.lead: Smoky and hot, and still packed
parts: The tunnels were made by digging up the street and covering it again. The smoke could not get out, and passengers and drivers alike were miserable. Yet the opening day carried 38,000 trips, and the first year 9.5 million.

paras.lead: Switch to electricity, and dig deeper
parts: In 1890 the City and South London Railway put electric locomotives to use, and became the first electrified underground railway. The round tunnels gave the London Underground its nickname, the “Tube.” The earliest carriages had no windows. The designers thought there was no need to look outside in a tunnel.

paras.lead: One person could drive the whole train
parts: In 1897 the American inventor Sprague tried out “multiple-unit control” in Chicago. One driving position could control every motor on the train, and from then on a metro did not have to be hauled by a locomotive.

In 1896 Budapest opened the first electrified metro on the European continent. In 1900 the Paris metro opened. Its full name copied London’s “Metropolitan Railway,” and the short form, métro, was later borrowed by many languages. In 1904 the first section of the New York subway opened.
In 1927 Tokyo opened the first metro in Asia. The Beijing metro began operating in 1971. Shanghai opened Line 1 in 1993.

paras.lead: The largest network now is in China
parts: By the end of 2025, 58 cities in mainland China had opened urban rail transit, 13,071.58 kilometers in all, of which the metro was about 10,000 kilometers. In 2023 the Beijing metro became the longest metro in the world by mileage. The Shanghai metro’s busiest day carried 13.397 million trips.

paras.lead: Wanting to build is not the same as being allowed to
parts: In 2018 the General Office of the State Council issued a document: a city applying to build a metro had to meet all of these at once: general public-budget revenue above 30 billion yuan, regional gross product above 300 billion yuan, and a permanent urban population above 3 million.

blocks.title: A door added on the platform
blocks.text: The Singapore metro opened in 1987. It was the world’s first heavy-rail metro to fit platform screen doors in underground stations. The glass door separates the platform from the track, and opens only when the train has stopped.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: City governments | View: a metro can hold up a city’s expansion and property development. ; Interest: a city’s competitiveness, building new districts, and a record of achievement. ; Worry: falling behind other cities for lack of a metro. ; Basis: in 2025 mainland China added 910.8 kilometers of urban rail in operation (China Association of Metros).

The central regulators | View: a metro should be built within one’s means, so that local borrowing does not run away. ; Interest: controlling the risk of local debt. ; Worry: a line with too little ridership losing money for a long time after it is built. ; Basis: the 2018 document of the General Office set thresholds of 30 billion yuan in fiscal revenue, 300 billion yuan of GDP, and a population of 3 million, and required a line’s early ridership intensity to be no lower than 7,000 passenger-trips per kilometer per day.

Passengers | View: a metro should be on time, cheap, and not packed. ; Interest: the time of the commute, and the fare. ; Worry: crowding at the peak, transfers that are too far, and fares going up. ; Basis: weekday ridership on the Shanghai metro is often above 10 million trips, about 73% of the city’s public-transport journeys; Beijing’s fare is charged by distance, starting at 3 yuan.

Operating companies, and investors | View: a metro can be a business that makes money. ; Interest: fares, advertising, the gains from developing along the line, and the share price. ; Worry: ridership falling, and costs rising. ; Basis: Tokyo Metro listed in October 2024 and raised about 348.6 billion yen, the largest IPO in Japan since 2018.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Cities want to build more. The center tightens with thresholds and ridership requirements. The two pull back and forth over “how much to build.”
Passengers want a cheap fare. Operators have to cover the cost. The difference often lands on a local fiscal subsidy.
Tokyo Metro’s listing shows that a metro can make a profit, but that depends on an extremely high density of ridership, which many cities do not have.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: A new line built in a new district where the people have not yet come is either “build the road first, and the people gather later,” or “built for nothing.” Which it is can be known only years later, from the ridership.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: There is no single published set of figures for the losses and the subsidies of urban rail in the various cities, and this piece cites no specific number.
Countries do not count a “metro” the same way. Some include light rail and suburban rail, and some do not, so the rankings change with the definition.

pieces.title: The refineries earned more than the wells: ExxonMobil’s third quarter
pieces.short: ExxonMobil’s third quarter
pieces.hook: On October 30, ExxonMobil reported third-quarter results: net profit under accounting rules of $15.4 billion, and per…
pieces.imageAlt: The Baytown refinery in Texas, photographed by satellite
pieces.imageCredit: NASA/METI/AIST/Japan Space Systems, and the U.S./Japan ASTER Science Team · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 30, ExxonMobil reported third-quarter results: net profit under accounting rules of $15.4 billion, or $3.72 a share. A year earlier it was $7.5 billion, about double.
Stripping out one-off items, earnings were $4.23 a share, above the analysts’ average estimate of $4.08.

paras.lead: The refineries overtook the oil fields
parts: This quarter, the business of refining and selling oil products earned $7.169 billion, and the business of extracting oil and gas earned $7.088 billion. Stripping out one-off items, the gap is wider still, about $9 billion against $7.3 billion. Reuters said this is the first time in at least six years that refining has earned more than extraction.

The war of the United States and Israel with Iran nearly cut off the Strait of Hormuz, and refineries in Russia and Saudi Arabia were attacked as well. Diesel and gasoline were tight, and refining margins jumped. The company’s refineries along the Gulf of Mexico ran at full tilt.

paras.lead: The oil price, meanwhile, went down
parts: Extraction did less well. Brent was lower than in the second quarter, and adjusted upstream profit was about 20% less than the quarter before. Output was about 4.5 million barrels of oil equivalent a day.
This quarter the company distributed $9.4 billion to shareholders, including $4.3 billion in dividends and $5.1 billion in buybacks, and it also announced $20 billion of buybacks for 2027.

An executive at Chevron said refining margins may stay high into next year. But this good result rests on tight supply. Once the strait is open to shipping again, this part of the profit may fall back.

In August, Trump said Chevron and Exxon “made too much money off the shortage.” The chief financial officer, Hansen, answered that high oil prices put real pressure on households, and that the company’s way is to increase supply. The higher the profit, the greater that pressure may be.

blocks.title: Why diesel
blocks.text: The chief executive, Woods, said diesel is where supply is tightest this time. Trucks, farm machines, and ships all depend on diesel. Every extra barrel a refinery makes can be sold at a good price.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: ExxonMobil’s management | View: the good result comes from years of cost control and of investment in refining. ; Interest: holding on to the profit and the return to shareholders, and avoiding being cast as “profiting from the war.” ; Worry: profit falling back once supply recovers, and political pressure growing. ; Basis: cumulative structural cost savings of $16.9 billion since 2019; Hansen said the answer is to increase supply.

Shareholders, and Wall Street | View: profit and cash flow both beat expectations, and the buybacks will be stepped up. ; Interest: dividends, buybacks, and the share price. ; Worry: the good times are temporary, and will not hold next year. ; Basis: operating cash flow of $25.7 billion, and free cash flow of $19.1 billion; after the results the share price rose about 2%.

The White House (Trump) | View: the oil companies made too much money off the shortage. ; Interest: pushing the oil price down, and easing the burden on voters. ; Worry: a high oil price hurting the election. ; Basis: in August Trump said Chevron and Exxon “made too much money off the shortage.”

Households and businesses that drive and use oil | View: fuel is too expensive. ; Interest: spending less, and prices not rising further. ; Worry: the diesel price pushing up freight and prices. ; Basis: Hansen acknowledged that high oil prices put “real pressure” on households; Woods said diesel is the tightest link in supply.

Peers, and rivals | View: this round of high refining margins will last a while yet. ; Interest: making more money while the margins are high. ; Worry: too much capacity, or demand falling. ; Basis: a Chevron executive said the margins may stay high into next year; Shell, Total, and BP also beat expectations in the third quarter, and BP set a record.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The more the company earns, the easier it is for the White House to blame it for the high oil price. The company answers with “produce more,” and stays off the subject of “cutting the price.”
Shareholders hope for a larger distribution. Households hope the oil price will come down. The two demands collide in the same barrel.
The war pushed refining margins up. Once the war eases, the profit that falls back first is this one too.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Whether the high profit counts as “the market’s reward” or as “profiting from the war” depends on who caused the tight supply, and on whether the profit has turned into new capacity. That is not yet clear.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: How long the profit can last is only a forecast by company executives and by analysts. There is no certain answer.
“The first time in at least six years” comes from Reuters’s count. The company’s own report does not put it that way.

pieces.title: Four days before the election, a judge stops the Department of Justice: an order protecting election officials
pieces.short: An order protecting election officials
pieces.hook: On October 30, Trina Thompson, a federal judge in the Northern District of California, issued a temporary restraining order, barring nationwide…
pieces.event: The ruling on October 30, 2026; the Department of Justice appealed on October 31
pieces.imageAlt: The federal courthouse in San Francisco
pieces.imageCredit: Marincyclist · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 30, Trina Thompson, a federal judge in the Northern District of California, issued a temporary restraining order, barring the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security, nationwide, from threatening or intimidating election officials.

The two departments may not require officials to set aside, not count, or delete the ballots of voters alleged to be “not qualified,” and they may not threaten prosecution. The Department of Justice must also notify officials who have received the relevant letters, and say whether there is a search warrant or a grand-jury subpoena under way.

The plaintiffs are the Service Employees International Union and other unions, and civil-rights groups including the NAACP and the League of United Latin American Citizens. They charge that these practices violate the Voting Rights Act, and also infringe the states’ power to run elections.

paras.lead: How it escalated, step by step
parts: In July, Dhillon, head of the Civil Rights Division at the Department of Justice, wrote to the 50 states and the District of Columbia, warning of possible lawsuits. After that the department asked California to set aside, for the time being, the mail ballots of about 20,000 voters alleged to be noncitizens. On October 28 another federal judge, Carter, rejected that request, and said the list was unreliable.

paras.lead: Subpoenas in the hands of the people who count
parts: The Department of Justice also sent grand-jury subpoenas to election workers in Los Angeles County, requiring them to appear on November 4, the day after the election.
Thompson wrote in the order that these practices “are likely to interfere with the administration of the election, and to deprive lawful voters of the right to vote.”

The order expires on November 16, and a further hearing is set for November 13. The Department of Justice appealed on October 31. By the evening of October 30, about 49.56 million early votes had been cast nationwide. Election day is November 3.

blocks.title: A reminder from another judge
blocks.text: On October 31, Chutkan, a federal judge in the District of Columbia, said in another case that the Department of Justice’s letters would produce a “chilling effect,” and that the data in the letters was inaccurate in places.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The Department of Justice (Dhillon, head of the Civil Rights Division) | View: noncitizen voting has to be checked, to protect the integrity of the election. ; Interest: the power to enforce the law, and the government’s election policy. ; Worry: unlawful ballots affecting the result. ; Basis: Department of Justice filings say California has admitted registering more than 1,500 noncitizens; it has already appealed the order.

The plaintiff unions, and the civil-rights groups | View: the Department of Justice is intimidating officials and suppressing lawful voters. ; Interest: the voting rights of members, and of minority voters. ; Worry: lawful ballots being set aside, or not counted. ; Basis: the complaint cites the Voting Rights Act; the judge found the plaintiffs’ chance of winning enough to issue a temporary order.

Election officials in California, and in Los Angeles County | View: elections are run by the state and the county, and the list is unreliable. ; Interest: finishing the count on time, and by the law. ; Worry: being sued, being summoned, and the count being disrupted. ; Basis: on October 28 Judge Carter found the Department of Justice’s list unreliable; Los Angeles election workers received subpoenas to appear on November 4.

The federal courts | View: interference with the election has to be prevented before election day. ; Interest: upholding legal procedure, and the right to vote. ; Worry: the ruling being taken as meddling in politics. ; Basis: Thompson, Carter, and the Ninth Circuit made decisions unfavorable to the Department of Justice, one after another; Chutkan mentioned a “chilling effect.”

People who have already voted early | View: their own ballots will be counted in the ordinary way. ; Interest: the right to vote, and the credibility of the result. ; Worry: a ballot being set aside because of an error on a list. ; Basis: about 49.56 million people have already voted early (a count by the University of Florida Election Lab); the Department of Homeland Security’s data matching has been criticized for counting citizens in by mistake.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The Department of Justice presses with lawsuits and subpoenas. State and county officials, and the civil-rights groups, go to court for an order. Both sides are racing for these few days before the election.
The courts reject the Department of Justice again and again, and the department appeals again and again. In the end a higher court may have to decide in a very short time.
Checking unlawful votes, and protecting lawful voters, are both things an election has to do. The disagreement is over whether the list is accurate, and over who should do the checking.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The Department of Justice’s list has about 20,000 people. The figure it itself cites for what “California has admitted” is more than 1,500. How many on the list really are noncitizens has not yet been fully checked in court.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The Department of Justice’s claim that California “admitted registering more than 1,500 noncitizens” comes from the department’s own court filings. This piece has not found California’s reply.
A temporary restraining order is only a preliminary ruling. It does not represent the court’s final judgment of the case.

2026-11-02.fallbackLine: Take one deep breath, then turn to the next page.

pieces.title: He printed the Bible, and lost the workshop: Gutenberg
pieces.short: Gutenberg
pieces.hook: Whether an idea can change the world often depends on whether a string of parts can be fitted into a whole process. Gutenberg lost the lawsuit, and the process he had fitted…
pieces.takeaway: Whether an idea can change the world often depends on whether a string of parts can be fitted into a whole process. Gutenberg lost the lawsuit, and the process he had fitted together spread across Europe.
pieces.imageAlt: A Gutenberg Bible at the New York Public Library
pieces.imageCredit: NYC Wanderer (Kevin Eng) · CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

paras.lead: A rich man’s son in Mainz
parts: Gutenberg was born about 1400 in Mainz, on the Rhine. No one knows the exact year. Scholars put it between 1393 and 1406. His father was an aristocratic merchant of the city, and also held a post at the mint. His mother came from common stock, and that, it is said, kept him from succeeding to his father’s place.

paras.lead: First, a business that lost money
parts: Around 1439, in Strasbourg, he made small mirrors to sell to people going on pilgrimage to Aachen. That year there was a great flood, the fair was put off a year, and he could not get his capital back. In 1448 he returned to Mainz and borrowed a sum from relatives, very likely for printing.

paras.lead: The real invention was a whole process
parts: Movable type was not his first. In the eleventh century, Bi Sheng of the Northern Song had already used clay type, and in 1377 Korea printed Jikji, the earliest surviving book in metal type. Gutenberg’s skill was to fit an alloy of lead, tin, and antimony, a handheld type mold, oil-based ink, and a screw press into a production line that could turn books out in quantity. The Latin alphabet has few characters, and that suited it.

Around 1450 he borrowed 800 gulden from the moneylender Fust, and later borrowed another 800 to print the Bible. In 1455 the Latin Bible, 42 lines to the page, was finished: about 180 copies, three quarters of them on paper, the rest on vellum.

According to the record, a copy sold for 30 florins, about three years’ wages for a clerk. But set against a manuscript that a scribe would take more than a year to copy, it was already much cheaper. According to the record, the books seem to have sold out as soon as they were printed, and some buyers were as far away as England.

Fust later demanded the money back, and sued in the archbishop’s court, saying the loan had been diverted to other uses. Principal and interest had risen to 2,026 gulden, and a legal document of November 1455 records the case. The court found for Fust, and the workshop that printed the Bible went to him.
In 1457 Fust, and Schoeffer, who later became his son-in-law, printed the Mainz Psalter, the first book to carry the printer’s name and a date. Gutenberg is not mentioned in it.

In 1465 the Archbishop of Mainz gave him the title of a courtier, with an annual stipend, a set of court clothes, 2,180 liters of grain, and 2,000 liters of untaxed wine. He died in 1468. The burial ground was later destroyed, and the grave cannot be found. Not even his appearance survives. The portraits we have were imagined by later people.

blocks.title: His name is not on his books
blocks.text: The books Gutenberg printed never carry a name or a date. Judging today which ones came from his hand can only be done by comparing the type, and by evidence from the side. So how much he actually printed is something scholars have still not settled.
