critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Gutenberg himself | View: printing was the “business and craft” he had worked at for years, and the borrowed money all went into it. ; Interest: the technical result, and control of the workshop. ; Worry: the money running out before the technology could be turned into cash. ; Basis: a legal document of 1455 records the partnership of the two sides “to make books”; Fust accused him of diverting funds.

The backer Fust, and Schoeffer | View: money lent has to be recovered as agreed, and the workshop should pass to the side that put up the money. ; Interest: the principal of 1,600 gulden and interest of 6%, and the book business that followed. ; Worry: the inventor caring only for experiments, and not for getting the money back. ; Basis: the court found for Fust; in 1457 they published the Mainz Psalter in their own names, with no mention of Gutenberg.

The Church, and the archbishop | View: printing could copy indulgences and scripture in quantity. ; Interest: the Church’s income, and the spread of doctrine. ; Worry: once there were many books, the power to interpret doctrine would also scatter. ; Basis: in 1454–1455 Gutenberg’s workshop printed thousands of indulgences; in 1465 the archbishop gave him a court title.

Scholars of East Asian printing | View: the “first” of movable type was not in Europe. ; Interest: recording faithfully Bi Sheng’s clay type, Wang Zhen’s wooden type, and Korean metal type. ; Worry: calling Gutenberg “the man who invented movable type,” and wiping out the earlier East Asian technology. ; Basis: Wikipedia and other sources record Bi Sheng’s clay type in the eleventh century, and the Korean metal-type book Jikji in 1377.

Economic historians | View: the press had a measurable effect on the growth of cities. ; Interest: testing, with data, the claim that “printing changed Europe.” ; Worry: the effect being exaggerated, or mixed up with other factors. ; Basis: research by the economist Dittmar says that cities with a press before 1500 grew about 60% faster in population in the sixteenth century.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The inventor needs money. The backer needs a return. Once the technology can make money, who owns the workshop matters more than who thought of the method.
The Church used the printing of indulgences to increase its income, and at the same time faced the loosening of thought that came with a flood of books. The same machine was used at both ends.

East Asian scholars and the European story compete over “who was first.” The later consensus is that East Asia had movable type first, and that Gutenberg’s contribution was a system of mass production.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Gutenberg’s books carry no name and no date. What he actually printed, and which of it was finished after he lost the workshop, is hard to decide.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: There is no reliable record of the year of his birth, of his early life, or of his appearance. Many of the stories come from later guesswork.
The print run of the Bible is given as 158 copies and as 180. Both rest on the retelling of a letter of 1455.

pieces.title: From a son’s tricycle to more than two billion a year: a hundred and eighty years of the tire
pieces.short: A hundred and eighty years of the tire
pieces.hook: Early natural rubber turned sticky in the heat and brittle in the cold.
pieces.imageAlt: Bibendum, the tire man, on an 1898 Michelin poster
pieces.imageCredit: O’Galop · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

paras.lead: First the rubber had to stand heat and cold
parts: Early natural rubber turned sticky in the heat and brittle in the cold. In 1839 the American Goodyear, in Massachusetts, found that rubber heated with sulfur became tough and elastic. That is “vulcanization.” He received a patent in 1844, and spent years after that in patent lawsuits.

In 1847 the Scot Thomson applied for a patent on a pneumatic tire, but it was never put into production. In October 1887 Dunlop, a veterinarian in Belfast, made a pneumatic tire for his ten-year-old son’s tricycle, so the boy would be jolted less. He received the patent in December 1888.

paras.lead: The patent was later held invalid
parts: Two years later his patent was held invalid, because Thomson’s came first. At the end of 1890 his company in Belfast began mass-producing bicycle tires. In 1895 he sold his shares, and from then on he had nothing more to do with it, and did not make a fortune from the invention.

paras.lead: Michelin: a tire you could take off
parts: In 1889 the Michelin brothers took over a farm-machinery plant in Clermont-Ferrand, in France, that was close to failing. At the time, repairing a tire glued fast to the rim took more than three hours. The brothers made a pneumatic tire that could be removed, and received a patent in 1891. In 1895 they put pneumatic tires on a car and entered the Paris–Bordeaux–Paris race.

Marius Mignol, a researcher at Michelin, made the radial tire: the cords run at right angles to the direction of travel, with a belt around them. It wore better, and used less fuel, than the old bias-ply tire. In 1948 the Citroën 2CV used it. Citroën then belonged to Michelin.

In 1968 Consumer Reports confirmed the advantage of the radial tire. In 1970 the Lincoln Continental Mark III became the first American car to have radials as standard. By the 1980s the North American market had switched entirely to radials.

Since 2021 Michelin has been the world’s largest tire maker by revenue, with revenue of €25.99 billion in 2025. Second is Bridgestone, founded in 1931. The name comes from the surname of the founder, Shojiro Ishibashi: “ishi,” stone, and “hashi,” bridge. There are about 450 tire plants in the world, and output in 2021 was about 2.27 billion tires.

paras.lead: A new trouble: the dust that wears off
parts: The particles from tire wear are drawing more and more attention. Some research holds that they are an important source of microplastics in the ocean. A breakdown product of the rubber antioxidant 6PPD has been found toxic to coho salmon. Under the European Union’s Euro 7 rules, from July 2028 tires for new passenger cars must pass certification against an abrasion limit.

blocks.note: Drawn from the Wikipedia entries Radial tire and Tire

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The tire giants (Michelin, Bridgestone, and others) | View: technology and brand set the premium, and wear and safety rest on research. ; Interest: premium tires, the replacement market, and a return on research spending. ; Worry: low-price competition, and ever stricter environmental rules raising the cost. ; Basis: Michelin has been first by revenue since 2021; the radial-tire patents and the Bibendum brand have lasted a hundred years.

The car makers | View: a tire has to fit the fuel use, the range, and the handling of the whole vehicle. ; Interest: the cost of the vehicle, and the test results. ; Worry: a change of tire raising the cost and cutting the range. ; Basis: the Citroën 2CV in 1948 and the Lincoln Mark III in 1970 made radials standard, one after the other, and pushed them into general use.

The regulators (the European Union, UN WP.29) | View: tire-wear particles need to be regulated, just as exhaust does. ; Interest: the quality of air and of water. ; Worry: test methods that are not uniform, and a limit that is disputed whether it is set tight or loose. ; Basis: Euro 7 requires tires for new passenger cars, from July 2028, to pass certification against an abrasion limit; the United Nations drew up the R186 test regulation.

Environmental researchers | View: tire particles are an underestimated source of pollution. ; Interest: the ecology of rivers and oceans, and public health. ; Worry: a pollutant left outside regulation for a long time. ; Basis: a 2020 study cited on Wikipedia says tires account for 78% of the mass of marine microplastics; 6PPD-quinone is toxic to coho salmon and other fish.

Ordinary drivers | View: a tire should be safe, durable, and reasonably priced. ; Interest: spending less, and driving steadily. ; Worry: a greener new tire being more expensive, or wearing less well. ; Basis: because radials lasted longer and used less fuel, they filled the North American market in the 1980s.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Makers hope to answer drivers and regulators at once with “wears better,” because wearing better both saves money and sheds less dust. On that point the three sides’ interests coincide.

But grip for safety and resistance to wear often rise and fall against each other. The stricter the regulatory limit, the more makers worry about sacrificing performance such as braking on a wet road.
Researchers push to bring tire dust under regulation. Makers would rather the limits tighten in stages, according to the test data, and the United Nations rules therefore use a two-stage approach.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Abrasion tests differ greatly with the road surface, the weight of the vehicle, and driving habits, and a single standard is hard to set.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “Tires account for 78% of marine microplastics” comes from a single study. The methods of estimation differ, and the conclusions are far apart.
Whether Dunlop or Thomson should count more as “the inventor” depends on whether one looks at the patent or at mass production.

pieces.title: Profit at a new high, and $42.4 billion of cash flowing out in a year: Amazon’s third quarter
pieces.short: Amazon’s third quarter
pieces.hook: On October 29, Amazon reported third-quarter results for the period ending September 30: revenue of $201.9…
pieces.imageAlt: An aerial view of an AWS data-center campus in Oregon
pieces.imageCredit: Tedder · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On October 29, Amazon reported third-quarter results for the period ending September 30: revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12% from a year earlier; operating profit of $28.1 billion, and an operating margin of 13.9%, which the company said was the highest on record.

paras.lead: The brightest part is the cloud
parts: Amazon Web Services, AWS, had revenue of $46 billion, up 39.3%, the fastest in nearly five years, and on an annualized basis already a scale of $184 billion. AWS operating profit was $17.8 billion, more than six tenths of the company’s operating profit.

paras.lead: But the cash is flowing out
parts: Over the past 12 months, operating cash flow was $168.3 billion, but buying equipment and building machine rooms spent a net $210.7 billion, and free cash flow turned into a net outflow of $42.4 billion. A year earlier it was still an inflow of $14.8 billion. The company said the main reason was investment in artificial intelligence.

In the third quarter alone, purchases of equipment and property cost $77.3 billion. The company restated full-year capital expenditure of about $220 billion. Long-term borrowing rose from $65.6 billion at the end of last year to $173.1 billion, and the third quarter borrowed a further $48.1 billion.

paras.lead: Why net profit was instead a little less
parts: Third-quarter net profit was $20.7 billion, a little less than the $21.2 billion of a year earlier. The reason is that last year’s quarter included $9.5 billion of mark-to-market gain on the Anthropic shares it held, and this year there is none.

Revenue and earnings per share were both a little below the analysts’ estimates. Capital expenditure was about $20 billion more than estimated. The share price fell about 7% at one point after hours, and another 1.4% the next day. Several investment banks cut their price targets, but still gave a buy rating.

The figures above are all facts the company published. Whether the investment in AI can turn, a few years from now, into profit just as high is for now only the company’s expectation and the analysts’ inference. It also depends on customer demand, and on the supply of chips, electricity, and the like.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Amazon’s management | View: spending more now is to take the AI orders already signed. ; Interest: AWS’s long-term share, and its profit. ; Worry: chips and electricity not keeping up, and capacity not matching demand. ; Basis: the release says capital expenditure for 2026 is about $220 billion, and AWS growth in 2027 and 2028 is expected to exceed 40%.

Shareholders, and analysts | View: bullish for the long run, but the short-term cash flow looks too poor. ; Interest: the share price, and the timetable of the return. ; Worry: how long the money spent will take to come back, and whether AI demand will cool. ; Basis: the share price fell about 7% at one point after hours; Morgan Stanley called it an “expectation gap,” and Goldman Sachs mentioned investors’ worry that the spending will continue after 2027.

Cloud rivals (Microsoft, Google) | View: the contest in the AI cloud is about who has more computing power, and more customers. ; Interest: enterprise customers, and model partners. ; Worry: a price war, and too much capacity. ; Basis: an Emarketer analyst said AWS’s pace of growth did not meet the bar that Microsoft and Google had raised; the same week Microsoft cut its full-year spending outlook from $175 billion to $170 billion.

Retail sellers, and consumers | View: faster delivery, and more AI tools, are a good thing. ; Interest: fees, traffic, and price. ; Worry: the platform putting more resources into the cloud, and retail growth slowing. ; Basis: North American retail grew 6%; a report carried by BusinessLine said core e-commerce growth was the slowest in three years; third-party seller services brought in $46.5 billion.

Communities where the data centers sit | View: a data center can bring tax revenue, and it also takes electricity and water. ; Interest: jobs, the price of electricity, and water. ; Worry: pressure on the grid, and on water use. ; Basis: Amazon announced a “Built Together” program of $1 billion in the communities where its data centers sit.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Management uses orders and growth expectations to reassure shareholders. Shareholders use the share price to express worry about the cash flow. The two pull against each other over “how long until it pays back.”
The rivals’ pace of spending has become the reference. Microsoft trimmed its spending, Google held steady, and Amazon did not cut. Investors will compare who spends more effectively.
The community and the grid are a hard constraint. A data center needs electricity and water, and the company puts up community investment in exchange for local support.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: How much of the demand for AI computing power will last as long-term contracts is something outsiders cannot see in a complete order book.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “Two trillion-dollar businesses” is the chief executive’s outlook, not a financial figure.
The claim of “the slowest e-commerce growth in three years” is affected by the members’ sale having been moved to the second quarter, so the year-over-year comparison is limited.

pieces.title: Two days before the vote, she turned and backed her opponent: a “defection” in Michigan’s Senate election
pieces.short: A “defection” in Michigan’s Senate election…
pieces.hook: The U.S. midterm elections are voted on November 3.
pieces.event: November 1, 2026 (U.S. Eastern Time, a Sunday); voting on November 3
pieces.imageAlt: The official House photograph of Haley Stevens
pieces.imageCredit: U.S. House of Representatives · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: The U.S. midterm elections are voted on November 3. On Sunday, November 1, Haley Stevens, a Democratic member of the U.S. House from Michigan, appeared with the Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers at a church in Detroit, and then posted a video announcing her support for Rogers.

In the Democratic primary in August, Stevens lost to Abdul El-Sayed by less than one percentage point, and afterward she said she supported El-Sayed. The disagreement between them was mainly over Israel: she demanded that he condemn an outside group’s advertisement blaming American food prices on Israel, and she also criticized his dealings with the streamer Hasan Piker.

In the video she said: “I am not part of Abdul’s campaign.” She also said she is “still a proud Democrat,” and will go on voting with the party for the rest of her term. The Associated Press reported that she had been set to appear with El-Sayed that day, and that the invitation was cancelled beforehand.

paras.lead: The party cut her off at once
parts: About an hour later, the state party chair, Hertel, wrote on X that she “is not now, and will not be, a member of the Michigan Democratic Party.” Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, called it a “shameful betrayal.” Her chief of staff and several aides resigned that day.

paras.lead: The reaction on the other side
parts: Trump praised her as “brave,” and said he hoped she would join the Republican Party. At the same time he called El-Sayed a “jihadist.” USA Today pointed out that this is not true. El-Sayed, for his part, said he “actually doesn’t think about Haley Stevens,” and that he would put his attention on the price of fuel and of food.

The Senate now has 53 Republicans and 47 Democrats. On the RealClearPolitics polling average, El-Sayed leads Rogers by 3.5 percentage points. If he is elected, he will be the first Muslim U.S. senator.
On the same polling average, the Democratic candidates in Maine and Texas lead by only one or two percentage points.

One account tells her choice as “the Democrats splitting over Israel.” Another tells it as “the opponent knows only how to apply a religious label.” Both have a basis in fact, and both tell only half: the reasons she herself gave include Israel, being shut out by the campaign, and the dealings with Piker. What one endorsement actually does to the vote will be known only after the count.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Haley Stevens | View: she said this was about “leadership and integrity,” and that the other side shut her out first. ; Interest: her own political position, and her consistent stand on Israel. ; Worry: being treated as a traitor inside the party, and her political future being damaged. ; Basis: her endorsement video; according to The Hill, she said it was “a personal decision,” and that she would still vote with the party.

El-Sayed, and the Michigan Democratic Party | View: the disagreement inside the party was settled in the primary vote, and the party should unite behind the nominee. ; Interest: holding this seat, and contesting a Senate majority. ; Worry: news of a split in the last two days before the vote affecting the will to turn out. ; Basis: Roberson, the state party’s first vice chair: “Disagreements inside the party are settled at the ballot box, and they have been settled.”

Rogers, and the Republicans | View: people from inside the Democratic Party have come over, which shows the opponent is too radical. ; Interest: taking this seat, and winning swing voters. ; Worry: being criticized for attacking the opponent by way of religious identity. ; Basis: Trump called Stevens “brave”; Speaker of the House Johnson said she “stood on the side of the truth.”

The national Democratic leadership | View: this is a betrayal, and the caucus supports the nominee as one. ; Interest: control of the Senate, and party discipline. ; Worry: the split inside the party over Israel growing wider. ; Basis: Schumer called it a “shameful betrayal”; Mamdani, the mayor of New York, said she betrayed working-class voters.

Voters, and observers | View: one endorsement need not change very many votes. ; Interest: practical issues such as the cost of living. ; Worry: emotional news before the vote crowding out a discussion of policy. ; Basis: the RealClearPolitics average: El-Sayed leads by 3.5 percentage points; he himself said voters care more about the price of fuel and of food.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The Republicans use Stevens’s endorsement to speak to swing voters. The Democrats use “no longer a member” to draw a line. Both sides are contesting the same swing voters.
The question of Israel sets the progressives and the moderates inside the Democratic Party against each other. Winning or losing the primary did not make the disagreement disappear.
Trump put a religious label on El-Sayed. The Democratic side, and USA Today, call it a false attack. The same event is used by both sides to mobilize their own supporters.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: What procedural basis the state party had for declaring that she “is not a member” is something the reporting does not explain in detail.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: How many votes this endorsement can move is something for which there are no reliable figures before the election.
Why she was taken off the joint appearance is mostly reported from unnamed people with knowledge. Neither side has made the full course of it public.

pieces.title: Taking the handle off a pump: John Snow and his cholera map
pieces.short: John Snow and his cholera map
pieces.hook: Evidence does not have to wait for a perfect explanation. Snow did not know what the germ was, but he counted clearly “who had drunk the water from where,” and…
pieces.takeaway: Evidence does not have to wait for a perfect explanation. Snow did not know what the germ was, but he counted clearly “who had drunk the water from where,” and that was enough to have the handle taken off first.
pieces.imageAlt: Snow’s cholera map of 1854
pieces.imageCredit: John Snow · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: John Snow was born on March 15, 1813, in York, England, the eldest of nine children. His father worked in a coal yard by the River Ouse. The neighborhood was poor, often flooded by the river, and the street and the river were both filthy. At 14 he went to be an apprentice near Newcastle, and in 1832, in the mining village of Killingworth, he met cholera for the first time and treated quite a few patients.

In 1847, only a year after ether reached Britain, he wrote a guide to its use, and also designed an apparatus for giving ether to a patient and a mask for chloroform. On April 7, 1853, when Queen Victoria bore her eighth child, Leopold, she asked him to ease the pain with chloroform. She asked him again in 1857, for the birth of Princess Beatrice, and obstetric anesthesia became easier to accept from then on.

paras.lead: He did not believe in “bad air”
parts: The mainstream view then was the “miasma theory”: cholera came from the bad air given off by rotting matter. In 1849 Snow published On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, arguing that the disease was drunk in. There was no germ theory yet, and he could not say what the thing was that did the harm.

On August 31, 1854, cholera broke out around Broad Street in Soho, London. 127 people died in three days. A week later, three quarters of the residents had fled, and in the end 420 people died. Snow and the curate Whitehead went from door to door, and found that the dead had almost all lived near the Broad Street pump.

Of the dead who lived closer to some other pump, there were only 10. Of those, 5 households said they preferred to fetch water from Broad Street, and 3 were children who went to school near Broad Street.

Not one worker at a nearby brewery fell ill. They had a beer allowance every day, and did not drink the water from that well, and the wort is boiled in brewing. On the evening of September 7, Snow set these facts before the vestry of the parish of St James, and the next day the pump handle was taken off.

paras.lead: He himself could not be sure
parts: Snow later wrote that, before the handle was removed, cases had already fallen sharply, and the flight of the residents had also brought deaths down, so it was “impossible to decide” whether the well water was still carrying the disease at that point. It was later found that the well was only 3 feet (about 0.9 meters) from an old cesspit. An infant who had caught the disease elsewhere had dirty water from the washing of diapers seep into the cesspit.

paras.lead: The harder evidence was in two water companies
parts: He also compared two water companies in south London. The Southwark and Vauxhall company drew water from a stretch of the Thames polluted by sewage. The Lambeth company had already moved its intake upstream. The two companies’ pipes were laid in an interleaving pattern, and neighbors on the same street might use different companies’ water.
In the first seven weeks of the 1854 outbreak, 315 people died for every 10,000 households of the former, and only 37 of the latter.

paras.lead: It was not accepted in his lifetime
parts: After the outbreak, officials put the handle back. The Board of Health in the end attributed this outbreak to miasma. On June 16, 1858, Snow died of a stroke, only 45. Not until 1866 did the statistician Farr, who had opposed him, order, while investigating another cholera outbreak in east London, that unboiled water was not to be drunk.
In 2013 The Lancet issued a correction to that short obituary of 1858.

blocks.title: The handle comes off once a year
blocks.text: The John Snow Society holds a “pump-handle lecture” every September. Before 2015 they would also take the handle off the memorial pump at the original site and put it back, as a reminder that reform in public health always meets resistance.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Snow himself | View: cholera spreads through contaminated drinking water, not through bad air. ; Interest: proving the cause with data, and pushing for better water supply. ; Worry: the Broad Street outbreak was already fading, and residents had fled in large numbers, so one well alone was not persuasive enough. ; Basis: the death map in the enlarged edition of 1855, and the comparison of death rates among the customers of the two water companies.

The Board of Health, and the miasma theorists | View: the disease came from the bad air given off by rotting matter, and the main thing was to clean and to remove the smell. ; Interest: keeping the sanitary policy and the conclusions already in place. ; Worry: accepting that “disease enters by the mouth” would mean facing the awkward fact that a city’s sewage was flowing into its drinking water. ; Basis: the Board of Health in the end attributed the 1854 outbreak to miasma; Simon, London’s medical officer, called Snow’s theory “peculiar.”

The vestry of the parish of St James | View: take the handle off first, and stop the loss in an emergency. ; Interest: calming the panic, and protecting the residents of the parish. ; Worry: being held responsible if the wrong thing was removed, while the theory was not yet proved. ; Basis: on the evening of September 7 it heard Snow’s account, and the handle came off the next day; after the outbreak the handle was put back.

The curate Whitehead, and the residents | View: at first they too believed in miasma, and later the investigation convinced them. ; Interest: the life and death of the neighborhood. ; Worry: putting the cause on the well everyone drank from every day would shake ordinary life. ; Basis: Whitehead had originally believed the miasma theory, and later, with Snow, traced the leaking cesspit and the infant who fell ill first.

Later historical researchers | View: “taking the handle off ended the outbreak” is a legend that has been simplified. ; Interest: recovering what happened, and seeing clearly the role of the data and of the collaborators. ; Worry: a hero story covering the more important comparison of the water companies. ; Basis: Snow himself wrote that cases had already fallen sharply before the handle was removed; Wikipedia says removing the pump had little effect on an outbreak in which nearly 3,000 people died across the city.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The parish accepted Snow’s advice to remove the handle, and did not accept his theory. The action and the theory came unhooked, and once the outbreak was over the handle went back on.
Both sides were speaking with data. The statistics collected by Farr, a miasma theorist, later helped Snow’s view to stand, and Farr himself turned in 1866.
The doctor and the clergyman filled in for each other. Snow had the method. Whitehead knew the neighborhood. Together they found the infant who fell ill first.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The cholera vibrio had already been isolated in 1854, but it was decades before that was generally accepted. In Snow’s lifetime he could not produce evidence that pointed to the cause under a microscope.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “A 14-fold difference in the death rates of the two water companies’ customers” appears on Wikipedia. “315 against 37 per 10,000 households” is the figure, in Snow’s book, for the first seven weeks of the outbreak. The two are not on the same basis.
How much removing the handle actually did to end the outbreak is something Snow himself said he could not judge.

pieces.title: The first one burned for only 24 days: more than a hundred and fifty years of the traffic light
pieces.short: More than a hundred and fifty years of the traffic light
pieces.hook: The record shows that as early as 1722, London Bridge posted three constables to direct the traffic crossing the bridge.
pieces.imageAlt: A traffic tower in the middle of an intersection in Detroit, around 1920
pieces.imageCredit: Burton Historical Collection, Detroit Public Library (author unknown) · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

paras.lead: Police first, and the light later
parts: The record shows that as early as 1722, London Bridge posted three constables to direct the traffic crossing the bridge. By the nineteenth century there were more and more carriages, and the gate of the Palace of Westminster was often jammed solid.

On December 9, 1868, a signal designed by the railway engineer John Peake Knight went into use in front of the Houses of Parliament. The post was 22 feet high (6.7 meters). By day it used semaphore arms, and at night red and green gas lamps, worked by a policeman with a lever. The idea was taken straight from railway signals. On January 2, 1869, 24 days after it opened, it exploded. The policeman operating it was injured (some accounts say he was killed), and the apparatus was taken down at once.

In 1912 Lester Wire, a policeman in Salt Lake City, made the first electric signal, with only red and green. In August 1914 the American Traffic Signal Company installed red and green electric signals at the intersection of East 105th Street and Euclid Avenue in Cleveland.

paras.lead: Where the yellow light came from
parts: In 1920 William Potts, a Detroit police officer, worried that officers in four directions could not change the lights at the same moment, and added a third color, amber. That color also came from railway signals. In 1921 he fitted automatic three-color lights on 15 traffic towers in Detroit.

From 1922, automatic control by a timer became more and more common. According to the record, New York had had 6,000 traffic police, and after the change to timed signals only 500 were left, saving $12.5 million. Garrett Morgan, an African American inventor in Cleveland, saw a car and a horse-drawn carriage collide in 1922, and designed a hand-cranked three-position signal. He received the patent in November 1923, and later sold the patent rights to General Electric for $40,000.

In 1952 Denver used a computer to control 120 signals. In 1967 Toronto used a computer, over telephone lines, to control 159, and could adjust the length of the green light according to the traffic. Later, incandescent lamps were replaced by LEDs, which save electricity and are bright. But an LED gives off no heat, and in winter it cannot melt the snow, so the housing has to be heated as well.

paras.lead: More lights are not always better
parts: Between 1979 and 1988 Philadelphia removed surplus signals at 199 intersections, and crashes fell by 24% on average. A traffic light can reduce side collisions, but it may increase rear-end collisions by as much as 50%. Hans Monderman, a Dutch traffic engineer, said: “We only put up traffic lights where they are useful, and I have not yet found a useful place.

Google’s “Green Light” uses AI and driving data from maps to suggest signal timings, and city engineers decide whether to adopt them. Boston announced in June 2025 that it had adjusted 114 intersections on the suggestions. Unnecessary stops fell by 20% on average, and delay by 13.5% on average.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: City traffic departments | View: the efficiency of an intersection rests mainly on signal timing. ; Interest: capacity, and less congestion. ; Worry: aging equipment, and timings that cannot keep up with changes in traffic. ; Basis: Boston’s traffic center makes more than 1,000 real-time adjustments a month, and asked INRIX to evaluate the effect of AI timing.

Road-safety researchers | View: a traffic light does not necessarily make an intersection safer. ; Interest: fewer crashes, and protection for people walking and cycling. ; Worry: more lights, and the risk of rear-end collisions and of harm to pedestrians may rise. ; Basis: after Philadelphia removed lights, crashes fell 24%; Wikipedia says signals can increase rear-end collisions by as much as 50%.

Technology companies (Google) | View: with data and AI, existing signals can be rebuilt at a low cost. ; Interest: getting the technology into use, emissions targets, and the value of map data. ; Worry: cities adopting it slowly, and the effect being hard to verify independently. ; Basis: Google says stops can be cut by as much as 30%, and intersection emissions by 10%; as of June 2025 it was running in 18 cities on four continents.

Environmental and health researchers | View: frequent stopping and starting at an intersection worsens local air pollution. ; Interest: the air quality of nearby residents, schools, and hospitals. ; Worry: a signalized intersection becoming a pollution hot spot. ; Basis: research cited by the World Economic Forum says peak concentrations of particulate matter at a signalized intersection can reach about 29 times those of free-flowing traffic.

Drivers, and pedestrians | View: less waiting at lights, and crossing the street has to be safe. ; Interest: time, and safety. ; Worry: waiting too long, and stopping and starting again and again. ; Basis: in 2023 Boston ranked 8th in the world for traffic delay; after AI timing, unnecessary stops at some intersections fell by about a third.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Traffic departments want to raise efficiency. Safety researchers remind them that the light itself also brings rear-end collisions. The side collisions a traffic light reduces are more likely to injure people, so the extra rear-end collisions are often treated as an acceptable price.
The technology company only makes suggestions. The decision stays with the city’s engineers, and the effect is then handed to a third party to evaluate. The three sides check one another.
Saving money has always been a driver. In the 1920s the timer replaced the traffic police. Today AI timing is treated as a cheaper method than replacing the hardware.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Whether to install a light has no simple answer. American rules say a light may be installed only when an intersection meets certain conditions, but meeting the conditions only shows that it “may be suitable.” Sometimes a roundabout is better.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Whether the policeman operating the signal in the explosion of 1869 was injured or killed is something the accounts do not agree on.
The effects of AI timing are mostly published by the project side and the partner cities. Independent long-term evaluations are still few.
The yellow light is often said to be Morgan’s invention. In fact Potts’s design of 1920 already had a yellow light.

pieces.title: Enterprise customers overtook the government for the first time: Palantir’s third quarter
pieces.short: Palantir’s third quarter
pieces.hook: Palantir makes data-analysis software. For a long time, the U.S. government, the military, and the intelligence agencies were its main cust…
pieces.event: Third-quarter results released on November 2, 2026 (U.S. Eastern Time)
pieces.imageAlt: Palantir’s booth at an NHS conference in Britain
pieces.imageCredit: Rathfelder · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Palantir makes data-analysis software. For a long time, the U.S. government, the military, and the intelligence agencies were its main customers. In recent years it has sold an AI platform to enterprises. The chief executive is Alex Karp.

After the close on November 2, Palantir reported third-quarter results for the period ending September 30: revenue of $2.313 billion, up 96% from a year earlier, the first quarter above $2 billion; net profit of $1.128 billion, against about $476 million a year earlier. Revenue and earnings per share were both above the analysts’ estimates.

Revenue from U.S. enterprise customers was $984 million, up 148%, and for the first time it exceeded U.S. government revenue of $953 million (up 96%). CNBC said its U.S. enterprise revenue has risen, in two years, to more than five times what it was.

paras.lead: A margin that is rarely this high
parts: Adjusted operating profit was $1.427 billion, a margin of 62%. The operating margin under accounting rules was also 47%. Operating cash flow was $1.205 billion. On the “Rule of 40” the company often cites (the pace of revenue growth plus the margin), this quarter scored 158%.

paras.lead: There are also figures that slowed
parts: The total value of contracts newly signed this quarter was $2.918 billion, up only 6% from last year. Of that, U.S. enterprise contracts were $1.463 billion, up 11%, far below the pace of revenue. But the part of U.S. enterprise contracts not yet recognized as revenue was $6.517 billion, up 79%.

The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of about $2.65 billion, and full-year revenue of about $8.53 billion, growth of about 91%. The full-year outlook given last quarter was $8.15 billion to $8.16 billion.

On the day of the results the share price closed down about 3% in the regular session, and moved only a little after hours. CNBC reported a fall of about 2%, and Fortune a rise of about 1.5%. The options market had earlier priced a move of as much as 13%. Investing.com counts the share price at about 114 times expected earnings per share for 2026.

Fortune noted that the week before, Alphabet recorded its largest single-day drop since listing, and Intel fell about 29% in a week. The market worries that investment in AI is running ahead of the return. On the day of the results the Nasdaq also fell more than 1%.

The financial figures above are facts the company published. Whether the growth can last, and what the slowing of newly signed contracts means, are for now only the separate judgments of management and of analysts.

blocks.text: Karp told CNBC: “I do not think anyone, in the history of software AI, has had a run of results like this.” He also said the growth of the business “does not depend on salespeople.”

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Palantir’s management | View: enterprises are adopting its AI platform on a large scale, and the growth can last. ; Interest: long-term contracts, and the valuation. ; Worry: being written down by the market along with the rest of an “AI bubble.” ; Basis: the letter to shareholders says that every industry will “either be remade, or simply set aside”; the full-year outlook for U.S. enterprise revenue was raised to more than $3.559 billion.

The bullish analysts | View: revenue, profit, and guidance all beat expectations. ; Interest: room for the share price to rise. ; Worry: the pace of growth will slow in the end. ; Basis: according to Investing.com, around the results Oppenheimer moved its target to $235, Citi to $250, and Rosenblatt to $260.

Those who doubt the valuation | View: the results are good, but the share price is already too dear. ; Interest: avoiding the risk of buying at a high. ; Worry: once the pace of growth falls back, the share price will correct sharply. ; Basis: the Royal Bank of Canada keeps a “sell” rating and a target of $90, on the ground that the valuation is far above peers.

Enterprise customers | View: use an AI platform to pull data together and raise efficiency. ; Interest: lower costs, and higher efficiency. ; Worry: spending on AI that does not come back as a return one can see. ; Basis: a net dollar retention rate of 165%, which means old customers are using more and more; Fortune, citing S&P Global, said AI spending will approach $2 trillion within two years.

Government customers | View: defense and the public sector need tools for analyzing data. ; Interest: the needs of the mission, and the safety of the budget. ; Worry: the budget cycle changing, and contracts that can be ended early. ; Basis: U.S. government revenue rose 96%; the company notes in the release that most contracts contain a clause allowing termination at any time.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Management answers the doubt about valuation with figures that beat expectations. The doubters hold that beating expectations was already in the share price. The result is bright figures, and very little movement in the price.
Enterprise revenue overtaking the government reduces dependence on a single large customer, but enterprise budgets rise and fall more easily with the economy and with the heat of AI.
Revenue grew 96%, and the value of newly signed contracts grew only 6%. The bulls look at the $6.5 billion of contracts not yet recognized. The bears look at the slowing of new signatures.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Many contracts contain a clause allowing early termination. How much of what has been signed but not yet recognized will in the end become revenue is hard for an outsider to estimate.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “Rule of 40, 158%” is a measure the company chose for itself, and it uses adjusted profit.
On the direction of the share price after hours, the reports do not agree.

pieces.title: The first woman elected president, and fewer than three in ten people voted: Bulgaria’s presidential runoff
pieces.short: Bulgaria’s presidential runoff
pieces.hook: On November 1, Bulgaria held the second round of its presidential election.
pieces.event: The runoff vote on November 1, 2026; the final result published on November 2
pieces.imageAlt: The official presidential portrait of Yotova
pieces.imageCredit: Presidency of Bulgaria · CC BY 2.5 bg, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On November 1, Bulgaria held the second round of its presidential election. On November 2 the Central Election Commission published the full count: the acting president, Yotova, and her running mate Valchev received 1,093,852 votes, 57.56%; the former caretaker prime minister, Gyurov, and his running mate Kandev received 750,251 votes, 39.48%; and another 2.95% chose “I support no one.”

Yotova is 61. She was a journalist at the national television, a member of the European Parliament from 2007, and from 2017 to 2026 vice president to President Radev for nine years. In January of this year Radev resigned to form a party and run for parliament, and she took over as acting president.
With this election she becomes Bulgaria’s first woman elected president. The new term begins on January 22, 2027.

paras.lead: Where the two of them differ
parts: Yotova argues for restoring a dialogue with Moscow, and opposes sending weapons to Ukraine. In a podcast on October 30, asked whether Russia is an enemy, she answered: “Absolutely not. Russia is part of our history.

” Gyurov has the support of pro-Western reformist parties. As caretaker prime minister he signed a security-cooperation agreement with Kyiv. In a television debate on October 29 he said, “Russia must end the aggression before the next step can be taken,” and “Let us say which country the threat comes from.” A few days before the runoff, Borisov, the leader of the old party GERB, also said he supported him.

In the month before the election, at least six merchant ships trading with Ukraine, inside Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, were struck by drones. Reuters said at least 24 seafarers were killed. The most recent strike was on October 28. The prime minister, Radev, summoned the Russian ambassador, and said the result of the strikes “benefits Russia,” but he did not accuse Moscow directly, and said responsibility would be assigned after an investigation.

Gyurov led in the capital, Sofia, and also took about 56% of the overseas vote: among Bulgarian voters in the United States he took about 67.5%; among voters in Russia, Yotova took 84%. Younger people voted more for Gyurov, and small towns more for Yotova.
According to figures from the polling firm Alpha Research, a large part of the votes she newly gained in the second round came from supporters of the pro-Russian Revival party.

The real power in Bulgaria lies mainly with parliament. “Progressive Bulgaria,” led by Radev, holds 131 of the 240 seats, and overturning a presidential veto takes only 121. The president’s weightier tools are to send a law to the Constitutional Court (4 of the 12 judges are appointed by the president), and to sign the decrees appointing the prosecutor general and the presidents of the two supreme courts, with the power to refuse a nomination once.

paras.lead: The accounts of turnout do not agree
parts: The Central Election Commission published a turnout of 19.33% as of 4 p.m. The parallel-count body Trend estimated 27.5%. The national radio reported about 27%. Novinite said it was under three in ten, the lowest of any presidential runoff.

One account is that “Bulgaria is turning toward Moscow.” Another is that “the establishment joined hands and was rejected by the voters.” Both tell only half. Yotova’s own words were “Russia is not an enemy.” Some people retold that as “Russia is a friend,” which Novinite points out is not accurate. And a president’s real power is limited. The diplomatic line still depends on how the government and parliament go.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Yotova | View: the voters chose “dialogue, not division.” ; Interest: carrying out the office of president with a fairly broad mandate. ; Worry: being seen as Radev’s dependent. ; Basis: her victory speech; she said that in nearly 30 years in politics, “no one has yet been able to tell me what to do.”

Radev, and “Progressive Bulgaria” | View: the result shows that voters support the new government’s line. ; Interest: the government and the presidency pointing the same way, so policy moves more smoothly. ; Worry: being criticized for an excessive concentration of power. ; Basis: Yotova’s thanks that evening: “Mr. Radev, without you we could not have done it”; the sociologist Dimitrova said, “We have never had such a concentration of the resources of power.”

Gyurov, and the pro-Western reformers | View: it should be said plainly that the threat comes from Russia, and Ukraine should be firmly supported. ; Interest: a European and Atlantic line. ; Worry: the president no longer checking the government. ; Basis: his words in the television debate, “Let us say which country the threat comes from”; after the defeat he said he accepted the result, “This is the result of the citizens’ vote.”

Revival (pro-Russian) | View: it claims to have decided the result of this election. ; Interest: having the new president hear its opposition to the euro, and to aid for Ukraine. ; Worry: its demands being ignored. ; Basis: the account of the party leader, Kostadinov, and Alpha Research’s figures on where the newly gained votes came from (according to Novinite).

The European Union, and the neighbors | View: willing to cooperate on security, defense, and energy. ; Interest: security in the Black Sea, and stability on NATO’s eastern flank. ; Worry: a member state’s position on Russia loosening. ; Basis: von der Leyen listed shared priorities including security, defense, competitiveness, and energy independence; the Romanian president, Dan, mentioned cooperation on Black Sea security, and invited her to visit.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The governing party’s 131 seats can overturn any veto, so a presidential veto is mainly a public statement, and a delay of a few weeks. What can really stop a law is sending it to the Constitutional Court.

Part of Yotova’s newly gained votes came from Revival supporters. That widens her mandate, and it also brings pressure against the euro and against aid to Ukraine. The European Union and the neighbors want her cooperation on Black Sea security. Both sides are pulling.

Three former prime ministers, Borisov, Denkov, and Kostov, accused Yotova and the government of underestimating the Russian threat, and turned to support Gyurov. But the reformers and GERB had been opponents, and this temporary joining did not manage to add the votes together.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Who struck the merchant ships in the Black Sea is something the government says looks consistent with Russia’s interest, but there is as yet no evidence pointing directly at Moscow, and responsibility has still not been assigned.
The new government’s target for the 2027 budget deficit is above 3% of GDP. Whether she signs it or sends it back will be the first test before the new term.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The turnout figures of 19.33%, about 27%, 27.5%, and 29.1% differ in what they count and in when they were counted.
“Revival’s supporters decided the result” comes from one polling firm’s data, and from the party’s own account.

pieces.title: An awl took the light, and he gave it back to everyone with six dots: Louis Braille
pieces.short: Louis Braille
pieces.hook: A good invention is often a matter of taking away: Barbier gave him the idea of “raised dots,” and Braille cut 12 dots down to 6…
pieces.takeaway: A good invention is often a matter of taking away: Barbier gave him the idea of “raised dots,” and Braille cut 12 dots down to 6, so that one finger could feel a whole character at a single touch.
pieces.imageAlt: A portrait of Louis Braille
pieces.imageCredit: Anonymous (a print of 1925) · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Louis Braille was born on January 4, 1809, in the small town of Coupvray, about 30 kilometers east of Paris. His father was a craftsman who worked leather harness. At three, in his father’s workshop, he was copying the adults and punching holes in leather with an awl. The awl slipped, and went into one eye.

The wound was badly infected, and later the other eye went blind as well, very likely from “sympathetic ophthalmia.” By five he could see with neither eye, and at first he often asked the adults why the sky was always dark. His father whittled him a cane, and he learned to walk the village paths by himself.

paras.lead: The whole school had three books
parts: In February 1819, at ten, he entered the Royal Institute for Blind Youth in Paris, one of the earliest schools for blind children in the world. The textbooks pressed raised Latin letters into thick paper. They were large and heavy. When the school first opened there were only three in all. Students felt their way through them very slowly, and could not write for themselves at all.

In 1821 the retired officer Charles Barbier brought his “night writing” to the school: up to 12 raised dots, in two columns, standing for 36 sounds. It could be felt, and it could be written, but a single symbol was too tall for a fingertip to take in at once, and it had no punctuation, no numerals, and no music.

Braille cut 12 dots down to 6, in two columns of three rows. One letter was exactly the size of a fingertip, and a single touch could recognize it. In 1825, at fifteen or sixteen, he showed the scheme to his classmates for the first time. In 1829 he published the first manual, and music could be written in it too. The second edition of 1837 took out the short dashes, which were hard to feel.

paras.lead: The school banned it, and then used it
parts: After graduating he stayed on. In 1833 he became a regular teacher, of history, geometry, and algebra, and he also played the organ in churches in Paris. In 1840 the principal who supported him, Pignier, was forced out. His successor, Dufau, opposed teaching the dots, and it was restored only in 1844, when the school moved into a new building.

paras.lead: Official only two years after his death
parts: He had a respiratory illness for a long time, long thought to be tuberculosis, and around 40 he had to stop teaching. On January 6, 1852, he died in the school infirmary, two days after his 43rd birthday. In 1854, after the blind students insisted again and again, the school formally adopted his dots.

An international meeting in Paris in 1878 proposed that each country’s braille match the Latin alphabet by sound. American schools for the blind formally adopted it in 1916, and in 1932 English braille had a unified standard. In 1952, the centenary of his death, his remains were moved to the Panthéon in Paris, while his hands were left to be buried in his hometown of Coupvray.

Once screen-reading software spread, fewer people learned to read braille. Of the 57,425 legally blind students registered in the United States in 1998, only about 10% used braille as their main way of reading and writing. But some scholars point out that there is still no reliable count of braille literacy.

blocks.title: A script “that sighted people can read too”
blocks.text: In 1839 Braille also designed “decapoint”: a blind person, with a special slate, punched dots that formed ordinary letters a sighted person could recognize, so as to write to the family. His friend Foucault made a faster writing machine from it, and showed it at the Paris exposition of 1855.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Braille himself | View: what blind people need is not pity, but a tool with which they can read and write for themselves, and communicate with sighted people as equals. ; Interest: letting blind people read quickly, write for themselves, and reach more books. ; Worry: a blind person who can only feel raised letters has a pitifully small store of knowledge, and can only have others write for them. ; Basis: Wikipedia quotes him: “We do not need pity…… We must be treated as equals, and communication is the way to achieve it.”

Barbier (the inventor of night writing) | View: raised dots let a person read and write without eyes, and the method could also be used in the army and in hospitals. ; Interest: having his script adopted, and spread. ; Worry: the original encoded 36 sounds, had no capitals, punctuation, numerals, or music, and the symbols were too tall for one finger to take in. ; Basis: he published the scheme in 1815; the Institute for Blind Youth adopted it in 1821; in 1823 it won a bronze medal at the industrial exhibition in Versailles; a pamphlet of 1832 stressed military and hospital uses.

The school’s management | View: the principal, Pignier, allowed braille to be taught; his successor, Dufau, opposed teaching it. ; Interest: deciding what textbooks the school used, and on what principles it taught blind children. ; Worry: (Wikipedia does not record in detail the reasons for Dufau’s opposition.) ; Basis: in 1840 Pignier was forced out, and braille stopped being taught; in 1844 it was restored with the support of the teacher Gaudet.

The students of the Institute for Blind Youth | View: braille was far more usable than raised Latin letters, and should be formally adopted. ; Interest: being able to read and write for themselves, to take notes, and to write music. ; Worry: the school’s policy changing with the principal, and the standing of braille being unsteady. ; Basis: Wikipedia: in 1854 the school formally adopted braille under the students’ “overwhelming insistence.”

Researchers and advocates today | View: braille is still the key tool by which blind people master written language, including spelling and punctuation. ; Interest: having blind children meet braille early, and keeping the basis of literacy and of employment. ; Worry: screen reading spreading, a shortage of qualified teachers, and the use of braille declining. ; Basis: about 10% of the blind students registered in the United States in 1998 used braille as their main method; an article in the Journal of Visual Impairment & Blindness points out that there is at present no reliable count of braille literacy.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Barbier supplied the raised dots and the tools. Braille remade the code. The credit for the invention is both an inheritance and a replacement.
The school and the students pulled back and forth. Management could stop the teaching. The students, by going on using it and by insisting, “voted” the dots back in.
Technical progress lets blind people “listen to books,” and it also reduces the motive to learn braille. The pull between advocates and the education budget continues to this day.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Reading by sound or reading by the fingers is not a choice of one or the other. Reading software is faster and cheaper. Braille is better for mastering spelling and written expression. There is no single answer for how to mix the two.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The medical cause of Braille’s blindness in both eyes is a later inference (sympathetic ophthalmia). Whether his illness really was tuberculosis is only something “long thought” to be so.
Why Dufau opposed braille is something the common accounts do not agree on, and this piece does not infer it.
“Adults who learn braille have a lower unemployment rate (44% against 77%)” comes from a preliminary study. It can show a connection, and cannot prove a cause.

pieces.title: The sender pays a penny first: more than a hundred and eighty years of the letter post
pieces.short: More than a hundred and eighty years of the letter post
pieces.hook: In Britain in the 1830s, postage was calculated by distance and by the number of sheets, and was usually more than 4 pence,…
pieces.imageAlt: The Penny Black stamp
pieces.imageCredit: General Post Office · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: In Britain in the 1830s, postage was calculated by distance and by the number of sheets, and was usually more than 4 pence, and in general the recipient paid. A recipient could refuse the letter. So some people wrote a code on the envelope, glanced at it, and sent it back, spending nothing.

paras.lead: And a group of people paid nothing
parts: Nobles, high officials, and members of Parliament enjoyed the privilege of “franking.” In the 1830s at least 12.5% of letters were sent free in this way. The post office had to register and price every letter, which took time and people.

In 1837 Rowland Hill, who had been a teacher, wrote the pamphlet Post Office Reform: Its Importance and Practicability. He and the mathematician Babbage found that the bulk of the cost of the post was not in carrying the letters, but in the fussy pricing and collecting at both ends. If the sender paid in advance, at one price for the whole country, the cost could fall a great deal.

From January 10, 1840, a letter of up to half an ounce (about 14 grams) cost a uniform 1 penny across the country. On May 1 the first adhesive stamp, the “Penny Black,” was issued, and it came into formal use from the 6th. The call for designs drew about 2,600 submissions, and not one was chosen. What was used in the end was a profile of the queen drawn from Wyon’s portrait of 1834.

paras.lead: No one would buy the envelopes
parts: The prepaid postage envelopes launched with the stamps, printed with an allegorical design by the painter Mulready, were widely mocked. Material from the British Postal Museum says stationers who feared for their livelihoods helped it along, and in the end the government used them to send official papers, and destroyed many.

paras.lead: A loss first, and a gain later
parts: In the first few years of the reform, postal revenue fell sharply, and in financial terms it was at one point called a “disaster.” But the letters sent in Britain in 1840 more than doubled, and doubled again within ten years. Within three years Switzerland and Brazil followed, and by 1860, 90 countries were using stamps.

The U.S. Postal Service’s “First-Class Mail” (mainly letters, bills, and greeting cards) reached a peak of about 103.66 billion pieces in 2001. After email and online bill-paying spread, it slid all the way down. In fiscal 2025 only about 42.18 billion pieces were left, less than half the peak.

According to PostNord, the volume of letters in Denmark has fallen by more than nine tenths since 2000. On December 30, 2025, the state postal company PostNord delivered its last letter in Denmark. The country’s 1,500 red postboxes have been taken down one after another. After that, letters are taken on by the private company DAO, and PostNord concentrates on parcels.

The weight of the postal business is shifting from “delivering letters” to “delivering parcels,” and the volume of online-shopping parcels is still growing. The Universal Postal Union reminds us that about 2.6 billion people in the world are still not online, and for them a paper letter is still a necessity.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The reformer, Rowland Hill | View: the cheaper it is to send a letter, the more people will send them, and revenue will rise again in the end. ; Interest: a cheap, uniform, prepaid way, so that ordinary people could afford to write. ; Worry: revenue falling in the early stage of the reform, and being criticized as not worth the cost. ; Basis: the pamphlet cites Babbage’s finding that the cost was mainly in handling at both ends, not in carriage; in 1840 the volume of letters more than doubled, and doubled again within ten years.

Nobles and members of Parliament with the franking privilege | View: (The record does not contain a collective statement from them.) ; Interest: keeping the privilege of sending letters free. ; Worry: the reform abolishing the privilege, so that they too would have to pay postage. ; Basis: in the 1830s at least 12.5% of letters went by franking; after uniform postage the privilege was abolished.

The stationers | View: prepaid postage envelopes would take away the business in paper and envelopes. ; Interest: keeping their own trade in stationery. ; Worry: officially printed envelopes crowding the market. ; Basis: material from the British Postal Museum says stationers stirred up the mockery of the Mulready envelope, and the envelope was in the end abandoned.

Postal companies today (PostNord, as an example) | View: there are too few letters to support a national delivery network, and the company should concentrate on parcels. ; Interest: putting resources into the growing business of online-shopping parcels. ; Worry: keeping a letter network that is running emptier and emptier, and losing more and more. ; Basis: PostNord: the volume of letters in Denmark has fallen by more than nine tenths since 2000, and on December 30, 2025, it delivered its last letter.

Spokespeople for the elderly, and for people offline | View: digitization must not leave behind people who cannot get online. ; Interest: letting the elderly, remote places, and poor people go on sending and receiving letters. ; Worry: the new letter service has to be paid for online, and is hard for people who are not online to use. ; Basis: a spokesperson for the Danish association of the elderly told CNN that DAO’s pickup service can be paid for only online; the Universal Postal Union says about 2.6 billion people in the world are still not online.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Hill persuaded the government with “cut the price, and gain the volume.” The price was a fall in revenue for the first few years. The privileged class, and the stationers, were the ones who lost directly in the reform.

Postal companies want costs they can control. People offline want a universal service. Denmark’s method was to hand the letters to a private company, and the tension moved to the price of the service and to how convenient it is.
The parcel business grows larger, and the letter business grows smaller. Inside the same delivery network, the two compete for resources.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Whether “universal service” should be kept, and who should pay for it, is something on which governments, postal companies, and users still have no agreed answer.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: What one penny in 1840 is worth today, on a 2013 estimate, runs from 32 pence to 4 pounds, depending on whether one converts by prices or by incomes.
The story that “a girl could not afford the postage, and refused her fiancé’s letter,” and that this prompted Hill’s reform, is something Wikipedia says may have been invented.
There are several candidates for “inventor” of the stamp, such as James Chalmers, and the attribution is still disputed.

pieces.title: Revenue at a new high, and free cash flow down by more than six tenths: AMD’s third quarter
pieces.short: AMD’s third quarter
pieces.hook: AMD’s third-quarter revenue was $13.38 billion, up 45% from a year earlier, a record; the data cen…
pieces.event: Third-quarter results released after the close on November 3, 2026 (U.S. Eastern Time)
pieces.imageAlt: Lisa Su, chief executive of AMD
pieces.imageCredit: Genevieve Martin (Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, Oak Ridge National Laboratory) · CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: AMD’s third-quarter revenue was $13.38 billion, up 45% from a year earlier, a record. The data-center business was $8.55 billion, nearly double. The results beat the analysts’ estimates, and the share price rose about 8% after hours.

The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of about $17 billion (plus or minus 3%). The midpoint is up about 66% from a year earlier, above the analysts’ average estimate of about $16.2 billion. Gross margin is expected at about 55%, a little below the third quarter’s 56%.

Almost all the growth came from the data center: Instinct AI accelerators and EPYC server processors sold best. Lisa Su said Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud are already using the first Helios rack systems.

The client and gaming businesses together were $3.72 billion, down 8% from a year earlier. Notebook processors lifted the client business 7%, but gaming fell 40%, mainly because fewer custom chips for game consoles, and fewer graphics cards, were sold.

paras.lead: Profit and cash do not match
parts: Under generally accepted accounting principles, quarterly net profit was $2.43 billion, nearly double. But free cash flow was only $554 million, against $1.53 billion a year earlier. The main reason is that inventory piled up by about $3 billion more in one quarter, and receivables by about $1.9 billion. Payables rose by about $2.3 billion, which offset part of it.

This quarter AMD issued about $4.73 billion of new debt, and total debt rose from $3.23 billion the quarter before to $7.08 billion. The release says the fourth quarter will expand production of Helios and of the next-generation “Venice” processors. Stocking up ahead fits that, but the release does not split the specific uses item by item.

The income statement has a line of $1.097 billion for “the change in the fair value of warrant liabilities,” from warrants issued to some customers. The higher the share price, the larger this book loss. In October 2025, when AMD signed with OpenAI, it gave the other side warrants for up to 160 million shares.

According to CNBC, last week Intel’s data-center revenue also rose 78%, but because the guidance was weak the share price fell 29% on Friday. AMD’s Helios rack system, for its part, is aimed directly at Nvidia’s Vera Rubin.

blocks.title: Ten years ago it nearly could not hold on
blocks.text: In 2011 and 2012 AMD laid off a tenth of the staff, and then fifteen percent. Wikipedia records that later supplying chips for the PlayStation 4 and the Xbox One was seen as what kept it from bankruptcy. In 2014 Lisa Su became chief executive. In 2022 AMD’s market value passed Intel’s for the first time.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: AMD’s management | View: data-center demand is still accelerating, fourth-quarter growth will be faster, and the supply chain can keep up. ; Interest: showing that it can take a larger piece of the AI-chip market from Nvidia. ; Worry: whether demand can last, and whether capacity can ramp on time. ; Basis: Lisa Su: the fourth quarter will expand production of Helios and of “Venice,” and she is “confident” of keeping very strong revenue growth; the chief financial officer, Jean Hu: non-GAAP earnings per share rose 74%.

Wall Street analysts, and investors | View: revenue, profit, and guidance all beat expectations, and demand for AI infrastructure is still strong. ; Interest: a rising share price, and the continuation of the main line of investment in AI. ; Worry: the whole industry “spending too much” on AI infrastructure. ; Basis: CNBC: AMD’s share price is already up 129% this year, but it has pulled back lately on worry about excessive investment in AI.

The competitors, Intel and Nvidia | View: (Neither has spoken on AMD’s results; the market’s reaction and their own results are the reference.) ; Interest: holding their share of server chips and of AI accelerators. ; Worry: share being eaten away by AMD. ; Basis: CNBC: Intel’s data-center revenue rose 78% last week, but because the guidance was weak and its ability to supply was questioned, the share price fell 29% in a single day.

The large customers (AI companies, and cloud providers) | View: they need a second supplier besides Nvidia, to spread the risk and to press the cost down. ; Interest: getting more computing power, and having one more card in the bargaining. ; Worry: a single supplier squeezing them, and a price that is too high. ; Basis: the release: Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud are already running Helios; AMD once gave OpenAI warrants for up to 160 million shares.

Opponents of data centers, and the doubters | View: data centers use too much electricity, will push the price of power up, and should slow down. ; Interest: protecting local power prices, and land. ; Worry: investment in AI running too hot, and coming to nothing in the end. ; Basis: Nikkei Asia: voters of different political positions are opposing data centers, on the ground that they use a great deal of electricity and that power prices may rise; Ohio is a state worth watching.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Management and investors look at revenue and guidance. The doubters look at cash flow and inventory. From the same release, each side takes what it needs.
Issuing warrants to large customers can lock in orders, but the higher the share price, the larger the book loss. The interests of customers and of shareholders are tied together.
AMD’s growth rests on the capital spending of the cloud companies, and the cloud companies’ expansion is in turn checked by local opposition to data centers.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Whether the demand comes from real use, or from everyone rushing to stockpile computing power, is something the present data cannot separate.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “The rise in inventory is stocking up for the fourth quarter” is an inference from what management said. The release does not split the uses of the inventory.
Which customers the $1.097 billion change in warrants corresponds to is something the release says only as “some customers.” The link to the OpenAI agreement is an inference.
The after-hours rise, “about 8%” and “more than 7%,” is not the same from one report to another. The next day’s regular trading is the standard.
Third-quarter net profit includes an income-tax benefit of $555 million. The quality of the business cannot be read from net profit alone.

pieces.title: The polling places are closing one after another, and the result is not out yet: a few figures from election day in the U.S. midterms
pieces.short: A few figures from election day in the U.S. midterms
pieces.hook: November 3, U.S. Eastern Time, is election day for the U.S. midterms: all 435 seats in the House, and 3… in the Senate
pieces.event: Election day, November 3, 2026 (U.S. Eastern Time); as of 7 a.m. Beijing time on November 4, the main results were not yet known
pieces.imageAlt: An “I Voted” sticker from the 2026 election in New York State
pieces.imageCredit: lurkingherern · CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: November 3, U.S. Eastern Time, is election day for the U.S. midterms: all 435 seats in the House, 35 seats in the Senate, and the governors of 36 states are chosen at once. At the time of writing (the morning of the 4th, Beijing time), polling places in the states are closing in batches, and control of the House and the Senate is not yet decided.

paras.lead: How many seats the Democrats have to flip
parts: The Associated Press’s account is that the Democrats have to gain a net 4 seats in the Senate and a net 3 in the House to take both chambers from the Republicans. According to The Guardian, the Democrats now have 212 seats in the House, and a majority needs 218.

According to a count by the University of Florida Election Lab, 59.10 million early and mail ballots had already been cast nationwide before election day, more than half the total vote of the 2022 midterms. Early voting in South Carolina was up more than 80% from the last election.

A survey by the AP-NORC Center from October 8 to 12 shows that 85% of voters listed the economy as one of the most important issues, 84% chose the cost of living, and after that health care (69%) and the Iran war (64%). Trump’s overall approval is 36%. Of his handling of the cost of living, 79% disapprove.

The Associated Press reported that problems on election day were, on the whole, few. Stormwater flooded Florida, and some polling places in 8 counties had to move. In North Carolina, 5 polling places in 4 counties extended their hours.

The Department of Justice announced that it was sending about 1,000 election monitors and observers to all 50 states, calling it the largest scale on record, and the first time every state was covered. Some state election officials and civic groups worry that this may intimidate voters, or interfere.

paras.lead: Why the result will be slow
parts: The states vote at different times, and the results come out in batches. Alaska’s polling places do not close until after midnight Eastern Time. Close districts may also be recounted, or go to court. Control of the Senate may come down to a few states where the vote is close.

Nikkei Asia cited the expectation of an economist at Nomura Securities: whichever party controls Congress, “more aggressive trade news” may appear after the election, because the Trump administration can use executive power to add tariffs.

blocks.note: Drawn from the Associated Press, The Guardian, and the Wikipedia entry “2026 United States elections”

blocks.title: Read the “early voting” figures with care
blocks.text: Of the early vote, those registered as Democrats were 43%, and Republicans 31.4%. But a registered party is not the same as whom a person votes for, and the ballots cast on election day itself have not yet been counted in.
