critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The Democrats | View: voters are unhappy with the way things are, and there is a chance to take Congress back and check the president. ; Interest: taking back the House, and contesting the Senate. ; Worry: a net gain of 4 seats in the Senate is hard; an advantage in party registration among early voters may not turn into votes. ; Basis: the Associated Press: the Democrats need a net gain of 4 seats in the Senate and of 3 in the House; in the AP-NORC survey, Democratic favorability is about 40%, a little above the Republicans’ 36%.

Trump, and the Republicans | View: hold the congressional majority, and let the president’s policies, including tariffs, go on. ; Interest: holding majorities in both chambers, and keeping room to govern for the president’s next two years. ; Worry: the president’s approval is only 36%, and 79% disapprove of the way he handles the cost of living. ; Basis: Wikipedia: in 2024 the Republicans gained a net 4 seats in the Senate and took the majority; Trump is pushing several states to redraw House districts in the middle of the decade.

The federal Department of Justice | View: send people to monitor, and make sure the federal voting-rights laws are observed. ; Interest: showing federal oversight of the election. ; Worry: (The Department of Justice says the purpose is a compliance check.) ; Basis: Nikkei Asia, citing the Department of Justice: about 1,000 monitors covering all 50 states, the largest scale on record; there has been a practice of sending people since the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

State election officials, and civic groups | View: elections are run by the states and the localities, and a large federal deployment may disturb voters. ; Interest: protecting the independence of the state’s election, and the order of the voting. ; Worry: voters being intimidated, or the voting being interfered with. ; Basis: Nikkei Asia, citing local media: some state officials and groups have expressed worry at the surge in monitors.

Voters | View: the economy and the cost of living matter most, and the country needs “a large change.” ; Interest: prices, health care, and energy bills. ; Worry: not very satisfied with either party, and only about one in ten feeling optimistic about politics. ; Basis: the AP-NORC survey of October: 85% weigh the economy, and 84% the cost of living; eight in ten think the country needs a large change or a complete transformation; Democratic favorability is about 40%, and Republican 36%.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The Democrats tell the election as “checking the president.” The Republicans want to hold the majority and continue the present policies. The same election is told as two stories.

The Department of Justice’s deployment and the worries at the state level check each other. The federal government wants to supervise. The states want autonomy. In the end the courts have to draw the line.
Even if the Democrats take the House, the president can still use executive power to push policies such as tariffs. How far Congress can check him depends on which party the Senate belongs to.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The Senate may depend on a very few close states. If there is a recount or a lawsuit, the final result may drag on for several days, or longer.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Neither pre-election polls nor the party registration of early voters can be converted directly into the final vote.
This piece was written while polling places were closing. Every statement about the result is only a forecast. What the Associated Press and other organizations formally announce is the standard.
“Data centers have become an election issue” comes mainly from reporting by Nikkei Asia, and there is as yet no systematic figure for how large the effect is.

pieces.title: He photographed the bones of his wife’s hand, and would not patent the X-ray: Wilhelm Röntgen
pieces.short: Wilhelm Röntgen
pieces.hook: When you meet a phenomenon you cannot read, do not rush to explain it. Test it again and again first. Röntgen shut himself in the laboratory for weeks, and tried every condition he could think of…
pieces.takeaway: When you meet a phenomenon you cannot read, do not rush to explain it. Test it again and again first. Röntgen shut himself in the laboratory for weeks, and tried every condition he could think of, before he dared to make the “X” public.
pieces.imageAlt: A portrait of Wilhelm Röntgen
pieces.imageCredit: Anonymous (a photograph of about 1900) · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was born on March 27, 1845, in Lennep, in the Rhineland of Germany (now part of Remscheid), the only son of a cloth merchant. At three he moved with his parents to the Netherlands, where his mother’s family lived, and for about forty years after that he had no nationality.

paras.lead: He took the blame for someone else
parts: In 1865, nearly two years into his studies at a technical school in Utrecht, in the Netherlands, someone drew a caricature of a teacher. He was taken for the author, and, it is said, would not name the person who had really drawn it. He was expelled, and never received a secondary-school diploma. Without the diploma, at a Dutch university he could only be an auditor.

He turned to Switzerland, passed the entrance examination of the Federal Polytechnic in Zurich, received a diploma in mechanical engineering in 1868, and the next year a doctorate in physics from the University of Zurich. In Zurich he was the favorite student of the physicist Kundt, and later followed Kundt first to Würzburg and then to Strasbourg.

The University of Würzburg at one point would not let him qualify to teach, because he had no secondary-school diploma. He taught in turn at the University of Strasbourg, the agricultural college at Hohenheim, and the University of Giessen. In 1888 he regained German nationality, returned to Würzburg as professor of physics, and later became rector.

paras.lead: The young woman in the café
parts: In 1866, in a Zurich café called “the Green Glass,” he met Anna Bertha Ludwig, the owner’s daughter. She was six years older than he was, and of ordinary means. Röntgen’s father was not very much in favor. They were engaged for three years, and married on July 7, 1872, in Apeldoorn, in the Netherlands.
After the marriage the family cut off its support, and at first they were not well off. In 1887 Anna’s only brother died, and they adopted their niece Josephine, who was 6.

paras.lead: A light behind the black paper
parts: November 8, 1895, was a Friday. Around then he was repeating the cathode-ray experiments of Lenard and others. In the evening he wrapped a Crookes tube tightly in black cardboard, darkened the room, and meant first to make sure the cardboard let no light through.

Just then he noticed a faint glow on the workbench a few steps away. He struck a match, and what was glowing was a small screen coated with barium platinocyanide, set out for the next step. He did not know what it was, and named it “X,” the letter for an unknown.

Over the weekend he repeated the experiment again and again, and wrote the first notes. Once he held a small piece of lead in front of the rays, to see what material would stop them, and on the screen he saw the moving shadow of the bones of his own hand. It was the first X-ray image he saw.

paras.lead: Seven weeks behind a closed door
parts: For the next few weeks he ate and slept in the laboratory. On December 22 he made a picture of his wife Anna Bertha’s hand. The bones and the ring were perfectly clear. She is said to have looked at it and said: “I have seen my own death.” On December 28 he handed in the paper On a New Kind of Rays.

Early in January 1896 he sent the paper and the pictures to a number of colleagues, and on January 5 an Austrian newspaper reported it. In the year 1896 alone there were about 49 papers on X-rays, and more than a thousand articles. Doctors were soon using them to find bullets and to look at fractures.
His paper also prompted the French physicist Becquerel to look for similar rays, and the same year Becquerel discovered natural radioactivity.

In 1901 he received the first Nobel Prize in Physics. He was shy by nature, and disliked speaking in public, and he even declined the Nobel lecture. Like the Curies, he did not patent the X-ray, hoping the whole of society could use it. The Nobel money he also gave to the University of Würzburg.

The physicist Lenard, who had given him a ray tube with an aluminum-foil window, later accused Röntgen of taking his discovery. In 1896 the Royal Society in Britain awarded the Rumford Medal to both men at once. Early on, people did not understand protection. Dally, Edison’s glassblower, died in 1904, and is often taken to be the first person to die of X-rays.

In 1900, at the repeated invitation of the Bavarian government, he moved to the University of Munich. He had relatives in Iowa, in the United States, and had accepted an appointment at Columbia University in New York. The transatlantic ticket was already bought. The outbreak of the First World War kept him in Munich.

In 1919 his wife, his companion of 47 years, died. The inflation after the war left him nearly bankrupt, and in his later years he lived in a country house at Weilheim. On February 10, 1923, he died of intestinal cancer in Munich, at 77. By his will, his private and scientific correspondence was almost entirely destroyed.
In 2004, element 111 was named roentgenium.

blocks.title: A “novelty” that was later banned
blocks.text: From the 1920s, many American shoe shops set out an “X-ray shoe-fitting machine.” A customer put a foot in and could see whether the bones and the shoe fitted. Later people came to understand the harm of the radiation, and machines of this kind were banned one after another in the United States in the 1960s.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Röntgen himself | View: the discovery should belong to all of humanity, and should not be locked up by a patent. ; Interest: letting the scientific world, and doctors, use X-rays as soon as possible. ; Worry: (He rarely spoke of himself in public, and most of the correspondence was destroyed by his will.) ; Basis: he did not patent the X-ray, and gave the prize money to the University of Würzburg; within days of the paper he sent the pictures to colleagues.

The physicist Lenard | View: Röntgen had used his own research, and the credit should be shared. ; Interest: being recognized in the history of the discovery. ; Worry: his own contribution being passed over in a phrase. ; Basis: a PMC article: in 1894 Lenard had sent Röntgen an aluminum-foil window, and later accused Röntgen of “taking” the discovery; in the Nazi period Germany for a time renamed X-rays “high-frequency rays” and gave the credit to Lenard.

Doctors, and hospitals | View: X-rays can see inside the body, and are a sharp tool for diagnosis. ; Interest: finding fractures, foreign bodies, and disease faster. ; Worry: early equipment was crude, and the exposure was long. ; Basis: Wikipedia: on January 11, 1896, a doctor in Britain had already used X-rays to find a sewing needle in a hand; about 49 papers were published in 1896.

Shopkeepers, and a curious public | View: X-rays were novel and amusing, and could be used to draw business. ; Interest: selling more goods, and satisfying curiosity. ; Worry: (Early on, very few people worried about the radiation.) ; Basis: from the 1920s, shoe shops commonly used X-ray shoe-fitting machines, and in the 1960s they were banned one after another in the United States.

The early victims, and later advocates of radiation protection | View: X-rays are harmful, and the dose must be limited and the protection strengthened. ; Interest: protecting the health of operators and of patients. ; Worry: people seeing only the benefit, and ignoring the long-term harm. ; Basis: Dally, Edison’s glassblower, was exposed to X-rays for a long time and died in 1904, and is often taken to be the first person to die of X-rays.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Röntgen’s giving up the patent let the technology spread quickly, and hospitals and shopkeepers both benefited. But the faster it spread, the more it was used without protection.
Lenard’s accusation and Röntgen’s silence stand in contrast. And because Röntgen destroyed the correspondence, the dispute over credit lacks a complete account from the people involved.
Shopkeepers pursued novelty. Advocates of protection demanded limits. In the end a regulatory ban drew the line.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: How to count the “first credit” for a discovery: how much recognition the person who supplied the key apparatus and the idea should get, and how much the person who first recognized the new phenomenon, has no standard answer.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The sentence “I have seen my own death” is widely repeated, but the source is mostly a later retelling.
“He would not name the classmate who drew the caricature” is a common account. The English Wikipedia says only that he was mistaken for the author.
The exact sum of the Nobel prize is given differently in different sources, and this piece does not write a specific figure.
Whether Dally was the “first” person to die of X-rays is only a common account.
How far the screen was from the ray tube when Röntgen made the discovery runs, in the various sources, from a few feet to two meters.

pieces.title: From the Pantheon in Rome to 3.8 billion tonnes a year: two thousand years of cement
pieces.short: Two thousand years of cement
pieces.hook: The English word “cement” can be traced to what the ancient Romans called opus caementic…
pieces.imageAlt: The interior of the dome of the Pantheon in Rome
pieces.imageCredit: Wilfredor · CC0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: The English word “cement” can be traced to what the ancient Romans called opus caementicium: a masonry that used rubble as the aggregate and burnt lime as the binder, very like today’s concrete. Later, the volcanic ash and powdered brick that were added to the lime, so that it could harden in water, were called cementum, and that evolved into today’s cement.

The ancient Romans mixed lime with volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, and made a concrete that could harden under water. The architect Vitruvius wrote the recipe down around 25 BCE: one part lime to three parts volcanic ash.

paras.lead: A dome that has not fallen in two thousand years
parts: The Pantheon in Rome, finished about the year 126, has a dome 43.3 meters across, and it is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. After Rome fell, the technique was largely lost in western Europe for more than a thousand years. Only in a few places, such as the Rhineland in Germany, did medieval masons still use a local volcanic ash called trass to make a hydraulic mortar.

In 1756 the English engineer Smeaton had to rebuild the lighthouse on the Eddystone rocks. The mortar had to set in the dozen or so hours between two high tides. He found that lime burnt from a limestone that contained clay could harden in water. The lighthouse was finished in 1759.

Smeaton’s discovery did not spread quickly. Early in the nineteenth century the French engineer Vicat found the same principle on his own: mix chalk and clay finely, and then burn them. In 1817 he made “artificial cement,” taken to be the chief forerunner of Portland cement.
Vicat also worked out the chemistry behind the hardening of this kind of cement.

On October 21, 1824, Joseph Aspdin, a bricklayer in Leeds, England, took out a patent and called the product “Portland cement,” because once set it looked like the stone of the Isle of Portland in England. He was also prosecuted twice for digging up the road to get his raw material.

paras.lead: The son made the real version
parts: Aspdin’s product was not burnt hot enough, and it was not today’s cement. Around 1843 his son William, at a works in Northfleet, in Kent, made the first cement that steadily contained “alite,” the chief source of cement’s strength. That is modern Portland cement.

The method needed more lime, and a higher temperature. The clinker that came out was so hard that it quickly wore out the millstones, and the cost was a good deal higher. But it set steadily, and gained strength quickly. From 1859 the new sewer system in London used it in quantity.

The French gardener Monier found clay flowerpots too brittle, and wooden tubs too quick to rot. He buried a wire mesh in concrete, showed it at the Paris exposition of 1867, and took out a patent. In 1875 he designed and built the first reinforced-concrete bridge. Concrete is weak in tension, and steel is strong in tension. The two together held up the tall buildings and the great bridges that came later.

In 1885 the Englishman Ransome took out a patent for the rotary kiln. Raw material is fed in at one end of a slowly turning long cylinder, and burnt to about 1,450 degrees Celsius, with the hottest part of the flame reaching 1,800 degrees. Material keeps coming in, and clinker keeps coming out. There is no need to let the fire go out kiln by kiln, and the cement that comes out is stronger and more even.
Today more than 95% of the world’s cement comes from a kiln of this kind.

paras.lead: How a bag of cement is made
parts: Today’s method is much the same everywhere. Limestone and clay are ground, proportioned, and sent into the kiln to be burnt into pellets of “clinker,” from a few millimeters across to two or three centimeters. About 5% of gypsum is added, and the whole is ground to a powder. That is the most common ordinary Portland cement. Burning one tonne of clinker consumes 3 to 6 gigajoules of fuel, mostly coal and petroleum coke.

According to the U.S. Geological Survey, the world produced about 3.8 billion tonnes of cement in 2025, and China about 1.7 billion tonnes. Figures from China’s National Bureau of Statistics show national cement output in 2025 of 1.693 billion tonnes, down 6.9% from a year earlier, the lowest since 2010.

paras.lead: The emissions that cannot be gone around
parts: Cement production accounts for about 8% of global carbon-dioxide emissions. About six tenths of that comes from the heating and breakdown of the limestone itself, not from burning fuel, so a switch to clean energy can cut only part of it. France and Poland are building carbon-capture projects.

Another path is to use less clinker: mix in slag left from ironmaking, volcanic ash, and other materials. China produces several million tonnes of calcium sulfoaluminate cement a year. It is burnt at a lower temperature, and uses less limestone. Carbon-dioxide emissions are about half those of ordinary clinker, but sulfur-dioxide emissions are usually higher.
More than four tenths of the heat at cement plants in the European Union already comes from waste and from biomass fuel.

blocks.title: It turns out there was a way
blocks.text: Research has found that small leftover grains of lime in Roman concrete can react again when they meet water, and fill cracks. That may be one reason the old buildings have lasted. Modern researchers are trying to put this “self-healing” idea into new materials.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Cement companies | View: cement is a necessity of infrastructure, emissions cuts have to come step by step, and they need technology and money. ; Interest: keeping the use of capacity, and the profit, while controlling the cost of cutting emissions. ; Worry: falling demand piled on spending to cut emissions, and profit squeezed from both sides. ; Basis: China’s National Bureau of Statistics: output in 2025 of 1.693 billion tonnes, down 6.9% from a year earlier; several European companies are building carbon-capture projects jointly with gas companies.

Construction, and the infrastructure industry | View: concrete is cheap, durable, and easy to get, and hard to replace in the short run. ; Interest: controlling cost, and the time of the work. ; Worry: low-carbon cement being more expensive, or its performance not yet proved over a long time. ; Basis: Wikipedia: concrete is one of the man-made materials used in the greatest quantity, and Portland cement, by mass, is the third most manufactured man-made material.

Climate researchers, and environmental groups | View: cement is one of the hardest industries in which to cut emissions, and the process has to be changed as soon as possible. ; Interest: pressing down global carbon-dioxide emissions. ; Worry: changing the fuel alone is not enough, because about six tenths of the emissions come from the breakdown of the raw material. ; Basis: the Wikipedia entry “Cement”: cement accounts for about 8% of global carbon-dioxide emissions (2018).

Some other researchers | View: concrete reabsorbs part of the carbon dioxide while it is in use, and the net emissions are not so high. ; Interest: calculating the industry’s carbon account more accurately. ; Worry: looking only at the production end overstates the emissions. ; Basis: Wikipedia: one study estimates that concrete can reabsorb about three tenths; but an analysis in 2024 holds that this climate benefit is about six tenths smaller.

Governments | View: they want both infrastructure and jobs, and emissions targets. ; Interest: keeping a balance between economic growth and the commitment on carbon emissions. ; Worry: too much capacity and high emissions at the same time. ; Basis: the U.S. Geological Survey: in 2025 China about 1.7 billion tonnes, India about 470 million tonnes, and India is still growing.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Companies want cost. Researchers want emissions cuts. Governments are caught between growth and climate targets.

Whether “concrete reabsorbing carbon dioxide” can be counted as an emissions cut is something on which researchers’ estimates differ greatly, and it directly affects how much responsibility the industry should bear.
Demand in China is falling, and demand in India is rising. World output is on the whole flat. The pressure to cut emissions is not the same from country to country.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: About six tenths of the emissions come from the breakdown of the limestone itself. Unless the raw material is changed, or carbon is captured on a large scale, they are hard to remove. And carbon capture is still expensive, and still small in scale.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The difference between Aspdin’s product and modern cement rests mainly on later analysis of his process.
The mechanism of the “self-healing” of Roman concrete is still being studied, and cannot simply be treated as settled.
The fall in China’s output in 2025 is often attributed to a fall in property investment, and this piece has not quantified that.
The U.S. Geological Survey’s country figures are estimates, and they differ slightly in definition from the official statistics of the countries.
“Emissions about halved” for calcium sulfoaluminate cement is an estimate cited on Wikipedia, and the specific figure depends on the recipe and the process.

pieces.title: The restaurants sold $38 billion, and the books record only $7.2 billion: McDonald’s third quarter
pieces.short: McDonald’s third quarter
pieces.hook: McDonald’s third-quarter revenue was $7.16 billion, only 1% more than a year earlier, below the analysts’ estimate of about $7.2…
pieces.event: Third-quarter results released before the open on November 4, 2026 (U.S. Eastern Time)
pieces.imageAlt: A McDonald’s in Indianapolis, in the United States
pieces.imageCredit: Valerie Everett · CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: McDonald’s third-quarter revenue was $7.16 billion, only 1% more than a year earlier, below the analysts’ estimate of about $7.29 billion. But adjusted earnings per share were $3.57, above the expected $3.38. Net profit was $2.49 billion, up 9%, and the share price closed up more than 6% that day.

McDonald’s more than 45,000 restaurants worldwide sold more than $38 billion in all this quarter, up 4% from last year. That is called “systemwide sales.” But about 95% of the restaurants are run by independent franchisees. Most of the money for the hamburgers goes into the franchisees’ books. McDonald’s mainly collects rent, and a royalty taken as a share of sales, so revenue is only about $7.2 billion.

McDonald’s writes in the release that a franchised restaurant’s sales do not count as the company’s revenue. Revenue has only three parts: all the sales of the company-operated restaurants, the rent and the royalty the franchisees pay, and a small piece of “other revenue.” When a franchised restaurant sells a meal, what is entered on McDonald’s books is only the share it takes by the proportion. When a company-operated restaurant sells a meal, the whole amount is entered.
The company still publishes systemwide sales, because the royalty is calculated on them, and because they also show how the franchisees are doing.

Franchise revenue this quarter was $4.49 billion, up 3%. Company-operated restaurant sales were $2.48 billion, down 3%. Other revenue was $190 million, up 26%. Franchise revenue, after $690 million of occupancy cost, still left about $3.8 billion. The company-operated restaurants sold $2.48 billion, and the restaurants’ own costs alone were $2.09 billion.
So revenue hardly rose, and operating profit still rose 7%, to $3.6 billion.

paras.lead: The other half of the profit
parts: The growth in profit did not all come from selling hamburgers either. The release says the growth this quarter came mainly from an increase in “other operating income” and from higher franchise profit. Other operating income rose from about $40 million last year to about $140 million. The company is also steadily buying back stock. The diluted share count is about 1% lower than last year, so adjusted earnings per share (up 11%) rose even faster than net profit (up 9%).

paras.lead: Fewer guests in the United States
parts: Global same-store sales rose 1.5%, but in the United States they fell 0.2%, while a year earlier they had still risen 2.4%. According to the restaurant-industry publication NRN, this is the first decline after five quarters of growth in the United States. The release says visits in the United States fell, and a higher amount per order made up most of it. Drinks such as a Red Bull specialty helped. Reuters, citing figures from Placer.ai, said third-quarter store traffic was 4.6% lower than last year.

paras.lead: One step that did not go well
parts: The problem was this year’s price changes. According to industry reporting, McDonald’s replaced the old offer, “buy one, and add $1 for another,” with a menu of “10 items under $3.” Quite a few customers felt this amounted to a price rise in disguise. In August the company acknowledged that about one third of franchisees had not taken part, and the same month it also changed the president of the U.S. business.

After that the company restored the offers in the app, such as a $2 breakfast sandwich, and fries with a purchase of $1. The chief financial officer, Borden, said the United States was down in July and August, and turned positive in September.

The chief executive, Kempczinski, said on the earnings call that lower-income customers are still under pressure. “What they want is a very good entry price, and on that point we have not yet done as well as we would like.” He said that, looking at menu prices, McDonald’s regular prices for chicken, beef, and drinks are on the whole below the main rivals, and the $5 and $6 meals also sell well. What is missing is the entry price.

International operated markets rose 1.4% (4.3% a year earlier). Germany and Australia did well, France was weak, and the call also mentioned a drag from Ukraine. International developmental licensed markets rose 4.2%. Japan led, and China was negative.

Starting last week, the company is running an 8-week test in about 1,900 U.S. restaurants, comparing two kinds of entry-price meal: one the customer assembles, and one a fixed combination. The example the Associated Press gave was a McChicken plus a small fries for $3.50. Among the rivals it faces, Taco Bell has a menu of 10 items, each at $3 or less.
The company plans to choose one early in 2027 and roll it out nationwide.

paras.lead: Where the money comes from, and where it goes
parts: The quarterly dividend was raised 4%, to $1.93 a share. The loyalty program brought about $41 billion of sales across 70 markets over the past year, and more than $11 billion this quarter alone. App members in the United States are above 45 million.
The new “Next” restaurant remodel costs about $800,000 each, most of it borne by the franchisee. The company also expects a “mid-single-digit” rise in food and paper costs in 2027.

blocks.title: Franchisees acted on their own
blocks.text: According to reports, the franchisees of about 4,000 restaurants did not wait for the test results, and have already launched entry-price meals locally on their own. Together with the restaurants in the test, about four tenths of U.S. stores now have an entry-price meal. Headquarters wants a uniform method, but the price has to be decided by the franchisee.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: McDonald’s management | View: the pricing strategy needs adjusting, but the franchise model and the loyalty program can hold the profit steady. ; Interest: using value meals to pull guests back into the restaurants, while keeping a high margin. ; Worry: lower-income customers spending less, and the U.S. market staying weak. ; Basis: the release: operating profit up 7%, and the dividend raised 4%; the chief financial officer, Borden, said the United States was down in July and August and turned positive in September.

Franchisees | View: a low-priced meal can draw traffic, but the cost and the remodel fall on them. ; Interest: protecting the profit of the single store. ; Worry: the rise in costs such as beef, a remodel of about $800,000 a store, and food and paper costs rising again in 2027. ; Basis: industry reporting: most of the remodel cost is borne by the franchisee; the franchisees of about 4,000 restaurants launched entry-price meals on their own; in August about one third of franchisees did not take part in the “under $3” menu.

Investors | View: revenue does not matter. Profit and the return to shareholders matter more. ; Interest: earnings per share, and a dividend that grows steadily. ; Worry: a continued fall in U.S. traffic dragging on future growth. ; Basis: CNBC: adjusted earnings per share of $3.57, above the expected $3.38, and the share price closed up more than 6% that day.

Ordinary customers | View: fast food is getting more expensive, and they wait for a deal before they go. ; Interest: spending less on a meal. ; Worry: the meal price still looking high compared with before. ; Basis: the release: visits in the United States fell, and were made up by a higher check; industry media: the “10 items under $3” was taken by quite a few customers as a price rise in disguise.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Headquarters wants a low price to pull people back, but the discount is borne mainly by the franchisee’s profit. The two sides have to work the price out again and again.
Investors look at profit. Customers look at price. The higher the margin, the more the room to cut the price is questioned.
The franchise model lets headquarters collect in good times and bad. But when store traffic falls, the franchisee feels the pressure first.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Whether the fall in U.S. traffic is a short-term effect of economic pressure, or a change in habits, is something the present data cannot yet separate.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: That the “under $3” menu was poorly received, and taken as a price rise in disguise, rests mainly on media reports. The company has not published the specific sales.
Placer.ai’s traffic figures are a third-party estimate, and they are not on the same basis as the company’s “visits.”
Systemwide sales of “more than $38 billion” are an approximate figure McDonald’s published.
Whether the turn to positive in September can last rests on only a month or two of data, and should not be read for more than it holds.

pieces.title: 54 seats in the Senate, and a majority in the House: the two years in Washington after the Democrats take Congress
pieces.short: The two years in Washington after the Democrats take Congress…
pieces.hook: The results of the U.S. midterm elections are largely in: the Democrats have taken both the Senate and the House.
pieces.event: Voting on November 3, 2026 (U.S. Eastern Time), with results published in succession from the 4th; figures as of the morning of November 5, Eastern Time
pieces.imageAlt: The United States Capitol
pieces.imageCredit: Martin Falbisoner · CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: The results of the U.S. midterm elections are largely in: the Democrats have taken both the Senate and the House. Senate Democrats (including two independents who caucus with them) have at least 54 seats. Alaska and Mississippi are still undecided. In the House, the Democrats are already securely past the majority line of 218.

On a preliminary estimate by the University of Florida Election Lab, about 48.8% of eligible voters cast a ballot, the highest turnout in a midterm election in more than a hundred years, after only 2018.

According to a count by The Guardian as of the early hours of November 5, Eastern Time, of the 387 seats already called, the Democrats have 240 and the Republicans 147, a net Democratic gain of about 30 seats. According to the election-data site Ballotpedia, 23 Republican incumbent members of the House have already lost to Democrats, and no Democratic incumbent has lost. More than forty seats are still without a result. Jeffries expects the Democrats to end with at least 255.

The Democrats flipped Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, and Texas. Kansas elected a Democratic senator for the first time since 1932. In Texas, Talarico, 37, defeated the state attorney general, Paxton.
By Ballotpedia’s standard, the net change in the Senate is at least 7 seats, enough to count as a “wave election.”

According to Associated Press figures, Alaska is about three quarters counted. The Democrat Peltola leads the incumbent senator, Sullivan, 48.2% to 47.9%, by about 640 votes, but neither is over half. If no one is ever over half, on November 18, under ranked-choice voting, the other candidates’ votes are transferred to the voters’ second choice. Local media, working from the ballot records already public, reckon that after the transfer Sullivan might instead lead by a little. The result depends on about 75,000 ballots not yet opened.

Mississippi is about 96% counted. The Democrat Colom leads the incumbent senator, Hyde-Smith, by about 1,100 votes, 49.0% to 48.9%. About 3,600 mail ballots are still uncounted. Ballots that need to be cured are to be dealt with by November 10, and the counties are to certify the result by November 13. This state has not elected a Democratic senator since 1982.

The Democrats won the governorship in Texas, Georgia, Nevada, Ohio, Iowa, and other states, and for the first time in 16 years hold a majority of the governorships. Bottoms, in Georgia, becomes the first Black woman governor in the United States.

paras.lead: The redrawn districts did not hold
parts: Before the election, 9 states redrew House districts in the middle of the decade. On paper, the seats favorable to the Republicans gained a net of about 9. But according to Ballotpedia, the Democrats instead gained a net 15 seats in these states, and redrawn states such as Texas and Florida could not hold off the losses either.

According to CBS News, 89% of voters said the cost of living was an important or a decisive factor in their vote. At the time of the election Trump’s approval was only 38%, a historical low for a midterm. Reuters counted that, in about 2,100 counties already counted, the Republican vote share fell in 99% of them, compared with the last election.

Speaker of the House Johnson said he would not continue as the Republican leader. Representatives Jordan and Scalise both said they want the place. Vice President Vance said: “The reason we lost is the war.” Trump said: “I wasn’t on the ballot,” and stressed that he holds the veto.
Jeffries said: “We don’t work for Trump.”

Both parties choose new leadership in mid-November. The old Congress still has to pass a government appropriation before the end of the year. After the new Congress is seated in January, House Democrats have already planned a number of investigations of the administration, and the White House has warned them not to run “investigations.”
Jeffries said no one in the party has raised impeaching Trump.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The Democrats | View: the voters are asking for a check on the president, and for a lower cost of living. ; Interest: pushing an “affordability” agenda, and strengthening oversight of the administration. ; Worry: the president holds the veto, and many bills can only stop at the door of the White House. ; Basis: Jeffries: the priorities are affordability, accountability, and “American values”; Schumer said he will be elected majority leader again.

Trump, and the White House | View: this election was not a vote on the president himself. ; Interest: keeping executive power, and pushing policies such as tariffs. ; Worry: congressional investigations, and appropriations being blocked. ; Basis: Trump: “I wasn’t on the ballot,” “I have the veto”; White House officials warned the Democrats not to push investigations.

Republicans in Congress | View: the reasons for the defeat have to be thought over, and the party reorganized. ; Interest: winning voters back before 2028. ; Worry: the Iran war and prices leaving the party on the defensive, and people inside blaming one another. ; Basis: Johnson will no longer serve as party leader; Vance: “The reason we lost is the war”; DeSantis called it an “extinction-level event.”

Voters | View: the cost of living and the war are the main concerns, and a change is needed. ; Interest: prices, tariffs, jobs, and safety. ; Worry: neither party has really solved the problems. ; Basis: CBS: 89% of voters said the cost of living was an important or a decisive factor; Reuters: the Republican vote share fell in 99% of about 2,100 counties; an NBC exit poll shows about 32% of young men voted Republican, against 49% who voted for Trump in 2024.

Election officials in the undecided states | View: every lawful ballot has to be counted under the law, and the result cannot be rushed. ; Interest: keeping the count lawful, and credible. ; Worry: a result that drags on so long that it draws challenges or lawsuits. ; Basis: the Associated Press: Alaska’s overseas ballots may arrive within 15 days after the election, and the ranked-choice count is on November 18; Mississippi’s counties certify by November 13, and if the margin is very small an application for a recount may still have to be dealt with.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Legislation from Congress has to pass the president. The president’s policies have to pass Congress’s appropriations. Each side holds a tool that can stop the other.
The Democrats’ plan of investigations and the White House’s warning stand point against point. The line between congressional oversight and executive privilege may have to be drawn by the courts.
Inside the Republican Party the accounts of why they lost do not agree: the war, prices, or the candidates. That affects which way they adjust over the next two years.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The government appropriation that must pass before the end of the year is the first test. The old Congress is still controlled by the Republicans, and the new Congress is not yet seated. Both sides may drag the talks into next year.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The total number of House seats is still being updated, and the media do not count it the same way (for example, the figures at CBS and Ballotpedia are a little lower than The Guardian’s, and NBC estimates the Democrats may end with more).
“After the transfer, Sullivan might lead” in Alaska is only a media calculation from part of the ballot record. It is not a result.
The results in Alaska and Mississippi may change the final number of Senate seats.
“Lost because of the war” and “lost because of prices” are things politicians say. An exit poll can show a connection, and cannot prove a cause.
The specific wording of the White House “warning” comes from a media retelling.

pieces.title: She wrote a program for a machine that had not yet been built: Ada Lovelace
pieces.short: Ada Lovelace
pieces.hook: It matters more to say clearly “what a machine can do” than to argue “who wrote which line first.” Ada’s notes took the Analytical Engine from abacus-style…
pieces.takeaway: It matters more to say clearly “what a machine can do” than to argue “who wrote which line first.” Ada’s notes took the Analytical Engine from abacus-style arithmetic to a general operation that can handle symbols.
pieces.imageAlt: A portrait of Ada Lovelace
pieces.imageCredit: Alfred Edward Chalon · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Augusta Ada Byron was born in London on December 10, 1815, the poet Byron’s only legitimate child. A month after the birth, her mother, Annabella, left with her. Byron soon went far off to Europe, and died in Greece in 1824. Ada was eight, and had never really met her father.

Byron had hoped for a “glorious boy,” and was disappointed to learn it was a daughter. The child was named Augusta Ada, but the household called her only Ada. A separation agreement was signed quickly. The father never sought custody, and only occasionally asked his sister for news of her.

Her mother was convinced that mathematics could hold down a Byronic impulse, and from early on hired people to teach her arithmetic and science. Ada was often ill as a child. From eight she had migraines. After measles in 1829 she was nearly paralyzed for a year, and in 1831 she still walked with a crutch. At twelve she studied the anatomy of birds in earnest, meant to write a book called Flyology, and even imagined wings driven by steam.

On June 5, 1833, Ada, then eighteen, was introduced by her tutor Mary Somerville and met him for the first time at one of Babbage’s Saturday evenings, and afterward went to see the prototype of the Difference Engine. Babbage later called her the “Enchantress of Number.”

In 1835 she married William King. In 1838 her husband was made Earl of Lovelace, and she became Countess of Lovelace. They had three children. She went on studying higher calculus with De Morgan, and in her letters often compared the changing of a formula to a sprite in a fairy tale, shifting its shape.

paras.lead: Nine months of translation and notes
parts: In 1840 Babbage lectured on the Analytical Engine in Turin. The Italian engineer Menabrea wrote the points down in French, and published them in 1842. Babbage’s friend Wheatstone asked Ada to translate them into English. Over nine months in 1842 and 1843 she wrote seven long notes, A through G, about three times as long as the translation itself. They appeared in September 1843 under the initials AAL.

Note G sets out in detail the steps and the tables for recursively computing the Bernoulli numbers on the Analytical Engine, and it is often called “the first computer program to be published.” The Analytical Engine was never built, and this program was never run on a real machine.

As the manuscript was about to appear, Babbage wanted to insert a statement criticizing the government as an unsigned preface. The journal required a signature, and he instead told Ada to withdraw the paper. Ada refused. The two of them fell out briefly, and later resumed writing. In 1851, when she was seriously ill, she wrote to ask him to be the executor of her will.

In the notes she stressed that the Analytical Engine was not only arithmetic. So long as the relations among the objects could be expressed by rules of operation, it could also handle symbols. She gave the example of musical harmony. Later people have taken this leap, “from calculation to a general operation on symbols,” as a key step in the history of the idea of computing.

She called her method “poetical science”: grasping the formula, and also asking how people and machines are to live together. Watching a Jacquard loom weave a pattern from punched cards, she connected it to the Analytical Engine, which could also be directed by cards. Later writers often take this as the key intuition by which she stepped past “pure arithmetic.”

She also wrote that the Analytical Engine “has no pretensions whatever to originate anything.” It can do only what we order it to do. Turing’s paper of 1950 called this sentence “Lovelace’s objection,” and used it to discuss whether machines can think.

Babbage’s autobiography says the Bernoulli algorithm was his own proposal, revised after she found errors. The historian Bromley pointed out that Babbage had already written dozens of unpublished programs in 1837–1840. Others, such as Stephen Wolfram, hold that it was Ada who explained the machine’s abstract operations clearly, and that Babbage never on his own wrote an account equally clear.

In her later years she was absorbed in horse racing, and at one point owed several thousand pounds in gambling debts. On November 27, 1852, she died of cervical cancer in London, at 36, and was buried beside her father, as she had asked. In 1980 the U.S. Department of Defense named a programming language Ada, and the military standard number MIL-STD-1815 was taken from the year of her birth.

blocks.title: A machine that had not yet been built
blocks.text: The Analytical Engine was to take instructions and data on punched cards, with a “store” to hold numbers and a “mill” to do the operations. In theory it was a general-purpose computer. The British government in the nineteenth century was unwilling to keep spending, and the whole machine was never finished. What the Science Museum in London shows today is a modern reconstruction of Difference Engine No. 2, not the Analytical Engine.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Later admirers, and the commemorations | View: she was the first person to see clearly the potential of general-purpose computing, and deserves to be called a pioneer among programmers. ; Interest: raising the visibility of women in STEM. ; Worry: the credit being pushed to the edge of the history of engineering. ; Basis: Ada Lovelace Day, the Ada language, and an illustration in a British passport are named for her; Wolfram and others defend her exposition.

Babbage, and some historians of science | View: the algorithm and the program were mainly Babbage’s work, and Ada was an outstanding interpreter and popularizer. ; Interest: assigning the credit in the history of invention accurately. ; Worry: the public story simplifying “the first” into one person. ; Basis: Babbage’s autobiography; Bromley: Babbage had written dozens of unpublished programs earlier.

The scientific community of the Victorian age | View: the Analytical Engine was too far ahead, and too expensive, and the government should not go on funding it. ; Interest: spending limited funds on engineering that was more “visible.” ; Worry: however fine the concept, if it cannot be built it is of no use. ; Basis: the Analytical Engine was never built; the Difference Engine project had also stopped over money and management.

Programmers and computer scientists today | View: Note G is a publishable description of an algorithm, with the structure of a program. ; Interest: finding their own lineage in history. ; Worry: fitting today’s standard of “programmer” onto 1843 will distort it. ; Basis: Note G contains step-by-step operations and data tables; Turing discussed “Lovelace’s objection.”

Ada herself (from the letters and the notes) | View: she wanted to do “poetical science,” binding imagination and analysis together. ; Interest: making clear how far the Analytical Engine could actually reach. ; Worry: a body often ill, and society’s prejudice against a woman mathematician. ; Basis: she called herself Analyst (& Metaphysician); the notes discuss music and operations on symbols.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: A commemoration needs a clear “first person.” The history of science tends to separate “who wrote the algorithm, who wrote the exposition, and who published first.”
Babbage wanted money to build the machine. Ada wanted to make clear the logical boundary of the machine. The two aims did not wholly coincide, and they once quarreled over the signed preface.
“A machine cannot originate” has been used both to limit the imagination of AI, and by Turing as a target that had to be answered.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: On the premise that a real machine was never built, whether “the program is correct” cannot be tested by running it. It can only be tested by reasoning on paper, and by later people reproducing it.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Whether the original of “Enchantress of Number” is Number or Numbers is something the quotations often do not agree on.
The details of the gambling debts and of her private life come mostly from biographical conjecture, and the accounts differ.
“The first programmer” is a label conferred after the twentieth century, not a way she described herself in 1843.

pieces.title: Without a safety brake, there is no skyscraper: more than a hundred and seventy years of the elevator
pieces.short: More than a hundred and seventy years of the elevator
pieces.hook: The Roman architect Vitruvius records that Archimedes built a lifting device around 236 BCE. The Colosseum had about…
pieces.imageAlt: An engraving of Otis’s safety demonstration at the Crystal Palace
pieces.imageCredit: Anonymous (an engraving of the 1854 demonstration) · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: The Roman architect Vitruvius records that Archimedes built a lifting device around 236 BCE. The Colosseum had about 25 lifts, worked by human power to raise wild animals onto the arena. Medieval and early-modern palaces also had rope-hung cars, but a broken rope meant a fall, and a passenger elevator was slow to amount to anything.

In the nineteenth century, mines and factories first used steam to drive hoists for coal and goods. In 1846 Armstrong invented the hydraulic crane, using water pressure to push a plunger, and it was soon used on the docks. London later also built a high-pressure water network, to power thousands of elevators and cranes.

In 1852 Elisha Graves Otis made a hoist with an automatic safety brake: if the hoisting rope broke, the jaws would grip the guide rails. In 1854, at the Crystal Palace exposition in New York, he cut the rope in public, and the car stopped steadily. On March 23, 1857, the first passenger safety elevator was installed at 488 Broadway in New York.

Otis received elevator-related patents in 1861. The safety brake turned “the fear of falling” into a risk that could be calculated, and insurers and the advertising of buildings were both willing to follow. The Otis company later grew into one of the world’s largest elevator firms, and the story of safety has always been the core of the selling.

paras.lead: The shaft first, and the elevator after
parts: When the Cooper Union building in New York was begun in 1853, a circular elevator shaft was already reserved. The builder, Peter Cooper, believed a safe elevator would appear soon. The Equitable Life Building, finished in 1870, is often taken to be the first office building fitted with passenger elevators.

In 1880 Siemens built an electric elevator. Frank Sprague then added leveling control, automatic running, and more safety devices, and both speed and load passed steam and hydraulics. When he sold the company to Otis in 1895, 584 had already been installed.
A hydraulic elevator suits a low building. Above about 7 floors, steel-rope traction is usually used instead.

The steel frame made the building tall, and the elevator took people up. Without vertical transport one could trust, a high office or apartment was hard to rent. Geared traction, gearless high-speed traction, counterweights, and compensation cables let the travel and the speed keep rising. Today an elevator in a supertall building can exceed more than ten meters a second, and the car also needs pressure regulation, to ease the discomfort in the ears.

The elevator shaft and the lobby take floor area. Too few cars, and there is a long line at the morning peak. Traffic calculation has gone from the empirical charts of the early twentieth century to today’s destination dispatch and double-deck cars, all in order to move more people with fewer shafts. A supertall building will also set a sky lobby, and change cars in stages.

paras.lead: An elevator with no one to run it
parts: There were fully automatic elevators as early as the start of the twentieth century, but passengers did not trust them. After the New York elevator operators’ strike of 1945, automatic doors, an emergency button, an intercom, and prompt announcements spread together, and the operator’s job gradually disappeared.

China is one of the world’s largest markets by the number of elevators in place. Italy and Spain have long been near the front in elevators per person. The machine-room-less elevator (MRL) has been popular since KONE’s MonoSpace in 1996. It saves space, and uses comparatively less electricity, but the space for maintenance is tighter.
Regenerative braking can send the energy of a full car going down, or an empty car going up, back to the grid.

Makers such as thyssenkrupp in Germany have tested concepts of electromagnetically driven cars that can also move sideways, trying to break the bottleneck of “one car to a shaft.” Real use on a large scale is still constrained by the rules, the cost, and reliability. Carbon-fiber ropes are being used to challenge the limit that a steel rope’s own weight sets on a very long travel.

blocks.title: The performance of cutting the rope
blocks.text: The point of the Crystal Palace demonstration was not that “an elevator can rise.” It was that “if the rope breaks, a person can still live.” The safety brake turned the passenger elevator from an adventure into infrastructure that could be insured, and that could sell a building. From then on a real-estate advertisement could write “a high-floor view” with an easy mind.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Elevator manufacturers | View: safety and speed are the selling points. The stricter the standard, the more the product is worth. ; Interest: selling more equipment, and maintenance contracts. ; Worry: an accident destroying the brand; an upgrade of the code pushing up the cost of research. ; Basis: Otis, KONE, thyssenkrupp, and others keep releasing safer and more efficient models; countries adopt standards such as ASME A17 and EN 81.

Developers, and architects | View: the elevator decides how tall a building can be, and how much area the core of circulation takes. ; Interest: maximizing the area that can be rented or sold, and the rent. ; Worry: the shaft and the machine room eating floor area, and a wait that is too long hurting the reputation. ; Basis: early cases such as the Equitable Life Building wrote the elevator into the competitiveness of an office building; MRL is used to save the machine room.

Passengers, and tenants | View: it should be fast, accurate, and steady, and reliable in a power cut and in a fire. ; Interest: less waiting, less panic, and access without barriers. ; Worry: being trapped, rumors of a fall, and worries about hygiene. ; Basis: the spread of the automatic elevator came with an emergency telephone and voice prompts; accessibility rules require the buttons and the prompts to meet the code.

Maintenance workers, and safety regulators | View: the more complex the equipment, the more it depends on licensed maintenance and regular inspection. ; Interest: a steady income from maintenance, and a safety responsibility that can be enforced. ; Worry: designs such as the machine-room-less elevator making the space for repair more dangerous, and more cramped. ; Basis: Wikipedia: deaths related to elevators are mostly in the course of maintenance; the states adopt different versions of the safety code.

Cities, and fire departments | View: the elevator is part of evacuation and rescue, but it cannot take the place of a smoke-protected stair. ; Interest: a controlled recall in a fire, for the fire service to use. ; Worry: a breakdown at the peak, or a power cut, causing congestion and the risk of a crush. ; Basis: fire-service mode, and the requirement for backup power, are written into a number of elevator codes.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Manufacturers use safety standards to raise the threshold. Developers complain about the cost and the area. In the end the rent and the regulations price it together.
Passengers want “fully automatic.” Maintenance people want “enough room to work.” MRL writes the contradiction into the shaft.
The skyscraper makes vertical transport a necessity, and in a power cut or a disaster the fragility of the whole building rises with it.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: A supertall building wants speed, and the pressure in the ear and the energy use limit the acceleration. Pressure regulation and energy recovery can ease it, and they do not remove the physical boundary.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “Without a safety brake there is no skyscraper” is a simplification of a causal story. The steel structure, fire protection, and the water supply are equally key.
Countries do not count the number of elevators in place the same way, and this piece is only a reference for the order of magnitude.
The images of the Crystal Palace demonstration are mostly later engravings, and the detail may have been worked up for art.

pieces.title: One film, The Odyssey, held up a record quarter: IMAX’s third quarter
pieces.short: IMAX’s third quarter
pieces.hook: IMAX reported the best single quarter in the company’s history: revenue of $174.6 million (about $175 million, in the way it is put),…
pieces.event: Third-quarter results published on November 5, 2026 (for the period ending September 30)
pieces.imageAlt: The interior of an IMAX auditorium
pieces.imageCredit: Shahzaib Damn Cruze · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: IMAX reported the best single quarter in the company’s history: revenue of $174.6 million (about $175 million, in the way it is put), up 64% from a year earlier; gross profit of $126.3 million, up 88%; net profit of $117.1 million, a net margin of about 67%; adjusted EBITDA of $120.9 million, a margin of about 69%. Global IMAX box office was $712 million, breaking the previous quarterly record of about $372 million.

Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey became the highest-grossing film in IMAX history. Global IMAX box office was more than $550 million, more than 30% of the film’s total global box office. The release says that, of this quarter’s IMAX box office, The Odyssey was about $538 million, and Spider-Man: Brand New Day about $58 million.

The company says that this quarter IMAX, with less than 1% of the world’s screens, took about 6.7% of global box office. The North American share was about 9.3%, also a quarterly record. That is to say, when audiences “chose a screen,” they put their budget more concentratedly into the large format.

Content-solutions revenue was $94 million, up 110%, with a gross margin of about 76%. Technology products and services were $77.3 million, up 28%, mainly from rental shares tied to the box office. At the end of the quarter there were 1,820 commercial multiplex IMAX systems, and 1,887 in the network, covering 91 countries and regions.

Net profit attributable to common shareholders includes a reversal of about $36.7 million in a valuation allowance on deferred tax assets (about $0.63 of diluted earnings per share). Adjusted diluted earnings per share were $2.21, up 370% from a year earlier. Even after deducting the effect of this tax item, the company still says a number of measures set records.

Signings of systems so far this year are more than 100 (about 105, on the call), of which about 65% are new locations. The third quarter installed 32. The backlog is about 409. Management raised the outlook: full-year global box office will be well above the original target of $1.4 billion, and the adjusted EBITDA margin is expected to reach about 50%.

The company named strong presales in December for Dune: Part Three (more than $30 million in the first month, second in the company’s history), and Avengers: Doomsday in China, the Avatar series, and more projects “shot for IMAX.” On the call, management summed the phenomenon up this way: when AI content is flooding in, people are more willing to pay for a scarce, shared viewing.

paras.lead: Who benefits, and who is under pressure
parts: IMAX, the studios that shoot “for the big screen,” and the theaters that can share in a high ticket price have plainly taken the benefit of the event film. Ordinary screens, and streaming windows, are more easily diverted by a big film in the same slot. For IMAX itself, the risk is whether the next quarter can repeat “one film carrying half a quarter.” The fourth quarter still has the presales of Dune 3 and the like, but the concentration is hard to match The Odyssey every week.

IMAX collects, on one side, content-solutions fees from the studios for conversion and distribution, and on the other, system sales, rentals, and maintenance from the theaters. The higher the box office, the rental share and the content revenue rise together, so the gross margin is magnified by “operating leverage” in a hit quarter. The other way around, in a slack quarter both sides soften together.

blocks.title: “Shot for the big screen”
blocks.text: The Odyssey is one of the first feature films shot entirely with IMAX cameras. The company treats it as a sample of what the platform can do: the same network can collect, on the content side, a share of conversion and distribution, and can also collect a share of the hardware and the rental. The higher the box office, the two sides are magnified together.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: IMAX’s management | View: this is an “awakening,” in which the platform’s ability was seen, and not only a lucky quarter. ; Interest: raising the full-year guidance, selling screens faster, and tying in more films “shot for IMAX.” ; Worry: when the next quarter has no film of the same scale, the pace of growth will fall back. ; Basis: the chief executive, Gelfond: the record margin shows the advantage of the model; signings of more than 100 systems, and raised guidance for box office and margin.

The studios and directors of Hollywood blockbusters | View: an IMAX window can raise the share of the box office, and the talk. ; Interest: using the big-screen premium to justify the cost of production. ; Worry: depending too much on a single format may affect the scheduling of ordinary screens. ; Basis: The Odyssey’s IMAX share was above 30%; the company says it is the highest in IMAX history.

Theater exhibitors | View: the event film saves the day, and the high-priced IMAX screen contributes more. ; Interest: raising attendance and revenue per seat, and deciding whether to sign a new system. ; Worry: the cost of the equipment and of the revenue-share terms is not low; the screens sit idle in a gap between films. ; Basis: the quarterly report: technology-services revenue rose with the box-office rental; a backlog of 409 systems.

Investors | View: they look at whether the margin and the free cash flow can last. ; Interest: a valuation that reflects “platform leverage,” and not a one-time hit. ; Worry: the tax reversal inflating the profit; the supply of content swinging widely. ; Basis: adjusted earnings per share of $2.21; the announcement disclosed a $36.7 million reversal of a valuation allowance.

Ordinary audiences | View: willing to queue and pay a premium for a film one “has to see in IMAX.” ; Interest: the one-time sense of ceremony of a large screen. ; Worry: a high ticket price, few showtimes, and not enough motive when it is not an event film. ; Basis: the company stresses that young audiences are looking for “a shared experience bigger than a phone”; 70mm locations contributed about $92 million of box office.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The studios and IMAX raise each other’s story that “you have to see it in a theater.” The theaters bet on the next film with an investment in the system. Once the slate thins, the three sides’ expectations have to be talked over again.
Investors take the record margin as the new normal. Management, on the call, has to separate “operating leverage” from “a one-time tax item.”
The event film takes the calendar. The room for smaller films on ordinary screens is squeezed further.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The business model magnifies a hit, and it also magnifies a gap. When the size of the network is fixed, quarterly results are highly sensitive to one or two films.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The specific figure for The Odyssey’s total global box office is not wholly the same from one media report to another. This piece stresses only the company’s figure, an IMAX share of “30% and more.”
The prior-year global box office is given both as $368 million and as $372 million.
The phrase “the first shot entirely with IMAX cameras” follows the company and the industry reporting, and needs to be checked against the studio’s technical notes.

pieces.title: A guilty plea brought it down to the statutory minimum: Joshua Wong sentenced to ten years for conspiracy to collude with foreign forces
pieces.short: Joshua Wong sentenced for conspiracy to collude with foreign forces…
pieces.hook: On November 5, 2026, the High Court of Hong Kong ruled that Joshua Wong was guilty of “…
pieces.event: Sentence pronounced by the High Court of Hong Kong on November 5, 2026
pieces.imageAlt: The High Court of Hong Kong
pieces.imageCredit: Mk2010 · CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On November 5, 2026, the High Court of Hong Kong found Joshua Wong guilty of “conspiracy to collude with foreign or external forces to endanger national security,” and sentenced him to 10 years in prison. He had already pleaded guilty.

Judge Andrew Chan took 13 years as the starting point. For the guilty plea and the plea in mitigation he subtracted 3 years, and landed on 10 years, the statutory minimum for that category of “a serious case.”

The Hong Kong national-security law was passed by the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress in 2020 and put into effect in Hong Kong. It covers secession, subversion of state power, terrorist activity, and collusion with foreign or external forces. For collusion that is “serious,” the statutory range is high. The judge made clear in the reasons that this case falls in that band, so the floor after the reduction is 10 years.

paras.lead: How it is counted with the old sentence
parts: According to RTHK, the BBC, and others, 2 months and 2 days of the new sentence run concurrently with another subversion sentence he is serving, and the rest is largely cumulative. For the subversion case related to the “35+” primary of 2020, he was sentenced in November 2024 to 4 years and 8 months, and had been expected to be released about January 2027. The media estimate that, after this sentence, release is put off to about the end of 2036.

paras.lead: What the prosecution and the reasons say
parts: The court said that he and Nathan Law, who is in exile, and others, after the national-security law took effect, still divided the roles, and had allies overseas publicly call for hostile measures such as sanctions and a blockade, while he wrote from inside Hong Kong in response. The judge said the offense was “serious,” and that his role was to provide “underground support” and to draw foreign attention.

Joshua Wong is 30 this year. During the Umbrella Movement of 2014 he was still a secondary-school student, and was on the cover of Time. In the 2019 wave against the extradition bill he became a focus of the international media again. According to The Guardian, he is at present the only social-movement figure to be prosecuted twice in Hong Kong under the national-security law, and he has been in custody for nearly six years since the end of 2020.

According to reports, he appeared in dark clothes, and nodded toward the public gallery. Outside the court, people queued, the police presence was increased, and diplomats were also in court to observe. It was a day that local media and international media watched at the same time, and the pictures from the scene are easily cut into headline images for different positions.

The chief executive, John Lee, and the government of the special administrative region stressed that the evidence of collusion with external forces was solid, that a heavy sentence has a deterrent effect, and that the property involved will be pursued. The U.S. Consulate General in Hong Kong “strongly condemned” the sentence and demanded immediate release. A spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs asked the parties concerned to respect China’s sovereignty and Hong Kong’s judiciary, and to stop “irresponsible” comment.
Nathan Law said the sentence shows that the authorities mean to put out hope for freedom and democracy. Amnesty International said the national-security law is being used to punish dissent.

paras.lead: The relation to the primary case
parts: He has already been in custody for nearly six years. The previous case was conspiracy to subvert, related to the primary. This prosecution focuses on words and acts, “after the national-security law took effect, of still pushing foreign sanctions,” and so in the telling it is written as “once, and then again.” For the Hong Kong government this is a reason for treating a repeat offense more heavily. For the critics, it is a second use of the same set of legal tools.

One frame is “a just court punishing treason”: every piece of lobbying abroad is defined as collusion. Another is “a legal tool for suppressing dissent”: the whole of the national-security litigation is seen as a political settling of accounts. There is also a frame that talks only of “foreign interference,” or only of “a human-rights checklist,” and does not set out the guilty plea, the statutory range, and the detail of the concurrent sentence.
Pulling the figure of the sentence out of the procedure and the statute easily turns it into an advertisement for a position.

items: The government of the Hong Kong special administrative region, and the prosecution | View: the evidence is sufficient, collusion with external forces endangers security, and it must be punished severely. ; Interest: protecting national security and social stability, and forming a deterrent. ; Worry: outside criticism weakening the authority of the judiciary. ; Basis: the government news release: John Lee named Wong, Law, and others; it welcomed the heavy sentence, and will pursue the property involved.

The court (from public reports of the reasons) | View: the offense is serious, but a guilty plea and a plea in mitigation can reduce the sentence, under the law, to the lowest threshold. ; Interest: a sentence that can be explained, inside the range of the national-security law. ; Worry: the reduction being taken by one side as too light, and by the other as going through the motions. ; Basis: RTHK: a starting point of 13 years, minus 3, makes 10; concurrent for 2 months and 2 days.

Joshua Wong’s supporters, people in exile, and some human-rights organizations | View: this is peaceful advocacy being punished as a national-security crime. ; Interest: pressing for release, and for international attention. ; Worry: very little room to speak in support openly in Hong Kong, so the talk is mainly overseas. ; Basis: Nathan Law’s statement; Amnesty International’s comment; the U.S. consulate’s demand for release.

Beijing, and statements connected to the central government | View: Hong Kong’s judicial sovereignty does not allow interference, and outside comment is unacceptable. ; Interest: consolidating the story of order after the national-security law took effect. ; Worry: the international contest of opinion continuing. ; Basis: the Ministry of Foreign Affairs: respect China’s sovereignty and Hong Kong’s law, and stop irresponsible comment.

Ordinary Hong Kong residents who are still watching | View: what they care about is whether life is stable, and whether speech and the boundary of a livelihood will be affected. ; Interest: a legal red line one can anticipate, and ordinary order. ; Worry: the cost of understanding the text is high, and a chilling effect is hard to measure. ; Basis: outside the court, residents queued and diplomats observed (media reports); public opinion is hard to present in full locally.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The Hong Kong government and Beijing write the sentence as “deterring foreign agents.” The United States and human-rights organizations write it as “suppressing dissent.” The same facts are set into two stories told outward.

The guilty plea bought the statutory minimum. Supporters still treat it as compelled. The prosecution treats it as evidence that cannot be argued with. The “guilty plea” itself becomes a point of attack and defense.
The concurrent days are very small, and the cumulative effect is very large. The focus of the argument easily slides from “10 years” to “another ten years still to be locked up.”

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Under the framework of the national-security law, the boundary between “lobbying abroad / calling for sanctions” and “endangering national security” is drawn mainly by the practice of enforcement and of the courts. Observers in different legal systems lack a common ruler.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “Release about the end of 2036” is a media calculation under the rules of concurrency. The formal release date follows the documents of the correctional service and of the legal execution.
The detail of the full reasons follows what the court publishes. This piece relies on summaries by news agencies and public broadcasters.
Scene details such as the number of people queuing outside, and who the diplomats were, are not wholly the same from one draft to another.

pieces.title: Giving a passport to people without a country: Fridtjof Nansen
pieces.short: Fridtjof Nansen
pieces.hook: First settle “who you are, and whether you can cross a border,” and then talk about resettlement: Nansen turned identity papers into a workable international tool, rather than…
pieces.takeaway: First settle “who you are, and whether you can cross a border,” and then talk about resettlement: Nansen turned identity papers into a workable international tool, rather than a word of sympathy.
pieces.imageAlt: Portrait of Fridtjof Nansen
pieces.imageCredit: Henry Van der Weyde · Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Fridtjof Nansen was born on October 10, 1861, on the outskirts of Oslo. He was a zoologist, an explorer who skied across Greenland, and the humanitarian diplomat behind the “Nansen passport,” winning the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922.

In 1888 he led five companions skiing west from Greenland’s east coast, deliberately leaving no line of retreat. They crossed the ice sheet for about two months in temperatures near minus 45°C, reached the west coast in early October with first-hand records of the interior, and he earned his doctorate that same year.

paras.lead: Freezing the ship into the ice
parts: On September 22, 1893, the Fram drove into the pack ice off Siberia, betting that ocean currents would carry it near the North Pole. In August 1896 the ship broke free of the ice near Spitsbergen after roughly thirty-five months.

In March 1895, seeing the ship would not pass over the Pole, he and Johansen set out north with dog sleds. In twenty-three days they covered about 140 miles, reaching roughly 86°14′ N—a new farthest-north record—before turning back and reuniting with the Fram the following year.

paras.lead: Half a million people brought home
parts: In 1920 the League of Nations asked him to repatriate prisoners of war. Despite tight funds, he arranged for roughly 450,000 people to return home in about a year and a half. Speed and execution became the hallmark of his refugee work.

In 1921 Soviet Russia stripped émigré Russians of their citizenship, leaving roughly 800,000 refugees suddenly “stateless.” Nansen championed a 1922 Geneva agreement to issue identity certificates for stateless persons—the Nansen passport. By 1942 about 52 countries recognized it, and around 450,000 were issued in total.

paras.lead: The Peace Prize and its aftermath
parts: He also coordinated famine relief in Russia and assisted in the Greek-Turkish population exchange. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922 and died on May 13, 1930. The Nansen International Office for Refugees won the Peace Prize again in 1938.

blocks.title: Crossing borders without a state
blocks.text: The Nansen passport was not citizenship, but internationally recognized travel identity. For people who had lost their embassies, it turned “who are you” into a sheet of paper that more than fifty countries were willing to stamp. Rachmaninoff, Chagall, Nabokov, and others held or were associated with such documents.
