critical.label: Another way to see it
items: League of Nations and humanitarian agencies | View: an enforceable identity tool was needed before cross-border resettlement could work. ; Interest: stabilizing order and proving the League’s usefulness. ; Worry: insufficient funding and major powers’ reluctance to take in refugees. ; Basis: the 1922 Geneva arrangement; accounts from the Nobel Foundation and UNHCR.

Stateless refugees | View: the passport was a lifeline—allowing travel, job hunting, and less risk of summary deportation. ; Interest: legal stay and family reunification. ; Worry: border officials could still interpret the papers arbitrarily. ; Basis: roughly 450,000 issued; lists of notable holders on Wikipedia.

Recognizing governments | View: recognition meant accepting certain transit and admission obligations. ; Interest: controlling borders while responding to international pressure. ; Worry: being accused of opening the floodgates or interfering politically. ; Basis: recognized by about 52 countries by 1942.

Home-country authorities | View: revoking citizenship was a sovereign right; refugees should “sort themselves out.” ; Interest: consolidating power and cutting off exiled opposition. ; Worry: international isolation and narratives of humanitarian disaster. ; Basis: the 1921 decree stripping émigré Russians of citizenship prompted the arrangement.

The public and donors | View: polar prestige could be converted into fundraising and bargaining capital. ; Interest: turning a heroic narrative into relief resources. ; Worry: the halo could obscure statistical and policy disputes. ; Basis: the 1922 Peace Prize; wide variation across sources on famine relief numbers.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Host countries wanted border control, refugees wanted passage, and the League wanted to prove itself—the passport was the bare minimum where their interests overlapped.
Personal credibility sped up agreements, but also made the mechanism dependent on a “celebrity executive.”
Figures for famine lives saved were written in vastly different orders of magnitude, turning the debate itself into a propaganda battle.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: A document can open a border, but it cannot automatically provide a job or housing; beyond the passport, resettlement capacity remained the hard constraint.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “About 450,000 passports” and “52 countries” are commonly cited orders of magnitude; archival counts vary slightly.
Estimates of the number of people saved in the famine span a wide range, so only the broad interval is noted here.
Lists of famous holders were compiled later and require case-by-case verification.

pieces.title: The quartz wave nearly wiped out Swiss watches: from crisis to mechanical revival
pieces.short: From crisis to mechanical revival
pieces.hook: After the Second World War, Swiss mechanical watches once held about half the global market.
pieces.imageAlt: Seiko Astron quartz wristwatch
pieces.imageCredit: Deutsches Uhrenmuseum · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: After the Second World War, Swiss mechanical watches once held about half the global market. Neutrality had allowed Switzerland to keep making civilian timepieces during the war, and its supply chain was deep and wide; when electronic timekeeping arrived, that guild-like structure reacted slowly.

On December 25, 1969, Seiko released the Astron, widely called the world’s first quartz wristwatch—more accurate and eventually much cheaper. Switzerland introduced the Beta 21 in 1970, but the story of mass production was seized by Seiko, Citizen, and Casio.

Swiss watchmakers shrank from roughly 1,600 firms in 1970 to about 600 in 1983, while industry employment fell from around 90,000 to roughly 28,000 by 1988. Around 1978, quartz sales overtook mechanical watches.

In 1983 ASUAG and SSIH merged, later becoming the Swatch Group, as Nicolas Hayek pushed for fewer parts and automation. With a plastic case, about 51 parts, and fashionable colors, Swatch pitched itself as a “second watch,” and the account that it sold more than 2.5 million pieces in under two years is widely cited.
Rolex, Patek Philippe, and others redefined mechanical movements around craftsmanship and status rather than “greater accuracy.” Quartz handled precision; mechanics handled storytelling.

After 2015, smartwatches rewrote the wrist again with sensors, notifications, and payments. High-end mechanical watches still sell heritage and value retention, while quartz and smartwatches divide everyday timekeeping. There is no longer a single “right” technological path.

blocks.text: The key to Swatch was not inventing a more accurate movement, but admitting that the mass market had been rewritten by quartz—using Swiss branding and low-cost manufacturing to win back young buyers while letting mechanical watches find new pricing at the high end.

The Swatch / Hayek line | View: win back counter space first, then support the high-end portfolio. ; Interest: group profits and Swiss jobs. ; Worry: a “plastic watch” could be accused of hurting prestige. ; Basis: the 1983 merger and accounts of strong early Swatch sales.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The mass market wanted low prices, the national brand wanted prestige, and workers wanted jobs—Swatch was a compromise, not a resurrection of every old workshop.
High-end mechanical watches rely on narrative while smartwatches rely on features, competing for the same wrist.
“Swiss Made” rules and movement supplies became bargaining chips inside and outside the industry.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Accuracy is no longer the main battlefield for mechanical watches; they must continually prove that “redundant complexity” is still worth paying for.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Employment and firm-count reference years (1983 vs. 1988) vary slightly across sources.
“2.5 million in under two years” is a widely repeated secondary figure.
Whether smartwatches represent a “second quartz crisis” remains an open debate.

pieces.title: Bookings up twenty percent, yet profit looks cut in half: Uber’s third quarter
pieces.short: Uber’s third quarter
pieces.hook: Uber’s third-quarter Gross Bookings reached $59.8 billion (+20%), with revenue…
pieces.event: Third-quarter results released on November 4, 2026 (for the period ended September 30)
pieces.imageAlt: Uber office buildings in San Francisco
pieces.imageCredit: HaeB · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Uber reported third-quarter Gross Bookings of $59.8 billion (+20%), revenue of $14.8 billion (+10%), and GAAP net income of $512 million (-92%). Trips reached 4.06 billion (+16%), and monthly active platform consumers (MAPCs) rose to 215 million (+14%).
Orders were hot, while net profit looked cold.

paras.lead: The drop is in the base
parts: The footnotes spell out why: third-quarter 2025 net income included roughly $4.9 billion from releasing a tax valuation allowance, plus about $1.5 billion in net unrealized gains on equity investments; in third-quarter 2026, Uber instead booked roughly $476 million in net investment revaluation losses.

GAAP operating income rose to $1.45 billion (+30%), Non-GAAP operating income reached $2.3 billion (+38%), and Non-GAAP diluted EPS was $0.88 (+35%). It was the fifth straight quarter with Gross Bookings growth of 20% or more.

Mobility revenue was $7.52 billion (-2%), Delivery $5.49 billion (+23%), and Freight $1.76 billion (+34%). Mobility looked “slimmer” mainly because of a UK business-model change: driver payments were reclassified as a reduction of revenue, trimming reported revenue by roughly $1.1 billion while leaving economic substance unchanged.

The CEO said roughly 700 fully autonomous vehicles should be running on the platform by year-end, and more than 2,000 in 2027—discussing driver supply with one hand while betting on automation with the other.
Fourth-quarter guidance calls for Gross Bookings of $63.25–65.25 billion and Non-GAAP EPS of $0.95–0.99. Investors have to watch underlying booking momentum and GAAP “optics” at the same time.

pieces.title: A digital bank collapsed, and the president fell with it: Paraguay’s Peña removed
pieces.short: Paraguay’s Peña removed
pieces.hook: On November 5, 2026, Paraguayan President Santiago Peña…
pieces.event: Resigned on November 5, 2026; removed by the Senate on November 6
pieces.imageAlt: Santiago Peña
pieces.imageCredit: U.S. Department of State · Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On November 5, 2026, Paraguayan President Santiago Peña announced his resignation; on November 6, the Senate unanimously removed him for malfeasance in office (mal desempeño), with all 44 senators present voting in favor. Vice President Pedro Alliana prepared to assume the presidency under the constitution.

Around November 2, the central bank placed digital lender Ueno Bank under intervention, freezing the deposits of roughly 3 million account holders. The bank had expanded rapidly during Peña’s term and once claimed to reach about 60% of the adult population.

paras.lead: Public funds and conflicts of interest
parts: Reports indicated the bank held roughly $800–850 million in state and pension-related deposits; Peña had previously held shares tied to the group and said he had divested them. The opposition accused him of conflicts of interest and ignoring regulatory warnings.

The Chamber of Deputies unanimously approved impeachment articles on November 5. Had Congress merely accepted a “dignified resignation,” he might still have claimed lifelong senatorial immunity; pushing through removal stripped that shield and exposed him to potential criminal proceedings.

Peña took office in August 2023 for a term meant to run until 2028. Alliana has also faced allegations of links to the affair, which he denies. For depositors, the first test remains when frozen funds will be released and who will cover the losses.

paras.lead: Three layers to read the news
parts: One layer is everyday livelihoods when people cannot withdraw their money; a second is the constitutional mechanics of impeachment and removal; a third is the competing narratives of “anti-corruption” versus “political purge.” With roughly 3 million depositors alongside a unanimous vote, any single-layer story is too thin.

pieces.title: He paid out of his own pocket to print Newton’s book, and predicted a comet he did not live to see: Edmond Halley
pieces.short: Edmond Halley
pieces.hook: Helping bring someone else’s great idea into the world is a contribution in itself: Halley first got Newton’s book into print, and then used Newton’s laws to calculate…
pieces.takeaway: Helping bring someone else’s great idea into the world is a contribution in itself: Halley first got Newton’s book into print, and then used Newton’s laws to calculate a comet’s return.
pieces.imageAlt: Portrait of Edmond Halley
pieces.imageCredit: Thomas Murray · Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Edmond Halley was born on November 8, 1656, in Haggerston, east of London—making today the 370th anniversary of his birth. His father, a wealthy soapmaker, paid for his schooling at St Paul’s School and Queen’s College, Oxford.

paras.lead: Going to university with a telescope
parts: When he entered Oxford in 1673, he brought along a telescope about 7.3 meters long, said to have been paid for by his father. While still an undergraduate, he published papers on the solar system and sunspots.

paras.lead: Leaving without a degree to map the southern sky
parts: In 1676, before taking a degree, he left Oxford and sailed to Saint Helena in the South Atlantic to set up an observatory. In a year he charted 341 southern stars, published his Catalogue of the Southern Stars in 1679, and observed a transit of Mercury.

paras.lead: A degree won by a letter from the King
parts: Upon his return in 1678, Oxford refused him a degree for breaking residency rules. After King Charles II wrote on his behalf, the university awarded him a Master of Arts on December 3 of that year—just days after the 22-year-old had been elected a Fellow of the Royal Society.

In August 1684 he visited Newton in Cambridge to ask how one could prove that planets move in ellipses. Newton replied that he had already proved it, had not published it, and could not find the papers. Halley asked him to recalculate and send it on, then returned to Cambridge to arrange publication—and Newton expanded it into the Principia.

paras.lead: The Society had no money, so he paid
parts: Because the Royal Society had just blown its publishing budget on a History of Fishes, Halley bore the printing costs of the Principia himself, bringing it out in the summer of 1687. When Robert Hooke disputed priority and Newton threatened to withdraw Book III in anger, it was Halley who talked him out of it.

Comparing historical records, he noticed that the comets of 1531, 1607, and 1682 followed nearly the same orbit and concluded they were the same comet returning roughly every 76 years. In his 1705 Synopsis of the Astronomy of Comets, he published the calculation and predicted its return in 1758.

paras.lead: A confirmation he did not live to see
parts: Halley died in 1742. On December 25, 1758, Johann Georg Palitzsch, a German farmer and amateur astronomer, was the first to spot it again. With the prediction fulfilled, the comet has been known ever since as Halley’s Comet.

In 1691 he built a diving bell and descended with five companions to about 18 meters in the Thames for over an hour and a half. In 1693 he used birth and death records from Breslau (now Wrocław, Poland) to construct a life table that let the British government price life annuities by age, shaping modern actuarial science.

Starting in 1698, commissioned by King William III to command HMS Paramour, he made two Atlantic voyages to measure compass variation and in 1701 published the first sea chart showing lines of equal magnetic declination. In 1720 he succeeded John Flamsteed as Britain’s second Astronomer Royal.

blocks.title: Paid in unsold fish books
blocks.text: Halley was then Clerk to the Royal Society, which had promised him an annual salary of 50 pounds. After he paid out of his own pocket to print the Principia, the Society said it could not pay him in cash and settled his arrears with unsold copies of the History of Fishes.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Halley | View: strong results should be put into print quickly so others can test them. ; Interest: advancing astronomy while building his own scientific standing. ; Worry: Newton pulling the manuscript and the Society lacking funds. ; Basis: published the Principia at his own expense in 1687 and talked Newton out of dropping Book III.

Newton | View: hated public quarrels and would rather not publish at all. ; Interest: protecting priority of discovery and his own peace of mind. ; Worry: Hooke claiming credit. ; Basis: had worked out the proof by 1684 without publishing, and threatened to suppress Book III over Hooke’s claims.

The Royal Society | View: backed publication in principle, but the money was already spent. ; Interest: the Society’s prestige and continued operation. ; Worry: tight finances. ; Basis: budget tied up in the History of Fishes; used unsold copies toward Halley’s 50-pound salary.

Robert Hooke | View: he had thought of a similar inverse-square gravity relation himself. ; Interest: securing credit for the discovery. ; Worry: Newton monopolizing the recognition. ; Basis: asserted priority in 1686, though without a mathematical proof.

Flamsteed and churchmen | View: questioned Halley’s character and religious orthodoxy. ; Interest: upholding academic and theological authority. ; Worry: unorthodox views spreading. ; Basis: when Halley applied for Oxford’s Savilian chair of astronomy in 1691, Flamsteed and the Archbishop of Canterbury opposed him, and he was passed over.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Newton wanted peace and quiet, Hooke wanted credit, and the Society wanted prestige—Halley used his own money and patience to hold all three together in a single book.
The Society could not afford the bill yet held the imprimatur, leaving editor-publisher and financier rolled into one person.
Flamsteed both mentored Halley early on and later blocked his chair, tangling personal feud with scientific judgment.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: A prediction for a 76-year comet took 53 years to test; by the time verification arrived, the man who made it had been dead for 16 years.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Details such as “his father paid for the telescope” rest on later biographical inference and are noted as “said to be.”
Identifying the 1066 comet with Halley’s Comet was a later backward calculation, not Halley’s own conclusion.
Popular anecdotes about drinking with Tsar Peter the Great and wheelbarrows have disputed sources and are omitted here.

pieces.title: Its inventor never patented it, yet it filled the world: more than 130 years of the vacuum flask
pieces.short: More than 130 years of the vacuum flask
pieces.hook: The vacuum flask has hardly changed in over a century: two walls with a near-vacuum between them.
pieces.imageAlt: Portrait of James Dewar
pieces.imageCredit: Thomas William Dewar · Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: The vacuum flask has hardly changed in over a century: two walls with a near-vacuum drawn between them. Because heat cannot easily escape by air conduction or convection, hot liquids stay hot and cold ones stay cold—and with cold drinks, almost no condensation forms on the outside.

Around 1892, the Scottish chemist James Dewar was studying liquefied gases at the Royal Institution in London. To keep super-cold liquids from evaporating too quickly, he made a double-walled vacuum vessel—known ever since in laboratories as the “Dewar flask.”

paras.lead: He never took out a patent
parts: Dewar did not patent the design. In 1904 two German glassblowers, Reinhold Burger and Albert Aschenbrenner, enclosed the glass liner in a protective metal casing, began commercial production, and named it Thermos.
Dewar later sued to claim his rights and lost.

The Viennese inventor Gustav Robert Paalen refined the design further and licensed patents to Thermos companies in the United States, Canada, and Britain. Mass production in Norwich, Connecticut, brought prices down and put vacuum bottles into everyday lunchboxes.

paras.lead: So famous it lost its name
parts: Thermos became so well known that in 1963 a U.S. court ruled lowercase “thermos” a generic term that any maker could use for a vacuum bottle. Uppercase THERMOS remains a registered trademark to this day.

Glass liners shattered easily when dropped. In 1978 Nippon Sanso (now Nippon Sanso Holdings) introduced the world’s first stainless-steel vacuum bottle. In 1989 it acquired the Thermos companies in the United States, Britain, and Canada, bringing all three under Japanese ownership.

Large Dewar flasks still hold liquid nitrogen for flash-freezing biological samples. NMR and MRI machines use double-walled vacuum vessels to limit liquid-helium boil-off, and in the 1960s and 1970s NASA’s Saturn rockets used the same principle on a giant scale for propellant tanks.

According to official figures from Yongkang, Zhejiang, the city has more than 300 insulated-drinkware makers producing over 600 million tumblers and flasks a year—about 80% of China’s output, or “one in every three insulated cups in the world.” Leading contract maker Haers supplies brands such as YETI, while Cali-Tech is deeply tied to Stanley, whose parent PMI accounts for 87% of its overseas revenue.

Insulated tumblers have shifted from durable hardware to fashion accessories, where colorways, straw lids, and capacity drive sales. Contract manufacturers say winning orders now hinges on how fast they can develop new models, even as they build their own brands and open plants in Thailand and Vietnam to spread risk.

Branding and trend appeal capture the lion’s share; under FOB shipping terms, tariffs are borne mainly by the buyer.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: The inventor, James Dewar | View: it was a scientific apparatus, not something he set out to monetize. ; Interest: advancing his liquefied-gas research. ; Worry: others commercializing his design without recognizing his claim. ; Basis: did not file a patent and lost his later lawsuit against Thermos.

The Thermos brand | View: the name and quality are its moat. ; Interest: defending the trademark and price premium. ; Worry: the brand name becoming a generic noun. ; Basis: a U.S. court ruled lowercase “thermos” generic in 1963, while uppercase THERMOS remained protected.

Competitors | View: the everyday word for a vacuum bottle should not be monopolized by one firm. ; Interest: selling their own products under a common term. ; Worry: trademark infringement suits. ; Basis: the 1963 King-Seeley Thermos v. Aladdin case.

Chinese contract manufacturers | View: win orders through R&D and rapid prototyping. ; Interest: retaining major U.S. clients while building own-brand sales. ; Worry: tariff shifts and client price pressure. ; Basis: Yongkang makes 600M+ units a year; Haers and Cali-Tech rely heavily on overseas revenue.

U.S. lifestyle brands | View: sell insulated tumblers as fashion items. ; Interest: high brand premiums. ; Worry: supply chains concentrated in a single country. ; Basis: the 35-yuan ex-factory vs. $35–45 retail example; over 90% of U.S. insulated drinkware is imported from China (Haers data).

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Leaving the invention unpatented let the technology spread fast, while handing the consumer name and profits to commercializers.
The brand owner wanted trademark exclusivity, competitors wanted a common noun, and the court drew the line between uppercase and lowercase.
Contract factories grew up on orders from global brands, and now want to build their own brands in the same market.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Because the core physics is long public and the barrier to entry is modest, differentiation comes down to industrial design and branding—no one can hold a long-term monopoly on the technology alone.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Stories such as “accompanying Peary to the North Pole in 1909” come from Thermos marketing materials and are not treated as verified fact here.
Yongkang’s “600M+ units and 80% national share” are local government figures; industry estimates vary by definition.
The 35-yuan vs. $35–45 comparison is an illustrative example from an executive, not an industry-wide average.

pieces.title: 64.9 million people check in daily, yet paid subscribers grew by just over a tenth: Duolingo’s third quarter
pieces.short: Duolingo’s third quarter
pieces.hook: On November 3 (U.S. Eastern Time), language-learning app Duolingo reported third-quarter…
pieces.event: Third-quarter results released on 2026-11-03 (ET); shares surged on 11-04
pieces.imageAlt: Luis von Ahn
pieces.imageCredit: Jarek Tuszyński · CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On November 3 (U.S. Eastern Time), language-learning app Duolingo reported third-quarter results: daily active users (DAUs) reached 64.9 million, up 29% year-on-year, with growth accelerating for a second straight quarter. The stock jumped about 26% the next day.

Revenue rose 14% to $309 million; total bookings grew 12% to $316 million; paid subscribers increased 14% to 13.1 million; and monthly active users rose 13% to 153.1 million. Both revenue and earnings per share beat Wall Street expectations.

paras.lead: Why net income fell nine tenths
parts: GAAP net income was $27.17 million, compared with $292 million a year earlier. The drop was not because the business soured: in the prior-year quarter, Duolingo released a valuation allowance on deferred tax assets, booking a one-time tax benefit of about $222.7 million that set an unusually high comparison base.
Even so, operating income did slip from $35.16 million to $24.20 million as operating expenses rose 24% and R&D spending climbed 30% to $108 million.

paras.lead: More users staying on the free tier
parts: With DAUs up 29% and paid subscribers up 14%, most new users remained on the free tier. The company said it prioritized “teaching better” and user growth this year, and will “gradually shift more focus to bookings growth” without hurting the free experience. CEO Luis von Ahn said the long-term goal is one billion learners.

Subscription revenue rose 18% to $270 million, nearly nine tenths of total revenue. Advertising was roughly flat at $20.82 million, in-app purchases fell 38% to $6.88 million, and the Duolingo English Test edged up 2% to $9.85 million.

Roughly 60% of revenue this quarter was processed through Apple and about 23% through Google. The 10-Q notes that payment-processing fees to those platforms make up the bulk of cost of revenues, alongside servers and third-party AI costs; gross margin edged up to 72.9%, which the company attributed to lower AI feature costs.

Duolingo raised full-year revenue guidance to roughly $1.22 billion, putting both bookings and revenue growth near the top end of its initial 2026 targets (10%–12% and 15%–18%), with adjusted EBITDA projected at $323 million. Cash and equivalents stood at about $1.24 billion.

Even after the post-earnings surge, the stock was still down roughly 8% year-to-date as of November 4 coverage. On October 7, shareholders also filed a putative securities class action against the company and certain executives, which Duolingo says it will vigorously defend.

blocks.title: Tying bonuses to daily active users
blocks.text: Duolingo set up a company-wide bonus pool that pays out if fourth-quarter DAUs grow more than 25% year-on-year. The company accrued about $11.4 million for it this quarter—$8.9 million of that inside R&D—effectively writing “users coming back every day” straight into employee paychecks.

items: Management | View: grow the user base and learning outcomes first, then monetize gradually. ; Interest: DAU expansion and the one-billion-learner goal. ; Worry: pushing monetization too hard hurts word-of-mouth; moving too slowly gets punished by Wall Street. ; Basis: shareholder letter prioritizing teaching and user growth this year, plus the company-wide DAU bonus plan.

Free users | View: keep using it as long as it is free and fun. ; Interest: learning a language without paying. ; Worry: more ads or features moving behind a paywall. ; Basis: DAUs rose 29%, and the company pledged not to degrade the free experience.

Paid subscribers | View: willing to pay an annual fee for better features. ; Interest: learning experience and value for money. ; Worry: price hikes or watered-down perks. ; Basis: subscription bookings rose 16%, driven by both volume and pricing.

Investors and analysts | View: user growth eventually has to convert into revenue. ; Interest: share-price returns. ; Worry: fast DAU growth paired with slower paid conversion and rising R&D costs. ; Basis: shares jumped about 26% in a day; William Blair noted the quarter “began to answer” monetization doubts.

Apple and Google | View: app stores are the primary billing rails. ; Interest: commission revenue and ecosystem control. ; Worry: developers steering users to web checkout. ; Basis: roughly 60% of revenue processed through Apple and 23% through Google.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Management wants user scale while investors want monetization speed—the DAU bonus pool and “gradual monetization” are designed to reassure both sides at once.
The free tier brings people in and the paid tier funds the company; every tweak to ads or paywalls shifts the balance between the two.
The more revenue flows through mobile app stores, the more platform fees act like a fixed toll.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: When paid conversion grows more slowly than DAUs, every additional free user is both a future monetization opportunity and an immediate server and AI cost.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: DAU and subscriber counts are tracked by internal company systems and are not independently audited (as noted in the 10-Q).
The “about 26%” stock jump comes from Yahoo Finance coverage; exact percentages vary by intraday vs. closing timestamps.
The “about $11.4 million” bonus figure comes from media summaries; the line-item breakdown in the 10-Q sums to roughly $11.5 million.

pieces.title: The prime minister handed in his resignation, and the King refused it: Belgium stuck on a 10-billion-euro budget gap
pieces.short: Belgium stuck on a 10-billion-euro…
pieces.hook: On Monday, November 2, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever submitted his resignation to King Philippe after budget talks broke down…
pieces.event: Resignation submitted on 11-02; refused by the King on 11-06; report due 11-16
pieces.imageAlt: Bart De Wever
pieces.imageCredit: Dati Bendo (European Commission) · CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On Monday, November 2, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever submitted his resignation to King Philippe after coalition budget talks collapsed. The King initially held his decision in abeyance and met one by one with the leaders of the five governing parties starting Tuesday.

On Friday, November 6, the royal palace announced that the King had “decided to refuse the prime minister’s resignation,” asking him to “immediately resume budget negotiations” and report back on November 16.

In Belgium, federal government formation and crisis mediation are overseen by the monarch. This time the King secured a “formal commitment” from all five party leaders that each side was ready to make concessions to reach an agreement quickly within the government, stressing a fair balance between social cohesion and economic growth.

Sworn in on February 3, 2025, the government is known as the “Arizona coalition” because the colors of its five parties match the flag of the U.S. state of Arizona: the New Flemish Alliance (N-VA), the Francophone Reformist Movement (MR) and Les Engagés, and the Dutch-speaking Vooruit and Christian Democratic and Flemish party (CD&V). De Wever is Belgium’s first Flemish nationalist prime minister.

The goal is to close a fiscal gap of roughly 10 billion euros by 2029, and the dispute is over who pays. N-VA and MR want to rely mainly on spending cuts and structural reforms, while Vooruit, CD&V, and Les Engagés want wealthier households to shoulder more.
Vooruit has pushed for higher taxes on top earners, which MR rules out alongside any VAT adjustments.

An OECD report this week noted that Belgium’s public debt exceeded 100% of GDP in 2025 and its deficit topped 5%, both well above EU reference thresholds; Brussels has ordered Belgium to correct its excessive deficit by 2029. ING Belgium chief economist Peter Vanden Houte said that even with 10 billion euros in savings over three years, the deficit would still sit near 4% of GDP, short of the 3% line.

Without a new budget, the government has to run on provisional twelfths—generally spending no more each month than one twelfth of the prior year’s appropriations. De Wever admitted in the Chamber of Representatives this week that 2027 will have to start that way again, just as 2026 did, calling it a “terrible failure” for the government.

paras.lead: Forming a cabinet is hard to begin with
parts: Because Belgium’s main parties are split along linguistic lines, assembling a federal coalition is notoriously difficult. After the 2010 election it took 541 days to form a government, and the current coalition took nearly eight months after the June 2024 vote.

The prime minister reports back to the King on November 16. The three main trade-union confederations have called a national demonstration in Brussels for November 23, while Pieter Timmermans, head of the Federation of Enterprises in Belgium, warned that financial markets are watching closely and “now is not the time to provoke a political crisis.”

items: De Wever and N-VA | View: the fiscal hole has to be plugged through spending cuts and structural reform. ; Interest: defending their fiscal line and the prime ministership. ; Worry: coalition collapse and dragging on under provisional twelfths. ; Basis: resignation refused by the King; called provisional budgeting a “terrible failure.”

Vooruit, CD&V, and Les Engagés | View: wealthier households should bear a larger share. ; Interest: social fairness and their own electoral bases. ; Worry: health care and social benefits being cut too deeply. ; Basis: Xinhua reports the three parties demanded greater contributions from the wealthy.

Business groups and financial markets | View: do not trigger a political crisis right now. ; Interest: fiscal predictability and borrowing costs. ; Worry: widening spreads against German bunds and negative rating outlooks. ; Basis: warnings from FEB chief Pieter Timmermans and ING economists.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: All five parties pledged to compromise without saying on what—between “willing to talk” and “closing a deal” sits a 10-billion-euro spreadsheet.
Cutting spending runs into the unions, while raising taxes runs into MR; whichever side gives ground has to explain it to its own voters.
The King’s refusal bought ten days of time, while turning November 16 into a public deadline.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The arithmetic is unforgiving: even saving 10 billion euros leaves the deficit near 4% rather than under 3%, and closing more of the gap means someone has to absorb more pain.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The five parties’ detailed negotiating texts have not been made public in full; the table summarizes media reporting.
“A deficit still near 4%” is an estimate from a single bank economist.
Talks remain underway, and positions could shift before or after the November 16 deadline.

pieces.title: Missing for six years, found by a reporter: David Livingstone
pieces.short: David Livingstone
pieces.hook: He treated fame as a tool for something larger. He said the source of the Nile mattered “only in that it gives weight to what I say among people…
pieces.takeaway: He treated fame as a tool for something larger. He said the source of the Nile mattered “only in that it gives weight to what I say among people”—and he wanted that weight for the fight against the slave trade.
pieces.imageAlt: David Livingstone
pieces.imageCredit: Thomas Annan · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: David Livingstone (1813–1873) was a Scottish doctor, missionary, and explorer. On this day 155 years ago—10 November 1871—the American journalist Stanley found him at Ujiji, beside Lake Tanganyika in what is now Tanzania. The greeting is said to have begun, “Dr. Livingstone, I presume?

paras.lead: Into the spinning mill at ten
parts: He was born on 19 March 1813 in a cotton-mill tenement at Blantyre, Scotland, the second of seven children. At ten he went into the mill as a piecer, working from 6 in the morning until 8 at night, and after work he still went to the village school.

He read a pamphlet urging that “a missionary should study medicine first,” and he meant to practice and preach in China. With the First Opium War about to begin, the London Missionary Society did not send him. In November 1840 he qualified as a doctor in Glasgow and was ordained; he sailed that same month and reached southern Africa in March 1841.

paras.lead: A lion crushed his left arm
parts: In February 1844, at Mabotsa in what is now Botswana, he shot at a lion that was attacking the flocks. As he reloaded, the lion sprang and crushed his left arm. Mebalwe, an African church deacon, fired and drew the lion off, and that saved him. He could never raise that arm above his shoulder again.
In January 1845 he married Mary Moffat, who had nursed him.

He was later called “Africa’s greatest missionary,” yet the record shows only one formal convert: Sechele, chief of the Kwena. Sechele kept the rainmaking rite. Neil Parsons of the University of Botswana argues that Sechele’s part in spreading Christianity through nineteenth-century southern Africa was almost greater than that of any European missionary.

From 1852 to 1856, with guides and porters sent by the Kololo chief Sekeletu (27 at first, later 114), he walked west from the middle Zambezi to Luanda on the Atlantic, then back and east to Quelimane on the Indian Ocean. On 16 November 1855 he became the first European on record to see the falls local people called “the smoke that thunders,” and he named them Victoria Falls after the queen.

paras.lead: A celebrity, and a new employer
parts: He was back in Britain at the end of 1856. The next year Missionary Travels and Researches in South Africa became a bestseller. The London Missionary Society said it could not readily fund a trade-route expedition “so remote from preaching the gospel,” so in 1857 he resigned, returned to Africa as a British consul, and took £5,000 from the government.

The Zambezi expedition of 1858–1864 went badly. The Kebrabasa rapids blocked the river; the steamer could not pass. His wife Mary died of malaria in April 1862. John Kirk, the expedition’s doctor, wrote that he was “a most unsafe leader.” In 1864 the government recalled the party, and many newspapers called it a failure.

paras.lead: Looking for the source of the Nile
parts: In 1866 he set out from Zanzibar to find the source of the Nile. His medicines were stolen, and when he was very ill he could only travel with a slave traders’ caravan. On 15 July 1871, at the market of Nyangwe on the Lualaba, he watched Arab slave traders massacre about 400 Africans. The shock was severe, and he gave up going farther north.
For those years he was almost cut off. Of 44 letters he sent, only one reached Zanzibar.

paras.lead: A greeting that may have been composed later
parts: James Gordon Bennett of the New York Herald paid for the search. Stanley reached Zanzibar in March 1871, raised a party, walked about 1,100 kilometres, and found him at Ujiji on 10 November. The famous sentence is not in Stanley’s diary from the time—he tore out the relevant pages—and it is not in Livingstone’s own record either.

He did not go back with Stanley. On 1 May 1873 he died at Chitambo, in what is now Zambia, aged 60. His attendants Chuma and Susi buried his heart under a tree, then carried his body and his diary for 63 days and more than 1,600 kilometres to Bagamoyo on the coast. From there he was taken to Britain and buried in Westminster Abbey.

His books and diaries moved the British public against the East African slave trade. The slogan “Christianity, commerce, and civilization” was borrowed, in the decades after his death, by European colonial expansion. In the anti-colonial mood of the 1960s he was for a time “debunked.” Livingstone in Zambia, and Blantyre in Malawi, named for his home town, still keep those names.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Livingstone himself | View: Christianity plus “legitimate trade” could replace the slave trade. ; Interest: opening a Zambezi trade route, his own name, and funds. ; Worry: the slave trade keeps expanding. ; Basis: the slogan “Christianity, commerce, and civilization”; he told a friend the source of the Nile mattered “only in that it gives weight to what I say among people.”

The London Missionary Society | View: money should go to mission work, not to exploring trade routes. ; Interest: mission stations, and the safety of missionaries. ; Worry: the plan was drifting ever farther from preaching. ; Basis: a letter saying the directors could hardly fund a plan “so remote from preaching the gospel”; several members of the mission he sent to the Kololo died of malaria, and the biographer Tim Jeal argues that he overstated local conditions.

The British government and the Royal Geographical Society | View: it was worth paying to test Britain’s trade prospects on the Zambezi. ; Interest: commerce, geographical knowledge, and influence. ; Worry: the money would be wasted. ; Basis: a government grant of £5,000 and a consulship; the expedition was recalled in 1864; the Society gave him its gold medal.

African people on the ground | View: cooperation was possible, but on their own terms. ; Interest: trade routes, safety, and their own beliefs and customs. ; Worry: Boers and slave traders. ; Basis: Sekeletu sent people with him across the continent; Sechele kept rainmaking and polygamy; Chuma and Susi carried the body for 63 days.

Later judges | View: from “national hero,” to “a myth that has been taken apart,” to something more complicated. ; Interest: how colonial history is told. ; Worry: a personal hero story hides what colonization did. ; Basis: the scholar Alvyn Austin’s summary in 1997; 98th place in the 2002 BBC poll of the 100 greatest Britons; many African places still carry his name.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: He opposed the slave trade, yet late in life he depended on slave traders’ caravans for his life and his supplies. The ideal and the fact tied each other down.
The Missionary Society wanted “preaching.” The government wanted “a trade route.” He changed employers, and he also took the charge that he sacrificed the people around him for the cause.
Stanley and the New York Herald sold papers on “finding Livingstone,” and along the way they rebuilt a reputation that had already been slipping.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: He wanted “commerce” to replace the slave trade. In the decades after his death, the roads into the interior became the roads of European colonization. There is still no agreed judgment on the gap between the motive and the result.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: “Dr. Livingstone, I presume?” is not in Stanley’s diary from the time. It may have been shaped afterward.
His estimate of deaths in the slave trade—“at most one in five lived to reach the market”—has been criticized as a serious exaggeration.
The detail of the Nyangwe massacre: spectral imaging of the original diary shows that the published text cut his doubts about his own attendants.

pieces.title: Forty thousand people queued for 13,000 pairs: ninety years of nylon
pieces.short: Ninety years of nylon
pieces.hook: On 4 January 1946 a queue formed outside a department store in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. People were there only…
pieces.imageAlt: Queueing to buy nylon stockings
pieces.imageCredit: Ed Westcott (U.S. Department of Energy) · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On 4 January 1946 a queue formed outside a department store in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. People were there only to buy a pair of nylon stockings. In those months, fights over stockings in several American cities became the “nylon riots.” In Pittsburgh, about 40,000 people queued for 13,000 pairs.

In 1927, on the advice of Charles Stine, director of its chemical department, DuPont set up small teams for “pioneering research” and brought Wallace Carothers, a lecturer at Harvard, to lead the work on polymers. At first he could stay with pure science.

In the spring of 1930 the team made two new polymers. One was neoprene, a synthetic rubber later used in quantity in the Second World War. The other was an elastic paste that became very tough when it cooled—the forerunner of nylon. After that the company told them to look for “a chemical combination suited to industrial use.”
On 28 February 1935 the first nylon, nylon 66, was synthesized. In 1938 Schlack at IG Farben made another: nylon 6.

paras.lead: He did not live to see the success
parts: Carothers had suffered from depression since he was young. In 1936 he became the first industrial organic chemist elected to the U.S. National Academy of Sciences, but he did not get better. He died in April 1937, sixteen months before nylon was shown to the public.

On 27 October 1938 DuPont announced nylon in New York: “the first man-made organic textile fiber,” made from “coal, water, and air,” “as strong as steel, as fine as a spider’s web.” Its first commercial use, though, was toothbrush bristles in 1938.
Later reports said nylon might be made from extracts of corpses. The panic made DuPont change the line and lead with “beautiful, and quick to dry.”

paras.lead: The first sale sold out in three hours
parts: On 24 October 1939 nylon stockings went on public sale for the first time in Wilmington, Delaware: 4,000 pairs were gone in three hours. On 15 May 1940 they went on sale nationwide, and 64 million pairs sold in the first year. They were not cheap. By weight they cost about 1.5 times silk ($4.27 a pound against $2.79).

DuPont later said the name was meant to be “No-Run,” but stockings do run, so that promise could not be made. The name was changed and changed again until it became nylon. The widespread story that it is New York (NY) plus London (Lon) is an urban legend.

From 11 February 1942 nylon was turned over to the military, for parachutes, tents, and rope. On the black market a pair of stockings sold for $20. Women without stockings drew a “seam” on their legs. From the end of the war until 1952, 80 percent of the world’s nylon went into stockings and underwear.

In China, nylon is called jinlun. In April 1958 the Jinzhou chemical plant made China’s first batch of caprolactam, and the Beijing fiber plant then spun it into filament. Because it was made in Jinzhou, the fiber was named jinlun.

paras.lead: Where it stands now: large, and under pressure
parts: Figures from the China Chemical Fibers Association: in 2025 China’s nylon output was 4.72 million tonnes, up 2.8 percent, and that growth was 3.5 percentage points slower than in 2024. The average operating rate was about 81 percent, down 8.64 percentage points. Longzhong Information counts domestic nylon 66 capacity in the first half of 2025 at about 1.271 million tonnes a year, up about 21 percent, with imports down by about a third.

Tough and long-lasting also means hard to break down. Discarded nylon fishing nets are one source of marine debris. Nylon is the fiber most used in American residential carpet, and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency estimates that in 2018 only 9.2 percent of carpet was recycled and 73 percent went to landfill.
Companies such as Italy’s Aquafil recycle old nets into clothing fabric, but recycling costs more than new material, and the scale is still small.

blocks.title: A bottleneck that lasted decades: adiponitrile
blocks.text: Nylon 66 needs hexamethylenediamine, and the key raw material for that, adiponitrile, was long controlled by foreign firms such as Invista and Ascend. In 2021 China’s own adiponitrile capacity was only 100,000 tonnes, while consumption was 312,000 tonnes. On 1 August 2022 Qixiang Tengda announced that Tianchen Qixiang’s 200,000-tonne-a-year adiponitrile unit in Zibo, Shandong, had run the whole process and produced premium-grade product. It was the first industrial adiponitrile plant in China to use the butadiene route.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: DuPont | View: turn basic research into a large business. ; Interest: patents and market position. ; Worry: consumers would not trust an “artificial fiber.” ; Basis: a patent in September 1938, and a quick monopoly of the fiber; to answer the rumors, the advertising shifted to “coal, air, and water” and “beautiful, and quick to dry.”

Carothers and the researchers | View: get the science straight first. ; Interest: freedom to research, and academic recognition. ; Worry: being told to turn toward “what is useful.” ; Basis: after 1930 the team was told to look for a combination “suited to industrial use”; in 1936 he was elected to the National Academy of Sciences.

Consumers, especially women | View: stockings that look good, last, and can actually be bought. ; Interest: price and supply. ; Worry: runs, stuffiness, static. ; Basis: 64 million pairs in the first year; the “nylon riots” of 1945–1946; pure nylon does not absorb sweat and runs easily, so blends became more common.

The U.S. military and the wartime government | View: strategic materials come first. ; Interest: a steady supply of parachutes and rope. ; Worry: Japanese raw silk being cut off. ; Basis: from February 1942 nylon was turned over to the military; after the embargo on Japan, the United States could not import raw silk.

China’s nylon firms today | View: break the raw-material bottleneck, and differentiate. ; Interest: cost, operating rate, and profit. ; Worry: a price war in ordinary grades, and high inventories. ; Basis: domestic adiponitrile in 2022; an operating rate of about 81 percent in 2025, down 8.64 percentage points (China Chemical Fibers Association).

Environmental and recycling groups | View: durable also means hard to break down. ; Interest: less marine debris and less microplastic. ; Worry: recycling is too expensive and still too small. ; Basis: the EPA’s 9.2 percent carpet recycling rate for 2018; Patagonia’s investment in Bureo, which makes products from old nets; Aquafil recycling nets into fabric.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: DuPont wanted the selling point “as strong as steel,” and it also feared promising too much. It would not even use a name that said “no run.”
The war took stockings out of consumers’ hands. The “nylon riots” afterward showed, the other way around, how large the demand was.
Domestic adiponitrile broke the monopoly and lowered the cost. Expanding capacity then pushed ordinary grades into a price war.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The virtues of nylon—tough, durable, cheap—are exactly its environmental problem. The recycling technology exists, but it costs more than new material, and the market has not yet put a strong enough price on the difference.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The crowd figures for the “nylon riots” (40,000 people for 13,000 pairs) are estimates from reporting at the time.
Sources give two dates for Carothers’s death, 28 April and 29 April.
That jinlun was named for Jinzhou rests mainly on popular accounts from the industry association and from companies.

pieces.title: Revenue up 28 percent, the share price down 18 percent in a day: Axon’s third quarter
pieces.short: Axon’s third quarter
pieces.hook: After the U.S. market closed on 5 November, Axon, which makes Tasers and body cameras, reported its third quarter (through…
pieces.event: Third-quarter results after the close on 2026-11-05 (U.S. Eastern time); the close on 11-06 was down 18.18 percent
pieces.imageAlt: An officer wearing a body camera
pieces.imageCredit: Tony Webster · CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: After the U.S. market closed on 5 November, Axon, which makes Tasers and body cameras, reported its third quarter (through 30 September): revenue of $909 million, up 28 percent, the company’s highest third quarter on record. The next day, 6 November, the share price closed down 18.18 percent, the largest one-day drop since 2013.

In 1993 the Smith brothers, Rick and Tom Smith, founded AIR TASER. With Jack Cover, a former NASA researcher who invented the stun gun, they changed the propellant from gunpowder to compressed nitrogen. The company listed in 2001, brought out its first body camera in 2008, and in April 2017 renamed itself Axon. Its headquarters are in Scottsdale, Arizona.

paras.lead: From selling the “gun” to selling the cloud
parts: It now has two parts: “connected devices” (Tasers, cameras, counter-drone equipment, and the like) and “software and services” (evidence cloud, AI report writing, 911 dispatch, and the like). This quarter software and services brought in $437 million, up 43 percent. Annual recurring revenue was $1.75 billion, up 40 percent. Net revenue retention from existing customers was 126 percent, which means those customers spent about a quarter more this year than last.

First, it missed expectations. Adjusted earnings were $1.72 a share; the LSEG analyst consensus cited by Reuters was $1.88. Revenue was also below the roughly $940 million expected. Second, it cut the full-year guide: revenue from $3.67–3.725 billion to $3.61–3.63 billion, and growth from 32–34 percent to about 30 percent, because three federal counter-drone deployments, about $130 million of revenue, were pushed out of this year.
Third, the fourth-quarter revenue guide of $990 million to $1.01 billion was below Wall Street’s roughly $1.06 billion.

The overall gross margin fell from 60.1 percent to 56.7 percent. The company’s explanation: a higher share of counter-drone equipment, more expensive memory chips, and new products still ramping. The gross margin on connected devices fell from 49.9 percent to 43.0 percent.

Operating cash flow this quarter was $20 million (against $60 million a year earlier), and free cash flow was an outflow of $19 million, mainly because the company spent about $100 million stocking inventory early against supply-chain risk. The full-year free-cash-flow guide was also cut, from about $450 million to $350–400 million.

paras.lead: The largest investment it has ever made
parts: The same day, Axon said it would invest another $1.2 billion, in cash and stock, in the drone company Skydio, taking its stake to about 37 percent and becoming Skydio’s exclusive distributor for public safety in the United States and Canada. Reuters reported a pre-money valuation of $5.2 billion for the deal.
The company called it “the largest single investment in Axon’s history.”

Axon is pushing “drone as first responder”: when a call comes in, send a drone before anyone else. Citing the company, Reuters said agencies using the setup cut response time on priority calls by as much as 65 percent, and that in about 80 percent of call-outs the drone arrived before the officer.

Needham kept a “buy,” but cut its target from $750 to $500, and warned that the company’s goal of “more than 30 percent growth in five-year orders” was at risk of being missed. Craig-Hallum cut the rating to “hold,” saying the Taser business was clearly short of expectations and that quarter-to-quarter swings could get larger.

The fact: revenue and orders are still growing, but growth is slower, the margin is thinner, cash has turned negative, and at the same time the company is spending $1.2 billion on a stake. The inference: for a company whose share price has long been set as “high growth,” the market often punishes not “no growth,” but “growth that has turned a corner.”

blocks.title: The orders are in fact still growing
blocks.text: “Future contracted bookings”—the part that is signed but not yet delivered—reached $15.8 billion, up 39 percent. The company expects 20–25 percent of that to be recognized in the next 12 months. Five-year orders signed so far this year are up 25 percent. Among this quarter’s large contracts was a $258 million AI package and body-camera expansion from a state corrections department.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Management (CEO Rick Smith) | View: demand is strong; three federal orders were only delayed. ; Interest: keep growth around 30 percent, and take the drone lane. ; Worry: the pace of federal purchasing, and supply-chain risk. ; Basis: the shareholder letter says that if the three deployments had been on time, full-year growth would be nearly 500 basis points above the current guide; he called drones “one of the defining technologies of this decade.”

Shareholders and analysts | View: slower growth and a lower guide cannot hold a high valuation. ; Interest: the share price, and certainty about growth. ; Worry: the order target is missed, and quarters swing more. ; Basis: the close on 11-06 was down 18.18 percent; Needham’s target went from $750 to $500; Craig-Hallum cut the rating to “hold.”

Police departments and government customers | View: they want a faster response and tools that save work. ; Interest: efficiency, evidence management, and the budget. ; Worry: a high price, and being tied to one supplier. ; Basis: net revenue retention of 126 percent; in 2023 three U.S. cities filed an antitrust class action saying it had raised body-camera prices (Wikipedia).

Civil-rights and privacy advocates | View: Tasers, AI, and drones are widening what the police can do. ; Interest: civil rights and accountability. ; Worry: surveillance, misuse, and AI getting it wrong. ; Basis: in 2022 Axon proposed drones armed with Tasers for school shootings; its ethics advisory board issued a unanimous objection and nine members resigned; an independent review questioned whether the AI report tool Draft One would “make things up.”

Skydio | View: it gets capital and the largest public-safety channel. ; Interest: scale and valuation. ; Worry: losing its independence. ; Basis: Skydio expects about $1 billion of orders this fiscal year; Axon says Skydio can still develop other industries “freely.”

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Management calls the cut a “delay in timing.” The market reads it as slower growth. The same numbers, two readings.
The company is stocking $100 million of inventory and investing $1.2 billion at the same time. Shareholders worry about cash and returns in the near term.
Drones get the police there faster, and they also make the privacy question sharper. The stronger the product, the larger the ethical dispute.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Axon’s growth depends more and more on large federal orders and on new businesses that are closer to hardware. That revenue arrives on an unsteady timetable and at a lower margin. Whether it can open a new lane and still keep a “software company” margin is the next gate.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The 18.18 percent drop at the close on 11-06 is compiled by the financial press from closing prices. The exchange is the authority.
“Response time cut by as much as 65 percent” and “the drone first in 80 percent of call-outs” are the company’s figures. They have not been checked independently.
Adjusted earnings per share and free cash flow are non-GAAP measures. Analyst expectations differ slightly by data vendor ($1.88 or $1.91).

pieces.title: One meeting, two hosts: COP31 opens, and money and fossil fuels are still the two hurdles
pieces.short: COP31 opens, and money and fossil…
pieces.hook: On 9 November the 31st U.N. Climate Change Conference (COP31) opened in Antalya, on the Mediterranean coast of…
pieces.event: Opened on 11-09 in Antalya, Turkey; scheduled through 11-20
pieces.imageAlt: Kurum at the COP30 venue
pieces.imageCredit: Xuthoria · CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On 9 November the 31st U.N. Climate Change Conference (COP31) opened in Antalya, on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, and runs through 20 November. Nearly 200 countries are taking part, and more than 90,000 people are expected.

Turkey and Australia both bid for this meeting. After the deadlock, a rare split of jobs was fixed last year during COP30 in Brazil. Turkey’s environment minister, Kurum, is president of COP31 and runs the “action agenda”—voluntary initiatives such as electrification, methane, and the circular economy. Australia’s minister for climate change and energy, Bowen, is “president of the negotiations” and chairs the formal talks. Pre-meetings have already been held in the Pacific island countries Fiji and Tuvalu.

paras.lead: A smooth start: the agenda passed quickly
parts: Opening sessions have often argued over the agenda for hours. The opening plenary in Baku in 2024 was delayed a long time for that reason. This time the agenda passed quickly. Bowen said a “presidency-led decision” would be drafted from the first day, rather than left to the last few days.

Already close to 1.5°C] On opening day the World Meteorological Organization reported that from January to September 2026 the global average surface temperature was about 1.47°C above the pre-industrial level, and that this year is likely to be one of the four hottest on record. In October the U.N. Environment Programme warned that going past 1.5°C for a sustained period is already unavoidable, and that current policies point to about 2.8°C of warming this century.

The U.N. Environment Programme estimates that by 2035 developing countries will need about $305 billion a year to adapt to climate change. In 2024 rich countries provided about $30 billion, one tenth of that. Last year in Belém, countries agreed to “at least triple” adaptation finance by 2035, but they did not write down which year the count starts from.
The first round of the loss-and-damage fund received $2.8 billion in requests and had only $342 million on hand.

paras.lead: A small friction in the agenda
parts: The “climate-finance work programme” set up at COP30 last year was put on the agenda. Carbon Brief reported that the European Union’s representative was “deeply concerned,” worried that last year’s compromise would be opened again. The African Group wanted “tripling adaptation finance” and trade listed as topics of their own. That was refused.

COP28 in Dubai in 2023 agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels,” but last year in Brazil the attempt to write a formal roadmap was blocked by some oil-producing countries. Last week Brazil itself published a voluntary roadmap, asking countries to produce national plans before 2028, with no date for ending coal, oil, and gas.
Turkey is pushing a voluntary target: electricity at 35 percent of global energy use by 2035—without requiring that electricity to be clean.

After Trump announced withdrawal from the Paris Agreement, the U.S. government is not in the negotiations. For the second year running there is no official delegation. A White House official said this summit “refuses to face reality.” About 20 members of Congress went on their own (RFI reported 19). They do not have the State Department’s usual support, and they cannot negotiate for the United States.

This meeting is not chasing a new landmark treaty. It is trying to put promises already made into practice. If it can produce a concrete arrangement on money and a “just transition,” that will be read as a sign that the multilateral machinery can still run. If the argument over money drags to the end, the result may again be a decision that does not bind.

One is to call the “Turkey–Australia split” a rupture. It was agreed last year. Another is to treat “the U.S. government is absent” as “no Americans are there.” Members of Congress are there; they just cannot negotiate. A third is to treat “1.47°C” as already breaching the Paris Agreement. The agreement’s 1.5°C is a multi-decade average, not a single year.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Turkey (the presidency, Kurum) | View: decisions have to land in cities, fields, and factories, and bring household power bills down. ; Interest: the host’s standing, and pushing electrification worldwide. ; Worry: a meeting with no practical result. ; Basis: the opening address (U.N. News); after visiting Tuvalu he said “not a minute, not a day, can be wasted”; the voluntary 35 percent electrification target (RFI).

Australia (president of the negotiations, Bowen) | View: seek the decision that is “the most ambitious and the heaviest on results that consensus will allow.” ; Interest: running the talks, and winning priority items for the Pacific islands. ; Worry: disagreements dragged into the last few days. ; Basis: quoted by U.N. News; in a Guardian interview he was asked whether it is a contradiction for a large fossil-fuel exporter to chair the negotiations.

Developing countries and the African Group | View: the money has to be predictable, and it should be grants, not loans. ; Interest: finance for adaptation and for loss and damage. ; Worry: promises that cannot be cashed, and heavier debt. ; Basis: the African Group chair, Amoah: “the question is not only how much, but on what terms”; Ado of Power Shift Africa: “adaptation is not an option, it is survival.”

The European Union and other developed countries | View: hold last year’s COP30 compromise, and do not reopen the money talks. ; Interest: limiting what they are obliged to pay. ; Worry: a compromise already reached being overturned. ; Basis: Carbon Brief quoted an EU representative as “deeply concerned”; the European Environment Agency reports that the EU can cut emissions about 54 percent by 2030, a little under the legal target of 55 percent.

The United States (the administration, and Democrats in Congress) | View: the administration: this summit “refuses to face reality”; the members of Congress: diplomatic continuity has to be kept. ; Interest: the administration: the fossil-fuel industry; the members: the international standing of the United States. ; Worry: the administration: being bound by climate policy; the members: damage from an empty American chair. ; Basis: the White House official’s remark (the Guardian); Representative Casten: “we have a lot of rebuilding to do.”

Pacific island countries | View: 1.5°C is a line of survival. ; Interest: protecting the ocean, and an easier path to money for sea walls and fresh water. ; Worry: the sea level rising. ; Basis: pre-meetings in Fiji and Tuvalu; a push for stronger ocean protection and easier access to finance (RFI).

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The Turkey–Australia split sends formal talks and voluntary initiatives down separate tracks. The formal text adds no new obligations, and the voluntary targets do not bind. Both are easier to move, and neither is hard enough.
Developing countries want the money question in every negotiating room. The EU wants to hold last year’s compromise. A small friction on the agenda can grow later.
The U.S. government’s absence removes one source of resistance, and also the largest potential payer. Members of Congress being there sends the signal “we will come back later.”

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: “At least triple” adaptation finance has no starting year, and the fossil-fuel roadmap has no end date. Without a number and a timetable, a promise is hard to test.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Outlets do not agree how many members of Congress went (19, or about 20).
The meeting has only just opened. What each side says now is an opening position. The final text may look very different.
“1.47°C” is the figure for January to September. The full-year result waits on the World Meteorological Organization’s formal report.
